title: “Describe two…”
content_html:
4 marks

“Describe two…”

Used in: America, 1920–1973

What the Examiner Wants

This is the simplest question on the paper. The examiner wants two separate, relevant things described with enough detail to show you know the topic. Each point gets up to 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying something relevant, and a second mark for adding supporting detail. No analysis or explanation is needed — just clear, factual recall.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
4 Two relevant points, each with supporting detail
3 Two relevant points, but only one has supporting detail
2 Two simple points without detail, or one well-developed point
1 One simple relevant point
0 Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify two things to describe — Read the question. What specific topic is it asking about? Think of two DIFFERENT aspects, features, or examples.
  2. 2
    Write point 1 — State one relevant thing. Then add a second sentence with specific detail (a date, name, statistic, or example) to develop it.
  3. 3
    Write point 2 — State a DIFFERENT relevant thing. Again, add supporting detail. Make sure it’s genuinely a new point, not a repeat of point 1.

Timing

Think
1 min Point 1
2 min Point 2
2 min

This is the quickest question on the paper. Two short paragraphs (2–3 sentences each) is all you need. Don’t waste time writing more — save it for the higher-mark questions.

Point 1

“One [feature/example/problem] was…”

“For example, [add specific detail: date, name, statistic]…”

Point 2

“Another [feature/example/problem] was…”

“This involved [add specific detail]…”

Describe two problems faced by immigrants to America in the 1920s. [4 marks]

Point 1 + Detail

One problem was discrimination in employment. Many immigrants, particularly those from Southern and Eastern Europe, were seen as a threat to American workers’ jobs. They were often forced to accept the lowest-paid and most dangerous work, such as in meatpacking factories or coal mines, because employers could exploit their desperation.

Point 2 + Detail

Another problem was the restriction of immigration through quota laws. The 1921 Emergency Quota Act limited immigration to 3% of each nationality already in the US (based on the 1910 census), and the 1924 National Origins Act reduced this further to 2% based on the 1890 census. This deliberately targeted immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe, making it much harder for them to enter the country.

Examiner: 4/4

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a 1-mark answer from a 2-mark one.

Describe two features of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. [4 marks]

1-Mark Answer

Vague point, no supporting detail

The KKK was a racist group that was against black people and immigrants.

2-Mark Answer

Clear point + specific detail

One feature of the KKK in the 1920s was its rapid growth in membership. By 1925, the Klan had around 4.5 million members, including politicians, police officers, and judges, which gave it significant political influence across Southern and Midwestern states.

Remember: you need TWO separate points like the strong example for full marks. This shows just one — you’d write a second paragraph on a different feature.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only making one point — You need TWO separate points for full marks. Even if your first point is brilliant, one point can only score 2 out of 4.
  • ❌
    Stating a point without detail — “Immigrants faced discrimination” gets 1 mark. Adding “They were given the worst jobs in meatpacking factories” gets the second mark. Always add a specific detail.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — This is a 4-mark question. Two short paragraphs (2–3 sentences each) is perfect. Writing half a page wastes time you need for the 8 and 12-mark questions.

title: “Explain the significance of…”
content_html:
8 marks

“Explain the significance of…”

Also asked as “Explain what was important about…” — Used in: Health & the People • Elizabethan England

What the Examiner Wants

“Significance” means WHY something mattered. The examiner wants you to explain what impact or importance something had — not just describe what happened. Think about: what changed because of it? Who was affected? What were the short-term and long-term consequences?

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Complex explanation of significance, showing multiple ways something mattered with specific supporting evidence
Secure Explains significance with relevant knowledge but doesn’t fully develop all points
Developing Describes what happened but doesn’t clearly explain WHY it was significant
Emerging General statements with limited relevant knowledge
— Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what you’re explaining — What person, event, or development does the question name? Write it down.
  2. 2
    Think of 2 reasons it was significant — Each reason is a separate paragraph. Think: What changed? Who was affected? What were the consequences (short-term AND long-term)?
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1 — State your first reason for significance. Support it with specific factual evidence (dates, names, numbers). Explain the impact clearly.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2 — State a different reason for significance. Again, support with evidence and explain the impact. If possible, link the two reasons together.

Timing

Plan
2 min Para 1
5 min Para 2
5 min

Two well-developed paragraphs are better than three rushed ones. Spend your time on evidence and explanation, not trying to cram in extra points.

Paragraph 1 (first reason for significance)

“One reason [topic] was significant is that…”

“For example, [specific evidence with dates/names]…”

“This was important because it meant that…”

Paragraph 2 (second reason for significance)

“[Topic] was also significant because…”

“Evidence for this includes [specific facts]…”

“As a result, [explain the wider impact or long-term consequence]…”

Explain the significance of Pasteur’s Germ Theory (1861). [8 marks]

Significance + Evidence

Pasteur’s Germ Theory was significant because it proved for the first time that microorganisms caused disease, overturning the miasma theory that had dominated medicine for centuries. In 1861, Pasteur used his swan-neck flask experiment to demonstrate that germs in the air caused decay, not ‘spontaneous generation.’ This was a turning point because it gave doctors a scientific basis for understanding illness. Before this, treatments were based on balancing humours or avoiding bad smells, which were ineffective.

Wider Impact + Long-Term

Pasteur’s discovery was also significant because it led directly to practical breakthroughs that saved millions of lives. Robert Koch built on Germ Theory to identify specific bacteria causing diseases like tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883), which allowed targeted treatments and public health measures. In surgery, Joseph Lister used Pasteur’s ideas to develop antiseptic techniques using carbolic acid in 1867, dramatically reducing death rates from infection after operations. Without Germ Theory, modern medicine — including vaccinations, antibiotics, and hygiene standards — would not exist.

Examiner: 8/8 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

Explain the significance of the Religious Settlement of 1559. [8 marks]

Developing Answer

Describes what happened, not why it mattered

The Religious Settlement was when Elizabeth made England Protestant again. She became Supreme Governor of the Church of England. The Act of Supremacy was passed and then the Act of Uniformity. Priests had to use the Book of Common Prayer. This happened in 1559 at the start of Elizabeth’s reign.

Mastering Answer

Explains significance with context

The Religious Settlement of 1559 was significant because it established a ‘Middle Way’ that aimed to unite a dangerously divided country. By making herself Supreme Governor rather than Supreme Head, Elizabeth avoided directly challenging Catholics who believed only the Pope could lead the Church. The deliberately vague wording of the 39 Articles meant that both moderate Catholics and Protestants could attend the same services without feeling they were betraying their beliefs. This prevented the kind of religious civil wars that tore apart France and the Netherlands during the same period.

A full Mastering answer would add a second reason for significance (e.g. its long-term impact on Puritan and Catholic challenges) — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing what happened instead of explaining significance — “Pasteur did an experiment with a flask” is description. You need to say WHY it mattered: “This proved germs caused disease, which transformed medicine.”
  • ❌
    Only giving one reason — Two developed reasons is the minimum for Mastering. One reason, however detailed, caps you at Secure.
  • ❌
    Forgetting to include evidence — General claims like “it was really important” score poorly. You need specific facts: dates, names, statistics, examples.
  • ❌
    Confusing significance with causes — The question asks why something MATTERED, not why it happened. Focus on impact and consequences, not background.

title: “Explain two ways… similar”
content_html:
8 marks

“Explain two ways… similar”

Used in: Health & the People

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner gives you two things from different time periods (e.g. medieval and Renaissance medicine) and asks you to find SIMILARITIES between them. You need to identify two clear points of comparison and explain each with evidence from BOTH periods. This tests your ability to see patterns across history.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Two developed similarities, each supported by specific evidence from both periods, with clear explanation of HOW they are similar
Secure Two similarities identified with relevant knowledge, but one or both lack full development or evidence from both periods
Developing One similarity explained, or two stated without development
Emerging General statements about the topic with limited relevant knowledge
— Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the two things being compared — What two periods, events, or developments does the question name? Write them both down.
  2. 2
    Find two similarities — Think about: methods, causes, beliefs, results, barriers, or attitudes. What patterns repeat across both periods? Each similarity becomes one paragraph.
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1: first similarity — State the similarity clearly. Give specific evidence from BOTH periods. Explain why this counts as a genuine similarity, not just a coincidence.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2: second similarity — A different similarity, again with evidence from both periods. Make sure it’s genuinely a different point, not the same idea rephrased.

Timing

Plan
2 min Para 1
5 min Para 2
5 min

The planning stage is critical here. Spend 2 minutes thinking of two distinct similarities before you write. Each paragraph MUST reference both periods mentioned in the question.

Paragraph 1 (first similarity)

“One similarity between [period A] and [period B] is that both…”

“In [period A], [specific evidence]…”

“Similarly, in [period B], [specific evidence]…”

“This shows that [explain the pattern/reason for the similarity]…”

Paragraph 2 (second similarity)

“Another similarity is that [both periods shared]…”

“For example, in [period A], [evidence]…”

“Likewise, in [period B], [evidence]…”

“This suggests that [explain the underlying reason]…”

Explain two ways in which ideas about the causes of disease in the medieval period were similar to ideas in the Renaissance period. [8 marks]

Similarity 1 + Both Periods

One similarity is that people in both the medieval and Renaissance periods believed that God sent disease as punishment for sin. In the medieval period, the Church taught that the Black Death (1348) was a punishment from God, and flagellants whipped themselves in public to show repentance. Similarly, during the Great Plague of 1665, which fell in the Renaissance period, many people still believed the epidemic was divine punishment, and days of fasting and prayer were ordered by the authorities. This shows that religious explanations for disease persisted across both periods, even as new scientific ideas began to emerge.

Similarity 2 + Both Periods

Another similarity is that both periods relied on the theory of the Four Humours developed by Hippocrates and Galen. Medieval doctors diagnosed illness by checking whether a patient’s humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were out of balance, using techniques such as urine charts and bloodletting. In the Renaissance, despite Vesalius correcting many of Galen’s anatomical errors in 1543, the underlying humoral theory remained dominant. Doctors still prescribed treatments like purging and bleeding to rebalance the humours well into the 1600s. This demonstrates that traditional theories about disease causation were extremely slow to change, even when new knowledge challenged them.

Examiner: 8/8 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

Explain two ways in which hospitals in the medieval period were similar to hospitals in the early modern period. [8 marks]

Developing Answer

Vague similarity, no evidence from either period

Both medieval and early modern hospitals looked after sick people. In medieval times hospitals were run by monks and nuns. In the early modern period hospitals still existed. They were similar because they both treated ill patients and tried to help people get better.

Mastering Answer

Specific evidence from both periods

One similarity is that hospitals in both the medieval and early modern periods were primarily places of care rather than cure. Medieval hospitals like St Bartholomew’s (founded 1123) focused on providing food, warmth, and prayer for the sick rather than medical treatment. Similarly, early modern hospitals continued this tradition — even after the dissolution of the monasteries in the 1530s, refounded hospitals like St Thomas’s still prioritised nursing care over active medical intervention, because without understanding of germ theory, doctors had few effective treatments to offer.

A full Mastering answer would add a second distinct similarity with evidence from both periods — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing about differences instead of similarities — Read the question carefully. If it asks for similarities, every point must be about what the two things have IN COMMON, not how they differ.
  • ❌
    Only giving evidence from one period — Each paragraph must reference BOTH periods. Evidence from only one side is incomplete and caps your mark.
  • ❌
    Stating similarities without explanation — “Both used herbal remedies” is a statement. You need to explain it: what herbal remedies, why, and what this tells us about the similarity.
  • ❌
    Making the two similarities too similar — “Both believed in God” and “Both thought disease was divine punishment” are really the same point. Choose genuinely distinct similarities (e.g. one about beliefs, one about treatments).

title: “How far do you agree?” / Factor Essay
content_html:
16 + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks

“How far do you agree?” / Factor Essay

Used in: Conflict & Tension • Health & the People

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants you to make a judgement about a statement. You must argue BOTH sides — the factor in the statement AND at least one other factor — then reach a clear conclusion about which matters most.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Complex explanation of stated factor AND other factors, with a clear judgement weighing them against each other
Secure Explains both the stated factor and other factors, but the judgement is missing or weak
Developing Describes relevant information about the topic but doesn’t clearly explain HOW or WHY factors matter
Emerging General statements or simple facts with little focus on the question
— Nothing relevant

spelling, punctuation and grammar Descriptors

Performance What You Need
High 4 Spelling, punctuation and grammar consistently accurate. Wide vocabulary. Paragraphs well structured.
Intermediate Generally accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar with some errors. Reasonable vocabulary. Some paragraph structure.
Low 1 Basic spelling, punctuation and grammar with frequent errors. Limited vocabulary. Little paragraph structure.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the statement carefully — Underline the factor in the statement (e.g. “the Treaty of Versailles”, “science and technology”). This is the factor you MUST write about first.
  2. 2
    Plan two+ factors — Jot down the stated factor plus 1–2 other factors. For each, note 2–3 specific facts (dates, names, statistics).
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1: the stated factor — Explain how the factor in the statement is important. Use specific evidence. Link back to the question.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2: another factor — Explain a different factor with its own evidence. Compare it to the first factor — is it more or less important?
  5. 5
    Write paragraph 3 (optional): a third factor — Adds complexity but only if you have time. Brief but specific.
  6. 6
    Conclusion: make your judgement — Directly answer “how far” you agree. State which factor you think matters most and WHY it outweighs the others. Don’t sit on the fence.

Timing

Plan
5 min Para 1
7 min Para 2
7 min Conclusion
4 min spelling, punctuation and grammar
2 min

This is the longest question on the paper. Don’t rush the plan — 5 minutes of planning saves time while writing because you know exactly what each paragraph will say.

Opening (stated factor)

“One reason [statement factor] is important is…”

“For example, [specific evidence]…”

“This shows/suggests that [link to question]…”

Counter-argument (other factor)

“However, [other factor] was also significant because…”

“For instance, [specific evidence]…”

“This challenges the statement because [explain why this factor might matter more/less]…”

Conclusion

“Overall, I [agree/disagree] with the statement to a [large/limited] extent because…”

“Although [other factor] was important, [stated factor] was ultimately [more/less] significant because…”

‘The main reason for the failure of the League of Nations was the absence of the USA.’ How far do you agree with this statement? [16 marks + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar]

Stated Factor + Evidence

The absence of the USA was a major reason the League of Nations failed. Without America, the League lost its most powerful potential member, which weakened both its economic sanctions and its moral authority. For example, when Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, the League could not impose effective trade sanctions because the USA — Japan’s biggest trading partner — was not a member. This meant the League’s main weapon was useless, making it easy for aggressive nations to ignore its rulings.

Other Factor + Comparison

However, the structure of the League itself was also a critical weakness. Decisions in the Assembly and Council required unanimous agreement, which meant any single member could block action. Britain and France, the League’s leading members, were often reluctant to act because they were recovering from the First World War and prioritised their own interests. During the Abyssinia Crisis in 1935, Britain and France secretly agreed the Hoare–Laval Pact to give Mussolini two-thirds of Abyssinia rather than confront him. This suggests the League would have struggled even with American membership, because its own decision-making process was fatally slow.

Judgement

Overall, I agree with the statement to a large extent. While the League’s structure was flawed, these weaknesses were magnified by America’s absence. With the USA inside the League, economic sanctions would have had real teeth and aggressive nations would have faced a united front. The structural problems could have been overcome with strong leadership, but without America there was no leader powerful enough to make the League work.

Examiner: 15/16 + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar = 19/20 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

‘Science and technology has been the main factor in the development of medicine since medieval times.’ How far do you agree? [16 marks + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar]

Developing Answer

Lists facts without explaining

Science helped medicine get better. Pasteur discovered germs and this was really important for medicine. Before that, people believed in the Four Humours and miasma. Koch found the bacteria that caused diseases like tuberculosis and cholera. Jenner also made a smallpox vaccine earlier, in 1796. These are all examples of how science improved medicine over time.

Mastering Answer

Explains with specific evidence

Science and technology was a significant factor in the development of medicine. Pasteur’s Germ Theory (1861) proved that microorganisms caused disease, overturning centuries of belief in miasma. This was crucial because it gave doctors a scientific target for the first time — Robert Koch built on this by identifying the specific bacteria causing tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883), allowing public health officials to tackle the real causes of epidemics rather than simply cleaning up bad smells.

A full Mastering answer would continue with a counter-argument (e.g. government action was equally important), then a conclusion with a clear judgement — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only writing about the stated factor — You MUST discuss at least one other factor to reach Secure+. The question asks “how far” you agree, which requires weighing alternatives.
  • ❌
    No judgement in the conclusion — “Both factors were important” is not a judgement. You must say which factor matters MORE and explain why.
  • ❌
    Telling the story without explaining — Describing what happened (narrative) only reaches Developing. You need to explain WHY factors were important and HOW they connect to the question.
  • ❌
    Ignoring spelling, punctuation and grammar — 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar is almost a full grade boundary. Use paragraphs, spell key terms correctly, and leave 2 minutes to proofread.
  • ❌
    Spending too long on this question — 25 minutes maximum. Students often overwrite the essay and run out of time for earlier questions worth easy marks.

title: “In what ways were lives affected?”
content_html:
8 marks

“In what ways were lives affected?”

Used in: America, 1920–1973

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants you to explain HOW people’s lives changed as a result of a specific event, development, or policy. Focus on the effects on real people — not just what happened, but what it meant for their daily lives, opportunities, rights, or living standards.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Detailed explanation of multiple ways lives were affected, with specific evidence and clear links to the lives of people
Secure Explains ways lives were affected with relevant knowledge but some points lack development
Developing Describes changes but doesn’t clearly explain how these affected people’s lives
Emerging General statements with limited relevant knowledge
— Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the event/development and the people — Who is the question asking about? Which group of people? What time period?
  2. 2
    Plan 2–3 ways lives were affected — Think about different aspects: economic (money, jobs), social (daily life, freedoms), political (rights, laws), cultural (attitudes, opportunities).
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1 — Explain the first way lives were affected. Use specific evidence (statistics, examples, named events). Make the link to people’s lives explicit.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2 — Explain a different way lives were affected. Again, evidence and clear link to lives. Try to cover a different aspect (e.g. if Para 1 was economic, make Para 2 social or political).

Timing

Plan
2 min Para 1
5 min Para 2
5 min

Focus on depth over breadth. Two well-evidenced ways are better than four vague ones. Always link facts back to how ordinary people experienced the change.

Paragraph 1 (first way lives were affected)

“One way [event/development] affected the lives of [people] was…”

“For example, [specific evidence with dates/statistics]…”

“This meant that [explain impact on daily life]…”

Paragraph 2 (second way lives were affected)

“[Event/development] also changed people’s lives by…”

“For instance, [specific evidence]…”

“As a result, [explain how this affected their opportunities/rights/living standards]…”

In what ways were the lives of Americans affected by the economic boom of the 1920s? [8 marks]

Economic Impact + Evidence

The economic boom of the 1920s transformed the daily lives of many Americans by making consumer goods affordable for the first time. Mass production techniques, pioneered by Henry Ford’s assembly line, cut the price of a Model T car from $850 in 1908 to $295 by 1927. By 1929, there were 23 million cars registered in America — roughly one for every five people. Hire purchase (buying on credit) meant even working-class families could afford radios, refrigerators, and washing machines. These products saved time on housework and connected people to entertainment and news, changing how they spent their leisure time.

Social Impact + Evidence

The boom also affected social attitudes and opportunities, particularly for women. The prosperity of the 1920s gave young women the financial independence to challenge traditional expectations. ‘Flappers’ wore shorter skirts, smoked in public, and went out without chaperones — behaviour that would have been scandalous before the war. The number of women in employment rose by 25% during the 1920s, with many working as secretaries, telephonists, and shop assistants in the growing consumer economy. However, these changes mainly affected white, middle-class women in cities — rural women and African Americans saw far fewer benefits from the boom.

Examiner: 8/8 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

In what ways were the lives of black Americans affected by Jim Crow laws? [8 marks]

Developing Answer

Lists facts without linking to lives

Jim Crow laws affected black Americans. They had to use separate facilities like schools, buses and drinking fountains. They couldn’t go to the same restaurants as white people. Life was very unfair for black Americans in the South because of segregation.

Mastering Answer

Explains impact on daily lives

Jim Crow laws affected the daily lives of black Americans by enforcing a rigid system of segregation that restricted their access to education and economic opportunity. Black schools received a fraction of the funding of white schools — in Mississippi in the 1930s, spending per white student was $52.01 compared to just $7.36 per black student. This meant black children received a poorer education, which in turn limited their job prospects and trapped families in cycles of poverty for generations.

A full Mastering answer would add a second way lives were affected (e.g. political rights, social humiliation) — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing the event instead of its effects on lives — “Ford used assembly lines to make cars” is description. You need: “Cheaper cars meant families could travel further for work and leisure, transforming daily life.”
  • ❌
    Being too vague about “lives” — “People’s lives got better” scores poorly. Be specific: which people? How exactly did their lives change? Use statistics and examples.
  • ❌
    Only covering one way — Two developed points is the target for Mastering. One point, even if detailed, limits your mark.
  • ❌
    Ignoring limitations — The best answers acknowledge that not everyone was affected equally. A brief mention of who missed out shows sophisticated understanding.

title: “Which had more impact?”
content_html:
12 marks

“Which had more impact?”

Used in: America, 1920–1973

What the Examiner Wants

The question gives you two bullet points (e.g. two events, policies, or developments) and asks which had MORE impact. You must write about BOTH bullets, not just one. The examiner wants to see you explain the impact of each and then COMPARE them to reach a judgement.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Detailed analysis of both bullets with specific evidence, plus a clear and supported comparison explaining which had more impact
Secure Explains both bullets with relevant knowledge but the comparison is underdeveloped or missing
Developing Describes both bullets but without clear explanation of impact or comparison
Emerging General statements or only addresses one bullet
— Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read both bullet points — Underline the key terms in each. Note the specific topic area they relate to.
  2. 2
    Plan: evidence for each bullet — For each bullet, jot down 2–3 specific facts (dates, statistics, names, events) that show impact.
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1: Bullet A — Explain the impact of the first bullet with specific evidence. Make it clear HOW and WHY it affected people’s lives.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2: Bullet B — Explain the impact of the second bullet with specific evidence. Begin to compare: was this impact bigger, smaller, or different in nature?
  5. 5
    Write paragraph 3: Judgement — Directly answer which had MORE impact. Explain your reasoning by comparing the scale, duration, or significance of each.

Timing

Plan
2 min Bullet A
5 min Bullet B
5 min Judgement
4 min

The judgement paragraph is crucial for Mastering. Don’t skip it even if you’re running short on time — even a brief comparison can push you up a level.

Bullet A

“[First development/event] had a significant impact on [group of people] because…”

“For example, [specific evidence with dates/statistics]…”

“This meant that [explain the effect on people’s lives]…”

Bullet B

“However, [second development/event] also had an important impact…”

“For instance, [specific evidence]…”

“This affected people’s lives because [explain]…”

Judgement

“Overall, I believe [bullet A/B] had more impact because…”

“While [other bullet] was important, [chosen bullet] had a [wider/longer-lasting/more significant] effect because…”

Which of the following had more impact on the lives of black Americans? • The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) • The Civil Rights Act (1964). Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points. [12 marks]

Bullet A + Evidence

The Montgomery Bus Boycott had a significant impact on the lives of black Americans because it was the first successful large-scale protest against segregation in the South. For 381 days, 40,000 black residents of Montgomery refused to use the city buses, costing the bus company 65% of its revenue. The Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional in Browder v. Gayle (1956). The boycott proved that non-violent direct action could defeat Jim Crow laws, and it made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. However, its direct impact was limited to bus segregation in one city.

Bullet B + Evidence

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had a much broader impact because it outlawed racial discrimination across the entire United States. The Act banned segregation in all public places, prohibited employment discrimination based on race, and strengthened voting rights enforcement. It was backed by federal law, meaning businesses and state governments could be taken to court if they discriminated. Within a year, segregation signs came down across the South and black Americans gained legal access to restaurants, hotels, and workplaces that had previously excluded them.

Comparison + Judgement

Overall, the Civil Rights Act had more impact because it affected every black American in every state, not just bus passengers in Montgomery. The boycott was a crucial catalyst — without it, the civil rights movement might not have gained momentum — but its direct impact was narrow. The Civil Rights Act turned the principles of the movement into enforceable law, creating permanent change rather than a single local victory. The boycott inspired the movement, but the Act delivered its results.

Examiner: 12/12 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

Which of the following had more impact on American society in the 1920s? • The growth of the motor car industry • Prohibition. Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points. [12 marks]

Developing Answer

Only covers one bullet

The motor car industry was really important in the 1920s. Henry Ford made cars on an assembly line and they became cheaper. The Model T was very popular. Lots of people bought cars and it created jobs. The car industry was a big part of the American economy and helped America become rich.

Mastering Answer

Covers Bullet A and begins comparison

The motor car industry had a transformative impact on American society. Ford’s assembly line cut the Model T’s price from $850 to $295, making car ownership possible for ordinary families — by 1929, there were 23 million registered cars. This didn’t just change transport: it created millions of jobs in related industries (rubber, glass, steel, road construction) and allowed suburbs to develop as workers could now commute. However, Prohibition arguably had a more disruptive social impact, because it fundamentally changed the relationship between American citizens and the law.

A full Mastering answer would continue with a developed Bullet B paragraph and a clear judgement — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only writing about one bullet — Both bullets must be covered. Writing brilliantly about one but ignoring the other caps you at Emerging.
  • ❌
    No comparison or judgement — “Both had an impact” is not a judgement. You must say which had MORE impact and explain WHY, comparing them directly.
  • ❌
    Describing events without explaining impact — The question asks about IMPACT on lives, not what happened. Always connect facts to how people’s lives changed.
  • ❌
    Unbalanced paragraphs — Give roughly equal space to both bullets. A full page on one and two sentences on the other suggests you only revised half the topic.

title: “Write an account of…”
content_html:
8 marks

“Write an account of…”

Used in: Conflict & Tension • Elizabethan England

What the Examiner Wants

This is a NARRATIVE question, not just description. The examiner wants you to tell the story of an event but with ANALYSIS woven in — showing causes, consequences, or how one thing led to another. Think of it as writing a mini-essay that reads like a story.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Mastering Complex analysis — shows how events connect, with a clear sense of cause and consequence throughout
Secure Explains causes or consequences with good knowledge, but connections between events aren’t fully developed
Developing Describes events accurately but without clear explanation of how they link together
Emerging General or vague statements about the topic
— Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the event and its scope — Read the question carefully. What specific event or development are you being asked about? Note the date range if given.
  2. 2
    Plan a chronological structure — Jot down 2–3 key stages or turning points. Arrange them in order. Each stage becomes a paragraph.
  3. 3
    Write paragraph 1: the beginning — Set the scene. What caused the event? What was the situation beforehand? Use specific facts.
  4. 4
    Write paragraph 2: the development — What happened next? How did the situation change? Use connectives like “As a result…” or “This led to…” to show the chain of events.
  5. 5
    Write paragraph 3: the outcome — What were the consequences? How did it end? What was the significance?

Timing

Plan
2 min Para 1
3 min Para 2
4 min Para 3
3 min

Don’t overthink the plan — 2 minutes is enough. The key to this question is writing a flowing narrative where each paragraph links to the next.

Opening (causes/context)

“In [date], [event] began because…”

“This was significant because…”

Development (escalation/change)

“As a result of this, [what happened next]…”

“This made the situation [worse/better/more complex] because…”

Outcome (consequences)

“Ultimately, this led to…”

“The significance of this was that…”

Write an account of how the remilitarisation of the Rhineland was a turning point in international relations. [8 marks]

Cause + Context

In March 1936, Hitler ordered 22,000 German troops to march into the Rhineland, which had been a demilitarised zone since the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Hitler gambled that Britain and France would not respond, and he was right. France was in the middle of an election and Britain believed Germany was simply ‘marching into its own backyard.’ This was a crucial moment because it was the first time Hitler had directly broken the Treaty of Versailles with military force.

Development + Analysis

As a result of the lack of opposition, Hitler became convinced that Britain and France were too weak to stop him. This emboldened him to pursue further aggressive actions, including the Anschluss with Austria in 1938 and the demand for the Sudetenland. Each success made the next gamble seem less risky. The Rhineland also convinced Mussolini that an alliance with Hitler was worth pursuing, leading to the Rome–Berlin Axis in October 1936.

Consequence + Significance

Ultimately, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland was a major turning point because it proved that appeasement would not stop Hitler. If Britain and France had acted in 1936, Hitler later admitted his troops had orders to retreat. By failing to act, the Western powers lost their best chance to stop German expansion without a full-scale war, making the outbreak of the Second World War significantly more likely.

Examiner: 8/8 (Mastering)

Compare these two responses to the same question. The annotations highlight what separates a Developing answer from a Mastering.

Write an account of how the threat of invasion from Spain developed. [8 marks]

Developing Answer

Describes without connecting events

Spain wanted to invade England. Philip II was angry at Elizabeth because she was Protestant and he was Catholic. He also didn’t like that English pirates were attacking his ships. Elizabeth had helped the Dutch rebels who were fighting against Spain. So Philip decided to send the Armada to invade in 1588.

Mastering Answer

Narrates with analysis

Relations between England and Spain deteriorated throughout the 1580s as religious and political tensions escalated. Philip II was already frustrated by Elizabeth’s support for Protestantism, but the turning point came when she signed the Treaty of Nonsuch in 1585, sending 7,000 troops to help Dutch Protestant rebels fighting against Spanish rule. This was a direct military challenge that made war almost inevitable. At the same time, Francis Drake’s raid on Cadiz in 1587 — destroying 30 Spanish ships — delayed the Armada by a year but hardened Philip’s determination to invade.

A full Mastering answer would continue with the outcome and consequences — see the model answer above.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Just describing what happened — “First X happened, then Y happened” without explaining WHY or what it LED TO only reaches Developing. Every paragraph needs a “this meant that…” or “as a result…” sentence.
  • ❌
    No chronological structure — The account should flow like a story with a beginning, middle, and end. Jumping randomly between events loses the narrative thread.
  • ❌
    Including irrelevant detail — Stick to the specific event in the question. If asked about the Rhineland, don’t write a paragraph about the Treaty of Versailles unless it directly sets up the Rhineland context.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — This is an 8-mark question. Three focused paragraphs in 12 minutes is ideal. Don’t write a full essay.

title: Map, Graph & Data Skills
content_html:
1–4 marks

Map, Graph & Data Skills

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

AQA Geography exams include questions that test your ability to read and interpret geographical data. These can involve OS maps, graphs and charts (bar, line, pie, climate graphs), photographs, and statistical data. The examiner wants you to extract information accurately and describe patterns using evidence from the resource.

Common Data Skills Questions

Type What You Do
OS map reading Give grid references (4 or 6 figure), measure distance, identify features, describe relief
Graph/chart reading Read values, identify trends, compare data sets, describe patterns
Calculations Percentages, percentage change, mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range
Photo interpretation Identify features, describe land use, explain processes visible in the photo

Key Skills to Practise

  1. 1
    Grid references — 4-figure: give the bottom-left corner of the square (along the corridor, up the stairs). 6-figure: estimate tenths within the square for greater precision. Always go along first, then up.
  2. 2
    Distance — Use the scale bar on the map. For curved routes, use a piece of string or paper edge to follow the path, then measure against the scale.
  3. 3
    Describing trends — Always state the general trend first (“overall increase”), then add specific data (“from 20% in 1990 to 65% in 2020”), then note any anomalies (“there was a slight dip in 2008”).
  4. 4
    Calculations — Always show your working. If asked for a percentage change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100. If your calculation is wrong but your method is correct, you can still earn method marks.

Timing

Data skills — 1 min per mark

The standard rule: roughly 1 minute per mark. A 3-mark graph question should take about 3 minutes. Don’t rush — read the resource carefully before writing.

  • Contour lines close together = steep slope. Far apart = gentle slope or flat land.
  • Learn common map symbols: PH (public house), Mus (museum), blue areas (water), green areas (woodland).
  • When describing relief, use compass directions: “The land rises steeply to the north-west, reaching 200m above sea level.”
  • For cross-sections, plot heights at regular intervals and join with a smooth line.
  • Always read the axes — check the units and scale before reading values.
  • Use data in your answer — “The temperature increased” scores less than “The temperature increased from 15°C in January to 28°C in July.”
  • For climate graphs: bars = rainfall (mm, left axis), line = temperature (°C, right axis).
  • When comparing two data sets, use connective phrases: “In contrast…”, “Similarly…”, “Whereas…”

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not using data from the resource — If the question gives you a graph, table or map, you must reference specific values from it. Don’t just describe what you remember from class.
  • ❌
    Getting grid references backwards — Remember: along the corridor first, then up the stairs. Easting before northing.
  • ❌
    Not showing working in calculations — Even if your final answer is wrong, you can earn method marks if your working is correct. Always write out your calculation steps.

  1. Read the resource carefully
  2. Use specific data in your answer

title: “Define…” / “What is meant by…”
content_html:
1 mark

“Define…” / “What is meant by…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

The simplest question on the paper. The examiner wants a clear, precise definition of a geographical term in one sentence. Some 1-mark questions are multiple choice instead — circle the correct answer and move on.

Marking

What You Need
1 A clear, accurate definition that shows understanding of the term
Incorrect, vague, or no definition given

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the term carefully — Make sure you know exactly which term they want. Don’t confuse similar terms (e.g. “weather” vs “climate”, “erosion” vs “weathering”).
  2. 2
    Write one clear sentence — State what the term means using precise geographical language. Aim for 10–20 words.
  3. 3
    Move on immediately — This is worth 1 mark. Don’t waste time adding examples or extra detail. Spend no more than 1 minute.

Timing

Define — 1 min

One minute maximum. Write the definition and move on. Every extra second here is time stolen from higher-mark questions.

Standard definition

“[Term] is [what it means].”

“[Term] refers to [what it means].”

Process-type term

“[Term] is the process by which [what happens].”

What is meant by the term ‘natural hazard’? [1 mark]

Full mark

A natural hazard is a natural event that poses a risk to people and property.

Examiner: 1/1

Define the term ‘urbanisation’. [1 mark]

0 marks — too vague

When people live in cities.

Full mark

Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of a country’s population living in urban areas.

Examiner: “People live in cities” doesn’t show the idea of growth or increasing proportion, which is the key concept.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Being too vague — “It’s when rocks break down” is not enough for ‘weathering’. You need: “The breakdown of rock in situ (in place) by physical, chemical or biological processes.”
  • ❌
    Confusing similar terms — Erosion vs weathering, weather vs climate, immigration vs migration. Read the question carefully.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — One clear sentence is all you need. Save your time for the 6-mark and 9-mark questions.

  2. Write one sentence
  3. Move on

title: “Discuss…” / “To what extent…” / “Evaluate…”
content_html:
9 marks (+3 spelling, punctuation and grammar)

“Discuss…” / “To what extent…” / “Evaluate…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-value question on the paper and the one that separates grade boundaries. The examiner wants you to weigh up both sides of an argument using detailed case study knowledge, then reach a supported conclusion. You also earn up to 3 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar (spelling, punctuation and grammar), so write clearly and use geographical terminology correctly.

Level Descriptors

Level What You Need
Secure Thorough and detailed discussion of both sides. Accurate, specific geographical knowledge with case study evidence. A clear, supported conclusion that weighs up the arguments.
Developing Some discussion of both sides with partial development. General knowledge used but may lack specific case study detail. Conclusion may be present but not well-supported.
Emerging Basic or one-sided statements with limited geographical knowledge. Points listed without development. No conclusion or a vague one.

spelling, punctuation and grammar Marks

What You Need
3 Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout. Geographical terminology used correctly and consistently.
2 Mostly accurate with occasional errors. Some geographical terminology used correctly.
1 Some accuracy but frequent errors. Limited use of geographical terminology.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan (2 minutes) — Jot down arguments FOR and AGAINST (or advantages/disadvantages). Note specific case study facts, statistics, and place names you will use.
  2. 2
    Paragraph 1: One side — Make 2–3 developed points supporting one side of the argument. Use specific case study evidence and chains of reasoning.
  3. 3
    Paragraph 2: The other side — Start with “However…” or “On the other hand…” Make 2–3 equally developed counter-arguments with evidence.
  4. 4
    Conclusion — Start with “Overall…” or “In conclusion…” State your judgement clearly and justify it by referring back to the strongest evidence. Do not sit on the fence — commit to a position.

Timing

Plan Side 1 Side 2 Conclude

About 15 minutes total. 2 minutes planning, 5 minutes on each side, 3 minutes on the conclusion. This is the question where time management matters most.

Three-part structure

Side 1: “There is strong evidence to suggest that [statement]. For example, [case study detail]. This shows that [developed reasoning]. Furthermore, [second point with evidence].”

Side 2: “However, it could also be argued that [counter-argument]. In [named place], [specific evidence]. This suggests that [reasoning]. Additionally, [second counter-point].”

Conclusion: “Overall, I believe that [clear judgement] because [strongest reason]. While [acknowledge the other side], the evidence from [case study] shows that [final justification].”

‘Soft engineering is always the best approach to managing coastal erosion.’ Do you agree? Use evidence to support your answer. [9 marks + 3 spelling, punctuation and grammar]

Top band (9/9 + 3 spelling, punctuation and grammar):

Soft engineering has several advantages over hard engineering when it comes to managing coastal erosion. Beach nourishment, for example, replaces sediment lost by longshore drift, creating a wider beach that absorbs wave energy and protects the cliffs behind it. At Lyme Regis in Dorset, sand was pumped onto the beach as part of a £22 million coastal protection scheme, and this has been effective at reducing wave impact on the seafront. Soft engineering also tends to look more natural and maintains the aesthetic appeal of the coastline, which is important for tourism-dependent areas.

However, soft engineering is not always the best option. Beach nourishment is temporary — storms can strip away imported sand within a single winter, meaning the process must be repeated regularly at significant cost. Hard engineering methods such as sea walls, while more expensive initially (£5,000–£10,000 per metre), provide a permanent physical barrier against wave attack. At Lyme Regis itself, a new sea wall was built alongside the beach nourishment because soft engineering alone was not sufficient to protect the town. Groynes trap sediment and slow longshore drift, extending the life of beaches far more reliably than nourishment alone.

Overall, I do not fully agree with the statement. While soft engineering is often more sustainable and environmentally sensitive, it is rarely sufficient on its own for areas where settlements and infrastructure are at serious risk. The most effective approach, as demonstrated at Lyme Regis, is to use an integrated strategy that combines both hard and soft engineering. The best method depends on the value of the land being protected, the budget available, and the severity of the erosion threat.

Examiner: 9/9 + 3 spelling, punctuation and grammar — Both sides thoroughly discussed with specific case study evidence (Lyme Regis, costs). Clear chains of reasoning. A strong, justified conclusion that doesn’t simply agree or disagree but evaluates. Geographical terminology used accurately throughout.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only arguing one side — A one-sided answer cannot reach Secure. Even if you strongly agree, you must discuss counter-arguments.
  • ❌
    No conclusion — The conclusion is where you demonstrate evaluation and judgement. Without it, you cap yourself at Developing.
  • ❌
    Sitting on the fence — “Both sides have good points” is not a conclusion. Commit to a clear position and justify it.
  • ❌
    Ignoring spelling, punctuation and grammar — 3 marks are awarded for spelling, punctuation and grammar. Use full sentences, check your spelling of key terms, and write neatly.

  2. Paragraph 1: Side A with evidence
  3. Paragraph 2: Side B with evidence

title: “Explain two…” / “Describe…”
content_html:
4 marks

“Explain two…” / “Describe…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

Two types of 4-mark question appear. “Explain two…” wants two developed points, each with a chain of reasoning (point + development = 2 marks each). “Describe…” wants a detailed description of a process, pattern, or distribution, with 4 separate valid points.

Marking

Type What You Need
Explain two 2 + 2 Two points, each with a developed explanation (1 for point + 1 for development, twice)
Describe 4 × 1 Four separate valid points or two developed descriptions

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the command word — “Explain” means give reasons (why/how). “Describe” means say what you see or what happens (the what, not the why).
  2. 2
    For “Explain two” — Write two short paragraphs. In each: state the point, then develop it with a “because…” or “which means…” chain. Don’t write three explanations — the examiner will only mark the first two.
  3. 3
    For “Describe” — Use specific detail: data, place names, compass directions, or process sequences. General statements like “it’s everywhere” will not score.

Timing

Explain / Describe — 5 min

About five minutes. Just over a minute per mark. Don’t write more than you need — two developed points or four clear descriptive statements.

“Explain two”

Point 1: One [reason/factor] is [point] (1). This means that [developed explanation / consequence] (1).

Point 2: Another [reason/factor] is [point] (1). This leads to [developed explanation / consequence] (1).

“Describe the distribution”

“[Feature] is mainly found in [location/direction] (1). There is a concentration in [specific area] (1). Very few are found in [area] (1). An exception is [named example] (1).”

Explain two reasons why people continue to live near tectonic hazards. [4 marks]

Full marks

Point 1: The soil near volcanoes is extremely fertile because volcanic ash breaks down into nutrient-rich minerals (1). This allows farmers to grow crops successfully, providing food and income for local communities (1).

Point 2: Many people cannot afford to move away from hazard-prone areas (1). In LICs like Haiti, poverty means families have no financial resources to relocate, so they must stay and accept the risk (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — two clearly separate reasons, each developed with a chain of reasoning.

Describe the distribution of tropical storms. [4 marks]

Full marks

Tropical storms are found between approximately 5° and 30° north and south of the equator (1). They form over warm ocean water in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans (1). They do not form on the equator itself because the Coriolis effect is too weak (1). The highest concentration is in the western Pacific, where they are called typhoons (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — specific latitudes, named oceans, exception at the equator, and a named concentration area.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing when asked to explain — “Describe” = say what happens. “Explain” = say why/how it happens. Mixing these up costs marks.
  • ❌
    Writing three points for “Explain two” — The examiner only marks the first two. A third point wastes time and cannot earn marks.
  • ❌
    Vague descriptions — “They are found everywhere” scores nothing. Use specific locations, compass directions, latitudes, and named places.

  2. Two developed points OR four descriptive statements

title: “Explain…” (with examples)
content_html:
6 marks

“Explain…” (with examples)

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

This is a levels-based question. The examiner wants a detailed explanation that uses specific case study knowledge and examples to support your points. You must show chains of reasoning — not just list facts, but explain how and why things happen. The best answers use named places, statistics, and precise details from case studies.

Level Descriptors

Level What You Need
Secure Detailed explanation with thorough understanding. Chains of reasoning with specific, accurate geographical knowledge. Named examples, data, and case study detail.
Developing Clear explanation with some understanding. Some development but may lack specific detail or case study knowledge.
Emerging Basic statements with limited explanation. Points listed without development.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan (1 minute) — Jot down 2–3 points you want to make. For each, note a specific example or piece of case study detail.
  2. 2
    Write 2–3 developed paragraphs — Each paragraph should: make a point, explain it with a chain of reasoning, and support it with a specific named example or statistic.
  3. 3
    Use PEE or PEE+ — Point → Explain → Example (with specific case study detail). Add a further development if you can.

Timing

Plan Write — 7 min

About 8 minutes total. Spend 1 minute planning, then 7 minutes writing 2–3 well-developed paragraphs.

PEE+ structure (repeat 2–3 times)

Point: One [reason/effect/factor] is [statement].

Explain: This is because [chain of reasoning].

Example: For example, in [named case study/place], [specific detail/statistic].

Extend: This shows that / This means / As a result, [further development].

Explain why deforestation of tropical rainforests has global consequences. [6 marks]

Top band (6/6):

Deforestation contributes to climate change because trees absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis. When they are cut down and burned, this stored carbon is released back into the atmosphere as a greenhouse gas. In the Amazon, deforestation releases an estimated 0.5 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year, accelerating global warming.

Rainforests also play a crucial role in the water cycle through transpiration. Trees release moisture into the atmosphere, which forms clouds and generates rainfall. When large areas are deforested, rainfall decreases — not just locally but in regions that depend on moisture carried by wind patterns. This can affect agriculture thousands of miles away.

Biodiversity is also lost on a global scale. Tropical rainforests contain over 50% of the world’s species, many of which have not yet been discovered. Deforestation destroys habitats, pushing species toward extinction. This matters globally because potential medicines, foods and genetic resources are lost before they are even studied.

Examiner: 6/6 — Three well-developed points with specific detail (0.5bn tonnes CO₂, 50% of species). Clear chains of reasoning throughout.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Listing without explaining — “Deforestation causes climate change, soil erosion and flooding” is a list. You need to explain how each one happens.
  • ❌
    No case study detail — Generic answers without named places or statistics cannot reach Secure. Always include specific examples.
  • ❌
    Writing too little — Two sentences will not score 6 marks. You need 2–3 developed paragraphs to demonstrate thorough understanding.

  2. Point → Explain → Example
  3. Use case study detail
  4. Extend with further reasoning

title: “State two…” / “Outline one…”
content_html:
2 marks

“State two…” / “Outline one…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

Two types of 2-mark question appear in AQA Geography. “State two…” wants two separate, brief points — one mark each. “Outline one…” wants one point with a brief development (1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the development).

Marking

What You Need
2 “State two”: Two correct, distinct points. “Outline one”: One correct point + development
1 One correct point (without development for “outline”)
Incorrect or irrelevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the command word — Is it “state” (two separate points) or “outline” (one point + development)?
  2. 2
    For “State two” — Write two separate points, each on its own line. Keep them short and distinct. Do not repeat the same idea in different words.
  3. 3
    For “Outline one” — Write one point, then develop it by giving a brief explanation or linking it to a consequence.

Timing

State / Outline — 2 min

Two minutes. Quick, focused answers. Don’t over-explain — save your depth for the 6 and 9-mark questions.

“State two”

1. [First point].

2. [Second point].

“Outline one”

“One [factor/effect/cause] is [point]. This means that [development/consequence].”

State two factors that affect hazard risk. [2 marks]

Full marks

1. The wealth of the country affected. (1)
2. The size and proximity of the population to the hazard. (1)

Examiner: 2/2 — two distinct, correct points.

Outline one way that tropical storms can affect people. [2 marks]

Full marks

Strong winds can destroy homes and buildings (1), leaving people homeless and without shelter, which increases their vulnerability to disease (1).

Examiner: 2/2 — clear point + developed consequence.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Repeating the same point in different words — “Flooding destroys homes” and “floods damage buildings” are the same point. You’d only get 1 mark.
  • ❌
    Giving only one point for “State two” — Always check how many points the question asks for. Two points = two marks.
  • ❌
    No development for “Outline” — Just stating the point without explaining it will only get you 1 mark. Add a “which means…” or “this leads to…” sentence.

  1. Read command word (state vs outline)
  2. Write two separate points OR one + development
  3. Keep it brief

title: “Describe…”
content_html:
2–3 marks

“Describe…”

Used in: R180 Written Examination

What the Examiner Wants

A describe question asks you to give detail about something — a process, an injury, a factor or a method. You do not need to explain why it happens. Just say what it is and develop the point with specific detail.

Marking

What You Need
2–3 Clear points with development and accurate use of sport science terminology
1 A basic point made but lacking detail or development
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer given

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the topic — What exactly are you being asked to describe? An injury type, a training method, a component of fitness? Underline the key word in the question.
  2. 2
    Make your point — State the thing clearly using correct terminology. For example: “A sprain is damage to a ligament.”
  3. 3
    Develop with detail — Add specific information to earn the second/third mark. Where does it happen? What does it involve? What does it look like? Use the pattern: Point + Development.

Timing

Describe — 3 min

About three minutes. Write your point, develop it with specific detail, and move on. Don’t slip into explaining why — that is a different command word.

Point + Development

“[Thing] is [what it is]. This involves/includes [specific detail about how, where, or what].”

Describing a process

“First, [step 1 happens]. Then [step 2 happens]. This results in [outcome].”

Describe one type of acute injury. [2 marks]

Full marks

A sprain is damage to a ligament caused by overstretching or tearing (1). This often occurs at the ankle joint when a performer lands awkwardly or changes direction quickly (1).

Examiner: 2/2 — Clear identification of the injury type with accurate terminology, plus specific development about where and how it occurs.

Describe one type of acute injury. [2 marks]

1 mark — no development

A sprain is when you hurt your ankle.

Examiner: The answer names a sprain but doesn’t describe what it actually is (ligament damage) or give any specific detail. “Hurt your ankle” is too vague for the second mark.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Explaining instead of describing — “Describe” means say what it is, not why it happens. Save your reasoning for “explain” questions.
  • ❌
    Lacking specific terminology — Saying “you hurt your leg” instead of “damage to a ligament” loses marks. Use the correct sport science terms.
  • ❌
    Making a point without developing it — One bare statement only earns 1 mark. Always add a second sentence with specific detail to pick up the remaining marks.
← Identify / State (1–2 marks) Explain (3–4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
3 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the topic
  2. Make your point
  3. Develop with detail

title: “Discuss…”
content_html:
8 marks (QWC)

“Discuss…”

Used in: R180 Written Examination

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-mark question on the paper and carries a Quality of Written Communication (QWC) assessment. The examiner wants you to consider multiple perspectives or factors, develop each one in detail, and reach a supported conclusion. Your spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of specialist terminology all contribute to the mark.

Marking

Level What You Need
4 7–8 Comprehensive, well-structured discussion with detailed knowledge, multiple perspectives considered, accurate terminology, and a clear conclusion. QWC: fluent writing with few errors.
3 5–6 Good discussion with developed points and some balance, but may lack depth in places or have a weak conclusion. QWC: generally clear with occasional errors.
2 3–4 Some relevant points made but limited development, one-sided argument, or weak use of terminology. QWC: meaning is clear but writing has noticeable errors.
1 1–2 Basic, superficial response with little or no development. QWC: poor spelling, punctuation and grammar that hinder communication.
— No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Introduction — Write one or two sentences that show you understand the question and signal that you will consider different sides. For example: “Risk assessments play an important role in sport, but their effectiveness depends on how thoroughly they are carried out.”
  2. 2
    Points in favour / for — Give 2–3 developed points supporting one side of the argument. Each should follow the pattern: point → because → this means → example.
  3. 3
    Points against / alternative view — Give 1–2 developed points presenting the other side or limitations. This shows balance and lifts your answer to the higher levels.
  4. 4
    Conclusion — Weigh up the arguments and give a clear, justified judgement. “Overall, I believe… because…” Never sit on the fence — commit to a position and support it.

Timing

Plan 2 min Write — 8 min Check 2 min

About twelve minutes total. Spend two minutes planning your for/against points, eight minutes writing, and two minutes checking your spelling, punctuation and grammar — QWC marks are easy to lose through careless errors.

Discussion structure

Intro: “[Topic] is an important consideration in sport because [brief context]. There are arguments both for and against [the statement].”

For: “One reason [topic] is important is [point]. This is because [development]. For example, [specific example].”

Against: “However, [counter-argument]. This suggests that [development]. For instance, [specific example].”

Conclusion: “Overall, I believe [judgement] because [justification based on the strongest arguments].”

Discuss the importance of a risk assessment in reducing the risk of sports injuries. [8 marks]

Top band (7–8 marks):

Risk assessments are a key part of health and safety in sport, but their effectiveness depends on how well they are carried out and followed up.

One reason risk assessments are important is that they identify hazards before an activity begins. By inspecting the playing surface, equipment and weather conditions in advance, a coach can spot potential dangers such as a waterlogged pitch or damaged goalposts. This means the hazard can be removed or managed before anyone gets hurt, directly reducing the chance of acute injuries such as fractures or concussions.

A second reason is that risk assessments encourage appropriate safety measures to be put in place. For example, if the assessment identifies that a gymnastics session involves a high risk of falls, crash mats and spotters can be provided. Without the assessment, these precautions might be overlooked, increasing the likelihood of injury.

Furthermore, risk assessments help coaches match activities to the ability of participants. By considering factors such as age, fitness level and experience, a risk assessment ensures that beginners are not exposed to advanced drills that could lead to overuse injuries or accidents. This is particularly important in school sport where ability levels vary widely.

However, risk assessments have limitations. They cannot predict every possible hazard — an unexpected collision between two players or a sudden change in weather may still cause injury regardless of planning. Additionally, a risk assessment is only useful if it is acted upon. If a coach identifies a risk but fails to implement control measures, the assessment itself offers no protection.

Overall, I believe risk assessments are very important in reducing sports injuries because they provide a structured way to identify and manage hazards before they cause harm. While they cannot eliminate all risk, they significantly reduce the likelihood of preventable injuries, especially when combined with proper follow-up actions.

Examiner: 8/8 — Comprehensive, well-structured discussion. Three distinct “for” points, each fully developed with specific examples. Balanced with a clear “against” paragraph acknowledging limitations. Strong conclusion with a justified judgement. Accurate use of specialist terminology throughout. QWC: fluent, well-punctuated, no errors.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    One-sided argument — Only writing “for” points without considering the other side caps you at Developing. You must show balance to reach Levels 3 and 4.
  • ❌
    No conclusion — Ending abruptly without a judgement loses marks. The examiner wants to see you weigh up the arguments and commit to a position.
  • ❌
    Ignoring QWC — Spelling, punctuation and grammar are assessed in this question. Sloppy writing, text-speak or missing full stops can drop you a level even if your content is good.
  • ❌
    Shallow breadth over depth — Listing six brief points is less effective than three well-developed ones. The examiner rewards depth of explanation, not just the number of points.
← Extended Response (6 marks) Identify / State (1–2 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
12 min total

Formula

  1. Introduction
  2. Points for (2–3 developed)
  3. Points against (1–2 developed)
  4. Conclusion with judgement

title: “Explain…”
content_html:
3–4 marks

“Explain…”

Used in: R180 Written Examination

What the Examiner Wants

Explain questions require you to give reasons why something happens. You must build cause-and-effect chains — not just state facts, but show how one thing leads to another. Each link in the chain earns a mark.

Marking

What You Need
3–4 Clear cause-and-effect chains with accurate terminology showing full understanding
1–2 Basic point(s) made but lacking development or reasoning
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer given

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Make your point — State the factor, reason or cause clearly. For example: “A warm up increases blood flow to the muscles.”
  2. 2
    Say “because” or “this means” — Extend the point by explaining the consequence. “This raises muscle temperature and makes them more elastic.”
  3. 3
    Complete the chain — Link back to the question. “This means the muscles can stretch further without tearing, reducing the risk of strains.”
  4. 4
    Repeat if needed — For 4-mark questions, you may need a second developed point or an additional link in the chain.

Timing

Explain — 5 min

About five minutes. Spend the time building clear chains of reasoning. Each “because” or “this means” is another potential mark.

Cause → effect chain

“[Factor] causes [effect] because [reason]. This means [consequence], which leads to [link back to question].”

Two-point explain

“One reason is [point 1] because [development]. Another reason is [point 2], which means [development].”

Explain why a warm up can reduce the risk of injury. [4 marks]

Full marks

A warm up increases blood flow to the muscles (1), which raises muscle temperature and makes them more elastic (1). This means the muscles can stretch further without tearing (1), reducing the risk of strains during the activity (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Excellent chain of reasoning. Each sentence builds logically on the previous one, moving from cause (increased blood flow) through mechanism (elasticity) to outcome (reduced injury risk).

Explain why a warm up can reduce the risk of injury. [4 marks]

1 mark — no chain of reasoning

A warm up gets your body ready for exercise so you don’t get injured.

Examiner: This is essentially just restating the question. There is no explanation of how or why a warm up reduces injury risk. You need to explain the mechanism — what happens in the body.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing instead of explaining — Saying what happens is not enough. You must say why or how it happens. Use connectives like “because,” “this means,” and “which leads to.”
  • ❌
    Breaking the chain — Each point must connect logically to the next. Jumping from a cause to an unrelated outcome without showing the link loses marks.
  • ❌
    Restating the question — “A warm up reduces injury because it stops you getting injured” is circular. You need to explain the mechanism behind the effect.
← Describe (2–3 marks) Extended Response (6 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Make your point
  2. Say “because” / “this means”
  3. Complete the chain
  4. Repeat if needed

title: Extended Response
content_html:
6 marks

Extended Response

Used in: R180 Written Examination

What the Examiner Wants

Extended response questions require a longer, well-structured answer that demonstrates detailed knowledge. You need to cover multiple points, develop each one fully, and use specific examples. The examiner is looking for depth, not just breadth — a few well-developed points beat a long list of shallow ones.

Marking

Level What You Need
3 5–6 Detailed and thorough response with well-developed points, accurate terminology, and clear logical structure
2 3–4 Sound response with some development but may lack detail or consistent use of terminology
1 1–2 Basic response with limited knowledge shown and little or no development of points
— No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Introduction — Write one sentence that shows you understand the question. For example: “A warm up has several different components, each serving a specific purpose in preparing the body for exercise.”
  2. 2
    Developed point 1 — Make your first point, then develop it with specific detail. Say what it is, how it works, and why it matters. Use a practical example.
  3. 3
    Developed point 2 — Move to a second point and develop it the same way. Make sure it is clearly different from point 1.
  4. 4
    Developed point 3 — Add a third point if needed. Three well-developed points is usually enough for full marks.
  5. 5
    Link back — End with a sentence that ties your answer back to the question, showing how all your points connect.

Timing

Plan 1 min Write — 6 min Check 1 min

About eight minutes total. Spend one minute planning your points, six minutes writing, and one minute re-reading to check your chains of reasoning are complete.

Extended response structure

“[Topic] involves several key [aspects/components/factors].”

“Firstly, [point 1]. This involves [detail]. For example, [specific example].”

“Secondly, [point 2]. This is important because [development]. In practice, [example].”

“Finally, [point 3]. This means [development and link back to question].”

Explain the different components of a warm up. [6 marks]

Top band (5–6 marks):

A warm up has several components that work together to prepare the body for physical activity.

The first component is a pulse raiser, which is a low-intensity cardiovascular activity such as jogging or cycling. This gradually increases heart rate and blood flow to the working muscles, delivering more oxygen and raising body temperature so the muscles become warmer and more pliable.

The second component is mobility exercises, which involve moving joints through their full range of motion. This could include arm circles or hip rotations. These exercises increase the production of synovial fluid in the joints, which lubricates them and reduces friction, lowering the risk of joint injuries.

The third component is stretching, specifically dynamic stretching where muscles are stretched through movement rather than held in a static position. For example, walking lunges stretch the hip flexors and quadriceps. This increases muscle elasticity and prepares the muscles for the specific movements they will perform.

Finally, a warm up should include sport-specific movements that replicate the actions used in the main activity. A footballer might practise dribbling or passing. This activates the neuromuscular pathways used during the activity, improving reaction time and coordination from the start.

Examiner: 6/6 — Four distinct components clearly identified and thoroughly developed. Each point includes what the component is, how it is done, and why it matters. Accurate terminology throughout (synovial fluid, dynamic stretching, neuromuscular pathways). Logical structure from start to finish.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Listing without developing — Writing “pulse raiser, stretching, sport-specific” as a list earns 1–2 marks at most. Each point must be developed with detail and reasoning.
  • ❌
    No structure or paragraphing — A solid wall of text is hard for the examiner to follow. Use paragraphs to separate each point clearly.
  • ❌
    Repeating the same point — Saying “it warms up the muscles” three different ways only counts once. Each point must be genuinely different.

← Back to Exam Technique

8 min total

  2. 2–3 developed points with examples
  3. Link back to question
