title: “Identify…” / “State…”
content_html:
1–2 marks

“Identify…” / “State…”

Used in: R180 Written Examination

What the Examiner Wants

The simplest question on the paper. The examiner wants you to name or state a specific term, fact or example. No explanation is needed — just a clear, direct answer. For 2-mark questions, give two separate points.

Marking

What You Need
1–2 One clear, correct point per mark — specific terminology used accurately
Incorrect, vague, or no answer given

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question carefully — Check exactly what the examiner is asking for. “Identify one” means one point; “state two” means two separate points.
  2. 2
    Write 1–2 clear, direct points — Use correct sport science terminology. Keep each point short and specific — one sentence is enough.
  3. 3
    Move on immediately — This is worth 1–2 marks. Don’t waste time adding extra detail or explanation. Spend no more than 1 minute.

Timing

Identify / State — 1 min

One minute maximum. Write your answer and move on. Every extra second here is time stolen from higher-mark questions worth 6 or 8 marks.

Identify one

“One [factor/type/example] is [answer].”

State two

“1. [First point]. 2. [Second point].”

Identify one extrinsic risk factor. [1 mark]

Full mark

The weather/playing surface conditions.

Examiner: 1/1 — Clear, specific extrinsic factor identified correctly.

Identify one extrinsic risk factor. [1 mark]

0 marks — too vague

Things outside the body.

Full mark

The weather/playing surface conditions.

Examiner: “Things outside the body” is a description of what extrinsic means, not an actual risk factor. You need to name a specific factor.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Being too vague — “Something external” does not earn a mark. Name the specific factor, such as “the playing surface” or “faulty equipment.”
  • ❌
    Writing too much — If the question says “identify” or “state,” you do not need to explain. A short, direct answer is all that is required.
  • ❌
    Repeating the same point twice — For 2-mark questions, each point must be different. Saying the same thing in two different ways only earns 1 mark.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
1 min total

Formula

  1. Read the question
  2. Write 1–2 clear points
  3. Move on

title: 8 marks — Structure Analysis
content_html:
Paper 1 Q3: Structure Analysis (8 marks)

What the Question Asks

This question asks you to explain how the writer has organised and sequenced the whole text to keep you interested as a reader. You are not analysing individual words or language techniques — you are looking at the big picture: how the text begins, how the focus shifts, what is revealed or withheld, and how it ends. Think of it as analysing the architecture of the text, not the paint on the walls.

Key Fact

This is about STRUCTURE, not LANGUAGE. If you find yourself analysing metaphors, similes, or word choices, you are answering the wrong question. Save that for Q2.

How Marks Are Allocated

LevelWhat the Examiner Wants
EmergingSimple awareness of structure. Typically just retells the order of events: "First this happens, then this happens." No effect on the reader explained. No structural terminology.
DevelopingSome understanding of structural choices. Attempts to explain an effect but it may be vague or general. May use one structural term but not confidently.
SecureClear, developed analysis of structure. Uses structural terminology accurately (e.g. "shift in focus," "withholding," "zoom in"). Explains the effect of choices on the reader with some detail.
MasteringPerceptive and sophisticated. Explains precisely how structural decisions shape the reader's experience — not just what the writer does, but why it works and what it makes the reader think or feel at that point. Confident, accurate use of structural terminology throughout.
Key Fact

The jump from Developing to Secure depends on two things: using structural terminology accurately, and explaining the effect on the reader rather than just describing what happens.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Skim the whole extract first (1–2 minutes). Before you write anything, read the full text quickly to see its overall shape. Ask yourself: what does the opening focus on? Where does the focus shift? What does the ending do differently from the beginning? Jot a quick mental map of the text's journey.
  2. Identify 3 structural features across the text. You need points from the beginning, middle, and end — the examiner wants to see you engaging with the whole text. Look for: a shift in focus (e.g. wide shot to close-up), a change in pace, a moment where information is withheld or revealed, a contrast between sections, a time shift or flashback, or a cyclical structure.
  3. For each feature, find a short quotation or line reference. You don't need long quotes — a phrase or even a line number will do. The point is to anchor your observation to a specific moment in the text.
  4. Explain the effect on the reader for each point. This is where most marks are won or lost. Don't just say "this keeps the reader interested." Explain how it affects the reader's experience: does it create suspense? Does it make the later action feel more shocking by contrast? Does it make the reader re-evaluate what they've already read?
  5. Use structural terminology in every paragraph. Terms like "shift in focus," "narrative perspective," "withholding," "zooming in," "cyclical structure," "juxtaposition of pace" — these signal to the examiner that you understand structure as a concept, not just plot sequence.
  6. Write 3 developed paragraphs. Three well-developed structural observations with effects will comfortably reach Mastering. You do not need to write an introduction or conclusion — get straight into your first point.

Timing

Spend 10–12 minutes on this question. Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes for 64 marks (reading) plus 40 marks (writing). The reading section should take roughly 1 hour, and Q3 is worth 8 marks — so 10–12 minutes is proportionate. Break it down like this:

  • 1–2 minutes: Skim the whole text and identify structural features
  • 8–9 minutes: Write 3 paragraphs
  • 1 minute: Re-read your answer to check you've explained effects, not just described events
Key Fact

Students often spend too long on Q3 and then rush Q4 (which is worth 20 marks). Set a timer. Three strong paragraphs in 10 minutes is enough for full marks.

Model Answer (Top band: 7–8 marks)

Paragraph 1: The writer opens the extract with a wide, panoramic description of the landscape before gradually zooming in to focus on a single figure. This movement from the general to the specific creates a sense of inevitability, drawing the reader's attention to the character as though they are the only person of significance in this world. The structural effect is cinematic — the reader feels as though a camera is slowly finding its subject, which builds anticipation before we know anything about who this person is or why they matter.

Paragraph 2: A structural contrast is built between the calm, measured opening and the frantic pace of the ending. The short, fragmented sentences in the final paragraph — "She ran. She didn't look back." — create urgency after the slow build, which makes the sudden action feel shocking and earned. By structuring the text with a gradual escalation, the writer ensures the shift in pace is not just noticed but felt by the reader — the ending disrupts the rhythm that the reader has become comfortable with.

Paragraph 3: The writer also uses withholding as a structural device: the identity of the figure on the hill is not revealed until line 20, keeping the reader in suspense for nearly half the text. This delayed revelation rewards careful reading and maintains interest throughout. Crucially, this structural choice forces the reader to project their own assumptions onto the figure, so when the identity is finally disclosed, it either confirms or subverts those expectations — either way, the reader is actively engaged.

Why this answer scores 7–8 marks:

  • ✅ Covers the beginning, middle development, and end — engages with the whole text
  • ✅ Uses accurate structural terminology: "zooming in," "structural contrast," "withholding," "delayed revelation," "shift in pace"
  • ✅ Every point explains the effect on the reader in specific, developed terms — not just "it keeps the reader interested"
  • ✅ Goes beyond identifying features to explaining why they work — e.g. the slow build makes the ending feel "earned," the withholding forces the reader to "project their own assumptions"
  • ✅ Short, embedded quotations used as evidence without over-quoting

Weak Answer (Emerging–2: 1–2 marks)

"The text starts by describing the landscape and then moves on to talk about the character. [❌ This is just retelling — what happens first, then what happens next. No structural term used. No effect explained.] This is an effective way to begin the story. [❌ "Effective" is vague — effective how? What does it make the reader think or feel?] Then at the end, the pace speeds up with short sentences. [❌ This is a valid observation but there's no quotation, no structural term beyond "pace," and no explanation of the effect.] The structure is good because it keeps the reader interested from start to finish. [❌ "Keeps the reader interested" is the most common dead-end phrase in Q3. It says nothing specific. Every text is structured to interest the reader — the question is HOW.]"

Why this answer scores only 1–2 marks:

  • ❌ Retells events in order rather than analysing structural choices
  • ❌ No structural terminology (no mention of "zoom," "shift in focus," "withholding," "contrast," etc.)
  • ❌ No quotations or line references to anchor observations
  • ❌ Effects are vague and generic: "effective," "keeps the reader interested," "good"
  • ❌ Only 4 sentences — underdeveloped for an 8-mark question

Common Mistakes

  • Analysing language instead of structure. If you're writing about "the adjective 'dark' creates a sinister tone," you've drifted into Q2 territory. Structure is about how the text is organised, sequenced, and shaped — not about individual word choices.
  • Retelling the plot in order. "First this happens, then this happens, then this happens" is not structural analysis. The examiner wants you to explain why the writer chose to present things in that order and what effect it has. Compare: "The text starts with the landscape" (retelling) vs. "The writer opens with a panoramic focus on the landscape before narrowing to a single figure, creating a sense of the character's isolation" (structural analysis).
  • Using "it keeps the reader interested" as your only effect. This phrase is so overused that it essentially means nothing. Push yourself further: how does it interest the reader? Does it create suspense? Shock? A sense of foreboding? Relief? Disorientation? Be specific.
  • Only writing about the beginning. You must cover the whole text. The bullet points in the question guide you through beginning, middle, and end. If you only write about the opening paragraph, you cannot score above Developing because you haven't engaged with how the structure develops.

Key Terminology

Use these terms in your answers to show the examiner you understand structure as a concept:

  • Shift in focus — when the writer moves attention from one subject, character, or setting to another
  • Zoom in / Zoom out — moving from a wide, general view to a close, specific detail (or vice versa), like a camera lens
  • Withholding information — deliberately not telling the reader something to create suspense or mystery
  • Delayed revelation — holding back a key piece of information until later in the text for dramatic effect
  • Flashback / Time shift — when the narrative moves backwards (or forwards) in time, disrupting chronological order
  • Cyclical structure — when the ending mirrors or returns to the beginning, creating a sense of completion or entrapment
  • Juxtaposition — placing two contrasting sections, images, or ideas next to each other for effect
  • Pace — how fast or slow the text feels; controlled through sentence length, paragraph length, and the amount of detail
  • Narrative perspective / distance — how close or far the narration feels from the character's thoughts and feelings
  • Cliff-hanger — ending on an unresolved moment of tension to leave the reader wanting more
  • Foreshadowing — structural hints early in the text that point towards later events
  • Opening / Exposition — the beginning of the text where setting, character, or situation is established
Key Fact

You don't need to use every term — 3 or 4 used accurately and confidently is far better than cramming in terminology you don't fully understand. Pick the terms that genuinely fit the text in front of you.

Quick Reference
Question: Paper 1, Q3
Marks: 8
Timing: 10–12 minutes
Paragraphs: 3 developed points
Focus: Whole-text structure, not language
Top tip: Cover beginning, middle shift, AND ending
Avoid: "It keeps the reader interested" with no further explanation
Remember: Structure = how the text is organised. Language = individual word choices. Don't mix them up.
Other Guides
4 marks — Retrieval 8 marks — Language Analysis 8 marks — Summary 16 marks — Comparison 20 marks — Evaluation 40 marks — Creative Writing

title: 40 marks — Creative Writing
content_html:
What the Question Asks

Paper 1 Question 5 asks you to produce a piece of creative writing — either a description or a narrative (story opening). You'll be given a choice: respond to an image with a description, or respond to a written prompt with a story. This is worth 40 marks — the single highest-value question on either paper. examiners are not looking for a complete story with a neat ending. They want crafted, controlled writing that shows you can use language and structure deliberately to create effects.

Key Fact

This question is worth 40 marks — that's 25% of the entire English Language GCSE. Every minute you spend here is worth more marks than anywhere else on the paper. Treat it seriously.

How Marks Are Allocated

Your marks are split across two Assessment Objectives:

AO5 — Content & Organisation (24 marks)

  • Top band (19–24): Compelling and crafted. Sophisticated vocabulary and structural choices. Individual voice sustained throughout. Structure actively enhances meaning. The writing feels deliberate and controlled — every paragraph earns its place.
  • Upper-mid band (13–18): Clear and effective. Deliberate language and structural choices that mostly convince. Engages the reader. Connected, coherent writing with a clear sense of direction.
  • Lower-mid band (7–12): Some attempt to engage the reader. Some conscious language and structural choices, but inconsistent. May lose focus or direction partway through.
  • Lower band (1–6): Simple, basic writing. Limited vocabulary. Little awareness of the reader. Minimal structure beyond chronological order.

AO6 — Technical Accuracy (16 marks)

  • Top band (13–16): Extensive, accurate vocabulary. Sophisticated punctuation (semicolons, colons, dashes, ellipses) used correctly and for effect. Sentence structures deliberately varied and controlled. Spelling is secure across ambitious vocabulary.
  • Upper-mid band (9–12): Accurate grammar and punctuation. Varied sentence types. Mostly secure spelling, including some complex words. Sentences shaped for effect.
  • Lower-mid band (5–8): Generally accurate in simple constructions. Attempts variety in punctuation but not always successful. Some spelling errors on more complex words.
  • Lower band (1–4): Simple sentences mostly accurate but frequent errors when attempting anything more complex. Limited punctuation range. Frequent spelling errors.
Key Fact

Technical accuracy is worth 16 marks — that's more than the entire Q2 on structure. Sloppy spelling and punctuation will cap your grade. Proofread.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Choose wisely (1 minute). Read both options. Pick the one that immediately gives you images, feelings, or a situation you can see clearly. If you're strong at atmosphere and detail, go for description. If you're better at voice, dialogue, and tension, go for narrative. Don't pick based on what sounds "harder" — pick what you can write well.
  2. Plan with purpose (4 minutes). Write a brief plan — not a plot summary, but a structural map. For a narrative: note your opening image, a shift or turning point, and where you'll end. For a description: plan 4–5 "zones" of focus (e.g., wide landscape → specific object → sound → memory → return to landscape). In your plan, jot down 3–4 specific words, images, or techniques you want to include. A plan stops you rambling and gives your writing shape.
  3. Open with impact (first 5 minutes of writing). Your first paragraph is the most important thing you write. It sets your tone, your voice, and the examiner's first impression. Start with something precise and deliberate — a short sentence, an unusual image, a detail that raises a question. Do NOT start with "Once upon a time" or "It was a normal day." Drop the reader into the middle of something.
  4. Write in controlled sections (25–30 minutes). Aim for 4–6 well-crafted paragraphs rather than 10 rushed ones. Each paragraph should do one thing well: establish a mood, shift perspective, slow time down, zoom in on a detail. Vary your sentence lengths consciously — follow a long, complex sentence with a short, blunt one. Use paragraphing as a structural tool: a one-line paragraph can create emphasis or a shift in tone. Remember: you are being marked on the quality of your writing, not the quantity.
  5. End with control (final 5 minutes of writing). Your ending doesn't need to resolve everything — in fact, it shouldn't. A strong ending echoes the opening, leaves an image in the reader's mind, or shifts perspective. Avoid cliché endings ("it was all a dream," "and then I woke up"). A single, precise final sentence is worth more than a rushed paragraph of plot summary.
  6. Proofread ruthlessly (5 minutes). Read your work back slowly. Check for: missing full stops, comma splices (two sentences joined with just a comma), spelling errors on common words (their/there/they're, where/were, would've not "would of"), and any sentences that don't make grammatical sense. This is where you protect your AO6 marks. Change at least 2–3 things. If you find nothing to fix, you're not reading carefully enough.

Timing

Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes total. You should spend the first 55–60 minutes on the reading section (Questions 1–4). That leaves 45–50 minutes for Question 5.

  • 1 minute: Choose your option
  • 4 minutes: Plan (structural map + key images/techniques)
  • 35–40 minutes: Write (aim for 400–550 words of quality prose)
  • 5 minutes: Proofread and correct errors
Key Fact

Do NOT write 3 pages of rushed storytelling. Two pages of crafted, controlled writing will outscore four pages of breathless plot every time. Quality over quantity.

Model Answer

Prompt: Write the opening of a story about someone who discovers an unexpected letter.

The letter was not addressed to her.

Maya turned it over twice as if repetition might change what she saw. The handwriting — cramped, urgent, leaning sharply to the right as though trying to escape — belonged to no one she knew. And yet her name sat in the centre of the envelope, underlined once, with a certainty that made her feel watched.

She placed it on the kitchen table and made coffee. The kind of thing you do to create time before a decision, as though the ritual of kettle and cup might somehow absolve you of choosing. The envelope didn't move. It wasn't supposed to. But somehow its stillness felt deliberate.

Outside, the street was already full of the ordinary machinery of a Tuesday: bins being wheeled out, a delivery van double-parked, a dog pulling against its lead with joyful determination. All of it as solid and unremarkable as gravity. Maya watched it through the window and felt, for the first time in years, like the world was made of something she could fall through.

Why This Is Strong

  • Opening sentence: Short, precise, and immediately raises a question. The reader is hooked in six words.
  • Controlled voice: The narrator has a distinctive, intelligent tone — slightly detached, slightly wry ("The kind of thing you do to create time before a decision"). This is what examiners mean by "individual voice."
  • Language as craft: The handwriting is personified ("trying to escape"), the envelope's stillness is made sinister ("its stillness felt deliberate"), and the metaphor of the world as something she "could fall through" is original and precise. These aren't random techniques — they build a single mood of unease.
  • Structure enhances meaning: The piece moves from the letter → to avoidance (coffee) → to the ordinary world outside → back to Maya's interior fear. This mirrors how a real person would process anxiety: distraction, then return. The structure is the characterisation.
  • Contrast: The mundane Tuesday morning (bins, vans, dogs) is deliberately placed against Maya's growing dread. This makes the tension sharper without needing anything dramatic to happen.
  • Technical accuracy: Semicolons, colons, dashes, and em-dashes are all used correctly and purposefully. Sentences range from 6 words to 30+. Vocabulary is ambitious but precise ("absolve," "machinery of a Tuesday"). Spelling is flawless.
  • It doesn't over-tell: The letter is never opened. The plot barely moves. And yet the reader is completely engaged — because the writing is doing the work, not the story.

Weak Answer

Prompt: Write the opening of a story about someone who discovers an unexpected letter.

The letter was on the mat when she woke up. She picked it up and looked at it. It had her name on it. She was confused because she wasn't expecting a letter. She made a cup of tea and then sat down to open it. She was nervous. The letter was from someone she didn't know. She started to read it. It was very strange and made her feel worried. She decided to call her friend and tell them about it. Her friend said she should open it. So she did.

What Goes Wrong Here

  • "She...She...She...": Almost every sentence begins the same way. This is the single most common problem in weak creative writing. It creates a flat, monotonous rhythm and shows no sentence variety — capping AO6 at Developing.
  • Telling, not showing: "She was confused," "She was nervous," "It was very strange" — these tell us what to feel instead of creating the feeling through imagery or detail. Compare this with the strong answer, which never once says Maya is afraid but makes you feel her fear.
  • No sensory detail: What does the letter look like? What does the handwriting look like? What does the kitchen smell like? There is nothing here that you can see, hear, or touch. The writing is a summary of events, not an experience.
  • Plot-driven, not craft-driven: This answer races through events (picks up letter → makes tea → reads it → calls friend → opens it) as though the point is to tell a story. At GCSE, the point is to write well. The strong answer covers far less "plot" but scores far higher.
  • No structural choices: The entire piece is a single paragraph with no variation in pace, focus, or perspective. There's no sense of where it's going or why paragraphs begin and end where they do.
  • Weak vocabulary: "Very strange," "made her feel worried," "looked at it" — this is everyday conversational language, not crafted prose. There is no word here that a Year 6 student couldn't write.
  • It resolves too quickly: The letter is opened by the end. The tension is used up. A strong opening withholds — it creates anticipation rather than answering every question it raises.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing a full story with a beginning, middle, and end. You have 45 minutes. If you try to write a complete narrative with a climax and resolution, you'll rush, your writing quality will drop, and you'll sacrifice the crafted detail that earns top marks. Write an opening or a moment — not a novel.
  • Ignoring the prompt entirely. If you choose the image-based option, your writing must be clearly suggested by the picture. If you choose the narrative prompt, your writing must connect to it. Going completely off-topic will cost you marks for content and communication.
  • Using techniques for the sake of it. Cramming in similes, metaphors, alliteration, and personification every other line doesn't impress examiners — it reads as a checklist. Use techniques when they earn their place. One perfect metaphor is worth more than five forced similes.
  • Forgetting to proofread. Students routinely throw away 4–6 marks on AO6 because they don't re-read their work. Comma splices, missing apostrophes, "would of" instead of "would have," and inconsistent tense are all fixable in 5 minutes — but only if you actually check.

Key Terminology

These aren't terms to name-drop in your answer — they're techniques you should be using in your writing, consciously and deliberately.

  • Imagery: Language that creates a vivid picture in the reader's mind through sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste). "The kitchen smelled of burnt toast and yesterday's rain" is imagery. "The kitchen was messy" is not.
  • Metaphor: Describing something as if it is something else, without using "like" or "as." "The world was made of something she could fall through." Used well, a metaphor can capture a complex feeling in a single image.
  • Simile: A comparison using "like" or "as." Effective when precise and original. "Her hands trembled like a held breath" works. "She was as white as a ghost" does not — it's a cliché.
  • Personification: Giving human qualities to non-human things. "The envelope's stillness felt deliberate" makes an object feel threatening. Use sparingly for maximum effect.
  • Pathetic fallacy: Using weather or environment to reflect mood or emotion. Rain for sadness, storms for anger, oppressive heat for tension. Effective but easy to overdo — be subtle.
  • Short sentence / minor sentence: A deliberately brief sentence used for impact, emphasis, or pace

title: Exam Technique
content_html:
Exam Technique

Step-by-step guides for every Drama (J316) question type. Learn the formula, study a model answer, and avoid the common mistakes that cost marks.

Section A: Blood Brothers

4 marks

Costume Design Questions

Suggest costume items for a character and explain what they communicate to the audience about status, personality, or mood.

 4 marks

Voice Skills Questions

Describe how you would use vocal skills — pitch, pace, pause, tone, accent, emphasis — to deliver a specific line.

 4 marks

Physicality & Movement Questions

Explain how body language, gesture, posture, gait, and facial expression would communicate character and emotion.

 4 marks

Staging & Performance Space Questions

Choose a staging type and explain how the performance space affects the audience’s experience of a scene.

 4 marks

Lighting & Sound Design Questions

Suggest lighting states, colour, sound effects, or music and explain their impact on atmosphere and meaning.

 8–10 marks

Director Interpretation Questions

The big Section A question. Explain how you would direct actors in a scene, covering staging, movement, voice, and overall interpretation.

 8 marks

Set Design Questions

Describe or sketch a set design for a scene, explaining how design elements communicate setting, mood, and themes.

Section B: Live Theatre

30 marks

Live Theatre Essay

The highest-value question on the paper. Evaluate a live performance you have seen, using SEAS paragraphs to analyse acting, design, and directorial choices.

title: Costume Design Questions [4 marks]
content_html:
4 marks

Costume Design Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner gives you a character and a moment in the play, then asks you to suggest costume items and explain what they communicate to the audience. You need to show you understand the character’s status, personality, age, or mood at that specific point — and that you can make practical design choices that an audience would read correctly.

Marking

What You Need
4Multiple specific costume items with clear explanation of what each communicates about the character at that moment
2–3Some relevant suggestions but lacking detail or explanation of meaning
1Vague or generic description with no connection to character or moment
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what the audience needs to understand — What should the costume tell us? Social class? Time period? Emotional state? For Blood Brothers, the class divide between Mickey and Edward is central, so costume choices must reflect this.
  2. 2
    Name specific items — Don’t say “smart clothes”. Say “a pressed white shirt, grey flannel trousers, and polished black shoes”. Examiners reward precise detail.
  3. 3
    Describe colour, fabric, and condition — A “faded, oversized hand-me-down jumper” tells the audience far more than just “a jumper”. Colour can suggest mood (dark = serious, bright = youthful).
  4. 4
    Explain what it communicates — Always connect back: “This would show the audience that…”. Every item must have a reason. This is where marks are won.

Timing

Costume Design — 5 min

About five minutes. Read the extract, picture the character at that moment, list 2–3 costume items with clear reasons, and move on.

Item + Detail + Meaning

“I would dress [character] in [specific item] made from [fabric/colour/condition]. This would communicate to the audience that [meaning], because [reason linked to the play].”

Contrast template (Blood Brothers)

“While [Character A] wears [items showing wealth/poverty], [Character B] would be dressed in [contrasting items]. This visual contrast would immediately show the audience the class divide that drives the play’s central conflict.”

Suggest how you would costume Mickey as a teenager. Explain what your choices would communicate to the audience. [4 marks]

Full marks

I would dress Mickey in faded, baggy jeans that are slightly too short, suggesting they are old and possibly second-hand (1). He would wear a worn grey hoodie with fraying cuffs, communicating to the audience that his family cannot afford new clothes and reinforcing his working-class background (1). On his feet would be scuffed white trainers with visible dirt marks, showing that he spends time outdoors unsupervised (1). His clothes would be untucked and creased, contrasting sharply with Edward’s neat appearance and visually representing the class divide at the heart of the play (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Four specific costume items, each with precise detail (colour, condition, fit) and a clear explanation of what it communicates about Mickey’s class and character.

Suggest how you would costume Mickey as a teenager. Explain what your choices would communicate to the audience. [4 marks]

1 mark — too vague

Mickey would wear scruffy clothes to show he is poor.

Examiner: The idea is right but “scruffy clothes” names no specific items and gives no detail about colour, fabric, or condition. The explanation is too brief.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Being too vague — “Nice clothes” or “casual outfit” earns nothing. Name the actual garments: shirt, trousers, shoes, accessories.
  • ❌
    Forgetting to explain meaning — Listing items without saying what they communicate is only half the answer. Always include “This would show the audience that…”
  • ❌
    Ignoring the specific moment — Mickey’s costume as a child should differ from his costume as a depressed adult. Read the extract carefully and design for THAT moment.
  • ❌
    Unrealistic suggestions — Keep it practical. A school production could realistically source what you describe.
Voice Skills (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify what audience needs to see
  2. Name specific items
  3. Describe colour, fabric, condition
  4. Explain what it communicates
Key Terminology
  • Silhouette
  • Fabric / texture
  • Colour palette
  • Period / era
  • Condition (worn, pristine)
  • Status / class
  • Accessories
  • Hair and make-up

title: Voice Skills Questions [4 marks]
content_html:
4 marks

Voice Skills Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner gives you a specific line or short section of dialogue and asks how you would use vocal skills to deliver it. You need to show you understand the character’s emotion and intention at that moment, and that you can describe precise vocal techniques that would bring the line to life for an audience.

Marking

What You Need
4Multiple specific vocal skills named and explained with clear connection to emotion and line meaning
2–3Some vocal skills identified but without enough detail or connection to the text
1Vague reference to voice with no specific skills named
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the line and identify the emotion — What is the character feeling? Angry, scared, excited, desperate? The vocal choices must match the emotional state. In Blood Brothers, emotions shift rapidly — check the context.
  2. 2
    Choose 2–3 specific vocal skills — Pick from: pitch (high/low), pace (fast/slow), pause, tone (warm/harsh/sarcastic), volume (loud/quiet/whisper), emphasis (stress on key words), accent (Liverpool working-class vs middle-class RP).
  3. 3
    Describe exactly how you would use each skill — Don’t just say “I would use a loud voice.” Say “I would raise my volume sharply on the word ‘never’ to show Mickey’s sudden anger.” Quote the specific words.
  4. 4
    Explain the effect on the audience — Why does this vocal choice matter? “The sudden pause before ‘brother’ would create tension and make the audience sense the weight of the revelation.”

Timing

Voice Skills — 5 min

About five minutes. Identify the emotion, pick 2–3 vocal skills, describe how you’d use them on specific words, and explain the effect.

Skill + Application + Effect

“On the line ‘[quote]’, I would use [vocal skill] by [how exactly]. This would communicate [emotion/meaning] to the audience because [reason].”

Contrast within a speech

“I would begin the line in a [description] voice, then shift to [different quality] on the word ‘[word]’. This contrast would show the audience that [character] is [emotional shift].”

How would you use vocal skills to deliver the line “I could have been him!” as Mickey? [4 marks]

Full marks

I would deliver “I could have been” at a low pitch and slow pace, with a bitter, regretful tone, as if Mickey is processing the injustice of his situation (1). I would then place a heavy pause before “him” to build tension and allow the weight of the realisation to hit the audience (1). The word “him” would be spoken with a sudden increase in volume and a cracking voice, as though Mickey is fighting back tears of anger (1). The overall effect would communicate Mickey’s resentment at the class divide that has shaped his life, making the audience feel sympathy for his frustration (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Three distinct vocal skills (pitch/pace, pause, volume) applied to specific words, with clear emotional reasoning and audience impact.

How would you use vocal skills to deliver the line “I could have been him!” as Mickey? [4 marks]

1 mark — no specific skills

I would say it in an angry voice to show Mickey is upset about Edward having a better life.

Examiner: “Angry voice” is not a specific vocal skill. Which techniques create anger? Volume? Pace? Tone? Name and describe the techniques, not just the emotion.

Vocal Skills Toolkit

The six vocal skills examiners expect to see:

  • Pitch — how high or low the voice is (high = panic, low = authority)
  • Pace — how fast or slow (fast = excitement/fear, slow = seriousness/grief)
  • Pause — deliberate silence for dramatic effect (builds tension, shows hesitation)
  • Tone — the quality/emotion in the voice (warm, cold, sarcastic, pleading)
  • Volume — how loud or quiet (whisper = secrecy, shout = anger)
  • Emphasis — stressing particular words to change meaning

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Saying “angry voice” instead of naming the skill — Emotions are not vocal skills. “Angry” describes the feeling; you need to say WHICH techniques create that anger (raised volume, fast pace, sharp tone).
  • ❌
    Not quoting the actual words — Refer to specific words or phrases. “On the word ‘never’ I would…” is far stronger than “at the end of the line.”
  • ❌
    Only using one vocal skill — A 4-mark answer needs 2–3 different techniques. If you only write about volume, you cap yourself at 1–2 marks.
  • ❌
    Ignoring the context — A line delivered in Act 1 when the twins are children sounds completely different from the same character in Act 2 as a desperate adult.
← Costume Design (4 marks) Physicality & Movement (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the emotion
  2. Choose 2–3 vocal skills
  3. Apply to specific words
  4. Explain the audience effect

title: Physicality & Movement Questions [4 marks]
content_html:
4 marks

Physicality & Movement Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner asks how a performer would use their body to communicate character and emotion at a specific moment. This covers gesture, posture, gait (how you walk), facial expression, eye contact, proxemics (use of space and distance), and levels. You must describe precise physical choices and explain what they tell the audience.

Marking

What You Need
4Multiple specific physical skills described with clear explanation of what each communicates
2–3Some relevant physical choices but lacking precision or explanation
1Vague or generic description (e.g. “look sad”)
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the character’s emotional state — Are they confident, afraid, angry, defeated? In Blood Brothers, Mickey’s physicality changes dramatically from the energetic child to the depressed adult.
  2. 2
    Choose 2–3 physical skills — Pick from: gesture (hand/arm movements), posture (how they hold their body), gait (walking style), facial expression, eye contact/line, proxemics (distance from others), and levels (standing, sitting, crouching).
  3. 3
    Describe each precisely — “Slumped shoulders with head bowed” is specific. “Looking sad” is not. Describe what the audience would SEE.
  4. 4
    Explain what it communicates — Connect every choice to character and meaning: “This hunched posture would show the audience that Mickey has been beaten down by unemployment and depression.”

Timing

Physicality — 5 min

About five minutes. Read the extract, picture the character’s body language, describe 2–3 physical choices with reasons.

Physical skill + Description + Meaning

“At this moment, [character] would [specific physical action]. This would communicate to the audience that [meaning] because [reason linked to the scene].”

Proxemics template

“[Character A] would stand [close to / far from] [Character B], with [body turned towards/away]. This use of proxemics would show the audience that [relationship dynamic].”

How would you use physicality to perform Mrs Johnstone during the scene where she gives away her child? [4 marks]

Full marks

Mrs Johnstone would stand with her arms wrapped tightly around herself, as if physically trying to hold herself together, communicating her internal conflict to the audience (1). Her gait as she moves toward Mrs Lyons would be slow and hesitant, with small shuffling steps, showing her reluctance and the weight of the decision (1). When handing the baby over, her hands would visibly tremble and she would extend her arms stiffly, keeping her body turned slightly away, conveying that she cannot bear to watch the moment of separation (1). Her facial expression would show a tight jaw and glistening eyes looking downward, avoiding eye contact with Mrs Lyons, suggesting shame and barely controlled grief (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Four distinct physical skills (posture, gait, gesture/hand movement, facial expression) each precisely described and linked to character emotion.

1 mark — too vague

Mrs Johnstone would look sad and move slowly because she doesn’t want to give away her baby.

Examiner: “Look sad” and “move slowly” are not specific physical descriptions. What does “sad” look like physically? Describe posture, gesture, facial muscles, eye line.

Physical Skills Toolkit

Physical skills examiners expect to see:

  • Gesture — hand and arm movements (pointing, wringing hands, clenching fists)
  • Posture — how the body is held (upright = confidence, slumped = defeat)
  • Gait — walking style (stride = power, shuffle = exhaustion, bounce = excitement)
  • Facial expression — eyes, mouth, brow (furrowed brow = worry, wide eyes = fear)
  • Eye contact — looking at or avoiding another character (dominance vs submission)
  • Proxemics — distance and positioning between characters (closeness = intimacy/threat)
  • Levels — standing, sitting, kneeling, lying (higher = power, lower = vulnerability)

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing about emotions instead of actions — “She would feel scared” is not physicality. Describe what the audience SEES: “Her hands would grip the edge of the table, knuckles white.”
  • ❌
    Confusing voice and body — This question is about physicality. Don’t write about pitch, pace, or tone — save those for voice skills questions.
  • ❌
    Only describing facial expression — Use the whole body. Combine posture, gesture, and movement for a complete physical performance.
  • ❌
    Generic descriptions — “Walking around the stage” is too vague. Say HOW they walk, WHERE to, and WHY.
← Voice Skills (4 marks) Staging & Performance Space (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the emotional state
  2. Choose 2–3 physical skills
  3. Describe each precisely
  4. Explain what it communicates

title: Staging & Performance Space Questions [4 marks]
content_html:
4 marks

Staging & Performance Space Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner asks you to choose or discuss a staging configuration and explain how it affects the audience’s experience. You need to know the main staging types and be able to justify why a particular configuration suits a specific scene in Blood Brothers. This includes how actors are positioned, where the audience sits, and how entrances, exits, and sightlines work.

Marking

What You Need
4Clear identification of staging type with specific explanation of how it enhances the scene for the audience
2–3Staging type named with some reasoning but lacking specific scene application
1Vague reference to staging with no clear understanding of types or impact
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer

Staging Types You Must Know

The five staging configurations:

  • Proscenium arch — audience faces the stage from one side through a frame. Best for: clear focus, set changes behind curtain, traditional productions.
  • Thrust — stage extends into the audience on three sides. Best for: intimacy, closer actor-audience relationship, soliloquies.
  • In the round — audience surrounds the stage on all sides. Best for: immersive experience, no hiding places for actors, community feel.
  • Traverse — audience on two opposite sides with stage in the middle. Best for: confrontation scenes, journey staging, two contrasting worlds.
  • Promenade — audience moves with the action through different spaces. Best for: immersive theatre, site-specific work.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Name the staging type — State clearly which configuration you would use. Use the correct terminology.
  2. 2
    Describe how actors would use the space — Where would key characters be positioned? How would entrances and exits work? Where is the focal point?
  3. 3
    Explain the audience experience — What does this staging type DO for the audience in this specific scene? Does it create intimacy, distance, tension, surprise?
  4. 4
    Link to the play’s themes — Blood Brothers explores class divide, fate, and superstition. How does your staging choice reinforce these themes?

Timing

Staging — 5 min

About five minutes. Name the type, describe actor positions, explain the audience impact, and link to themes.

Explain how you would use the performance space for the final scene of Blood Brothers. [4 marks]

Full marks

I would use a thrust stage so the audience is close to the action on three sides, creating an intimate and claustrophobic atmosphere for the climax (1). Mickey and Edward would be positioned at opposite ends of the thrust, forcing the audience to look between them, physically representing the divide that has torn the brothers apart (1). Mrs Johnstone would enter from the back of the auditorium through the audience, making her arrival feel desperate and unexpected, breaking the fourth wall as the Narrator has done throughout (1). The close proximity of the thrust stage would mean the audience can see every facial expression in detail, making the shooting feel visceral and unavoidable rather than distant (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Clear staging type named, specific actor positioning, audience experience described, and linked to the play’s themes of division and fate.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not naming a staging type — You must use the correct terminology. “The audience would be around the stage” is vague; “in the round” is precise.
  • ❌
    Describing set design instead of staging — Staging is about the configuration of the space and where the audience sits. Furniture, props, and scenery are set design — a different question type.
  • ❌
    No connection to the scene — Don’t just define the staging type. Explain why it WORKS for this particular moment in Blood Brothers.
  • ❌
    Forgetting sightlines — In the round and traverse have sightline challenges (audience behind actors). Show awareness of this in your answer.

← Back to Exam Technique

Formula

  1. Name the staging type
  2. Describe actor positions
  3. Explain audience experience
  4. Link to themes

title: Lighting & Sound Design Questions [4 marks]
content_html:
4 marks

Lighting & Sound Design Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner asks you to suggest lighting or sound design choices for a specific moment and explain their effect on the audience. You need to show knowledge of practical design elements — lantern types, colour gels, gobos, angles for lighting; live sound, recorded effects, underscoring, volume, and timing for sound — and explain how they create atmosphere and meaning.

Marking

What You Need
4Specific design choices using correct terminology with clear explanation of atmospheric and dramatic effect
2–3Some relevant ideas but lacking technical detail or explanation of effect
1Vague suggestion with no technical language or connection to meaning
Incorrect, irrelevant, or no answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the mood the scene needs — Is it tense, joyful, eerie, romantic, chaotic? The design must serve the drama. In Blood Brothers, the Narrator’s scenes often need an ominous, supernatural quality.
  2. 2
    Name specific equipment or effects — For lighting: Fresnel spot, profile spot, flood, colour gel (blue, red, amber), gobo, follow spot, blackout, cross-fade. For sound: underscoring, sound effect (gunshot, heartbeat), live music, recorded track, fade in/out.
  3. 3
    Describe when and how it changes — Design is about transitions. A sudden blackout is different from a slow fade. A sharp gunshot is different from a building drumbeat.
  4. 4
    Explain the effect on the audience — Why does this choice matter? “The cold blue wash would make the audience feel uneasy, reflecting the sense of fate closing in on Mickey.”

Timing

Lighting/Sound — 5 min

About five minutes. Identify the mood, name specific design choices with technical terms, and explain the audience impact.

Suggest how lighting could be used when the Narrator delivers his warnings. [4 marks]

Full marks

I would use a tight profile spot with a steel-blue gel focused solely on the Narrator, isolating him from the rest of the stage which would fall into a dim wash (1). The blue light would give his skin a cold, ghostly appearance, suggesting to the audience that he is a supernatural figure connected to fate and death (1). As he speaks, a gobo projecting a clock face could slowly rotate across the back wall, symbolising time running out for the twins (1). When he finishes, the spotlight would snap to blackout before the next scene’s warm amber wash fades in, creating a jarring contrast that unsettles the audience and reinforces the sense of foreboding (1).

Examiner: 4/4 — Four specific lighting choices (spot type, gel colour, gobo, blackout transition) with technical vocabulary and clear connection to mood and meaning.

1 mark — no technical language

I would make the lighting dark and scary to show the Narrator is a creepy character.

Examiner: “Dark and scary” uses no design terminology. What type of lantern? What colour? What angle? How does it change? Technical precision is essential.

Design Toolkit

Lighting terminology:

  • Fresnel — soft-edged wash light for general areas
  • Profile spot — hard-edged beam for precise focus
  • Flood — wide, even light covering large areas
  • Follow spot — manually operated spot that tracks an actor
  • Gel / colour filter — coloured plastic placed over lanterns (blue = cold, red = danger, amber = warmth)
  • Gobo — metal template that projects patterns (trees, windows, clock faces)
  • Blackout / snap / cross-fade — transition types between lighting states

Sound terminology:

  • Underscoring — music played beneath dialogue to set mood
  • Sound effect (SFX) — specific noises (gunshot, doorbell, rain)
  • Live music — performed on stage (Blood Brothers uses live piano/guitar)
  • Fade in / fade out — gradual volume change
  • Diegetic — sound characters can hear (radio, doorbell)
  • Non-diegetic — sound only the audience hears (underscoring, sound effects for mood)

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    No technical vocabulary — “Bright lights” or “scary music” is too vague. Use specific terms: Fresnel, profile spot, gel colour, underscoring, SFX.
  • ❌
    Describing what happens instead of designing it — Don’t narrate the scene. Explain your DESIGN CHOICES and why they work.
  • ❌
    Mixing up lighting and sound — If the question asks about lighting, don’t write about sound effects. Read the question carefully.
  • ❌
    Ignoring transitions — How lighting or sound CHANGES is as important as the static state. A slow fade creates a different mood from a snap blackout.
← Staging (4 marks) Director Interpretation (8–10 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique

5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the mood needed
  2. Name specific equipment/effects
  3. Describe how it changes
  4. Explain the audience impact

title: Director Interpretation Questions [8–10 marks]
content_html:
8–10 marks

Director Interpretation Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-mark question in Section A. The examiner asks you to explain how you would direct a specific scene or extract, covering multiple elements: how actors would move and use the space, their vocal delivery, the overall mood and atmosphere you want to create, and how your choices communicate the play’s themes to the audience. You must write as a director giving instructions to actors and designers.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureDetailed, creative direction covering multiple performance elements with clear justification linked to character and themes
DevelopingSome directorial ideas but lacking detail, range, or clear connection to the text
EmergingBasic ideas with limited understanding of the director’s role
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    State your overall interpretation — Open with a clear directorial vision. What is the MOOD of this scene? What do you want the audience to FEEL? This sets the framework for everything that follows.
  2. 2
    Direct the actors’ movement and positioning — Where do they enter from? Where do they stand in relation to each other (proxemics)? How do they move through the space? Use specific stage directions (downstage, upstage, centre).
  3. 3
    Direct the vocal delivery — How should key lines be spoken? Apply specific vocal skills (pace, pitch, tone, pause, emphasis) to 2–3 important lines from the extract.
  4. 4
    Direct the physicality — What gestures, posture, and facial expressions should the actors use? How do these change through the scene?
  5. 5
    Justify every choice — Everything must connect back to character, theme, or audience impact. Use phrases like: “I would direct this because…”, “This would show the audience that…”

Timing

Vision
2 min Direction
6 min Check
2 min

About ten minutes. Spend two minutes planning your vision, six minutes writing detailed direction, and two minutes checking you’ve covered movement, voice, and physicality.

As a director, explain how you would stage the scene where Mickey and Edward first meet as children. [10 marks]

Strong answer

My overall interpretation of this scene would emphasise the instant, natural bond between the twins, contrasting with the audience’s knowledge that this friendship is forbidden. I want the audience to feel joy and dread simultaneously.

I would direct Mickey to enter from stage left at a run, tripping slightly as he reaches centre stage, establishing his energetic, clumsy physicality. He would be bouncing on his toes, unable to stand still, with wide eyes and an open-mouthed grin. Edward would enter from stage right more cautiously, taking neat, measured steps, hands by his sides — physically reflecting his more sheltered, controlled upbringing.

When Mickey says “Gis a sweet,” I would direct him to deliver it at a fast pace with a rising pitch, leaning forward with an outstretched hand — direct, demanding, but playful. Edward’s response should be spoken with a slightly bewildered tone, wide eyes, and a delighted smile — he has never been spoken to so bluntly and finds it thrilling. I would direct Edward to hand over the whole bag of sweets with both hands, an excessive gesture that shows he doesn’t understand the value of things.

As the scene progresses and they discover shared interests, I would bring them physically closer until they are standing shoulder to shoulder, mirroring each other’s gestures unconsciously — sitting cross-legged, leaning in, matching each other’s energy. This mirroring would visually communicate their twin connection to the audience before the characters themselves know it.

The blood brother pact should be staged centre stage, both boys kneeling face to face at the same level. I would direct them to speak the oath in unison, slowly and seriously, with a sudden drop in pace and volume from their previous excited chatter. This shift would signal to the audience that something significant and irreversible is happening, building dramatic irony given what we know about their fate.

Examiner: 9–10/10 — Clear directorial vision stated up front. Covers movement, positioning, vocal delivery on specific lines, physicality, and proxemics. Every choice is justified through character or audience impact. Range of performance elements covered across the whole extract.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Retelling the plot — The examiner knows what happens. Don’t describe the story — direct the performance. Write as if giving instructions to actors.
  • ❌
    Only covering one element — For 8–10 marks, you MUST cover multiple elements: movement, voice, physicality. Only writing about blocking or only about voice will cap your mark at Developing.
  • ❌
    No overall vision — The best answers open with a clear statement of intent: “I want the audience to feel…” This frames everything that follows.
  • ❌
    Writing as a performer instead of a director — Use director language: “I would direct Mickey to…” not “I would walk across the stage.” You are the director, not the actor.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10 min total

Must Cover

  1. Overall interpretation / vision
  2. Movement and positioning
  3. Vocal delivery on key lines
  4. Physicality and gesture
  5. Justify every choice

title: Set Design Questions [8 marks]
content_html:
8 marks

Set Design Questions

Used in: Section A — Blood Brothers

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner asks you to describe or sketch a set design for a specific scene, explaining how your choices communicate setting, mood, social context, and themes. You need to think about: stage furniture, levels, materials, colours, backdrops, entrances/exits, and how the set might change between scenes. Blood Brothers moves between multiple locations (the Johnstone house, the Lyons house, the street, the field) so your design must be practical as well as meaningful.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureDetailed, practical set design with clear explanation of how elements communicate meaning. May include a labelled sketch.
DevelopingSome relevant design ideas but lacking detail or explanation of purpose
EmergingBasic ideas with limited design vocabulary or connection to the play
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what the set needs to show — Location, time period, social class, mood. For Blood Brothers, the contrast between the Johnstone and Lyons households is essential.
  2. 2
    Describe the key elements — Stage furniture (tables, chairs), levels (raised platforms, stairs), materials and textures (bare brick vs polished wood), colours (muted vs bright), backdrops or projections.
  3. 3
    Explain how the set communicates meaning — A cracked, bare-brick wall on one side and a pristine painted wall on the other could symbolise the class divide without a single word of dialogue.
  4. 4
    Consider practicality — How does the set change between scenes? A revolving set, trucks, projections, or a split stage? Show the examiner you understand how theatre works.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
5 min Sketch
3 min

About ten minutes. Plan your design, write the explanation, and add a quick labelled sketch if asked. The sketch does not need to be artistic — it needs to be clear and labelled.

Describe how you would design the set to show the contrast between the Johnstone and Lyons households. [8 marks]

Strong answer

I would use a split-stage design to show both households simultaneously, reinforcing the class divide that runs through the entire play.

Stage left (the Johnstone home) would feature a bare, cramped space with exposed brick walls painted in faded grey-brown tones. A small, scratched wooden kitchen table with mismatched chairs would be centre-left, cluttered with mugs and newspapers. The floor would be bare boards, slightly raised on a low 6-inch platform. A single overhead bare bulb on a cord would hang above the table, suggesting harsh, functional lighting. A washing line strung across the back with children’s clothes would communicate the large family and domestic labour of Mrs Johnstone’s life.

Stage right (the Lyons home) would be raised on a 12-inch platform to suggest superiority. It would feature a polished dark-wood sideboard, an upholstered armchair, and a side table with a vase of flowers. The walls would be smooth and painted cream, with framed pictures visible. A thick rug on the floor would contrast with the bare boards opposite. The overall colour palette would be warm and coordinated, suggesting wealth, order, and control.

The centre of the stage would remain a neutral, open space representing the street and the outside world where the twins meet. A simple lamp post could mark this area. Set changes between indoor and outdoor scenes would be achieved by lighting — fading up one side while dimming the other — rather than moving furniture, keeping transitions swift and the contrast always visible.

Examiner: 7–8/8 — Detailed, practical design with specific furniture, materials, colours, and levels. Clear explanation of how each element communicates class difference. Practical solution for scene changes. Shows strong understanding of Blood Brothers’ themes.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Too vague — “The set would look poor” is not design. Describe specific items, materials, colours, and their condition.
  • ❌
    Unrealistic or impractical — A rotating waterfall or full-size house is not feasible. Show you understand theatre budgets and practicality.
  • ❌
    No explanation of meaning — Describing the set without saying WHY you made those choices loses half the marks. Every element must communicate something.
  • ❌
    Confusing set with props or costume — Set design is the physical environment: walls, floors, levels, large furniture. Hand-held items are props; what actors wear is costume.

← Back to Exam Technique

10 min total

  2. Describe key elements in detail
  3. Explain how they communicate meaning
  4. Consider practical scene changes

title: Section B: Live Theatre Essay [30 marks]
content_html:
30 marks

Section B: Live Theatre Essay

Used in: Section B — Live Theatre Evaluation

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-value question on the entire paper, worth 30 marks. You must write an extended response evaluating a live performance you have seen. The examiner wants you to analyse specific moments — acting, design (set, lighting, sound, costume), and directing — and evaluate how effective they were in communicating meaning to the audience. You MUST write about a real production you attended, not a film or recording.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
Level 5Perceptive, detailed analysis of multiple production elements with sophisticated evaluation using subject-specific terminology throughout
MasteringDetailed analysis with clear evaluation and good use of terminology. Covers acting and design elements.
SecureSome analysis with evaluation but may lack range or detail in places
DevelopingDescription of the production with limited analysis or evaluation
EmergingBasic comments with little or no evaluation
No relevant response

The SEAS Paragraph Structure

Every paragraph should follow the SEAS structure. This ensures you always analyse AND evaluate, which is what separates Secure from Level 5.

SEAS — the formula for every paragraph:

  • S — State what you saw (specific moment, specific element)
  • E — Example with precise detail (name the actor, describe the exact choice)
  • A — Analyse the technique (WHY was it effective? What did it communicate?)
  • S — Synthesis — evaluate the overall impact on the audience (Was it successful? How did it make you feel?)

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Open with production details — Name the production, venue, date, and company. State your overall impression in one sentence: “Overall, I found this production to be [effective/powerful/thought-provoking] because…”
  2. 2
    Write 3–4 SEAS paragraphs — Each paragraph analyses a DIFFERENT element: one on acting/vocal skills, one on physical performance, one on a design element (lighting, sound, set, or costume), and optionally one on directing or overall atmosphere. Each paragraph must include a specific moment from the production.
  3. 3
    Use subject-specific terminology throughout — Vocal skills (pitch, pace, tone), physical skills (gesture, proxemics), design terms (gobo, Fresnel, cross-fade, underscoring). This is what separates Mastering from Level 5.
  4. 4
    Conclude with an overall evaluation — Briefly sum up the production’s effectiveness. Which element was most impactful? Would you recommend it? What stayed with you after leaving the theatre?

Timing

Plan
5 min Write
25 min Check
5 min

About 35 minutes total. Spend 5 minutes planning your 3–4 SEAS paragraphs (list the moments and elements you’ll analyse), 25 minutes writing, and 5 minutes checking terminology and evaluation depth.

SEAS in action

[State] One of the most powerful moments in the production was the use of lighting during the final scene. [Example] As Mickey raised the gun, a single tight profile spot with a deep red gel snapped on, isolating him in a circle of crimson light while the rest of the stage fell to near-blackout. Edward, downstage right, was lit by a cool blue wash that made him appear pale and vulnerable. [Analyse] The red light symbolised danger, violence, and the blood that connects and destroys the brothers, while the blue created a visual contrast that emphasised how different their lives have become despite their shared origin. The snap transition — rather than a slow cross-fade — mirrored the sudden, irreversible nature of the violence. [Synthesis] This was, for me, the most effective design choice in the entire production. The audience around me gasped audibly at the lighting change, and the image of Mickey bathed in red stayed with me long after the curtain fell. It transformed what could have been a melodramatic ending into something genuinely shocking and visually unforgettable.

Use these phrases to push your answer from description (Developing) into evaluation (Mastering–5):

  • “This was effective because it communicated to the audience that…”
  • “The impact on the audience was…”
  • “This choice was particularly successful in conveying…”
  • “As an audience member, I felt… which demonstrated the effectiveness of…”
  • “This contrasted with [earlier moment], which highlighted…”
  • “The most memorable aspect of the production was…”
  • “If I were to suggest one improvement, it would be…”
  • “Overall, the production succeeded in… because…”

What to Prepare Before the Exam

Your live theatre revision checklist:

  • Production name, venue, date, and company
  • 3–4 specific moments you can describe in detail
  • For each moment: which element you’ll analyse (acting, lighting, sound, set, costume)
  • Subject-specific terminology for each element
  • Your personal response — how did each moment make you feel?
  • An overall evaluation sentence ready to go

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Retelling the plot — The examiner does not want a summary of the story. They want you to analyse PERFORMANCE choices. Focus on how the story was told, not what happened.
  • ❌
    Only writing about acting — For the top marks, you must analyse design elements too. Include at least one paragraph on lighting, sound, set, or costume.
  • ❌
    No evaluation — Description without evaluation caps you at Developing. Always say how effective the choice was and why. Use the evaluation phrases above.
  • ❌
    Writing about a film — It MUST be a live theatre production. Writing about a film, NT Live screening, or YouTube recording will score zero.
  • ❌
    Vague descriptions — “The acting was really good” earns nothing. Name the actor (or character), describe the specific choice, and explain why it was effective.
