title: 40 marks — Transactional Writing
content_html:
What the Question Asks

Paper 2 Question 5 asks you to write a real-world non-fiction text — a letter, article, speech, or essay — for a specific purpose and audience. You must argue a viewpoint, persuade, inform, or advise, depending on the question. This is worth 40 marks (half the entire paper), so it deserves serious time and effort. Your writing must match the form (e.g. article = headline, subheading, paragraphs), the register (e.g. broadsheet = formal, sophisticated), and the audience (e.g. adults, newspaper readers).

Key Fact

This question is worth 40 marks — that's half of Paper 2. The marks split into 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). You need to perform well on BOTH to reach the top grades.

How Marks Are Allocated

AO5 — Content & Organisation (24 marks)

  • Sophisticated, assured writing throughout
  • Form, register, and language are precisely matched to purpose and audience
  • Compelling argument with a controlled, deliberate structure
  • Wide range of ambitious vocabulary used with precision
  • Ideas are linked seamlessly — the reader is guided through the argument
  • Communicates clearly for the stated purpose and audience
  • Form features are consistently used (e.g. headline, paragraphs, appropriate sign-off)
  • Ideas are organised logically with clear paragraphs
  • Persuasive or informative as required — tone is mostly appropriate
  • Some range of vocabulary and linguistic devices
  • Attempts to communicate with the reader
  • Some form features present but may be inconsistent
  • Tone shifts or becomes informal when it shouldn't
  • Some organisation, but paragraphing may be weak or formulaic
  • Limited range of vocabulary and persuasive techniques
  • Basic communication — reader struggles to follow the argument
  • Limited or no awareness of form, purpose, or audience
  • Little organisation; ideas may be random or repetitive
  • Simple vocabulary with no deliberate language choices

AO6 — Technical Accuracy (16 marks)

  • Top band (13–16): Extensive, accurate vocabulary; sophisticated punctuation (semicolons, colons, dashes, parentheses used correctly); sentences deliberately varied for effect; spelling consistently accurate, including ambitious words.
  • Upper-mid band (9–12): Accurate writing with varied punctuation; mostly secure spelling; sentences show some variety in structure and length.
  • Lower-mid band (5–8): Generally accurate with some punctuation variety; some spelling errors on more complex words; sentence structures mostly simple or compound.
  • Lower band (1–4): Mostly accurate simple sentences; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation, or grammar; limited sentence variety.
Key Fact

(technical accuracy) is worth 16 marks — that's 40% of this question. Spelling, punctuation, grammar, and sentence variety are not an afterthought. They are nearly half the battle.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Identify RALF (2 minutes). Before you write a single word, circle or underline the Register (formal? informal?), Audience (who are you writing to?), Language (argue? persuade? advise?), and Form (article? letter? speech? essay?). Write these at the top of your plan. Every decision you make should flow from these four things. For the example question: Register = formal; Audience = broadsheet newspaper readers (educated adults); Language = argue; Form = newspaper article.
  2. Plan your argument (3 minutes). Write a quick bullet-point plan with 4–5 paragraph ideas. Each paragraph should make one clear point. Include at least one counterargument paragraph — this is what separates Secure from Mastering. Decide on your opening hook and your closing line now. A plan prevents repetition and keeps your structure tight.
  3. Write a compelling opening (5 minutes). Your first paragraph must grab the reader and establish your voice. Do not start with "I think…" or "In this article I will…". Instead, open with a striking image, a provocative statement, a statistic, or a direct address to the reader. Establish your register immediately — if it's a broadsheet article, sound like a broadsheet columnist from sentence one.
  4. Develop your argument in structured paragraphs (25 minutes). Each paragraph should contain: a clear topic sentence, development or evidence, and a deliberate language choice (rhetorical question, list of three, emotive language, an analogy). Vary your paragraph lengths — a short, punchy paragraph between two longer ones creates emphasis. Include at least one counterargument that you then dismantle. Use discourse markers to guide the reader ("However", "What this fails to acknowledge", "The real question is").
  5. Write a powerful conclusion (5 minutes). Do not just repeat your introduction. Your conclusion should feel like an arrival, not a summary. End with a call to action, a thought-provoking question, or a line that echoes your opening. The examiner reads your first and last paragraphs most attentively — make both count.
  6. Proofread for (5 minutes). Read your work back slowly. Check for: comma splices (two sentences joined by a comma — fix with a full stop or semicolon), missing apostrophes, spelling errors on common words (definitely, separate, government, their/there/they're), and any sentences that run on too long. If every sentence starts the same way, rewrite one or two. This step is worth up to 16 marks — do not skip it.

Timing

Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes. Section A (reading questions 1–4) should take about 55–60 minutes. That leaves 45–50 minutes for Question 5. Here's how to spend them:

  • 2 minutes: Identify RALF — form, purpose, audience, register
  • 3 minutes: Plan your argument (bullet points, 4–5 paragraph ideas, counterargument)
  • 35–40 minutes: Write your response (aim for 450–600 words — quality over quantity)
  • 5 minutes: Proofread — this is where you pick up easy AO6 marks
Key Fact

Students who skip planning almost always repeat themselves, lose track of their argument, or forget to include a counterargument. A 3-minute plan saves you marks. Students who skip proofreading throw away easy AO6 marks. A 5-minute check catches the errors examiners are trained to look for.

Model Answer — Strong (Mastering)

THE PRESSURE PARADOX

We are raising the most scrutinised generation in human history. Before today's fifteen-year-old has finished breakfast, she has checked her phone seventeen times, absorbed a dozen curated versions of other people's lives, and received implicit notice of everything she is not. And then we ask her to sit quietly in an exam hall and prove herself against a mark scheme.

The argument that schools should do more for mental health is not merely a charitable impulse — it is an economic one. A student in crisis cannot learn. A teacher managing three students in crisis cannot teach. The externalities of failing to act fall, inevitably, on the very institutions we are asking to ignore the problem.

Critics of intervention — and they exist — will argue that resilience is built through adversity, that softening school environments produces graduates ill-equipped for the world. This is not wrong. But it mistakes the nature of what young people face. The pressures of social media, housing insecurity, and a climate crisis they did not create are not the character-building rigours of previous generations. They are structural problems, not personal weaknesses. Schools cannot solve them. But they can refuse to compound them.

The question is not whether schools should support students' mental health. The question is whether we have the honesty to admit that they already do — badly, reactively, and without adequate resources — and whether we are willing to change that.

Why this answer is strong:

  • Form: It reads like a real broadsheet article — headline, columnist's tone, no "Dear Sir/Madam" or "In conclusion". The form is embedded, not bolted on.
  • Opening hook: The first paragraph creates a vivid, specific image of a teenager's morning. It doesn't start with "I think" — it draws the reader in.
  • Counterargument: Paragraph 3 addresses the opposition view ("Critics of intervention… will argue…") and dismantles it with a distinction between structural problems and personal weakness. This is what examiners mean by "compelling" — it doesn't just disagree, it reframes.
  • Register: Formal, authoritative, and controlled throughout. Words like "externalities", "scrutinised", and "compound" show precise vocabulary without being showy.
  • Structure: Each paragraph does one job. The argument builds logically: problem → why it matters → counterargument → redefinition of the real question.
  • Conclusion: Ends by reframing the debate — "The question is not whether… The question is whether…" — which is more powerful than simply restating the argument.
  • Technical accuracy (AO6): Sentences are varied — long and complex, then short and punchy ("Schools cannot solve them. But they can refuse to compound them."). Dashes, colons, and commas are used correctly. Spelling is flawless. This alone would score highly on AO6.

Weak Answer — Common Mistakes

I think schools should do more to help students with their mental health. Lots of young people today are stressed because of exams and social media. Schools should have counsellors and mental health days. This would help students feel better. Some people might say that young people need to be resilient, but I disagree. Young people have more pressure than before and schools need to help. In conclusion, schools should do more because mental health is important.

What goes wrong and why:

  • ❌ No form features at all. The question asks for a newspaper article, but this has no headline, no subheading, and reads like a short paragraph from a school exercise. The examiner cannot award marks for form if the form is absent.
  • ❌ Opens with "I think". This immediately signals a personal opinion essay, not a broadsheet article. It also sets a flat, informal register from the start — and the writing never recovers from it.
  • ❌ Vague, undeveloped points. "Lots of young people today are stressed because of exams and social media" — this says nothing specific. Compare the strong answer's image of a fifteen-year-old checking her phone seventeen times before breakfast. Specificity is what makes writing compelling.
  • ❌ Counterargument is dismissed, not engaged with. "Some people might say… but I disagree" is a Developing move. The student mentions resilience but doesn't explain why the counterargument is wrong — they just reject it. The strong answer distinguishes between types of adversity. That's the difference.
  • ❌ "In conclusion" + repetition. The final sentence simply repeats the opening point. There's

title: 16 marks — Comparison
content_html:
Paper 2 Q4: Comparison (16 marks)

This is the biggest reading question on either paper. You must compare how two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about a given theme. You need to analyse the methods each writer uses (language, structure, tone) and explain how these methods reveal their attitudes. Crucially, you must compare — weaving both sources together throughout your answer, not writing about one and then the other.

Key Fact

This question is worth 16 marks — the most marks of any reading question on Paper 2. It tests your ability to compare, not just describe. Every paragraph you write should reference both sources.

How Marks Are Allocated

The examiner marks your answer against four levels. Read these carefully — they tell you exactly what separates a good answer from a great one.

  • Identifies simple differences or similarities between the writers' attitudes
  • Little or no analysis of the methods writers use
  • May deal with one source much more than the other
  • Evidence is limited or not well chosen

Typical student at this level: "Source A likes the city and Source B doesn't. Source A uses a metaphor." This just labels — it doesn't analyse or genuinely compare.

  • Comments on some differences and similarities in writers' perspectives
  • Some reference to methods, but analysis may be thin or undeveloped
  • Comparison is attempted but may not be sustained — might drift into writing about each source separately
  • Uses some relevant evidence

Typical student at this level: Makes valid points about attitude and quotes from both sources, but doesn't fully explain how language creates meaning. Comparison fades in and out.

  • Clear understanding of both writers' different perspectives
  • Analyses the methods of both writers in a detailed way
  • Comparison is sustained — both sources are discussed together, not in isolation
  • Well-chosen evidence supports each point

Typical student at this level: Consistently compares, picks precise quotes, and explains how specific word choices or structural decisions convey each writer's attitude. This is a solid, well-structured answer.

  • Nuanced, sophisticated understanding of both writers' perspectives — picks up on subtlety, ambiguity, or complexity in their attitudes
  • Analysis of methods is insightful and precise — explains exactly how and why a technique creates meaning
  • Comparison is convincing throughout — sources are interwoven seamlessly
  • Evidence is precisely selected and embedded fluently into sentences

Typical student at this level: Writes with authority and originality. Doesn't just say what each writer thinks — explores the complexity of their views, makes surprising connections, and shows how form and language enact meaning rather than just describing it.

Step-by-Step Method

Follow these six steps every time you answer this question. Practise the method until it becomes automatic.

  1. Read the question and identify the theme. Underline the key focus — e.g. "city life", "attitudes to nature", "childhood memories". Everything you write must connect to this theme. Don't drift.
  2. Annotate both sources (3–4 minutes). Go through each source and underline key quotes where the writer's perspective is clear. In the margin, jot a one-word note: what attitude does this reveal? Look for language techniques (metaphor, word choice, imagery, tone) and structural choices (how the piece opens, shifts, or ends).
  3. Plan 4–5 comparative points (2–3 minutes). Pair your annotations. For each point, you need: one quote/method from Source A, one quote/method from Source B, and a clear statement of how their perspectives differ or align. Write these as brief bullet points. A strong plan might look like:
    • Point 1: Both writers open differently — A moves towards city, B retreats from it → opposite attitudes to engagement
    • Point 2: A's metaphor "pulsed" = city as alive; B's verb "crowded out" = city as threatening
    • Point 3: A's listing enacts energy; B's fragmented syntax enacts disorientation
    • Point 4: A's overall tone is wonder; B's overall tone is anxiety
  4. Write a comparative opening sentence. Start with an overarching comparison that frames both writers' perspectives. For example: "Both writers respond to the intensity of the city, but while Source A's writer is energised by it, Source B's writer is diminished." This immediately signals to the examiner that you are comparing.
  5. Write 4–5 comparative paragraphs (15–18 minutes). Each paragraph should follow this pattern:
    • Comparative topic sentence — what both writers do or how they differ
    • Source A evidence + method analysis — quote, name the technique, explain how it conveys the writer's perspective
    • Connective that pivots to Source B — use "In contrast", "Conversely", "Similarly", "However", "While Source A…, Source B…"
    • Source B evidence + method analysis — quote, name the technique, explain how it conveys the writer's perspective
    • Brief evaluative comment — what does this comparison reveal about their different attitudes overall?
  6. Check your answer (1 minute). Quickly scan: have you compared in every paragraph? Have you analysed methods (not just quoted)? Have you addressed the specific theme the question asks about? If any paragraph only discusses one source, add a comparison sentence.
Key Fact

The golden rule: Never write a paragraph about only one source. Every paragraph must reference both. If you find yourself writing half a page on Source A alone, stop and bring in Source B immediately.

Timing

Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes total. The reading section should take approximately 1 hour, and Q4 is worth the most marks within it.

  • Spend 20–25 minutes on Q4. This is not a question to rush. It's worth 16 marks — more than Q2 and Q3 combined on this paper.
  • Planning: 5–7 minutes. Annotate both sources and plan your comparative points. This is not wasted time. A planned answer with four strong paragraphs will outscore a rambling unplanned answer with six weak ones.
  • Writing: 13–16 minutes. Aim for 4–5 developed comparative paragraphs. Quality over quantity — three perceptive paragraphs beat five superficial ones.
  • Checking: 1–2 minutes. Make sure every paragraph compares and every quote is followed by analysis of method.

If you're running out of time, write fewer paragraphs but make them count. One excellent comparative paragraph with precise evidence and method analysis is worth more than three paragraphs of vague description.

Model Answer

Question: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about city life. [16 marks]

Both writers engage with the energy of the city, but their perspectives on whether this energy is exhilarating or exhausting reveal fundamentally opposed attitudes to urban existence.

Source A's writer presents the city as a living, breathing force of opportunity. The metaphor 'the city pulsed' gives London a heartbeat — an organism rather than a space — suggesting the writer feels the city is alive with potential. This stands in sharp contrast to Source B, where the city is rendered through the verb 'crowded out', implying it displaces rather than enables the writer's sense of self. Where Source A's metaphor animates the city, Source B's verb choice positions the city as an aggressor — the writer is acted upon, not empowered.

The structural choices reinforce this divergence in perspective. Source A opens with the writer moving towards the city, actively seeking it; Source B opens with retreat, the writer already overwhelmed. This contrast in direction mirrors the contrast in attitude: one writer pursues the city, the other flees it. The way each text begins, then, immediately establishes the writer's relationship to urban space — one of desire versus one of displacement.

Source A uses an accelerating, list-heavy style — 'the sirens, the voices, the wheels, the light' — which enacts the city's vitality through form. The piling up of nouns mimics sensory overload, but the tone remains breathless and excited, suggesting the writer is thrilled rather than threatened by this multiplicity. Source B's syntax, by contrast, is fragmented and halting, mimicking the disorientation the writer experiences. Where Source A's form embodies enthusiasm, Source B's form embodies unease — both writers use the shape of their prose to make the reader feel their attitude, not just understand it.

Ultimately, both writers acknowledge the city's overwhelming sensory power, but they diverge sharply in how they interpret it. Source A reads urban intensity as a sign of life and possibility; Source B reads the same intensity as a threat to individuality and peace. This is not simply a difference in opinion — it is a difference in the writers' fundamental relationship to belonging, with Source A seeking connection in the crowd and Source B seeking escape from it.

Why this answer scores highly:

  • Comparison is constant. Every single paragraph discusses both sources. Connectives like "in sharp contrast", "by contrast", and "where Source A… Source B…" weave the sources together.
  • Methods are analysed, not just named. The answer doesn't just say "metaphor" — it explains what the metaphor does and how it reveals the writer's perspective.
  • It analyses structure as well as language. The paragraph on openings (direction of movement) shows the student can discuss structural choices — this is often overlooked.
  • The analysis is perceptive. Phrases like "an organism rather than a space" and "the writer is acted upon, not empowered" show genuine interpretive insight, not just technique-spotting.
  • It addresses the question's focus throughout. Every point connects back to "perspectives and feelings about city life" — there is no drift.
  • The final paragraph synthesises. It doesn't just summarise — it offers a deeper interpretation of what the comparison reveals about each writer's worldview.

Weak Answer

Question: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about city life. [16 marks]

Source A likes the city and Source B doesn't. ❌ This is a bare assertion with no evidence or method. It tells us the attitude but not how the writer conveys it.

Source A says the city 'pulsed' which is a metaphor. ❌ The technique is named, but there is no analysis of what the metaphor does or how it reveals the writer's perspective. This is "feature-spotting".

Source B says it was 'crowded out'. ❌ A quote is used, but there is no analysis and no comparison to Source A. This paragraph only discusses one source.

Both writers write about city life but they feel differently. ❌ This just restates the question. It adds nothing the examiner doesn't already know.

Source A is positive and Source B is negative. They both use descriptive language to show their feelings. ❌ "Descriptive language" is too vague to count as method analysis. "Positive" and "negative" are too general — what kind of

title: Exam Technique Guides
content_html:
AQA English Language (8700) is assessed through two exam papers, each lasting 1 hour 45 minutes and worth 80 marks. Together they test your ability to read critically and write effectively across fiction and non-fiction.

Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing focuses on fiction. In Section A, you read a literature extract and answer four reading questions worth 40 marks total. In Section B, you produce a piece of creative writing worth 40 marks. The reading questions move from simple retrieval (Q1, 4 marks) through language analysis (Q2, 8 marks) and structure analysis (Q3, 8 marks) to a more demanding evaluation task (Q4, 20 marks).

Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives focuses on non-fiction. Section A gives you two linked sources — one from the 19th century and one from the 20th or 21st century — and asks four reading questions worth 36 marks total. These cover retrieval (Q1, 4 marks), summary and synthesis (Q2, 8 marks), language analysis on one source (Q3, 12 marks) and a comparison of viewpoints across both sources (Q4, 16 marks). Section B asks you to write a transactional piece — such as an article, speech or letter — worth 40 marks.

Both writing tasks are marked out of 40, split between content and organisation (24 marks) and technical accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar (16 marks). This means that across the two papers, 80 out of 160 marks — exactly half — come from writing. Getting your exam technique right on every question type is essential. Use the guides below to learn exactly what each question demands, how to structure your answer and where the marks are won and lost.

4 marks

Retrieval

Paper 1 Q1 & Paper 2 Q1. Identify and list specific pieces of information from a defined section of the text. Straightforward marks that reward careful reading and precise selection — no analysis needed.
8 marks

Language Analysis

Paper 1 Q2 & Paper 2 Q3. Analyse how the writer uses language to achieve effects. Select specific words and phrases, identify techniques and explain in detail what they suggest, imply or make the reader feel.
8 marks

Structure Analysis

Paper 1 Q3 only. Analyse how the writer structures the whole text to interest the reader. Consider openings, shifts in focus, perspective changes, pace and how the ending connects back to the beginning.
8 marks

Summary

Paper 2 Q2 only. Summarise the differences or similarities between two non-fiction sources on a given topic. Use evidence from both texts and make clear, concise inferences rather than simply copying quotations.
16 marks

Comparison

Paper 2 Q4 only. Compare how two writers convey their different viewpoints and perspectives. Analyse the methods each writer uses — language, tone, structure, rhetoric — and draw out clear points of comparison throughout.
20 marks

Evaluation

Paper 1 Q4 only. Critically evaluate a statement about the text, exploring the extent to which you agree. Select evidence, analyse the writer's methods and develop a personal, well-supported critical response.
40 marks

Creative Writing

Paper 1 Q5. Write a creative piece — a description or narrative — inspired by a visual prompt or scenario. Marked for content and organisation (24 marks) and technical accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar (16 marks).
40 marks

Transactional Writing

Paper 2 Q5. Write to present a viewpoint — as an article, letter, speech or essay. Marked for content and organisation (24 marks) and technical accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar (16 marks). Persuade, argue or inform with flair.

title: Exam Technique
content_html:
Exam Technique

Step-by-step guides for every Food Preparation and Nutrition question type. Learn the formula, study a model answer, and avoid the common mistakes that cost marks.

Food Preparation and Nutrition (8585)

1 mark

"Define…" / "What is meant by…"

A one-sentence definition of a food science term or process. Precise language wins the mark.

 2 marks

"Name…" / "Identify…"

Name two specific items — a nutrient, ingredient, or function. No explanation needed; accuracy is everything.

 4 marks

"Explain…" (4 marks)

Give two developed points. Each point must link a cause to a food science effect — statement + reason.

 6 marks

"Explain…" / "Discuss…" (6 marks)

A longer explanation requiring three well-developed points covering a food science concept in depth.

 8 marks (QWC)

"Discuss…" / "Evaluate…" (8 marks)

The highest-value question. Quality of Written Communication assessed. Consider multiple factors, weigh them up, and reach a supported conclusion.

title: "Define…" / "What is meant by…" (1 mark)
content_html:
1 mark

"Define…" / "What is meant by…"

Used in: Section A & Section B

What the Examiner Wants

This is the quickest question on the paper. The examiner wants one clear, accurate sentence that shows you know what a food science term means. No examples, no explanation — just the definition.

Marking

What You Need
1A clear, accurate definition that correctly explains the term
Vague, circular, or incorrect definition

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the term precisely — Read carefully. "Denaturation" and "coagulation" are different processes. Make sure you define the right one.
  2. 2
    Write one accurate sentence — Use correct food science language. Aim for 10–20 words. The sentence must state what the term means, not just what it involves.
  3. 3
    Move on immediately — This is worth 1 mark. Spend no more than one minute. Do not add examples or extra detail.

Timing

Define — 1 min

One minute maximum. Write your definition and move straight to the next question.

Standard definition

"[Term] is [what it means]."

"[Term] refers to [what it means / what it does]."

Process-type term

"[Term] is the process by which [what happens]."

Define the term 'denaturation'. [1 mark]

Full mark

Denaturation is the process by which heat or acid causes a protein's structure to permanently unfold and change shape.

Examiner: 1/1 — clear, accurate, uses correct food science language.

What is meant by the term 'gelatinisation'? [1 mark]

Full mark

Gelatinisation is the process by which starch granules absorb water, swell, and burst when heated, thickening a liquid.

Examiner: 1/1

Define the term 'emulsification'. [1 mark]

0 marks — too vague

It is when you mix oil and water together.

Full mark

Emulsification is the process by which an emulsifier, such as lecithin in egg yolk, keeps oil and water mixed together in a stable suspension.

Examiner: "Mix oil and water" is too vague — you must explain the role of the emulsifier to show real understanding.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Circular definitions — "Gelatinisation is when gelatine forms" does not explain the process. Always say what happens and why.
  • ❌
    Confusing related terms — Denaturation (protein shape changes) and coagulation (denatured proteins bond together) are different. Know the distinction.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — One precise sentence earns full marks. Don't waste time writing a paragraph for a 1-mark question.
← Discuss (8 marks) Name / Identify (2 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
1 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the term
  2. Write one accurate sentence
  3. Move on

title: "Name…" / "Identify…" (2 marks)
content_html:
2 marks

"Name…" / "Identify…"

Used in: Section A & Section B

What the Examiner Wants

This question asks you to name or identify two specific items — nutrients, ingredients, functions, or food science processes. No explanation is required. Accuracy is everything: the right word earns the mark, the wrong word earns nothing.

Marking

What You Need
2Two correct, distinct items clearly identified
1One correct item
No correct items, or items are too vague / duplicated

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question category carefully — "Name two minerals" and "Name two vitamins" need completely different answers. Do not drift between categories.
  2. 2
    Write two distinct, specific answers — Be precise. "Vitamin C" not just "vitamins." "Calcium" not just "minerals." Use the correct scientific name.
  3. 3
    Check they are different — "Iron and iron-rich foods" is one answer written twice. You must give two genuinely separate items.

Timing

Name / Identify — 2 min

Two minutes maximum. Two short answers — no more. Move on quickly.

Naming two items

"1. [Specific item 1]"

"2. [Specific item 2]"

If the question says "state"

"[Item 1] and [Item 2]"

Name two fat-soluble vitamins. [2 marks]

Full marks

1. Vitamin A    2. Vitamin D

Examiner: 2/2 — both are correct fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K are all accepted).

Identify two high biological value (HBV) protein sources. [2 marks]

Full marks

1. Eggs    2. Fish

Examiner: 2/2 — HBV sources contain all essential amino acids. Meat, dairy, soya are also accepted.

Name two raising agents used in baking. [2 marks]

1 mark — too imprecise for second answer

1. Baking powder    2. Air

Full marks

1. Baking powder    2. Yeast

Examiner: "Air" is accepted by AQA as a raising agent (mechanical aeration). However, "yeast" or "bicarbonate of soda" are safer, more specific answers. Steam is also accepted.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Being too broad — "Vitamins" is not an answer to "name two vitamins." Give the specific name: Vitamin C, Vitamin B12, etc.
  • ❌
    Repeating the same answer twice — "Chicken and chicken breast" is one item, not two. Make sure your two answers are genuinely different.
  • ❌
    Mixing up HBV and LBV proteins — HBV (high biological value) = contains all essential amino acids (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, soya). LBV = missing one or more (pulses, nuts, cereals). Know the difference.
← Define (1 mark) Explain (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
2 min total

Formula

  1. Read the category
  2. Write two specific answers
  3. Check they are distinct

title: "Explain…" (4 marks)
content_html:
4 marks

"Explain…" (4 marks)

Used in: Section A & Section B

What the Examiner Wants

This question requires two developed points, each linking a food science cause to its effect. You cannot just state a fact — you must explain why or how. The mark schemes awards one mark for each correct statement and one mark for each correct development.

Marking

What You Need
4Two correct statements, each with a clear, accurate development (cause + effect)
3Two statements but only one developed, or one statement with full development plus an undeveloped point
2Two correct statements with no development, or one fully developed point
1One correct statement with no development
No relevant points

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Make your first point (P) — State a relevant food science fact directly answering the question. Be specific.
  2. 2
    Develop it (E) — Explain why or how. Link cause to effect. Use connective phrases: "because," "this means that," "as a result," "which causes."
  3. 3
    Make your second point (P) — A different, distinct reason or factor. Do not repeat the first point in different words.
  4. 4
    Develop it (E) — Explain this second point with a cause-effect chain. Aim for one or two clear sentences of development.

Timing

Plan
1 min Write
3–4 min

About five minutes. Spend one minute planning two points, then write two P-E pairs. Do not write an introduction or conclusion for a 4-mark question.

Point + Explain structure (P-E × 2)

"[Food science point 1]. This is because / This means that [development — cause or effect]."

"[Food science point 2]. As a result / This causes [development — cause or effect]."

Explain two reasons why eggs are important in cake making. [4 marks]

4/4

Point 1: Eggs act as an emulsifier in cake batter. This is because the lecithin in egg yolk has hydrophilic and hydrophobic properties, allowing it to bind the water and fat together, creating a smooth, stable batter that does not separate.

Point 2: Eggs also act as a raising agent through aeration. When eggs are whisked, air bubbles are trapped in the mixture; during baking, these bubbles expand with heat, causing the cake to rise and creating a light texture.

Examiner: 4/4 — Each point is clearly stated (P) and then fully developed with a food science explanation (E). The candidate goes beyond simply identifying the function to explaining the mechanism.

Explain two effects of heat on protein. [4 marks]

2 marks — statements only, no development

Heat causes denaturation. Heat also causes coagulation.

Full marks

Point 1: Heat causes denaturation of protein. This means the heat energy breaks the bonds that hold the protein's three-dimensional structure in shape, causing it to unfold and change permanently — for example, egg white turning from transparent to white when cooked.

Point 2: Continued heat causes coagulation. The denatured protein chains bond together and form a solid network, which is why a fried egg white sets firm and cannot be reversed to its liquid state.

Examiner: The weak answer names the processes correctly but scores only 2 marks because there is no development. Always explain the mechanism — what actually happens and why.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Listing without explaining — "Eggs add colour and flavour and structure" is three statements with no development. Each point must be followed by a "because" or "this means that" sentence.
  • ❌
    Writing the same point twice — "Eggs make cakes light" and "eggs add air" are very similar. The examiner will only credit distinct points. Plan first to ensure your two points are genuinely different.
  • ❌
    Writing an introduction — "In this answer I will explain two reasons why…" wastes time. Dive straight into Point 1.
← Name / Identify (2 marks) Explain (6 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

P-E × 2 Formula

  1. Point 1 (food science fact)
  2. Explain 1 (because / this means)
  3. Point 2 (different fact)
  4. Explain 2 (because / this causes)

title: "Explain…" / "Discuss…" (6 marks)
content_html:
6 marks

"Explain…" / "Discuss…" (6 marks)

Used in: Section A & Section B

What the Examiner Wants

A 6-mark question requires three well-developed points. It may be phrased as "explain," "describe and explain," or "discuss." The examiner is looking for a thorough response that covers the topic in breadth and depth, using accurate food science terminology throughout. Some 6-mark questions are level-marked (holistic), so a well-structured response with clear language gains more marks.

Mark Band Descriptors (level-marked)

BandWhat You Need
Band 3Detailed, accurate explanation covering multiple relevant aspects with correct terminology; response is logical and coherent
Band 2Some accurate explanation but lacks detail or range; terminology used but not always correctly
Band 1Basic points made with limited explanation; terminology limited or absent
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan three distinct points — Take 1–2 minutes to identify three different food science aspects relevant to the question. Write them as bullet points before you start writing.
  2. 2
    Write Point 1 (P + E + E) — State the point, explain why/how, then develop further with a specific example or food science detail. Use correct terminology.
  3. 3
    Write Point 2 (P + E + E) — A clearly different point with the same depth of explanation. Avoid repeating the first point reworded.
  4. 4
    Write Point 3 (P + E + E) — The third and final point, again with explanation and specific food science detail.
  5. 5
    Check your terminology — Re-read and ensure you have used the correct scientific vocabulary (e.g., "gelatinisation," "coagulation," "Maillard reaction," "emulsification").

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
6 min Check
2 min

About ten minutes. Planning is essential — students who plan three points before writing almost always score in Band 2 or 3.

P-E-E × 3 structure

"[Point 1]. This is because [explanation]. For example / In addition, [further development]."

"[Point 2]. This means that [explanation]. [Specific food science detail or example]."

"[Point 3]. As a result, [explanation]. [Specific food science detail or example]."

Explain the functional properties of fat in pastry making. [6 marks]

Band 3 — 5–6 marks

Fat acts as a shortening agent in shortcrust pastry. The fat coats the flour particles and prevents the gluten strands from joining together during mixing. This creates a crumbly, tender texture — hence the name "shortcrust." Without sufficient fat, the pastry would be tough and chewy because the gluten would overdevelop.

Fat also contributes to the colour and flavour of pastry. During baking, fat helps to conduct heat evenly across the pastry surface. The Maillard reaction between proteins and sugars — enhanced by fat — produces the golden-brown colour and rich, savoury flavour that makes well-made pastry appealing.

The type of fat affects the texture of the final product. Butter contains approximately 80% fat and 20% water; when heated, the water turns to steam, which helps to create layers and adds a rich flavour. Lard, which is almost 100% fat with no water, produces a shorter, more crumbly texture. The choice of fat is therefore a deliberate decision to control the final outcome of the pastry.

Examiner: Band 3, 6/6 — Three distinct functional properties explained in depth: shortening, colour/Maillard reaction, and the comparison of fat types. Correct food science terminology used throughout (gluten, Maillard reaction, shortening). Each point is developed well beyond a simple statement.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only making two points — For 6 marks you need three developed points. Two points with excellent explanation might reach Mid band (4 marks) at best. Always plan three before you start.
  • ❌
    No food science terminology — Answers written in everyday language ("fat makes pastry taste nicer") score Band 1. Use the correct terms: shortening, Maillard reaction, gelatinisation, coagulation, emulsification.
  • ❌
    Repeating a point in different words — "Fat stops gluten forming" and "fat prevents the pastry being tough" are the same point. Plan in advance to ensure your three points are genuinely distinct.
← Explain (4 marks) Discuss (8 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10 min total

P-E-E × 3 Formula

  1. Plan 3 distinct points
  2. Point + explain + develop (×3)
  3. Use food science terminology
  4. Check for repetition

title: "Discuss…" / "Evaluate…" (8 marks, QWC)
content_html:
8 marks (QWC)

"Discuss…" / "Evaluate…" (8 marks)

Used in: Section B

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-value question on the paper. Quality of Written Communication (QWC) is assessed, which means your spelling, punctuation, and grammar matter alongside your food science knowledge. The examiner wants a balanced, well-structured response that:

  • Covers the topic from multiple angles
  • Considers advantages AND disadvantages, or multiple factors
  • Uses accurate food science terminology consistently
  • Reaches a supported conclusion

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureDetailed, balanced discussion of multiple factors with accurate terminology; clear, logical structure; relevant conclusion supported by evidence
DevelopingSome discussion of more than one aspect but lacking balance or depth; terminology used but not always correctly; limited conclusion
EmergingBasic points with little discussion; one-sided or descriptive; limited use of terminology
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan before you write (2–3 minutes) — Identify three to four factors or viewpoints relevant to the question. Note positives and negatives for each where relevant. This planning stage separates Developing from Secure responses.
  2. 2
    Write a brief introduction — One or two sentences that show you understand the topic and the scope of your answer. Do not spend more than 30 seconds on this.
  3. 3
    Develop each factor in depth (P-E-E structure) — For each point: state it, explain the food science reason, then develop with a specific example or counterpoint. Use "However," "On the other hand," and "Furthermore" to create a balanced discussion.
  4. 4
    Write a conclusion — Reach a judgement. Which factor is most significant? Which approach is most suitable given the context? Your conclusion must be supported by evidence from your answer — not an opinion pulled from nowhere.
  5. 5
    Check QWC — Spend the final two minutes checking spelling (especially food science terms: gelatinisation, coagulation, emulsification), punctuation, and sentence structure.

Timing

Plan
3 min Write
10 min QWC check
2 min

About fifteen minutes. This question is worth nearly a fifth of your total marks — give it the time it deserves. Planning is not optional at this level.

Adding points

"Furthermore… / In addition… / A second factor to consider is…"

Contrasting / balance

"However… / On the other hand… / Despite this…"

Conclusion starters

"Overall, the most significant factor is… because…"

"In conclusion, [approach/method] is most suitable because… although it is important to consider…"

Discuss the factors a manufacturer should consider when modifying a traditional cheesecake recipe to meet the needs of different dietary groups. [8 marks]

Secure — 7–8 marks

When modifying a cheesecake recipe, a manufacturer must consider a range of dietary needs, including those following vegan, lactose-free, and gluten-free diets, as well as consumers reducing their sugar or fat intake for health reasons.

For vegan consumers, the manufacturer would need to replace all animal-derived ingredients. Full-fat cream cheese could be substituted with cashew cream or coconut cream, which set in a similar way due to their high fat content. Eggs, which act as a setting agent through coagulation, could be replaced with aquafaba or a commercial vegan setting agent. However, these substitutes may alter the texture and flavour profile of the cheesecake, so the manufacturer would need to conduct extensive product testing to ensure the modified version meets consumer expectations.

For lactose-intolerant consumers, lactose-free dairy alternatives such as lactose-free cream cheese could be used. These are produced using lactase enzyme to break down lactose into glucose and galactose, so the product retains a similar taste and texture to regular cream cheese without causing digestive discomfort. This modification is simpler than a full vegan adaptation and is less likely to alter the sensory properties of the product.

For consumers following a gluten-free diet, the biscuit base — typically made from wheat-based digestive biscuits — would need to be replaced with gluten-free alternatives such as oat-based biscuits (certified gluten-free) or ground almonds. The manufacturer must also ensure there is no cross-contamination during production, as even trace amounts of gluten can cause adverse reactions in people with coeliac disease.

Overall, the most complex modification is the vegan adaptation, because it requires replacing multiple functional ingredients simultaneously and the risk of compromising texture and flavour is highest. Manufacturers should prioritise clear labelling of all allergens (required by UK food law under the 14 major allergens) to ensure consumers can make safe and informed choices.

Examiner: Secure, 8/8 — Discusses three distinct dietary groups in depth. Each modification is explained with food science reasoning (coagulation, lactase enzyme, gluten cross-contamination). Considers both the benefits and limitations of modifications. Concludes with a supported judgement. QWC: well-structured, technical vocabulary used accurately, clear and logical throughout.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    One-sided response — If the question asks you to "discuss," you must consider more than one viewpoint or factor. A response that only argues one side is capped at Emerging–2.
  • ❌
    No conclusion — A discussion without a conclusion is incomplete. Even two sentences summarising your overall judgement are better than no conclusion at all. The examiner is looking for evidence that you can weigh up the factors you've discussed.
  • ❌
    Ignoring QWC — This is the only question on the paper where spelling, punctuation, and grammar are explicitly assessed. Misspelling key terms (e.g. "gelatinsation," "coagualtion") or writing in bullet points rather than prose will cost you marks.
  • ❌
    Surface-level points — "Vegans can't eat dairy" is a fact but it's not a discussion. Explain why the ingredient is present in the original recipe, what function it performs, and what the implications of removing or replacing it are.

  2. Brief introduction
  3. P-E-E for each factor
  4. Consider multiple viewpoints
  5. Supported conclusion
  6. Check QWC (spelling, punctuation and grammar)

title: Multiple Choice (1 mark)
content_html:
1 mark

“Which one of the following…” (Multiple Choice)

Used in: Component 1 & Component 2 — All papers and sections

What the Examiner Wants

This is the simplest question on the paper. The examiner wants you to identify the single correct answer from four options. There is no partial credit and no marks deducted for wrong answers, so always choose an answer even if you are unsure. One mark is awarded for the correct option — no explanation is needed.

Marking

What You Need
1The correct option selected
0An incorrect option selected, or no answer given

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question stem carefully — Identify exactly what is being asked. Key words such as “Christian”, “Muslim”, “belief about”, or “practice of” tell you which religion and which topic to focus on.
  2. 2
    Read all four options before choosing — AQA often includes plausible distractors that are true statements but do not answer the specific question. Read A, B, C, and D fully before selecting.
  3. 3
    Eliminate the clearly wrong options — Cross out any option you know is incorrect. Even eliminating one or two options significantly improves your chances if you are unsure between the rest.
  4. 4
    Select and move on — Mark your answer clearly (circle, tick, or write the letter as instructed). This question is worth 1 mark — spend no more than 30–45 seconds on it.

Timing

Multiple Choice — 30–45 seconds

Under one minute. Never spend more than a minute on a 1-mark question — every second here is better spent on the 12-mark evaluate question.

Which one of the following best describes the Christian belief in the Trinity? [1 mark]
A — God exists as three separate beings
B — God exists as one being in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
C — God only exists as Jesus Christ
D — God changes form throughout history

Correct answer: B

B — The doctrine of the Trinity holds that there is one God in three persons. Options A and D are common misconceptions (tritheism and modalism respectively). Option C is not mainstream Christian teaching.

Examiner: 1/1

Which one of the following is the Muslim declaration of faith? [1 mark]
A — Salah
B — Zakat
C — Shahadah
D — Sawm

Correct answer: C

C — The Shahadah (“There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger”) is the declaration of faith and the First Pillar of Islam. Salah = prayer, Zakat = charity, Sawm = fasting.

Examiner: 1/1

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not reading all four options — Students often pick the first option that looks correct. AQA designs distractors that are partially true. Always read every option before deciding.
  • ❌
    Leaving it blank — There is no negative marking on AQA RS. Always guess if you are unsure — a blank earns 0, but a guess gives you a 25% chance of scoring 1.
  • ❌
    Confusing religions or practices — The question may name a specific religion. An answer that is true for Christianity is not credited if the question asks about Islam. Check the question stem carefully.

30–45 seconds

  2. Read all four options
  3. Eliminate wrong answers

title: Evaluate a Statement (12 marks)
content_html:
12 marks

“‘[Statement]’ Evaluate this statement.”

Used in: Component 1 & Component 2 — AO2 Extended Writing

What the Examiner Wants

This is the highest-value question on the paper and accounts for 50% of the total mark. The examiner wants a balanced, well-argued response that considers different viewpoints, includes religious beliefs and teachings, and reaches a justified conclusion. This question assesses AO2 — your ability to analyse and evaluate.

Two critical rules:
  1. Must include two viewpoints — A one-sided response is capped at Lower-mid band (maximum 6 marks):
  2. Must include religious beliefs and teachings — An entirely secular response is capped at Lower-mid band (maximum 6 marks):

Marking (Levels of Response)

LevelWhat You Need
4A well-argued response with two or more developed viewpoints. Includes well-developed religious arguments. Evaluates the arguments with a justified conclusion. Clear judgements on the strength of arguments.
3Two viewpoints with some development and use of religious arguments. Some evaluation but conclusion may lack full justification.
2One-sided arguments, or arguments that lack religious content. Some relevant points but limited evaluation or development.
1Simple, relevant comments with little or no reasoning. May be descriptive rather than evaluative.
0Nothing relevant or no response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the statement and plan your response (1–2 minutes) — Identify what the statement is arguing. Quickly note arguments for and against. Decide your overall conclusion before you start writing.
  2. 2
    Paragraph 1 — Arguments supporting the statement — Present arguments that agree with the statement. Include specific religious beliefs, teachings, or sources of authority. Explain why these arguments support the statement.
  3. 3
    Paragraph 2 — Arguments against the statement — Present a contrasting viewpoint. Again include religious teachings where relevant. In Component 2 Themes, non-religious views may also be included.
  4. 4
    Paragraph 3 — Conclusion with evaluation — State your overall judgement clearly. Explain why you find one side more convincing. Evaluate the strength of the arguments: use phrases like “this argument is convincing because…” or “however, this view is weaker because…”. A justified conclusion is essential for the top level.

Timing

Plan
1–2 min For
4–5 min Against
4–5 min Conclusion
3–4 min

About 15 minutes — this question is worth half the total AO2 marks. Aim for approximately 250 words across three paragraphs. Write clearly and check your spelling.

Paragraph 1 — Supporting arguments

“Some [religious believers] would agree with this statement because [reason]. [Teaching/belief] supports this because [explanation]. This argument is [strong/convincing] because [justification].”

Paragraph 2 — Opposing arguments

“However, other [religious believers / non-religious people] would disagree because [reason]. [Teaching/belief/evidence] shows that [explanation]. This is a [strong/weak] argument because [justification].”

Paragraph 3 — Justified conclusion

“In conclusion, I believe [your judgement] because [main reason]. Although [acknowledge the other side], the evidence from [source/teaching] is more convincing because [final justification].”

“All Christians should believe the Genesis creation story as the truth.” Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give developed arguments to support this statement; give developed arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. [12 marks]

Paragraph 1 — Supporting the statement

Some Christians, particularly fundamentalists, would agree with this statement because they believe the Bible is the literal word of God and therefore every part of it, including Genesis, is factually true. They argue that God created the world in six days and rested on the seventh, exactly as described, because to say otherwise would be to question God’s authority and truthfulness. This is a significant argument because if Christians accept that the Bible is divinely inspired, then rejecting parts of it could undermine the whole foundation of their faith.

Paragraph 2 — Opposing the statement

However, many liberal Christians would disagree because they believe the Genesis story should be understood as a myth or metaphor rather than a literal account. They argue that the creation story teaches important truths — that God is the creator, that the world has purpose and meaning, and that humans are special — without needing to be scientifically accurate. Many Christians today accept the theory of evolution and the Big Bang as explaining how the universe was created, while Genesis explains why. This argument is convincing because it allows Christians to reconcile their faith with modern scientific evidence.

Paragraph 3 — Justified conclusion

In conclusion, I believe that not all Christians should be required to take the Genesis creation story literally. While the fundamentalist view is sincere and has a clear theological basis, the liberal interpretation is more robust because it allows Christians to maintain their belief in God as creator while acknowledging the overwhelming scientific evidence for evolution. The most important message of Genesis — that God is the source of all life — can be upheld without reading it as a scientific textbook.

Examiner: 12/12 — Mastering. Two well-developed viewpoints, both grounded in Christian teaching, with clear evaluation of argument strength and a justified conclusion. The response weighs the evidence and explains why one position is found more convincing.

Key Differences: Component 1 vs Component 2

Component 1 (Religions): Your answer must stay focused on the religion specified in the question. Non-religious views and comparisons with other religions will not be relevant. Both viewpoints should come from within that religion (e.g. different Christian denominations).
Component 2 (Themes): Non-religious views and perspectives from different religions can be included where relevant (though are not required). You have more flexibility in the viewpoints you use.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing a one-sided answer — This is the single most costly mistake. If you only argue one side, you are capped at Lower-mid band (maximum 6/12):. Always include at least two viewpoints, even if you strongly agree with one.
  • ❌
    No religious content — An entirely secular answer with no reference to religious beliefs, teachings, or sources of authority is also capped at Developing. Always include religious arguments even when discussing ethical issues.
  • ❌
    No conclusion or a weak conclusion — “In conclusion, both sides have good points” is not a justified conclusion. You must make a clear judgement and explain why you find one side more convincing. Top-level answers evaluate the strength of arguments.
  • ❌
    Writing too little — This question is worth 12 marks and deserves about 15 minutes and approximately 250 words. A short answer with undeveloped points cannot reach the top levels. Plan your time carefully.
  • ❌
    Describing instead of evaluating — Simply listing what different people believe is not evaluation. You must explain why those arguments are strong or weak and reach a judgement. Use evaluative language: “this is convincing because…”, “this argument is weak because…”

  2. Arguments FOR + religious teaching
  3. Arguments AGAINST + religious teaching
  4. Justified conclusion with evaluation

Mastering Checklist

  • Religious beliefs/teachings included

title: “Define…” (1 mark)
content_html:
1 mark

“Define…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section A (short answer)

What the Examiner Wants

This is the quickest question on the paper. The examiner wants one clear, accurate sentence showing you understand what a business term means. No examples, no lengthy explanation — just a precise definition.

Marking

What You Need
1A clear, accurate definition that correctly explains the business term
Vague, circular, or incorrect definition

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the exact term — Read carefully. “Revenue” and “profit” are different. “Fixed cost” and “variable cost” are different. Define precisely what is asked.
  2. 2
    Write one accurate sentence — Use correct business terminology. Aim for 10–25 words. State what the term means, not what it involves or why it matters.
  3. 3
    Move on immediately — This is worth 1 mark. Spend no more than one minute. Do not write a paragraph for a 1-mark question.

Timing

Define — 1 min

One minute maximum. Write your definition and move straight to the next question.

Standard definition

“[Term] is [what it means].”

“[Term] refers to [what it means / what it measures].”

Process or relationship

“[Term] is the [process / difference / relationship] between [A] and [B].”

Define the term ‘revenue’. [1 mark]

Full mark

Revenue is the total income a business earns from selling its goods or services, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.

Examiner: 1/1 — precise, uses correct formula language.

Define the term ‘variable cost’. [1 mark]

0 marks — too vague

Variable costs are costs that change.

Full mark

Variable costs are costs that change in direct proportion to the level of output — for example, raw materials used in production.

Examiner: “Costs that change” is too vague. You must state what they change with (output / production level).

Define the term ‘market share’. [1 mark]

Full mark

Market share is the percentage of total sales in a market held by one business, expressed as a proportion of the market’s total sales value or volume.

Examiner: 1/1 — correctly identifies it as a proportion/percentage of the total market.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Circular definitions — “Profit is when you make a profit” repeats the word. Always say what it is: “Profit is revenue minus total costs.”
  • ❌
    Confusing similar terms — Revenue vs profit, fixed vs variable costs, cash flow vs profit. Know the distinctions before the exam.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — One accurate sentence earns full marks. A long paragraph wastes time and earns no extra credit.
Outline (2 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
1 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the exact term
  2. Write one accurate sentence
  3. Move on immediately

  • Discuss — 6 marks
  • Justify / Evaluate — 9 & 12 marks

title: “Outline…” (2 marks)
content_html:
2 marks

“Outline…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section A

What the Examiner Wants

An “Outline” question asks you to identify one point and give it brief context or development. Two marks means two creditworthy things: a point and its development. This is not a full explanation — keep it concise and focused.

Marking

What You Need
2Relevant point identified (1) + brief, accurate development or context (1)
1Relevant point identified with no development, or a vague developed point
No relevant point, or answer is entirely incorrect

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    State your point clearly — Identify one relevant business fact, reason, or factor that directly answers the question. Be specific.
  2. 2
    Develop it briefly — Add one sentence of context, consequence, or clarification. Use “This means that…” or “For example…” or “This is because…”
  3. 3
    Stop at 2–3 sentences — This is a 2-mark question. Do not write a full paragraph. Two well-chosen sentences are ideal.

Timing

Outline — 2–3 min

Two to three minutes. Identify, develop briefly, move on.

Point + Development

“[Business point]. This means that [consequence / how it works / example].”

Point + Example

“[Business point]. For example, [specific business scenario].”

Outline one benefit to a business of having a USP. [2 marks]

Full marks

A USP (Unique Selling Point) differentiates a business from its competitors. This means customers have a specific reason to choose that business over rivals, allowing it to charge a premium price and increase revenue.

Examiner: 2/2 — clear point (differentiation) + development (premium pricing, revenue).

Outline one impact of a rise in interest rates on a business. [2 marks]

1 mark — no development

A rise in interest rates means borrowing costs go up.

Full marks

A rise in interest rates increases the cost of borrowing for businesses. This means that businesses with existing loans face higher monthly repayments, reducing their profit and cash flow and potentially forcing them to delay investment.

Examiner: The first answer states the point but does not develop the consequence. The improved answer shows the chain of effect on profit and investment decisions.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Stopping at the point — “It helps the business save money” earns 1 mark at most. Always add a development sentence.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — An “Outline” is not an “Explain.” Two focused sentences score full marks; a page of writing does not earn more.
  • ❌
    Giving two separate undeveloped points — This question asks for one point, developed. Two unconnected points without development may only earn 1 mark total.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
2–3 min total

Formula

  1. State the point clearly
  2. Develop briefly (1 sentence)
  3. Stop — don’t over-write

title: “Explain…” (3 marks)
content_html:
3 marks

“Explain…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section A & B

What the Examiner Wants

A 3-mark “Explain” question asks you to make one business point and develop it thoroughly — explaining the cause, the effect, and the context. The mark schemes typically awards: 1 mark for the relevant point, 1 mark for development (why/how), and 1 mark for a further development or application to the scenario.

Marking

What You Need
3Clear point (1) + development explaining cause or effect (1) + further development or application to context (1)
2Point with one development but no further depth
1Relevant point only, with no real development
No relevant points

Step-by-Step Formula: P → E → E

  1. 1
    Point (P) — State one relevant business factor, reason, or concept that directly answers the question. Be specific and use business terminology.
  2. 2
    Explain (E) — Explain why or how using a connector: “This is because…” / “This means that…” / “As a result…”
  3. 3
    Extend (E) — Push the explanation further: link to the scenario, add a specific example, or show a knock-on consequence. “This would result in…” / “In the context of [business name]…”

Timing

Explain — 4–5 min

Four to five minutes. A well-constructed paragraph earns full marks.

P → E → E Chain

“[Business point / factor]. This is because [reason / mechanism]. As a result, [consequence / application to context].”

Explain one reason why a business might use social media marketing. [3 marks]

Full marks

Social media marketing allows a business to reach a large audience at a low cost. This is because platforms like Instagram and TikTok enable targeted advertising to specific demographics without requiring a large budget. As a result, a small business can compete with larger rivals, increasing brand awareness and potentially driving higher sales without significantly increasing costs.

Examiner: 3/3 — clear point, developed cause (low cost, targeted), further development (competitive advantage, sales impact).

Explain one way a business could improve its cash flow. [3 marks]

1 mark — point only

The business could ask customers to pay quicker.

Full marks

The business could reduce its debtor days by offering customers an early payment discount. This means cash comes into the business sooner, reducing the gap between money going out (costs) and money coming in (revenue). As a result, the business is less likely to face a cash flow crisis and may not need to rely on expensive short-term borrowing such as an overdraft.

Examiner: The weak answer states the point but gives no mechanism or consequence. The improved version explains how and why it works, and links to the knock-on effect on borrowing.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Stopping at one sentence — “It increases profit” earns 1 mark. You need two more steps in the chain to reach 3 marks.
  • ❌
    Making two separate points — This wastes time. Develop one point fully rather than listing two shallow points.
  • ❌
    Ignoring the scenario — If the question gives a business context, use it. Referring to the specific business can secure the third mark.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
4–5 min total

Formula: P → E → E

  1. Point — state the factor
  2. Explain why/how
  3. Extend — consequence or context

title: “Calculate…”
content_html:
Calculate

“Calculate…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — throughout both sections

What the Examiner Wants

Calculation questions test whether you can correctly apply a business formula to given data. Marks are awarded for the correct answer, but crucially: showing your working can earn you method marks even if your final answer is wrong. Always show every step.

Marking

What You Need
All marksCorrect formula used, correct substitution, correct final answer with appropriate units or % sign
Method mark(s)Correct formula or method shown even if arithmetic is wrong
No working shown and wrong answer, or completely wrong formula

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what you need to calculate — Read carefully. Underline the key figures given in the question. Note whether the answer should be in £, units, or %.
  2. 2
    Write the formula — State the formula before substituting numbers. This earns a method mark even if your arithmetic is wrong: e.g. Profit = Revenue − Total Costs.
  3. 3
    Substitute the values — Replace each variable with the numbers from the question. Write this as a separate line: e.g. Profit = £80,000 − £55,000.
  4. 4
    Calculate and state the answer clearly — Write the final answer on its own line with the correct unit: e.g. Profit = £25,000. Do not leave the examiner to search for your answer.
  5. 5
    Check it makes sense — Does the answer seem reasonable in business context? A negative profit when the business is described as successful should prompt a recheck.

Key Formulas to Know

FormulaCalculation
RevenuePrice × Quantity sold
Total costsFixed costs + Variable costs
Variable costs (total)Variable cost per unit × Quantity
Profit / LossRevenue − Total costs
Gross profitRevenue − Cost of goods sold
Net profitGross profit − Expenses
Gross profit margin (%)(Gross profit ÷ Revenue) × 100
Net profit margin (%)(Net profit ÷ Revenue) × 100
Break-even output (units)Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
Contribution per unitSelling price − Variable cost per unit
Margin of safetyActual output − Break-even output
Average rate of return (ARR %)(Average annual profit ÷ Cost of investment) × 100
Market share (%)(Business sales ÷ Total market sales) × 100
Market growth (%)((New size − Old size) ÷ Old size) × 100

Timing

Calculate — ~1 min per mark

Allow approximately one minute per mark. A 3-mark calculation should take no more than 3 minutes. Always show your working — never just write the final answer.

A bakery sells cakes for £3.50 each. Variable costs are £1.20 per cake. Fixed costs are £920 per month. Calculate the bakery’s monthly break-even output. [3 marks]

Full marks

Step 1: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit
Contribution = £3.50 − £1.20 = £2.30

Step 2: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit
Break-even = £920 ÷ £2.30 = 400 units per month

Examiner: 3/3 — formula stated, correct substitution, correct answer with units. Even if the arithmetic was slightly wrong, showing the correct formula earns method marks.

A business has total revenue of £240,000. Its cost of goods sold is £96,000 and expenses are £64,000. Calculate the net profit margin. [4 marks]

Full marks

Step 1: Gross profit = Revenue − Cost of goods sold
Gross profit = £240,000 − £96,000 = £144,000

Step 2: Net profit = Gross profit − Expenses
Net profit = £144,000 − £64,000 = £80,000

Step 3: Net profit margin = (Net profit ÷ Revenue) × 100
Net profit margin = (£80,000 ÷ £240,000) × 100 = 33.3%

Examiner: 4/4 — all steps shown clearly, correct answer with % sign.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    No working shown — If you write only the answer and it’s wrong, you score 0. Show every step so the examiner can award method marks.
  • ❌
    Forgetting units or the % sign — A percentage without the % sign, or a revenue figure without £, may lose the final mark.
  • ❌
    Using the wrong formula — Confusing gross profit margin and net profit margin is a common error. Write the formula name before you use it.
  • ❌
    Rounding too early — Keep all decimal places until the final answer. Rounding intermediate steps causes errors in the final figure.
  • ❌
    Mixing up fixed and variable costs — Fixed costs do NOT change with output. Variable costs DO. Read the question carefully before substituting.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
~1 min per mark

Always Show

  1. Formula name
  2. Substituted values
  3. Final answer + units / %

  • Explain — 3 marks
  • Discuss — 6 marks
