title: “Analyse…”
content_html:
Analyse

“Analyse…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section B

What the Examiner Wants

An “Analyse” question asks you to apply business knowledge to a scenario and explore the chain of cause and effect in depth. Unlike “Explain,” analysis requires you to go further: unpick the business impact, consider knock-on effects, and relate your thinking specifically to the context. You are not expected to reach a final evaluative judgement — that is what “Discuss,” “Justify,” and “Evaluate” ask for.

Mark Band Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
Secure7–9 (typical)Detailed analysis with well-developed chains of reasoning; clearly applied to the context; accurate business terminology throughout
DevelopingSome analysis present but chains of reasoning are incomplete or not fully applied to context
EmergingBasic points identified but little development; mainly descriptive with few analytical links
No relevant response

Note: Analyse questions appear at varying mark allocations on the Edexcel papers (typically 6–9 marks). Always check the mark total and adjust your depth accordingly.

Step-by-Step Formula: Chain Analysis

  1. 1
    Identify the key business factor — What is the specific change, decision, or trend the question is asking about? Extract the key detail from the scenario.
  2. 2
    State your first analytical point (P) — Identify the first business impact or consequence of the factor. Be precise — use business concepts such as costs, revenue, cash flow, motivation, or market share.
  3. 3
    Build the chain (E → E → E) — Develop the consequence step by step: “This would lead to… which means… because… therefore…” A strong analysis has at least three links in the chain.
  4. 4
    Apply to context — At each step, reference the specific business, product, market, or situation given in the question. Do not write generically.
  5. 5
    Second chain of analysis — Identify a second business impact and build another chain. Use “Furthermore…” or “In addition…” to introduce it.

Timing

Plan Write

Approximately 10–14 minutes depending on the mark allocation. Spend 1–2 minutes planning your chains before writing.

Chain Analysis Template

“[Factor] would cause [first impact on business]. This means that [development 1], because [reason applied to context]. As a result, [development 2 — knock-on effect], which would [further business consequence].”

“Furthermore, [second chain starting point]. This would lead to [development], meaning [final business impact].”

A sports clothing manufacturer is considering moving its production to an overseas factory in Vietnam. Analyse the impact this decision might have on the business. [9 marks]

Secure — 8/9 marks

Moving production overseas to Vietnam would significantly reduce the manufacturer’s variable costs. Labour costs in Vietnam are considerably lower than in the UK, which means the cost of producing each unit of clothing would fall. This would reduce total costs and, if the selling price remained the same, increase the profit margin on each item sold. With higher profit margins, the business could reinvest in product development or marketing, potentially growing its market share in a competitive sportswear industry.

Furthermore, lower production costs could allow the business to reduce its selling price. This would make its products more price-competitive against rival brands, potentially attracting price-sensitive customers who previously chose cheaper alternatives. An increase in sales volume would raise total revenue, further improving overall profitability.

However, there are risks to analyse. Quality control may be harder to manage with production taking place thousands of miles away. If product quality falls and customers notice defects, this could damage the brand’s reputation. Negative publicity — particularly if poor working conditions in the overseas factory are reported — could lead to a customer boycott, significantly reducing demand and harming sales revenue.

Examiner: Strong Secure — two clear chains of analysis developed with multiple links, consistently applied to context. Third paragraph adds depth by identifying a risk chain. Full marks would require slightly more precision on the third chain.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Stopping too soon — “Costs would fall, so profits would rise” is a two-link chain. Push to three or four links: what happens next? What does that mean for the business?
  • ❌
    Being descriptive, not analytical — Describing what the business is doing is not analysis. Analysis explores why and what happens as a result.
  • ❌
    Ignoring the scenario — Generic points score lower. Always anchor your chains to the specific business type, size, or market mentioned in the question.
  • ❌
    Trying to evaluate — An Analyse question does not require a final judgement or conclusion. Save that for Discuss, Justify, and Evaluate questions.
← Justify / Evaluate Calculate →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10–14 min total

Chain Formula

  1. Identify the factor
  2. State first impact
  3. Build chain (E → E → E)
  4. Apply to context at each step
  5. Add second chain

Other Guides

  • Define — 1 mark
  • Outline — 2 marks
  • Explain — 3 marks
  • Discuss — 6 marks
  • Justify / Evaluate — 9 & 12 marks
  • Calculate

title: “Discuss…” (6 marks)
content_html:
6 marks

“Discuss…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section B

What the Examiner Wants

A “Discuss” question requires a balanced response that explores more than one side of a business issue. The examiner wants to see you weigh up advantages and disadvantages, or multiple factors, and show understanding of context. You must make a judgement — not just list points.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureWell-developed response considering both sides; judgements are made with supporting reasoning; business terminology used accurately throughout
DevelopingSome discussion of more than one aspect but reasoning lacks depth on at least one side; some business terminology present
EmergingOne-sided response or basic points with little development; limited use of terminology
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan (1–2 min) — Jot down one argument for and one against, or two contrasting factors. Identify the context from the question (type of business, market, size).
  2. 2
    Argument 1 (P → E → E) — Make your first point, explain the reason, and develop the consequence. Apply to the business context in the question.
  3. 3
    Argument 2 (P → E → E) — Make a contrasting point. Use “However…” or “On the other hand…” to signal the shift.
  4. 4
    Judgement — Reach a conclusion. Which argument is stronger in this context? Use “Overall…” and justify your view with reference to the scenario.

Timing

Plan Write Judge

Approximately 8–10 minutes total. Plan before you write — it prevents one-sided answers.

Four-paragraph structure

Para 1 (For): “[Business point in favour]. This is because [reason]. As a result, [consequence in context].”

Para 2 (Against): “However, [contrasting point]. This means that [reason / risk]. Therefore [negative consequence in context].”

Para 3 (Judgement): “Overall, [state which argument is stronger] because [justify with context — e.g. size of business, market, objectives].”

Discuss whether a small clothing retailer should sell its products online. [6 marks]

Secure — 6 marks

Selling online would allow the retailer to reach a much wider customer base beyond its local area. This is because e-commerce removes geographical barriers, meaning customers from across the UK can purchase products. As a result, sales revenue could increase significantly without the high fixed costs of opening additional physical stores.

However, moving online involves significant upfront costs and ongoing challenges. The business would need to invest in website development, digital marketing, and logistics such as packaging and delivery. For a small retailer with limited capital, these costs could outweigh the short-term revenue gains, and managing returns could create additional cash flow pressures.

Overall, selling online is likely to benefit the retailer in the long run, but only if it has sufficient cash flow to fund the initial set-up. A small business might consider starting with a platform like Etsy or Shopify to minimise initial costs before investing in a dedicated website.

Examiner: 6/6 — both sides well-developed, business terminology used accurately, conclusion is context-specific and justified.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    One-sided answers — Only writing advantages or only disadvantages caps you at Emerging. Always discuss both sides.
  • ❌
    No judgement — A Discuss question expects a conclusion. Without one, you cannot reach Secure.
  • ❌
    Generic answers — “It increases profit” is vague. Connect your points to the specific business and context given in the question.
  • ❌
    Too many shallow points — Two well-developed arguments score higher than four undeveloped bullet points.
← Explain (3 marks) Justify / Evaluate (9 & 12 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
8–10 min total

Structure

  1. Plan both sides (1 min)
  2. Argument 1 (P → E → E)
  3. Argument 2 — contrasting
  4. Judgement in context

Other Guides

  • Define — 1 mark
  • Outline — 2 marks
  • Explain — 3 marks
  • Justify / Evaluate — 9 & 12 marks
  • Analyse
  • Calculate

title: “Justify…” / “Evaluate…” (9 & 12 marks)
content_html:
9 / 12 marks

“Justify…” / “Evaluate…”

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2 — Section B (highest-tariff questions)

What the Examiner Wants

These are the highest-value questions on the Edexcel Business papers. Both require a structured argument: consider one or more options or factors, weigh up the evidence, and reach a well-reasoned conclusion supported by the business context. The key difference:

  • Justify (9 marks) — Often asks you to recommend one option from a choice (e.g. “Justify which method of promotion the business should use”). Argue clearly for your chosen option AND consider why alternatives are less suitable.
  • Evaluate (12 marks) — Often asks you to assess the importance of a factor or strategy. Weigh evidence on both sides and reach a nuanced conclusion.

Level Descriptors (9-mark Justify)

LevelWhat You Need
SecureWell-reasoned justification for chosen option; counter-argument acknowledged; conclusion supported by context; accurate business terminology throughout
DevelopingReasonable justification but limited counter-argument or weaker application to context
EmergingSome relevant points but one-sided or undeveloped; limited use of terminology
No relevant response

Level Descriptors (12-mark Evaluate)

LevelWhat You Need
MasteringDetailed, balanced evaluation; multiple factors considered; well-supported, context-specific conclusion; excellent use of terminology
SecureGood analysis with some evaluation; may lack full balance or depth in conclusion
DevelopingSome analysis but limited evaluation; mainly descriptive with few judgements
EmergingBasic points, little development, minimal use of terminology
No relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the context carefully — Underline key details: type of business, size, objectives, market, financial situation. Your conclusion must relate to these specifics.
  2. 2
    Plan in 2–3 minutes — Identify your main argument, one or two supporting reasons, a counter-argument, and the basis for your conclusion. Note relevant business concepts.
  3. 3
    Main argument (P → E → E) — Develop your primary point in depth. Apply it to the business scenario. Use precise language (break-even, cash flow, competitive advantage, etc.).
  4. 4
    Second supporting point — Add further depth or a second reason supporting your main argument. Keep it linked to the scenario.
  5. 5
    Counter-argument — Acknowledge the strongest opposing point. Use “However…” Show you understand the other side, then explain why your main argument still holds.
  6. 6
    Conclusion — State your final judgement clearly. Justify it with specific reference to the context. The best conclusions explain why this answer applies to this particular business.

Timing

Plan Write Conclude

9-mark question: approximately 14–16 minutes. 12-mark question: approximately 18–20 minutes.

Justify / Evaluate structure

Main argument: “[Option/factor] would be most beneficial because [reason 1]. This means that [consequence 1 in context]. Furthermore, [reason 2], which would [consequence 2].”

Counter-argument: “However, [opposing option/factor] could also [benefit]. This is because [reason]. Nevertheless, [why your main argument is stronger for this business].”

Conclusion: “Overall, [your judgement] is the most appropriate [recommendation/factor] for [this business] because [specific contextual reason — e.g. size, objectives, financial position, market].”

A small bakery has £5,000 to spend on promotion. It is choosing between social media advertising and a local newspaper campaign. Justify which method of promotion the bakery should use. [9 marks]

Secure — 8/9 marks

The bakery should use social media advertising. This is because platforms such as Instagram and Facebook allow highly targeted advertising to specific demographics — for example, people within a 5-mile radius who have shown interest in food and baking. This means the bakery’s £5,000 budget would be spent reaching the most relevant potential customers, maximising return on investment. Furthermore, social media allows the business to showcase visually appealing product images and build a loyal following over time, generating ongoing free exposure even after the paid campaign ends.

However, a local newspaper campaign could also be effective, particularly for reaching older customers who may be less active on social media. A print advertisement would build local brand recognition and may reinforce trust in a community-based business.

Overall, social media advertising is the stronger choice for the bakery. Given its limited budget of £5,000 and its need to attract a high volume of local customers quickly, the ability to target precisely and track performance in real time makes social media far more cost-effective than a newspaper campaign, which offers less measurable results and declining readership among younger demographics.

Examiner: Strong Secure — clear recommendation with well-developed justification applied to context, counter-argument acknowledged, conclusion context-specific and justified.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Ignoring the context — Generic answers score Emerging or 2. Every developed point must reference the specific business, market, or scenario given.
  • ❌
    No counter-argument — A one-sided answer cannot reach the top level. Acknowledge the strongest opposing view before explaining why your main argument wins.
  • ❌
    A vague conclusion — “Overall, both options have advantages” is not a judgement. Commit to a clear position and justify it with context-specific reasoning.
  • ❌
    Running out of time — These questions are worth the most marks but must not eat into time for other questions. Practice planning quickly so your writing is efficient.
← Discuss (6 marks) Analyse →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
14–20 min total

Structure

  1. Read context carefully
  2. Plan main + counter (2 min)
  3. Main argument (P → E → E)
  4. Counter-argument
  5. Context-specific conclusion

title: 1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer
content_html:
1 Mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer

These are the quickest questions on the Music Component 3 Appraising paper. They test whether you can identify a specific musical feature — such as a device, texture, dynamic, instrument, or musical term — from a short listening extract. You'll either choose from a set of options (multiple choice) or write a single word or short phrase as your answer.

Key Fact

There is only one correct answer for each 1-mark question. You either get the mark or you don't — there are no half marks. Precision and confidence in musical terminology are essential.

How Marks Are Allocated

The mark scheme for 1-mark questions is straightforward:

Mark Scheme

1 mark: The correct answer is given (e.g. the correct option is circled/ticked, or the correct musical term is written).

0 marks: An incorrect answer is given, more than one option is selected (where only one is required), the answer is left blank, or the response is too vague to be credited.

For multiple choice questions, the examiner simply checks whether you've selected the right option. For one-word or short-answer questions, the examiner looks for the precise musical term or an acceptable alternative. Spelling does not need to be perfect, but it must be close enough for the examiner to recognise the intended word. For example, "cresendo" would likely be accepted for "crescendo," but "getting louder" might not be accepted if the question specifically asks for the Italian term.

Step-by-Step Method

Follow these steps every time you encounter a 1-mark question:

Step 1: Read the question carefully before the extract plays. Identify exactly what musical element you're being asked about — is it dynamics, tempo, texture, instrumentation, structure, or something else? If it's multiple choice, read all the options before listening.

Step 2: Listen with focus. As the extract plays, direct your ear specifically to the feature being asked about. Block out everything else. If the question asks about dynamics, listen only for volume changes. If it asks about texture, listen for how many parts are playing and how they relate to each other.

Step 3: Commit to your answer quickly. Trust your first instinct. For multiple choice, eliminate any options you know are wrong first, then choose from what remains. For one-word answers, write the most precise musical term you know.

Step 4: Don't change your answer unless you're certain. If the extract is played again, use the second hearing to confirm your choice rather than second-guessing yourself. Only change your answer if you hear clear evidence that your first choice was wrong.

Step 5: Never leave it blank. If you're unsure, always put something down. For multiple choice, you have at least a 25% chance of getting it right by guessing. A blank answer guarantees 0 marks.

Timing

Key Fact

Spend no more than 30 seconds on each 1-mark question (excluding listening time). The total paper is 1 hour 15 minutes, and you need to save the bulk of your time for the higher-mark questions (especially the 10-mark and 12-mark questions). These quick-fire questions should be answered almost immediately after the extract finishes.

The listening time is controlled by the recording, so you can't speed that up. But the moment the extract ends, write your answer and move on. Don't agonise over a single mark when there are much larger questions ahead.

Model Answer

Example Question (Multiple Choice): Listen to this extract from Bach's Badinerie. Which woodwind instrument plays the melody?
A) Oboe    B) Flute    C) Clarinet    D) Recorder

Model Answer: B) Flute ✓

Why this works: The student recognised the bright, agile tone of the Baroque flute playing the fast-moving semiquaver melody in Bach's Badinerie (BWV 1067). This is a set work, so they knew the instrumentation. They selected one clear answer without hesitation.

Example Question (One-word): What Italian term describes the gradually getting louder effect heard in this extract from Toto's Africa?

Model Answer: Crescendo ✓

Why this works: The student used the precise Italian musical term rather than a description like "getting louder." One word, directly answering what was asked.

Weak Answer

Example Question (Multiple Choice): Listen to this extract from Bach's Badinerie. Which woodwind instrument plays the melody?
A) Oboe    B) Flute    C) Clarinet    D) Recorder

Weak Answer: The student circles both B) Flute and D) Recorder ✗

Why this fails: Even though one of the selected options is correct, the mark scheme states that selecting more than one answer when only one is required results in 0 marks. The student was unsure and hedged their bets — but this strategy never works in multiple choice.

Example Question (One-word): What Italian term describes the gradually getting louder effect heard in this extract?

Weak Answer: "It gets louder" ✗

Why this fails: The question specifically asks for the Italian term. While the student understood what was happening musically, they didn't use the correct terminology. "Crescendo" was required, and a description is not an acceptable substitute when a specific term is requested.

Common Mistakes

Avoid these pitfalls on 1-mark questions:

• Selecting more than one option in multiple choice. If the question asks you to tick or circle one answer, selecting two (even if one is correct) will score 0 marks. Be decisive.

• Using descriptions instead of musical terms. If a question asks "What is the tempo?" the answer is a term like "allegro" or "andante" — not "fast" or "medium speed" (unless the question specifically offers those as options). Learn your Italian terms thoroughly.

• Confusing similar-sounding instruments. Students often mix up flute and recorder, or trumpet and cornet. For the set works, make sure you know the exact instrumentation. Bach's Badinerie features a Baroque flute with strings and harpsichord continuo. Toto's Africa features synthesisers, drums, guitars, bass, and vocals.

• Leaving the answer blank. There is absolutely no penalty for guessing on the Eduqas paper. A blank answer is always 0 marks. An educated guess — or even a random guess on multiple choice — gives you a chance of picking up the mark.

Key Terminology

Make sure you can confidently identify and use these terms in 1-mark questions. They frequently appear as both correct answers and distractors:

Key Terminology to Know

Dynamics: pianissimo (pp), piano (p), mezzo piano (mp), mezzo forte (mf), forte (f), fortissimo (ff), crescendo, diminuendo/decrescendo

Tempo: largo, adagio, andante, moderato, allegro, vivace, presto, accelerando, rallentando/ritardando, rubato

Texture: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic/contrapuntal, heterophonic, unison, melody and accompaniment

Structure: binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo, strophic, verse-chorus, through-composed, coda, intro, bridge, middle 8, outro

Tonality: major, minor, modal, atonal, pentatonic, chromatic

Instruments: flute, harpsichord, strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass), synthesiser, drum machine, electric guitar, bass guitar

Devices: ostinato, riff, sequence, imitation, pedal note, trill, ornament, syncopation, anacrusis

For the set works specifically, make sure you know the following:

Bach — Badinerie (from Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, BWV 1067): Baroque era, B minor, 2/4 time, solo flute, strings (violins, violas, cellos), basso continuo (harpsichord + cello), binary form, semiquaver passages, sequences, trills, terraced dynamics.

Toto — Africa (1982): Pop/rock, F♯ minor (with modulations), 4/4 time, synthesisers (including the iconic marimba-like intro pattern), electric guitar, bass guitar, drums, backing vocals, verse-chorus structure, syncopation, layered textures, use of studio effects.

Quick Reference
Marks Available1 mark — right or wrong, no partial credit
Time to Spend~30 seconds (excluding listening time)
Golden RuleNever leave it blank — always guess if unsure
Multiple Choice TipOnly ever select ONE option, even if unsure
Terminology TipUse Italian terms when asked for musical terms
Other Guides
1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.) 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features) 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect) 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)

title: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
content_html:
1 Mark — Identification Questions (Bar Number, Instrument, Key etc.)

Identification questions are the quickest questions on the Music listening paper. They ask you to pinpoint a single, specific fact about the music you hear — such as which instrument is playing, what bar a feature occurs in, what key the piece is in, or what time signature is being used. You need to give a precise, concise answer. There is no need to explain or justify — just identify correctly.

Key Fact

These questions are worth 1 mark each. You either get it right or you don't — there are no half marks. Precision and confidence in musical terminology are essential.

How Marks Are Allocated

The mark scheme for 1-mark identification questions is straightforward:

  • 1 mark: The correct answer is given. This must be the specific term, bar number, instrument name, key, time signature, or other musical fact that the question asks for. The answer must be unambiguous.
  • 0 marks: An incorrect answer, a vague answer, or no answer at all. If two answers are given and one is wrong, the mark is not awarded — even if the other answer is correct.

For bar number questions, examiners typically accept the correct bar or a range of one bar either side (e.g. if the answer is bar 5, bars 4–6 may be accepted). However, this depends on the specific question and the examiner's discretion, so always aim for the exact bar number.

Key Fact

If the question asks you to name one feature or instrument, give only one answer. Writing two answers — hoping one is right — can lose you the mark if one of them is wrong.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the question carefully before the extract plays. Identify exactly what you are listening for: is it an instrument, a bar number, a key, a time signature, a dynamic marking, or something else? Underline or highlight the key word in the question.
  2. If a score or skeleton score is provided, scan it quickly. Locate the relevant section. For bar number questions, follow along with the score as the music plays, tapping or counting beats to track where you are.
  3. Listen with focused intent on the first playing. Don't try to listen for everything — zero in on the specific feature the question asks about. Trust your first instinct if you hear the answer clearly.
  4. Write a short, definitive answer immediately. Don't waste time writing sentences. A single word or number is usually all that's needed: "Flute", "Bar 12", "G major", "4/4".
  5. Use the second playing to confirm. If you're unsure after the first listen, use the repeat to verify. If you were confident, use this time to double-check and then move on to reading the next question.

Timing

The Eduqas Component 3 paper is 1 hour 15 minutes long and is worth a total of 72 marks. That gives you roughly 1 minute per mark as a general guide.

Key Fact

For a 1-mark identification question, you should spend no more than 30–60 seconds thinking and writing your answer. The listening time is controlled by the recording, so use the pauses efficiently. Write your answer quickly and move straight to reading the next question.

Remember that the audio controls the pace of the exam — you cannot go back and replay extracts. Use the reading time before each extract wisely by scanning all questions related to that extract so you know what to listen for.

Model Answer

Example question (Bach — Badinerie): "Name the instrument that plays the melody at the start of the piece."

Model answer: Flute

Why this works: The answer is a single, correct, specific instrument name. No unnecessary information is included. The student has used the correct instrument name rather than a vague term like "woodwind". In the context of Bach's Badinerie from Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, the solo instrument is indeed the flute, and this is one of the most recognisable features of the piece.

Example question (Toto — Africa): "What time signature is this piece in?"

Model answer: 4/4

Why this works: Clear, correct, and precise. The student has written the time signature in standard notation rather than writing "four-four time" or "common time" (though these would also typically be accepted).

Example question (Bar number identification): "In which bar does the flute first play a trill?"

Model answer: Bar 9

Why this works: The student gives the exact bar number. They have clearly been following the score during playback and identified the correct moment.

Weak Answer

Example question: "Name the instrument that plays the melody at the start of the piece."

Weak answer 1: "A woodwind instrument plays the tune at the beginning"

Why this loses marks: "Woodwind" is a family of instruments, not a specific instrument. The question asks you to name the instrument — the examiner needs to see "flute". The extra words add nothing and waste time.

Weak answer 2: "Flute or clarinet"

Why this loses marks: The student has hedged by giving two answers. Because "clarinet" is incorrect, the examiner can award 0 marks even though "flute" is also written. Never give two options for a 1-mark question.

Example question: "In which bar does the flute first play a trill?"

Weak answer: "Somewhere near the middle"

Why this loses marks: This is vague and not a bar number. The question specifically asks for a bar number, so the answer must be a number. This suggests the student was not following the score during playback.

Common Mistakes

  • Giving two answers when only one is needed. If you write "flute or oboe" and one is wrong, you score 0. Commit to one answer. If you're truly unsure, go with your strongest instinct — you have a better chance with one educated guess than with a contradictory pair.
  • Using vague or general terms instead of specific ones. Writing "woodwind" instead of "flute", or "fast" instead of "allegro", or "loud" instead of "forte" can cost you the mark. Always use the most precise musical term you know.
  • Not following the score during playback. For bar number questions, you must track the music against the score. Practise counting bars and following a score at home — this is a skill that improves with regular practice.
  • Leaving the answer blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always write something. An educated guess has a chance of earning a mark; a blank space never will.

Key Terminology

For identification questions, the examiner is looking for precise vocabulary. Make sure you are confident using the following terms where relevant:

Key Fact

Instruments: flute, harpsichord, strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass), bass guitar, electric guitar, synthesiser/keyboard, drums, percussion, voice/vocals

Key Fact

Keys: B minor, D major, F♯ minor, G major, A major (for Bach Badinerie). A major, F♯ minor, B major (for Toto Africa). Always state whether major or minor.

Key Fact

Time signatures: 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 6/8. Know how to count beats in each and identify them by ear.

Key Fact

Tempo markings: allegro, andante, moderato, adagio, lento, presto, accelerando, rallentando/ritardando

Key Fact

Dynamic markings: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, crescendo, diminuendo/decrescendo

Key Fact

Musical features to spot: trill, mordent, appoggiatura, sequence, imitation, pedal note, ostinato, riff, syncopation, anacrusis, modulation, cadence (perfect, imperfect, plagal, interrupted)

The golden rule for 1-mark identification questions: be specific, be brief, and be confident. These are free marks if you know your set works and can follow a score — practise both regularly in the weeks before the exam.

Quick Reference
Marks available1 mark — right or wrong, no partial credit
Time to spend30–60 seconds maximum
Answer lengthOne word or number — never a sentence
Golden ruleGive only ONE answer — two guesses can score 0
Score trackingCount bars along with the music — practise this skill
Never leave blankNo penalty for wrong answers — always guess
Other Guides
1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features) 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect) 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)

title: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
content_html:
What the Question Asks

Short feature identification questions worth 4 marks ask you to listen to a musical extract and either identify specific musical features (such as texture, dynamics, articulation, or structure) or give bar numbers where particular events occur. You might be asked to name where a feature first appears, where a section repeats, or to identify multiple features heard in a specific passage.

These questions typically appear as part of the set work section (Bach Badinerie or Toto Africa) where you'll have an annotated score or skeleton score in front of you. You may also encounter them in the unfamiliar listening sections. The question might be broken into sub-parts (e.g., 4 × 1 mark) or require four separate correct identifications for 4 marks.

Key Fact

These questions test your ability to connect what you hear with what you see on the score and what you know about musical terminology. Each correct identification or bar number typically earns 1 mark — so you need four correct points for full marks.

How Marks Are Allocated

4-mark short identification questions use a point-based marking scheme. There are no level descriptors — each mark is awarded for a specific correct answer. The mark scheme typically works as follows:

  • 1 mark — for each correctly identified feature, bar number, or musical element (up to a maximum of 4 marks)
  • Answers must be precise: if the question asks for a bar number, a vague answer like "near the beginning" will not earn the mark
  • If the question asks you to identify features, correct musical terminology is expected (e.g., "trills" rather than "wobbly notes")
  • Where bar numbers are required, examiners typically accept a tolerance of ±1 bar depending on the feature, but you should aim for accuracy
  • If you give more answers than asked for (e.g., six answers when four are required), examiners mark the first four only — extra answers are ignored
Key Fact

There is no partial credit within each point — you either get the mark or you don't. This means precision and correct terminology are essential. Writing "bar 5" when the answer is bar 9 scores zero for that point, even if your reasoning was partially correct.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the question carefully before the music plays. Identify exactly what you're being asked: are you giving bar numbers, naming features, or both? Underline key words in the question such as "identify," "give the bar number," "name two features," or "describe."
  2. Study the score excerpt during reading time. If a score or skeleton score is provided, scan it quickly. Note bar numbers, time signatures, key signatures, and any obvious features like dynamic markings, ornaments, or changes in texture. This gives you landmarks to follow during playback.
  3. Follow the score with your finger during playback. Track the music bar by bar so you can pinpoint exactly where features occur. If the question asks for bar numbers, jot down approximate bar numbers as soon as you hear the feature — don't wait until the end.
  4. Write your answers using precise musical terminology. Replace vague descriptions with proper terms: "trill" not "shaky note," "staccato" not "short and bouncy," "homophonic texture" not "everyone plays together." This is what examiners are looking for.
  5. Check you've given the right number of answers. If the question asks for four features, make sure you've written exactly four. Don't write five or six hoping for the best — only your first four will be marked.
  6. Use the second listening to verify. On the repeat playing, check each of your answers. Confirm bar numbers are accurate and that you haven't confused similar-sounding sections (e.g., the exposition and recapitulation in Badinerie).

Timing

The full Component 3 paper is 1 hour 15 minutes (75 minutes) and is worth approximately 72 marks. As a rough guide, you should spend just over 1 minute per mark.

Key Fact

For a 4-mark short identification question, aim to spend approximately 4–5 minutes including both listening plays. Use the first play to draft your answers and the second play to confirm and refine them. Don't overthink — these are meant to be quick, precise responses.

Model Answer

Question: "Identify four musical features used by Bach in bars 1–8 of the Badinerie." [4 marks]

Strong answer:

  • The flute plays semiquaver runs in a scalic pattern (bar 1). [1 mark]
  • The texture is melody and accompaniment (homophonic), with the flute as the solo melody instrument over the continuo. [1 mark]
  • The piece is in 2/4 time with a fast tempo, giving a lively dance-like character. [1 mark]
  • Trills (ornaments) are used by the flute in bar 4. [1 mark]

Why this scores full marks: Each point is distinct, uses correct musical terminology, references specific bar numbers where appropriate, and directly answers what was asked. The student has covered different musical elements (melody, texture, rhythm/metre, ornamentation) showing breadth of knowledge.

Weak Answer

Question: "Identify four musical features used by Bach in bars 1–8 of the Badinerie." [4 marks]

Weak answer:

  • The flute plays fast notes. [0 marks — too vague; needs to say "semiquaver runs" or "scalic passages"]
  • The music sounds happy and lively. [0 marks — this is a subjective description, not a musical feature with correct terminology]
  • There are lots of instruments playing. [0 marks — inaccurate and vague; the Badinerie has a small ensemble, and this doesn't identify a specific feature]
  • The flute does some fancy bits. [0 marks — the student likely means ornaments/trills but hasn't used the correct term]

Why this scores 0/4: Every answer lacks precise musical terminology. The student clearly heard things in the music but couldn't translate their observations into the language examiners require. "Fast notes" needed to be "semiquaver runs," "fancy bits" needed to be "trills" or "ornaments," and "sounds happy" is not a musical feature.

Common Mistakes

  • Using vague, everyday language instead of musical terminology. Examiners need to see words like "syncopation," "staccato," "riff," "pentatonic," or "call and response" — not "catchy beat," "jumpy notes," or "African-sounding." Always translate what you hear into proper musical vocabulary.
  • Giving the wrong bar numbers because you lost your place in the score. If you stop following the score for even a few seconds, you can easily be several bars out. Practise tracking scores with your finger during revision so this becomes second nature.
  • Repeating the same point in different words. If you write "the flute plays quick notes" and "the flute part moves fast with lots of notes," these are the same point and you'll only get 1 mark maximum. Make sure each answer identifies a genuinely different feature — try to cover different musical elements (melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, dynamics, timbre, structure).
  • Writing more answers than required. If the question asks for four features and you write six, only the first four are marked. If your best answer is number five, it won't count. Be selective and write your strongest, most precise answers first.

Key Terminology

Using the correct musical vocabulary is the single most important factor in scoring marks on these questions. Here are the essential terms organised by musical element:

Key Fact

For Bach Badinerie, make sure you know: Baroque, binary form, flute, continuo, harpsichord, strings, semiquavers, trills, mordents, ornaments, scalic, sequences, modulation, relative major, dominant, tonic, imitation, homophonic, polyphonic, staccato, legato, basso continuo, figured bass, 2/4 time.

Key Fact

For Toto Africa, make sure you know: introduction, verse, chorus, bridge, outro, synth, marimba, riff, syncopation, backing vocals, harmonies, pentatonic, call and response, crescendo, fade out, drum fill, guitar solo, key change (modulation), layered texture, reverb, panning, multitrack recording, hook, anacrusis.

General terms you should be confident using across any question:

  • Melody: conjunct, disjunct, scalic, arpeggio, sequence, ostinato, riff, motif, phrase, ornamentation, chromatic, diatonic, pentatonic
  • Harmony: major, minor, tonic, dominant, subdominant, perfect cadence, imperfect cadence, modulation, chord, triad, pedal note, suspension, dissonance, consonance
  • Rhythm & Metre: syncopation, dotted rhythm, triplet, semiquaver, quaver, crotchet, time signature, anacrusis, cross-rhythm, polyrhythm, swing
  • Texture: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic, melody and accompaniment, unison, antiphonal, contrapuntal, layered
  • Dynamics & Articulation: piano, forte, crescendo, diminuendo, staccato, legato, accent, sforzando
  • Timbre & Sonority: arco, pizzicato, muted, distorted, acoustic, electric, breathy, vibrato
  • Structure: binary, ternary, rondo, verse-chorus, strophic, through-composed, coda, introduction, bridge, middle 8
Quick Reference
Marks available4 marks — 1 per correct identification
Time to spend4–5 minutes (including both plays)
Key skillPrecise terminology + accurate bar numbers
Golden ruleNever write more answers than asked for
Follow the scoreTrack with your finger — don't lose your place
Cover different elementsMelody, rhythm, texture, dynamics, harmony — spread your answers
Other Guides
1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.) 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect) 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)

title: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
content_html:
10 marks — Extended Listening Response

The extended listening response is the highest-tariff single question in the Music listening paper. It requires you to write a detailed, structured answer explaining how musical elements are used to create a specific effect, mood, or describe something. This is your chance to show off your musical vocabulary and your ability to link what you hear to how it makes the listener feel or what it represents.

Key Fact

This question is worth 10 marks — that's a significant chunk of your total paper. You'll typically hear the extract played three times with pauses for writing. The question will usually ask you to "explain how" the music creates a particular mood, effect, or atmosphere, or how musical elements are used in the extract.

What the Question Asks

You will hear an extract of music — either from one of your set works (Bach's Badinerie or Toto's Africa) or an unfamiliar piece. The question will ask you to explain how the music creates a particular effect or mood. For example:

"Explain how the composer uses musical elements to create excitement in this extract."

"Explain how the music describes the scene/mood of..."

"Discuss how the performers use musical elements to create contrast in this extract."

The key word is "explain" — you must go beyond simply identifying features. You need to say what you hear, where you hear it (if possible), and how it contributes to the effect the question asks about. Every point should link a musical feature to the mood, effect, or description mentioned in the question.

How Marks Are Allocated

This question is marked using a best-fit level descriptor approach. Examiners read your whole answer and decide which level it best fits into, then fine-tune the mark within that level.

Level Descriptors

Top band (8–10 marks): A detailed and perceptive response. The answer demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of musical elements and context. Points are well-developed and consistently linked to the question focus. Accurate and extensive use of musical terminology throughout. Clear, coherent structure with well-supported points referencing specific moments in the music.

Level Descriptors

Upper-mid band (5–7 marks): A competent response showing sound knowledge and understanding. Most points are developed and linked to the question focus, though some may lack detail. Good use of musical terminology, mostly accurate. Some reference to specific moments in the music. The response is generally well-organised.

Level Descriptors

Lower-mid band (3–4 marks): A basic response showing limited knowledge and understanding. Some relevant points are made but they are often undeveloped or not clearly linked to the question focus. Some musical terminology is used but may be inaccurate or limited. The response may be disorganised or list-like.

Level Descriptors

Lower band (1–2 marks): A minimal response with very limited knowledge. Few relevant points, little or no use of musical terminology. Points are not linked to the question focus. The response may be very brief or largely inaccurate.

0 marks: No relevant content or no response given.

Step-by-Step Method

Follow this method every time you face a 10-mark extended listening question:

Step 1 — Read the question carefully before the first play. Identify exactly what effect, mood, or description you're being asked about. Underline or circle the key words (e.g., "excitement," "contrast," "sadness"). Everything you write must link back to this focus.

Step 2 — First listening: get an overview. On the first play, listen to the whole extract and jot down quick notes about the overall mood and the most obvious musical features. Think across all the musical elements: melody, harmony, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, texture, timbre/sonority, structure, and tonality.

Step 3 — Second listening: gather detail. On the second play, listen more carefully for specific details. Note down precise features — intervals, rhythmic patterns, specific instruments, changes in dynamics, harmonic devices. Try to note roughly where things happen (beginning, middle, end, or bar numbers if you can).

Step 4 — Organise your notes before writing. Quickly scan your notes. Aim for at least 5–6 well-developed points covering different musical elements. Prioritise the most significant features that directly relate to the question focus.

Step 5 — Write using the WHAT–WHERE–HOW structure. For each point, state:

  • WHAT — the musical feature you can hear (using correct terminology)
  • WHERE — when it occurs in the extract (if you can identify it)
  • HOW — how this feature creates the effect/mood the question asks about

Step 6 — Third listening: check and add. Use the final play to verify your points and add any extra detail you may have missed. Fill in gaps, correct errors, and make sure every point is linked to the question focus.

Step 7 — Review your answer. Quickly check that you've covered multiple musical elements, used correct terminology, and linked every point back to the question.

Key Fact

The golden rule: never describe a feature without explaining its effect. Saying "the dynamics are loud" earns very little. Saying "the fortissimo dynamics in the full ensemble passages create a sense of power and excitement" earns much more.

Timing

The whole paper is 1 hour 15 minutes (75 minutes) and the audio playback is controlled by the examiner, so your writing time is built into the listening gaps. However, you should plan your time wisely:

Timing Guide

Aim to spend approximately 12–15 minutes on a 10-mark question, including all three listenings. Use the first play for overview notes (2–3 minutes), the second play for detailed notes (2–3 minutes), then write your answer (5–7 minutes), and use the third play to refine and add to it (2–3 minutes). Don't rush — this is the question where detailed, well-linked points earn the most marks.

Model Answer

The extract creates a strong sense of energy and excitement through a combination of musical elements working together.

The tempo is moderately fast, which immediately gives the music a sense of forward momentum and drive. This is reinforced by the steady, syncopated rhythm in the drum part, which uses a repetitive pattern with off-beat accents that create a sense of urgency and groove, propelling the music forward.

The texture builds throughout the extract, starting with a relatively thin texture of synthesiser and drums before gradually layering in bass guitar, rhythm guitar, and backing vocals. This cumulative layering creates a growing sense of anticipation and excitement as more instruments are added, making the sound increasingly full and powerful.

The dynamics follow a similar trajectory — the extract begins at a mezzo-forte level and builds to forte in the chorus sections, where the full band plays together. The contrast between the quieter verse passages and the louder chorus creates a sense of release and energy each time the chorus arrives.

The melody in the chorus uses a rising contour and relatively stepwise movement with some leaps, giving it a memorable, anthemic quality that conveys excitement. The vocalist performs with an energetic, powerful timbre and uses some falsetto at the top of phrases, adding intensity and emotional urgency.

The harmony uses major tonality throughout, which gives the music a bright, uplifting character. The chord progression in the chorus is strong and decisive, using primary chords that create a sense of resolution and confidence. The use of keyboard/synthesiser pads adds richness and warmth to the harmonic texture.

Finally, the call-and-response between the lead vocal and backing vocals in the chorus creates a sense of communal energy, as though many people are joining in, which heightens the overall feeling of excitement and celebration.

Weak Answer

"The music is fast and loud which makes it exciting. There are drums and guitars playing. The singer sings high notes. The chorus is catchy. It sounds like pop music. The instruments are all playing together at the end which makes it sound big. It is in a major key."

Why this is weak (likely Developing, around 3 marks):

  • Lacks musical terminology — "fast and loud" instead of specific tempo markings and dynamic levels; "high notes" instead of describing the vocal range, falsetto, or melodic contour.
  • Points are not developed — each statement is a single sentence with no explanation of how the feature creates excitement.
  • Too vague — "drums and guitars playing" describes almost any pop song; there's no mention of specific rhythmic patterns, syncopation, or playing techniques.
  • No structure — the answer reads as a list of disconnected observations rather than a coherent analysis.
  • No reference to specific moments — doesn't mention verse vs. chorus, beginning vs. end, or any changes within the extract.
  • "Catchy" is a subjective opinion, not musical analysis.

Common Mistakes

Avoid these pitfalls that cost students marks every year:

  • Describing without explaining the effect. Simply listing features ("there are syncopated rhythms," "the texture is thick") without saying how they contribute to the mood or effect in the question earns minimal credit. Always complete the link: feature → effect.
  • Using vague, everyday language instead of musical terminology. Words like "fast," "loud," "high," and "catchy" are too imprecise. Use terms like "allegro tempo," "fortissimo dynamics," "ascending melodic contour," and "memorable, conjunct melody." The level descriptors specifically reward accurate musical vocabulary.
  • Only discussing one or two musical elements. A top-level answer covers multiple elements — melody, harmony, rhythm, dynamics, texture, timbre/sonority, structure. If you only write about rhythm and dynamics, you'll cap yourself at Developing or 3 no matter how good those points are.
  • Writing a narrative or storytelling instead of analysing. Don't write "this part sounds like rain falling on the savannah and then the sun comes out." Instead, identify the specific musical features and explain how they create imagery or mood. Keep it rooted in musical analysis, not creative writing.

Key Terminology

Using precise musical vocabulary is one of the clearest ways to move from Developing into Secure and Mastering. Make sure you are confident using these terms in your answers:

Melody & Harmony

Conjunct / disjunct — stepwise or leaping melodic movement. Ascending / descending contour — the direction of a melody. Sequence — a melodic pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch. Ornamentation / trills / mordents — decorative notes (especially relevant for Bach). Major / minor tonality. Diatonic / chromatic harmony. Perfect cadence / imperfect cadence. Pedal note / drone. Modulation — a change of key. Chord progression. Suspended chords. Riff / ostinato.

Rhythm, Tempo & Metre

Syncopation — accents on off-beats. Dotted rhythms. Triplets. Semiquaver runs (important for Bach). Cross-rhythms / polyrhythms. Allegro / moderato / andante — tempo markings. Rubato — flexible tempo. Anacrusis — an upbeat. Simple / compound time. Time signature.

Dynamics & Articulation

Pianissimo (pp) / piano (p) / mezzo-forte (mf) / forte (f) / fortissimo (ff). Crescendo / diminuendo. Sforzando (sfz) — a sudden accent. Staccato — short, detached notes. Legato — smooth, connected notes. Accents.

Texture & Sonority

Monophonic — single unaccompanied line. Homophonic — melody with chordal accompaniment. Polyphonic / contrapuntal — multiple independent melodic lines (key for Bach). Unison — all parts playing the same notes. Imitation — one part copies another.

title: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
content_html:
What the Question Asks

This question type is worth 12 marks and is based on one of your set works — either Bach's Badinerie or Toto's Africa. You will be given a printed score extract in your question booklet and will hear the extract played several times during the exam.

The 12 marks are split across multiple sub-questions (typically 5–8 shorter questions labelled a, b, c, etc.). These sub-questions test different musical elements and range from simple identification tasks (1 mark) to slightly longer explanations (2–3 marks). Because this is a prepared extract, examiners expect you to demonstrate knowledge you've gained from studying the set work — not just what you hear in the moment.

Sub-questions may ask you to:

  • Name an interval, chord, key, or time signature shown in the score
  • Identify a specific musical device (e.g. trill, sequence, syncopation)
  • Give bar numbers where a particular feature occurs
  • Name the instrument playing a particular line
  • Describe how a musical element is used (e.g. dynamics, texture, rhythm)
  • Complete missing notes or rhythms on the score
  • Explain the role of a part within the texture
Key Fact

You must know your set works inside out. The score is provided, but examiners expect answers that show detailed prior study — not just surface-level listening. Learn the structure, instrumentation, key features, and context of both Bach's Badinerie and Toto's Africa.

How Marks Are Allocated

Each sub-question has its own mark allocation, typically following these patterns:

  • 1-mark questions: Require a single correct answer — a key name, instrument, interval, device, or bar number. No explanation needed. The mark scheme lists acceptable answers; you either get it right or you don't.
  • 2-mark questions: May require two correct identifications, or one identification plus a brief description. For example: "Name the device used in bar 5 [1] and explain how it is used [1]." Each correct point scores 1 mark.
  • 3-mark questions: Require more detailed description. The mark scheme typically lists 4–5 acceptable points and you need to make 3 distinct, correct statements to gain full marks. These often relate to how a musical element (e.g. texture, rhythm, melody) is used across the extract.

Mark scheme descriptors for the sub-questions are typically point-based (not level-based). This means each valid musical observation or correct identification earns a mark, up to the maximum for that sub-question. The mark scheme will list all acceptable answers and common alternatives.

Key Fact

For point-based mark schemes, every distinct correct point scores. If a 3-mark question lists five acceptable answers and you make three of them, you get full marks. Always aim to write one more point than the marks available as insurance.

Step-by-Step Method

Follow these steps during the exam to maximise your marks on this question type:

  1. Read ALL sub-questions before the first playing. You have reading time before the extract plays. Use it wisely. Scan every sub-question so you know what to listen for. Underline key command words (name, describe, identify, explain, give the bar number).
  2. Study the printed score. Before the music plays, look at the score extract carefully. Identify the key signature, time signature, instruments, and any obvious features (trills, rests, repeated patterns, dynamic markings). Some questions can be answered from the score alone.
  3. First listening — get your bearings. Follow the score as the music plays. Don't panic-write. Focus on matching what you hear to what you see. Note where the extract sits within the overall set work — this helps you recall your revision notes about that section.
  4. Answer the easy questions first. After the first playing, immediately answer any questions you're confident about — especially 1-mark identification questions. These are quick wins.
  5. Second listening — target the harder questions. Focus specifically on the sub-questions you haven't answered yet. If a question asks about texture in bars 9–12, follow only those bars closely on this listening.
  6. Use precise musical vocabulary. Don't write vaguely. Instead of "the music gets louder," write "there is a crescendo from piano to forte." Instead of "the tune goes up and down," write "the melody uses a scalic ascending passage followed by a descending sequence."
  7. Give bar numbers when relevant. Even when the question doesn't explicitly ask for bar references, including them shows the examiner exactly what you're talking about and can help clarify your answer.
  8. Check your answers on the final listening. Use the last playing to verify what you've written. Correct any mistakes. If you have a blank answer, make your best educated guess — there is no penalty for wrong answers.

Timing

The total exam is 1 hour 15 minutes (75 minutes) and is worth approximately 68–72 marks in total (this varies slightly by year). As a rough guide:

Key Fact

Allow approximately 12–15 minutes for the 12-mark prepared extract question, including all listenings. That's roughly 1 minute per mark plus time for the playings themselves. The listenings are controlled by the recording, so your writing time is the gaps between playings and after the final playing.

Don't spend excessive time on any single sub-question. If a 1-mark question is stumping you, write your best answer and move on. The 2- and 3-mark sub-questions deserve proportionally more thought, but even these should take no longer than 1–2 minutes of writing time each.

Model Answer

Example sub-questions and model responses:

(a) Name the key of this extract. [1 mark]

B minor.

✅ Simple, correct, no wasted words.

(b) Name the ornament used by the flute in bar 3. [1 mark]

A trill.

✅ Precise musical term. The student has clearly studied the score notation.

(c) Identify the interval between the two notes circled in bar 7. [1 mark]

A perfect 4th.

✅ Includes the quality (perfect) and the number (4th) — both elements are needed for full marks.

(d) Name the instrument playing the bass line. [1 mark]

Harpsichord (playing basso continuo).

✅ Correct identification. Adding "basso continuo" shows contextual knowledge, though just "harpsichord" would score the mark.

(e) Describe the texture of this extract. [2 marks]

The texture is melody and accompaniment (homophonic) [1], with the flute playing the main melodic line over a basso continuo accompaniment provided by the harpsichord and cello [1].

✅ Two distinct points: names the texture type and explains which instruments fulfil which roles.

(f) Describe three features of the flute melody in bars 1–8. [3 marks]

The flute melody uses fast semiquaver runs that create a virtuosic, lively character [1]. There is a descending sequence in bars 5–6 where a melodic pattern is repeated at a lower pitch [1]. The melody also includes trills as ornamentation, which is typical of the Baroque style [1].

✅ Three distinct, well-described features. Each point uses correct terminology (semiquaver, sequence, trill, ornamentation, Baroque). Bar references are included where helpful.

(g) Name the musical period in which this piece was composed. [1 mark]

The Baroque period.

(h) From which larger work is the Badinerie taken? [1 mark]

Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor (BWV 1067).

✅ Demonstrates prepared knowledge. Even just "Orchestral Suite No. 2" would score the mark.

Weak Answer

(a) Name the key of this extract. [1 mark]

Minor.

❌ "Minor" alone is not enough — the examiner needs the full key name: B minor. This scores 0.

(b) Name the ornament used by the flute in bar 3. [1 mark]

A wiggly note.

❌ This is not a musical term. The correct answer is "trill." Always use proper terminology. This scores 0.

(c) Identify the interval between the two notes circled in bar 7. [1 mark]

A 4th.

⚠️ This may or may not score depending on the mark scheme. Some mark schemes require the quality (perfect, major, minor) as well as the number. Always give the full interval name to be safe.

(d) Name the instrument playing the bass line. [1 mark]

Piano.

❌ There is no piano in a Baroque ensemble of this type. The student hasn't revised the instrumentation. This scores 0.

(e) Describe the texture of this extract. [2 marks]

The texture is quite thin.

⚠️ "Thin" gives a vague sense but doesn't use correct terminology and doesn't explain which instruments are doing what. At best this might scrape 1 mark, but more likely 0.

(f) Describe three features of the flute melody in bars 1–8. [3 marks]

The flute plays fast and it sounds really nice. The melody goes up and down a lot. It's quite catchy and memorable.

❌ This answer uses no musical vocabulary at all. "Sounds really nice" and "quite catchy" are subjective opinions, not musical descriptions. "Goes up and down" is too vague — the student should specify scalic movement, sequences, intervals, or note values. This likely scores 0–1 marks at most.

(g) Name the musical period in which this piece was composed. [1 mark]

Classical.

❌ Bach is Baroque, not Classical. A common mistake from students who haven't learned the set work context. Scores 0.

(h) From which larger work is the Badinerie taken? [1 mark]

I don't know.

❌ Never leave an answer blank or write "I don't know." Always attempt a guess. This is pure recall from revision — the student needed to learn this fact beforehand.

Common Mistakes

  • Not learning the set works thoroughly enough. This question type rewards preparation. Students who only revise casually will struggle with context questions (key, period, instrumentation, structure) that cannot be answered from listening alone. Know your set works inside out — every instrument, every section, every key change.
  • Using vague, everyday language instead of musical terminology. Answers like "it gets louder," "the tune goes up," or "it sounds happy" will not score well. Examiners want terms like crescendo, ascending scalic passage, major tonality. The mark schemes are written in technical language, and your answers need to match.
  • Not reading the question carefully. If a question asks you to describe the melody, don't write about dynamics or texture. If it asks for three features, give three — not two. If it says "in bars 5–8," don't describe bars 1–4. Misreading costs easy marks.
  • Leaving answers blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers in Music. Always write something. Even a partially correct answer or educated guess can pick up a mark. A blank answer guarantees zero.

Key Terminology

Using correct musical vocabulary is essential for scoring marks. Here are the key terms you should be comfortable using, organised by musical element:

Key Fact

The examiner marks against a list of acceptable terms and descriptions. If your answer doesn't use recognisable musical vocabulary, it is very difficult for them to award marks — even if you understand the music.

Melody/Pitch: scalic, arpeggiated, conjunct (stepwise),

title: Exam Technique Guides
content_html:
Exam Technique Guides — GCSE Music (Eduqas)

Component 3: Appraising is the listening exam for Music. It accounts for 40% of your total GCSE grade and tests your ability to listen to music, analyse features, and communicate your understanding using correct musical vocabulary. This hub page explains how the exam works and links to detailed technique guides for every question type you will encounter.

Exam Format Overview

The Appraising exam lasts 1 hour 15 minutes and is taken under standard exam conditions with audio played to the whole room. You will hear a mixture of set works, related listening extracts, and unfamiliar music drawn from across the four Areas of Study.

Detail Information
Component Component 3: Appraising
Weighting 40% of GCSE
Duration 1 hour 15 minutes
Format Listening exam with written answers
Set Works Bach — Badinerie (AoS1); Toto — Africa (AoS4)

Audio extracts are played a set number of times during the exam — you cannot pause or replay them yourself. Some questions provide a skeleton score or full score to follow, while others rely entirely on your listening skills and memory of the set works.

How the Paper Is Structured

The exam paper is divided into several questions, each based on a different listening extract. Questions progress from shorter, lower-tariff items to longer, higher-tariff responses. You should expect the following broad structure:

  • Opening questions — Short-answer and multiple-choice items testing quick identification of musical elements such as instruments, keys, time signatures, and textures.
  • Middle questions — Feature identification tasks where you pinpoint specific moments in the music (often by bar number) or list musical characteristics heard in an extract.
  • Prepared extract question — A multi-part question on one of the two set works, typically accompanied by a score excerpt. This carries up to 12 marks and tests detailed knowledge.
  • Extended response — A longer writing task worth up to 10 marks asking you to explain how musical elements combine to create a particular mood, effect, or depiction.

The total mark for the paper varies slightly between series but is typically around 72 marks. Time management is essential: aim to spend roughly one minute per mark, leaving a few minutes at the end for checking.

Question Type Guides

Each question type on the paper demands a slightly different technique. The guides below break down exactly what the examiner is looking for, how to structure your response, and common mistakes to avoid.

Multiple Choice & One-Word Answer

1 mark

These are the quickest questions on the paper. You either select from given options or provide a single precise term. Speed and accuracy matter — there is no room for partial credit. This guide covers how to eliminate wrong answers and avoid common traps.

Identification Questions

1 mark

You are asked to identify a specific detail such as a bar number, instrument, key, time signature, or dynamic marking. These may require you to follow a score or rely purely on listening. This guide explains how to practise pinpointing details quickly and accurately.

Short Feature Identification

4 marks

These questions ask you to identify several features or locate specific moments in the music, often by giving bar numbers or naming techniques. You typically need to make four correct points. This guide shows you how to organise your listening and ensure you hit every mark.

Extended Listening Response

10 marks

The highest-tariff writing question on the paper. You must explain how music describes something or creates a particular effect, covering multiple musical elements in detail. This guide walks you through planning, paragraph structure, use of vocabulary, and how to hit the top mark band.

Prepared Extract with Score

12 marks (multiple sub-questions)

This question focuses on one of the two set works — Bach's Badinerie or Toto's Africa — and provides a score excerpt. Sub-questions range from 1-mark identifications to longer explanations. This guide covers how to revise the set works effectively and navigate score-based questions under timed conditions.

General Exam Tips

  • Read before you listen. Use the reading time before each extract is played to study the question carefully so you know exactly what to listen for.
  • Use musical vocabulary. Terms like staccato, syncopation, pedal note, and homophonic texture signal to the examiner that you understand the music at a technical level.
  • Be specific. Vague statements like "the music gets louder" score less than precise ones like "a crescendo from piano to fortissimo in bars 12–14 creates a sense of building tension."
  • Know your set works inside out. The prepared extract question rewards detailed, memorised knowledge. You should be able to describe what happens in every section of both Badinerie and Africa.
  • Manage your time. Don't spend five minutes on a 1-mark question. If you are unsure, write your best answer and move on — you can return at the end.
Quick Reference

Exam: Component 3 — Appraising

Board: Eduqas (C660U)

Weight: 40% of GCSE

Duration: 1 hour 15 minutes

Set Works:

  • Bach — Badinerie (AoS1)
  • Toto — Africa (AoS4)

Question Types:
