title: 20 marks — Evaluation
content_html:
What the Question Asks

Paper 1 Question 4 gives you a statement about the fiction text — usually something a student has said — and asks "To what extent do you agree?" You must take a clear position on the statement, support it with evidence from across the specified lines, and analyse the writer's methods. This is not a simple agree/disagree question: the best answers evaluate critically, showing where the statement is accurate and where it might be an oversimplification.

This is worth 20 marks — the highest-mark reading question on Paper 1. It tests your ability to think like a literary critic, not just a student spotting techniques.

Key Fact

This question is about evaluation, not description. You are being asked to judge the statement — is it fair? Is it the whole picture? Where does it hold up, and where does it fall short? Your answer must show your own critical thinking, not just agreement with the statement.

How Marks Are Allocated

Examiners use four levels to mark this question. Understanding the difference between them is essential:

Level Marks What It Looks Like
Mastering 16–20 Perceptive, compelling. Critically evaluates with sophisticated analysis of method and effect. Considers multiple readings. Uses precise, well-chosen evidence. Sustains a critical voice throughout.
Secure 11–15 Clear, detailed. Evaluates clearly using a range of evidence. Writer's methods are commented on with some analysis of effect.
Developing 6–10 Some understanding. Begins to evaluate the statement with some evidence. Methods may be mentioned but not analysed in depth.
Emerging 1–5 Simple. Paraphrase or basic comment. Little or no evaluation. Methods not analysed.
Key Fact

The jump from Secure to Mastering comes from critical evaluation — not just saying "the writer uses a metaphor to show fear" but judging how effectively that metaphor supports (or complicates) the statement. Mastering answers consider alternative interpretations and sustain a confident, analytical voice.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the statement twice and underline the key words. In the example, the key words are "feel", "completely overwhelming", and "fear". These are your anchors — every paragraph you write should connect back to these specific words. Ask yourself: does the text really do all of what the statement claims? The word "completely" is a gift — it invites you to challenge or qualify.
  2. Re-read the specified lines with the statement in mind. As you read, annotate evidence that supports the statement and evidence that challenges or complicates it. Aim for 4–6 pieces of evidence across the specified section — don't cluster all your quotes from one paragraph. Look for specific methods: word choices, sentence structures, imagery, narrative perspective, shifts in tone.
  3. Decide your position before you write. The strongest answers don't just say "I agree." They take a nuanced position — for example: "I largely agree, but the writer also introduces moments of X which complicate the picture." Write your position as your opening sentence. This gives the examiner confidence that you understand what evaluation means.
  4. Write 3–4 developed paragraphs, each evaluating a different aspect. Each paragraph should follow this pattern:
    • Evaluate — state how far this evidence supports or challenges the statement
    • Evidence — embed a precise, short quotation
    • Analyse method — name the technique and explain how it creates the effect
    • Effect on reader — explain what the reader thinks, feels, or understands as a result
    At least one paragraph should offer a counter-argument or qualification — this is what separates good answers from excellent ones.
  5. Consider structure and shifts across the passage. Does the writer's approach change from the beginning to the end of the specified section? If the fear builds, or if it breaks momentarily, this is rich material for evaluation. Commenting on how the passage develops shows the examiner you're reading critically, not just cherry-picking quotes.
  6. End with a brief conclusion that refines your position. Don't just repeat your opening. Show that your analysis has led you somewhere — e.g., "While the fear is powerfully conveyed, the writer's inclusion of self-conscious detail suggests it is not quite 'completely' overwhelming — there is always a flicker of awareness beneath the panic." Two or three sentences is enough.

Timing

Spend 25–30 minutes on this question. Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes total. The reading section (Questions 1–4) should take roughly 1 hour, and Q4 is worth the most marks — so it deserves the most time.

  • 3–5 minutes: Re-read the specified lines, annotate evidence, decide your position
  • 20–22 minutes: Write 3–4 developed evaluation paragraphs
  • 2–3 minutes: Write a brief conclusion and check your answer
Key Fact

Do not rush this question. Students who spend only 15 minutes on Q4 almost always end up in Developing — they don't develop enough points, they don't analyse method in detail, and they forget to evaluate. The 20 marks here are worth the same as Questions 1, 2, and 3 combined (4 + 8 + 8 = 20). Give Q4 the time it deserves.

Model Answer

I largely agree that the writer makes the reader feel the narrator's fear is overwhelming, though this is achieved through carefully controlled techniques rather than explicit statement — which makes the effect all the more powerful.

The most compelling evidence of overwhelming fear comes through the writer's use of free indirect discourse: 'He couldn't — he simply couldn't — go through that door.' The repetition and the dash-interrupted syntax enact the narrator's mental breakdown in real time, placing the reader inside the paralysis. We don't observe the fear from outside; we experience its irrationality from within, which creates a suffocating sense of helplessness.

Furthermore, the writer strips away sensory detail as the passage progresses. The opening lines contain vivid descriptions of colour and sound, but by the final paragraph the prose becomes almost bare — short, declarative sentences with no adjectives. This structural reduction mirrors the way extreme fear narrows perception, which reinforces the statement's claim.

However, there are moments where the fear does not feel overwhelming but almost absurd — the detail of the narrator straightening his tie before the confrontation introduces dark comedy. This suggests the writer intends something more nuanced: a character whose fear is real but whose response to it is self-conscious, even pitiful. The reader is made to feel sympathy and a degree of frustrated exasperation simultaneously. So while the fear is certainly powerfully conveyed, 'completely overwhelming' slightly overstates it — the writer preserves the narrator's self-awareness even in extremis.

Why this answer is Top band:

  • Clear, sustained position: The opening sentence establishes a nuanced stance ("largely agree… though") and this position is maintained and developed throughout.
  • Precise evidence: Quotes are short, well-chosen, and embedded fluently into sentences — not dumped in and left unexplained.
  • Sophisticated method analysis: The answer names specific techniques (free indirect discourse, dash-interrupted syntax, structural reduction) and explains how they create the effect, not just that they do.
  • Effect on the reader is specific: Instead of vague phrases like "the reader feels scared," it pinpoints exact responses — "suffocating sense of helplessness," "sympathy and frustrated exasperation simultaneously."
  • Critical evaluation with counter-argument: The third paragraph challenges the word "completely" in the statement, offering an alternative reading (dark comedy, self-awareness). This is what makes it an evaluation, not just an analysis.
  • Uses evidence from across the passage: References the opening, the progression, and specific moments — not just one section.

Weak Answer

I agree that the writer makes the reader feel the narrator's fear is completely overwhelming. The writer uses techniques like repetition and short sentences to show the fear. ❌ Techniques named but not demonstrated with evidence or analysed — this is a feature spot, not evaluation.

The narrator is very scared. ❌ Paraphrase, not analysis. No evidence. No method. Tells us nothing the examiner doesn't already know.

There is also a lot of description which shows how he feels. ❌ Vague — what description? What does it show? "A lot of description" is not a method.

The reader feels scared too because the writing is effective. ❌ Circular reasoning. Saying the writing is "effective" is not the same as explaining HOW or WHY it is effective.

Overall, the writer does make the fear feel overwhelming throughout the passage. ❌ Conclusion adds nothing new. The answer simply agrees with the statement without ever challenging, qualifying, or critically engaging with it.

Why this answer scores poorly:

  • No quotations at all — you cannot score above Developing without textual evidence.
  • No method analysis — techniques are named ("repetition," "short sentences") but never connected to a specific quote or explained.
  • No evaluation — the answer simply agrees without questioning the statement. There is no critical voice.
  • Vague reader response — "the reader feels scared" is too generic. The examiner wants to know how the writer makes the reader feel this way.
  • Very short — this answer could be written in 5 minutes. It doesn't reflect 25–30 minutes of thought.

Common Mistakes

  • Simply agreeing with the statement and never challenging it. The question says "to what extent" — this is an invitation to consider where the statement is accurate and where it might be incomplete, exaggerated, or too simple. Answers that only agree tend to plateau at Developing–3 because they lack critical evaluation.
  • Feature-spotting without analysis. Writing "the writer uses a simile" or "there is alliteration" means nothing if you don't quote the specific example, explain how it works, and connect it back to the statement. Naming a technique is not the same as analysing it.
  • Forgetting the reader. This question asks about the effect on the reader. Every point you make should explain what the reader thinks, feels, questions, or experiences. If your paragraph doesn't mention the reader's response, it's incomplete.
  • Using evidence from only one part of the specified text. Examiners want to see that you've engaged with the whole section, not just the first paragraph. Aim to reference at least three different moments across the specified lines — this shows range and demonstrates that you've read critically.

Key Terminology

Using precise terminology shows the examiner you can identify and discuss methods with confidence. Here are the most useful terms for Q4:

  • Evaluate / Evaluation — making a judgement about how effectively the writer achieves something, supported by evidence and reasoning.
  • Writer's method — any deliberate choice the writer makes, including word choice, imagery, sentence structure, narrative voice, tone, or structural techniques.
  • Connotations — the associations and implied meanings of a word beyond its literal definition (e.g., "crept" connotes secrecy and unease).
  • Imagery — language that creates a picture in the reader's mind, including simile, metaphor, and personification.
  • Tone — the overall mood or attitude conveyed by the writing (e.g., anxious, mocking, melancholy).
  • Narrative voice / perspective — who is telling the story and how their viewpoint shapes the reader's experience (first person, third person limited

title: Give / Name (1 mark)
content_html:
1 mark

“Give…” / “Name…”

Used in: Component 1 & Component 2 — All papers and sections

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants one accurate piece of information — a belief, teaching, practice, or term — relevant to what the question asks. Depending on the question, a single word may be enough. Students do not need to write full sentences. One mark is awarded for one correct, relevant response.

New for 2026: This replaces the old “Give two” (2-mark) question. You now only need to give one answer, and a single word or short phrase is often sufficient.

Marking

What You Need
1One correct and relevant answer (word, phrase, or short sentence)
0Nothing correct or relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question carefully — Identify which religion, topic, and type of information is being asked for. Check whether it asks for a belief, a practice, a person, a text, or something else.
  2. 2
    Give one accurate, specific answer — A single word or short phrase is fine. If the question asks “Give one of the Holy books, other than the Qur’an”, writing “Torah” is a perfect answer. Do not add unnecessary explanation.
  3. 3
    Move on quickly — This is worth 1 mark. A few seconds of thought and a few seconds of writing is all you need. Save your time for the higher-mark questions.

Timing

Give / Name — 20–30 seconds

Even quicker than multiple choice — you don’t have four options to read. Write your answer and move on immediately.

Give one of the Holy books, other than the Qur’an. [1 mark]

Full marks

Torah

Examiner: 1/1 — Correct, relevant, and concise. One word is all that’s needed.

Name one of the Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam. [1 mark]

Full marks

Khums

Examiner: 1/1 — Correctly identifies one of the Ten Obligatory Acts.

Give one Christian belief about the afterlife. [1 mark]

Full marks

Christians believe in resurrection.

Examiner: 1/1 — A short sentence is also acceptable. “Resurrection” alone would also score the mark.

Give one Christian belief about the afterlife. [1 mark]

0 marks — too vague

Christians believe in the afterlife.

Examiner: 0/1 — This restates the question rather than giving a specific belief. You need to name something specific: heaven, hell, resurrection, judgement, purgatory, etc.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Restating the question as the answer — “Give one Christian belief about God” answered with “Christians believe in God” scores zero because it doesn’t give a specific belief. Name the actual belief: omnipotence, Trinity, etc.
  • ❌
    Writing too much — This is 1 mark. Writing a full paragraph wastes time you need for higher-value questions. A word or phrase is often enough.
  • ❌
    Answering about the wrong religion — If the question asks about Islam, an answer about Christianity scores zero. Always check which religion is specified in the question.

title: Explain Influence (4 marks)
content_html:
4 marks

“Explain two ways belief in X influences…”

Used in: Component 1 — Beliefs and Teachings only (AO1.2)

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants you to explain how a specific religious belief impacts the life of believers — how it makes them feel, act, or think. This question assesses AO1.2 (influence on individuals, communities, and societies) and only appears in the Beliefs and Teachings section of Paper 1. Two developed points are needed.

Key word: “influences”
This is not asking you to describe the belief itself. It’s asking how the belief changes the way people live. Think about actions, feelings, decisions, and practices that result from holding the belief.

Marking

What You Need
4Two influences, each clearly explained/developed (2 marks × 2)
3Two influences identified, but only one is developed
2Two influences stated without development, or one influence well developed
1One relevant influence stated without development
0Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the belief named in the question — Make sure you understand exactly which belief is being asked about (e.g. judgement, resurrection, Tawhid, akhirah). You must link your answer back to this specific belief.
  2. 2
    State the first influence clearly — Write a clear opening sentence explaining one way this belief affects believers. Use phrasing like “Because Christians believe in [X], they might [Y]” or “This belief influences Muslims to…”
  3. 3
    Develop point 1 — Add a sentence explaining why or how this influence works in practice. Use connecting words like “because”, “this means that”, or “for example”. This is where your second mark for this point comes from.
  4. 4
    State the second influence — Give a genuinely different way the belief impacts believers. Do not repeat the same idea in different words.
  5. 5
    Develop point 2 — Again, add explanation showing how or why this influence plays out in believers’ lives.

Timing

Plan
30s Influence 1 + development
2 min Influence 2 + development
2 min

About four to five minutes. Two short paragraphs. Focus on showing the link between the belief and its real-world impact.

Influence 1 template

“Because [religion] believe in [specific belief], this influences them to [action/feeling/behaviour]. This is because [explanation of why the belief leads to this influence].”

Influence 2 template

“Another way this belief influences [religion] is that [different action/feeling/behaviour]. This means that [further explanation or real-world example].”

Explain two ways in which belief in judgement influences Christians today. [4 marks]

Influence 1 (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

Because Christians believe that God will judge them after death, this influences many to try to live a moral life by following the teachings of Jesus, such as loving their neighbour and caring for the poor. This is because they believe their actions on earth will determine whether they enter heaven or hell, so they are motivated to do good works and avoid sin.

Influence 2 (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

Another way this belief influences Christians is that it can bring them comfort when they see injustice in the world. They believe that even if wrongdoers are not punished in this life, God’s final judgement means that justice will ultimately be served, which helps them to remain faithful and trust in God’s plan.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two distinct influences, each clearly linked back to the belief in judgement and well developed with explanation.

Explain two ways in which belief in the incarnation of Jesus influences Christians. [4 marks]

Weak Answer (1/4)

Describes the belief instead of explaining influence

Christians believe Jesus is the incarnation of God. He came to earth as a human being. This is an important belief for Christians. They celebrate this at Christmas.

Strong Answer (4/4)

Influence 1 + development

Because Christians believe God became human through Jesus, this influences them to see all human life as sacred and valuable. If God chose to take on a human body, then the human body has immense worth, which motivates Christians to care for the sick, the vulnerable, and the unborn.

Influence 2 + development

This belief also influences Christians to celebrate Christmas as one of the most important festivals in the Church calendar. They attend special services, give gifts, and reflect on God’s love for humanity, because the incarnation shows that God was willing to enter the world and share in human suffering.

Examiner: The weak answer merely describes the belief and states it’s important. The strong answer explains how the belief changes behaviour and thinking, with clear development.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing the belief instead of its influence — “Christians believe in judgement” describes the belief. The question asks how this belief influences people. Always answer: “Because they believe X, they do/feel/think Y.”
  • ❌
    Giving the same influence twice — “They go to church” and “they attend worship services” are the same point in different words. Make sure your two influences are genuinely different.
  • ❌
    Not developing the points — Stating an influence without explaining why or how it works only earns half the available marks. Always add at least one sentence of explanation.
  • ❌
    Losing the link to the specific belief — Make sure each point clearly ties back to the named belief. If the question asks about “belief in the resurrection”, don’t drift into general points about being a good person.

title: Explain Similarities & Differences (4 marks)
content_html:
4 marks

“Explain two similar/different…”

Used in: Component 1 Practices (differences) & Component 2 Themes (similarities or differences) — AO1.3

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants two developed points that show either similarities or differences between religious beliefs, practices, or viewpoints. In Paper 1 Practices, the question will always ask for differences. In Paper 2 Themes, it could ask for either similarities or differences. Each point needs to be stated and then developed for full marks.

Who can you compare?
  • Two denominations or schools of thought within the same religion (e.g. Catholic vs Methodist)
  • Two different religions (e.g. Christianity vs Islam)
  • In Themes: the question may specify “the main religious tradition of Great Britain” (Christianity) — one view must then be explicitly Christian
You do not need to name denominations specifically. It is acceptable to write “some Christians…” and “other Christians…”

Marking

What You Need
4Two points of similarity/difference, each with clear development (2 marks × 2)
3Two points identified, but only one is developed
2Two points stated without development, or one point well developed
1One relevant point stated without development
0Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Check whether the question asks for similarities or differences — This determines the structure of your answer. Also check whether the question specifies religions or allows you to choose.
  2. 2
    Choose two groups or viewpoints to compare — For differences in Practices, think about two different ways the same practice is carried out (e.g. Catholic vs Methodist baptism). For Themes, think about two different perspectives on the issue.
  3. 3
    State the first similarity or difference clearly — Write a clear opening sentence identifying the first group and their belief/practice. For example: “Some Christians believe that…” or “In Catholicism, the practice of…”
  4. 4
    Develop point 1 — Add a sentence explaining why this group holds this view, or what it means in practice. Use “because”, “this is because”, or “this means that” to signal development.
  5. 5
    State and develop the second point — For differences, use a contrasting phrase: “In contrast…”, “However…”, “On the other hand…”. For similarities, use: “Similarly…”, “In the same way…”. Then develop with an explanation.

Timing

Plan
30s Point 1 + development
2 min Point 2 + development
2 min

About four to five minutes. Two short paragraphs of two to three sentences each. The marks reward clarity and genuine comparison, not length.

Differences template

“[Group A] believe/practise [X]. This is because [reason/theological basis].
In contrast, [Group B] believe/practise [Y]. This is because [different reason/theological basis].”

Similarities template

“[Group A] believe that [X]. This is because [reason/theological basis].
Similarly, [Group B] also believe that [X/related idea]. This is because [shared or parallel reason].”

Differences example (Practices)

Explain two different ways in which Christians practise baptism. [4 marks]

Point 1 (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

In the Roman Catholic Church, baptism is usually performed on infants by pouring water over the baby’s head. This is because Catholics believe baptism removes original sin, so it should happen as soon as possible after birth to welcome the child into the Church and God’s family.

Point 2 contrasting (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

In contrast, Baptists practise believer’s baptism, where adults are fully immersed in water. This is because they believe baptism should be a conscious, personal choice to follow Jesus, and that the act of going under the water symbolises dying to the old life and rising to a new one.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two genuinely different ways of practising baptism, each clearly developed with theological reasoning.

Similarities example (Themes)

Explain two similar religious beliefs about the sanctity of life. [4 marks]

Point 1 (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

Christians believe that all human life is sacred because humans were created in the image of God (imago Dei). This means that life should be protected from conception to natural death, which is why many Christians oppose practices like abortion and euthanasia.

Point 2 similar (1 mark) + Development (1 mark)

Similarly, Muslims believe that life is sacred because it is a gift from Allah and only He has the right to take it away. The Qur’an teaches that taking a life unjustly is like killing all of humanity, which reinforces the Muslim belief that life must be protected and respected.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two similar beliefs from different religions, each with a clear development explaining why the belief is held.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not making the comparison clear — The examiner needs to see that your two points are genuinely similar or different. Use comparison language: “In contrast…”, “However…”, “Similarly…”, “In the same way…”
  • ❌
    Giving similarities when differences are asked for (or vice versa) — Read the question carefully. If it says “different”, your two points must show contrast. If it says “similar”, they must show agreement.
  • ❌
    Not developing the points — Stating that “Catholics baptise babies and Baptists baptise adults” only earns 2 marks. You need to explain why each group does this to earn the development marks.
  • ❌
    Forgetting the Christianity requirement in Themes — When a Themes question asks about “the main religious tradition of Great Britain”, one of your viewpoints must be explicitly Christian.
