title: Explain with Sources of Authority (6 marks)
content_html:
6 marks

“Explain two beliefs/teachings… Refer to a source of authority.”

Used in: Component 1 & Component 2 — All papers and sections (AO1.1)

What the Examiner Wants

The examiner wants two developed points about beliefs, teachings, or practices, plus a named source of authority with a brief explanation of how it applies to the question. This question always assesses AO1.1 — it will never ask for influences, differences, or similarities. The question will always include the instruction: “Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.”

What counts as a source of authority?
  • Holy books: the Bible, Qur’an, Guru Granth Sahib, Torah, and sub-sections such as the Ten Commandments, Surah 96, the Parables
  • Religious leaders: founders (e.g. Prophet Muhammad, the Buddha), leaders of the faith (e.g. the Pope, Dalai Lama), or influential figures (e.g. Martin Luther King, Rabbi Sachs)
  • Religious writings: commentaries (e.g. the Mishnah), law (e.g. Shari’ah), set prayers (e.g. Lord’s Prayer), hymns
References can be paraphrased — students do not need to cite chapter and verse.

Marking

AreaWhat You Need
First belief2Detailed explanation of a relevant and accurate teaching
1Simple explanation of a relevant and accurate teaching
Second belief2Detailed explanation of a relevant and accurate teaching
1Simple explanation of a relevant and accurate teaching
Source of authority2Names a relevant source and applies it to the question
1Names a relevant source without application, or applies a source without naming it
No relevant source

Total: up to 6 marks (2 + 2 + 2)

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the topic and religion — Read the question carefully. Note what beliefs or teachings are being asked about. In Themes, you can use beliefs from the same religious tradition or from two different religions.
  2. 2
    Write point 1: state and explain — State a relevant belief or teaching clearly, then add explanation. Include your named source of authority here with a brief application. This is the recommended place for it.
  3. 3
    Apply the source — After naming the source, briefly explain how or why it connects to the point you are making. For example: “In the Bible it says humans were made in God’s image, which means that all life is sacred and should be protected.”
  4. 4
    Write point 2: state and explain — Give a second, different belief or teaching on the same topic. Develop it with explanation. You do not need a second source here, but you can include one if it strengthens your answer.
Recommended structure:
  1. Point → Explain → Named source + brief application
  2. Point → Explain

Timing

Plan
30s Point 1 + source
3.5 min Point 2
2.5 min

About six to seven minutes. Spend slightly longer on the first point where you include the source of authority. Two substantial paragraphs.

Point 1 + Source (recommended)

“[Religion] teach that [specific belief/teaching]. This means [explanation/development]. In [source name] it says [paraphrase or quote], which shows that [application to the question].”

Point 2

“[Religion] also teach that [different belief/teaching]. This is because [explanation/development/consequence for believers].”

Explain two Christian beliefs about the sanctity of life. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer. [6 marks]

Point 1 (2 marks) + Named source with application (2 marks)

Some Christians would be against violence because they believe that life is sacred. They believe this because in the Bible it says humans were made in God’s image and if something is in God’s image it should not be destroyed. This teaching from Genesis shows that all human life has a special, God-given value that must be respected and protected.

Point 2 (2 marks)

Christians also believe that only God has the authority to give and take life. This means that practices like euthanasia and abortion are seen by many Christians as wrong because they involve humans making decisions about life and death that should be God’s alone, which is why the Catholic Church teaches that life must be protected from conception to natural death.

Examiner: 6/6 — Two developed points with a named source (the Bible / Genesis) clearly applied to the argument. The source is named and its relevance explained.

Explain two Muslim beliefs about prophethood. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer. [6 marks]

Weak Answer (2/6)

No named source, limited development

Muslims believe in prophets. They think prophets were sent by God to teach people. Muhammad was the last prophet. Muslims believe he was very important and follow his teachings.

Strong Answer (6/6)

Point 1 + named source + application

Muslims believe that Allah sent prophets throughout history to guide humanity to the right path, including Ibrahim, Musa, Isa, and Muhammad. Muhammad is considered the “Seal of the Prophets” — the Qur’an states in Surah 33:40 that Muhammad is the last messenger, meaning no more prophets will come after him. This is significant because it means the Qur’an is the final and complete revelation from God.

Point 2 + development

Muslims also believe that all prophets delivered the same core message — that there is one God (Tawhid) and people should submit to His will. This means that Muslims respect all the prophets, not just Muhammad, and see them as part of a continuous chain of guidance. This belief in the unity of the prophetic message reinforces the importance of Tawhid in Islam.

Examiner: The weak answer has no named source and only simple, undeveloped points. The strong answer names the Qur’an (Surah 33:40) and explains how it applies, with two well-developed points.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Forgetting the source of authority entirely — This costs up to 2 marks. Always include at least one named source. Even a paraphrase counts, as long as you name where it comes from (e.g. “the Bible says…”, “the Qur’an teaches…”).
  • ❌
    Naming the source but not applying it — Writing “it says in the Bible” without explaining how this connects to your point only earns 1 of the 2 source marks. Always add a brief explanation of relevance.
  • ❌
    Using vague or generic references — “A holy book says life is important” is too vague. Name the specific source: the Bible, the Qur’an, the Ten Commandments, the Hadith, the Lord’s Prayer, etc.
  • ❌
    Only writing one point — You need two developed beliefs or teachings for full marks. One excellent point still caps you at 4 out of 6.
← Similarities & Differences (4 marks) Evaluate a Statement (12 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Multiple Choice 1 mark Give / Name 1 mark Explain Influence 4 marks Explain Similarities & Differences 4 marks Evaluate a Statement 12 marks
Quick Reference
6–7 minutes

Structure

  1. Point 1 + explain
  2. Named source + application
  3. Point 2 + explain

Source Marks

Named + applied = 2
Named only = 1
Applied only = 1

title: Quote Analysis — 4 marks
content_html:
4 marks

Quote Analysis

Used in: Paper 1 Section A (Shakespeare), Paper 1 Section B (19th-century novel), Paper 2 Section A (modern prose/drama)

What the Examiner Wants

Quote analysis questions ask you to look closely at a specific moment in the text — often a short extract or a single quotation highlighted in the question. The examiner wants to see you identifying a language technique, explaining the effect it creates on the reader, and linking your analysis to the writer's intentions or context. This is (critical response) and (language/form/structure) working together.

Key Fact

AO2 is the dominant assessment objective here. Simply saying what happens (AO1 plot summary) without analysing HOW language works will not score well. Always zoom in on specific words and techniques.

Mark Scheme Levels

What You Need
4Clear technique identified, effect explained with subject terminology, brief contextual link or inference about writer's intention
3Technique identified and effect explained, but contextual link is thin or absent
2Some awareness of technique or effect, but mainly descriptive or paraphrase-based
1Simple relevant comment on the text with no technical language
0Nothing relevant

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Identify the technique — Name the specific literary or language technique the writer is using (e.g. metaphor, sibilance, semantic field, juxtaposition). Be precise — “the writer uses language” is not enough.
  2. 2
    Embed the quotation — Weave a short, focused quotation into your sentence rather than copying out long chunks. One to five words is usually enough to anchor your point.
  3. 3
    Explain the effect — What does this technique make the reader feel, think, or understand? Use phrases like “this suggests”, “this implies”, or “the effect is” to signal your analysis.
  4. 4
    Link to context or intention — Connect your analysis to the writer’s purpose or historical/social context. Why might the writer have made this choice? What were they trying to show about society, a character, or a theme?

Timing

Read & select
1 min Write
3 min Check
1 min

You have roughly 4–5 minutes for a 4-mark quote analysis response. Keep it tight: one technique, one embedded quote, one explanation of effect, one contextual link. Do not write an essay — save your time for the higher-mark questions.

Point

“[Writer] uses [technique] when [character/narrator] says ‘[short quote]’…”

Effect

“This suggests / implies / conveys [effect on reader / meaning]…”

Context Link

“[Writer] may have chosen this because [contextual reason / writer’s intention]…”

How does Priestley use language to present Mr Birling in this extract? [4 marks]
(Extract includes: “a man has to make his own way”)

Technique + embedded quote

Priestley uses an imperative tone through Birling’s assertion that “a man has to make his own way”, presenting him as someone who believes firmly in individual responsibility over community.

Effect explained

The modal verb “has” implies necessity and inevitability, suggesting Birling sees self-interest not just as sensible but as a law of nature — a view the inspector (and Priestley) will systematically undermine.

Context link

Writing in 1945 but setting the play in 1912, Priestley uses Birling to critique the capitalist attitudes that he believed had contributed to the social inequalities driving two world wars.

Examiner: 4/4 — Clear technique, embedded quotation, well-explained effect, strong contextual link.

How does Priestley use language to present Mr Birling? [4 marks]

Weak Answer

Plot retelling, no technique named

Mr Birling says “a man has to make his own way”. This shows he is selfish and doesn’t care about other people. He is a bad person.

Strong Answer

Technique + effect + context

Priestley uses an imperative through Birling’s declaration that “a man has to make his own way”. The modal verb “has” conveys a sense of absolute necessity, implying Birling views self-reliance not as a choice but as a moral law. Priestley uses this to satirise the capitalist ruling class whose individualism, he believed, caused the social suffering symbolised by Eva Smith.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Naming a technique without explaining the effect — “Priestley uses a metaphor” scores 1 mark at most. You must say what that metaphor does to the reader.
  • ✗
    Copying out a long quotation — Examiners reward analysis, not transcription. Embed just the key words so your explanation is the focus.
  • ✗
    Telling the story — AO2 is about HOW the writer writes, not WHAT happens in the text. Avoid “this shows he is mean” without explaining the language that creates that impression.
  • ✗
    Skipping the context link — For 4 marks you need all four elements. A brief contextual sentence lifts a 3-mark answer to 4.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

P-E-E-C Structure

  1. Point (technique + quote)
  2. Effect (what it does)
  3. Elaborate (deeper meaning)
  4. Context link

Key AOs

  • Critical response & reference
  • Language/form/structure analysis
  • Context link

title: Extract Analysis — 8 marks
content_html:
8 marks

Extract Analysis

Used in: Paper 1 Section A (Shakespeare), Paper 2 Section A (modern prose/drama)

What the Examiner Wants

Extract analysis questions give you a passage from the text and ask how the writer uses language and structure to achieve a particular effect. You are expected to analyse specific language choices (AO2) while also showing you understand the text’s meaning and themes (AO1). The focus is on the extract itself, though brief links beyond it can strengthen your response.

Key Fact

AO2 is the primary focus: examiners are looking for analysis of language (word choice, imagery, tone) and structure (how the extract is organised, sentence length, paragraph position). Do not write a general essay about the theme — anchor every point to the text.

Mark Scheme Levels

LevelWhat You Need
7–8MasteringPerceptive, detailed analysis. Confident use of subject terminology. Convincing interpretation of writer’s methods and their effects.
5–6SecureClear explanation of how the writer uses language/structure. Relevant use of subject terminology to support analysis.
3–4DevelopingSome understanding of how language is used. Attempts to comment on effect. Terminology may be applied inconsistently.
1–2EmergingSimple comments. Mostly paraphrase or assertion without evidence of analysis.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the question focus — What does the question ask you to explore? A character’s emotions? The atmosphere? A relationship? Keep that focus in mind throughout.
  2. 2
    Annotate the extract — Underline three to four specific moments: a striking phrase, a pattern (e.g. repeated imagery), a structural choice (e.g. short sentence at a turning point). Each annotation becomes a paragraph.
  3. 3
    Write focused analytical paragraphs — For each point: name the technique, embed a short quotation, explain the effect on the reader, and explore the writer’s intention. Aim for two to three substantial paragraphs.
  4. 4
    Comment on structure — As well as language, consider how the extract is structured. Where does tension build? What is the effect of the extract’s opening or closing lines? Does sentence length vary for effect?
  5. 5
    Link beyond the extract briefly — A sentence or two connecting the extract to a wider theme or character development shows you know the whole text and can elevate a Secure to Mastering response.

Timing

Read & annotate
2 min Write
7 min Check & extend
1 min

Spend around 10 minutes on an 8-mark extract question. Use two minutes to read and annotate, then seven minutes writing. Aim for two or three well-developed paragraphs rather than five thin ones.

Language Point

“[Writer] creates [effect] through [technique]. The [word/phrase] ‘[quote]’ suggests [meaning/effect], implying [deeper interpretation].”

Structure Point

“Structurally, [writer] places [detail] at the [opening/end/centre] of the extract. This [effect], mirroring [character’s state/theme].”

How does Dickens use language and structure in this extract to present Scrooge’s transformation? [8 marks]

Language: technique + effect + interpretation

Dickens presents Scrooge’s transformation through a shift in his use of exclamatory language. Where earlier passages are characterised by cold, clipped commands, the extract sees Scrooge cry out “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel”. The anaphoric repetition of “I am” conveys an almost childlike self-discovery — as though Scrooge is surprised by his own capacity for joy, having suppressed it for decades.

Structure: sentence length / pace

Structurally, Dickens accelerates the pace in this extract through a series of short, exclamatory sentences. The staccato rhythm — “Glorious. Splendid. Magnificent.” — mimics the burst of energy Scrooge feels, contrasting sharply with the measured, slow prose of the opening stave. This structural shift signals to the reader that the transformation is not just emotional but physical: Scrooge is literally reanimated.

Examiner: 7–8 — Perceptive analysis of language and structure, confident use of terminology (anaphora, staccato, stave), convincing interpretation.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Analysing only language, not structure — AO2 covers both language AND form/structure. Always include at least one structural observation (sentence length, positioning, shifts in tone, paragraph breaks).
  • ✗
    Writing a general essay about the theme — You must be anchored in the given extract. Every paragraph must reference specific words or moments from the passage.
  • ✗
    Too many thin points — Two or three perceptive, well-developed paragraphs score higher than five surface-level observations. Depth beats breadth.
  • ✗
    Vague effect statements — “This creates tension” needs developing. Tension in whom? What does it make the reader anticipate? Push every analysis one sentence further.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10 min total

Structure

  1. Read & annotate (3–4 moments)
  2. 2–3 language paragraphs
  3. 1 structure paragraph
  4. Brief link beyond extract

Key AOs

  • Critical response
  • Language & structure (primary)

title: Extended Response — 12 marks
content_html:
12 marks

Extended Response

Used in: Paper 1 Section A (Shakespeare), Paper 1 Section B (19th-century novel), Paper 2 Section A (modern prose/drama)

What the Examiner Wants

The 12-mark extended response asks you to explore how a writer presents a character, theme, or relationship across the whole text (or in relation to a given extract plus beyond). You need to select your own evidence and build a sustained, analytical argument. This tests (your own interpretation, supported by evidence) and (analysis of language, form, and structure) equally.

Key Fact

You must show awareness of the whole text, not just one part. Use at least two or three separate moments from different points in the text to show a character or theme developing, changing, or remaining consistent.

Mark Scheme Levels

LevelWhat You Need
10–12MasteringPerceptive, well-structured argument. Convincing analysis of methods. Evidence selected from across the text. Subject terminology used accurately and meaningfully.
7–9SecureClear, explained analysis. Evidence from different points in the text. Relevant use of terminology.
4–6DevelopingSome relevant points. Evidence used but analysis may be surface-level. Partial coverage of the text.
1–3EmergingSimple observations. Limited or no textual evidence. Mainly plot retelling.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Plan before you write — Spend two minutes jotting down three to four moments from the text that show the character or theme in different ways. Think about beginning, middle, and end of the text for variety.
  2. 2
    Write a direct opening — State your main argument in your opening sentence. Do not rewrite the question or start with a general statement. Tell the examiner your interpretation straight away.
  3. 3
    Write analytical paragraphs (P-E-E-C) — For each moment you selected: make a Point about the character/theme, provide an Embedded quotation, Explain the effect of specific language choices, make a Context link to writer’s purpose or social/historical context.
  4. 4
    Show development or contrast — Does the character change? Does the theme develop? The strongest responses track a journey across the text, not just list separate observations.
  5. 5
    Write a brief conclusion — One or two sentences restating your overall interpretation in light of your analysis. Avoid simply listing what you said — reach a final judgement.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
11 min Conclude & check
2 min

Approximately 15 minutes for a 12-mark question. Three well-developed paragraphs (each around 100–130 words) with a brief introduction and conclusion is the target. Do not exceed this — the essay-length questions are worth more marks per minute.

How does Priestley present the theme of responsibility in An Inspector Calls? [12 marks]

Direct opening argument

Priestley presents responsibility as a moral obligation that the older generation wilfully avoids, using the younger characters and the Inspector to argue that collective accountability is the only path to social justice.

Paragraph 1: language analysis

Birling’s dismissal of shared responsibility is established early through his bombastic monologue, in which he declares that “a man has to make his own way”. The modal verb “has” positions individualism as natural law rather than a choice, revealing a world view Priestley regarded as the root cause of social inequality. This is deliberately exposed as dangerous — Birling’s confident pronouncements are shown to be wrong by the play’s end.

Paragraph 2: development / contrast

In contrast, Sheila’s arc enacts the acceptance of responsibility Priestley advocates. After the Inspector’s interrogation, she tells her parents “I know I’m to blame and I’m desperately sorry”. The adverb “desperately” conveys genuine remorse rather than polite regret, suggesting that true responsibility requires emotional engagement, not just acknowledgement. Priestley may be implying that the younger generation, represented by Sheila, still has the capacity for moral growth.

Brief conclusion

Ultimately, Priestley uses the contrast between the Birlings’ resistance and Sheila’s transformation to argue that responsibility is a choice society must consciously make — a message given urgent relevance by the play’s 1945 audience, rebuilding after the collective catastrophe of the Second World War.

Examiner: 11–12 — Clear argument sustained across the text, perceptive language analysis, strong contextual links.

Weak Opening

Restates question, vague

In An Inspector Calls, Priestley presents responsibility in many different ways throughout the play.

Strong Opening

Direct argument from line one

Priestley presents responsibility as a moral choice that the older Birlings evade while the younger generation — Sheila and Eric — begin to embrace it, suggesting that social change is possible but only through genuine self-reflection.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Using only one part of the text — A 12-mark response must show knowledge of the whole text. Draw evidence from at least two or three distinct moments.
  • ✗
    Retelling the plot — “Then the Inspector arrives and asks everyone questions” is AO1 plot summary, not analysis. Every sentence should be making an analytical point.
  • ✗
    Forgetting context — AO3 context marks are available here. Link to the writer’s historical/social context in at least one or two paragraphs.
  • ✗
    Vague opening sentence — “Priestley presents responsibility in many ways” wastes your first sentence. State your argument immediately.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
15 min total

Structure

  1. Direct opening argument
  2. 3 analytical paragraphs (P-E-E-C)
  3. Brief conclusion

Key AOs

  • Argument + evidence
  • Language analysis
  • Context links

title: Essay Response — 30 + 4 SPaG marks
content_html:
30 + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks

Essay Response

Paper 1 Section A (Shakespeare, 30+4 spelling, punctuation and grammar) • Paper 1 Section B (19th-century novel, 30+4 spelling, punctuation and grammar) • Paper 2 Section A (modern prose/drama, 30 marks)

What the Examiner Wants

The essay response is the highest-value question on each paper. You must write a sustained analytical essay exploring a theme, character, relationship, or writer’s method across the whole text. (your argument and evidence), (language analysis), and (context) all count. On Paper 1 and Paper 2 Section A, an additional 4 marks are awarded for spelling, punctuation and grammar — spelling, punctuation, and grammar.

Key Fact

spelling, punctuation and grammar marks (Paper 1 both sections and Paper 2 Section A only): these 4 marks reward accurate spelling of subject-specific vocabulary, correct use of punctuation (especially commas and apostrophes), and grammatically sound sentences. They are easy to earn if you proofread.

Key Fact

Paper 2 Section A (modern prose/drama) has two questions: one on a named character and one on a theme. You choose one. Both are 30 marks but do NOT carry spelling, punctuation and grammar marks — those are on Paper 2 Section A only for the prose/drama text you studied.

Mark Scheme Levels (30 marks)

LevelWhat You Need
25–30MasteringPerceptive, coherent argument. Convincing analysis of language/structure/form. Well-selected evidence from across the text. Assured use of terminology. Strong contextual understanding (AO3).
19–24SecureClear, explained analysis. Good range of evidence. Relevant terminology. Context linked to the text’s meaning.
13–18DevelopingSome analytical points with supporting evidence. Coverage of the text but analysis may be surface-level or uneven.
7–12EmergingSimple observations with limited evidence. Mostly descriptive or plot-based.
1–6FoundationVery basic response. Little evidence. No clear argument.

Paper 1 vs Paper 2: Key Differences

FeaturePaper 1Paper 2 Sec A
TextsShakespeare + 19th-century novelModern prose or drama
Question formatExtract given + “and the rest of the play/novel”No extract — whole text essay
spelling, punctuation and grammar marksYes (4 marks, both sections)Yes (4 marks, Section A only)
Time suggested~50 min per section~45 min

On Paper 1, you are given an extract to analyse first, then must go “beyond” it to discuss the rest of the text. On Paper 2 Section A, you write a whole-text essay with no extract provided — your choice of evidence is entirely your own.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Decode the question carefully — Identify the key word (How? Why? To what extent?), the focus (character, theme, method), and any specific instruction (“starting with this extract”).
  2. 2
    Plan in two minutes — Note four or five key moments from across the text and a clear overarching argument. Your plan does not need full sentences — key words, moments, and quotes are enough.
  3. 3
    Write a one-sentence thesis opening — State your argument directly. This tells the examiner your interpretation immediately and gives your essay a clear direction.
  4. 4
    Write four to five analytical paragraphs — Each paragraph: Point (topic sentence), Evidence (embedded quotation), Explanation (language technique + effect), Context (writer’s purpose/historical context). Show development: how does the theme/character shift across the text?
  5. 5
    Write a concise conclusion — Return to your thesis. Reflect on what your analysis shows about the writer’s overall message. Avoid introducing new evidence here.
  6. 6
    Proofread for spelling, punctuation and grammar (Paper 1 / Paper 2 Sec A) — In the final two minutes, scan for spelling errors (especially names: Priestley, Dickens, Macbeth), misplaced apostrophes, and sentence fragments. spelling, punctuation and grammar marks are straightforward to earn.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
40 min Conclude & spelling, punctuation and grammar
8 min

Aim for 45–50 minutes on the 30-mark essay. Four to five developed paragraphs (each 120–150 words) plus introduction and conclusion. Quality over quantity — a focused 700-word essay with strong analysis beats a 1,200-word plot summary.

How does Shakespeare present ambition in Macbeth? Write about: how ambition is presented in this extract and how it is presented in the play as a whole. [30 + 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks]

Thesis: one sentence, clear argument

Shakespeare presents ambition as an inherently destructive force that, once unleashed, corrupts not only the individual but all those around them, transforming Macbeth from a celebrated warrior into a tyrant driven by fear and paranoia.

Paragraph: P-E-E-C in action

In the extract, Macbeth’s ambition is conveyed through the soliloquy’s imagery of violence: the “dagger of the mind” is a metaphor that externalises his murderous intent, making his ambition a tangible, almost physical presence. The phrase “proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain” suggests a feverish loss of rational control, implying that ambition in Shakespeare’s world is a kind of madness. Contextually, Jacobean audiences would have recognised the link between unchecked ambition and disorder — James I, for whom the play may have been performed, had survived the Gunpowder Plot, a real act of violent political ambition only months earlier.

Examiner: Strong Secure/Mastering opening. Clear thesis, confident AO2 analysis, relevant AO3 contextual link.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Starting with a vague introduction — “Shakespeare wrote Macbeth in the Jacobean era” wastes your opening. State your argument in sentence one.
  • ✗
    Forgetting spelling, punctuation and grammar under time pressure — Reserve two minutes at the end specifically for proofreading. These 4 marks are easier to earn than analytical marks and students often lose them through rushing.
  • ✗
    Only writing about the extract (Paper 1) — Paper 1 questions explicitly ask you to write about the extract AND the rest of the text. Evidence from elsewhere in the play/novel is required for Secure and above.
  • ✗
    Context as background information only — Don’t just mention when the text was written. Connect the context directly to the language choices: why would the writer make THIS choice for THAT audience at THAT time?
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
50 min total

Structure

  1. Thesis opening (1 sentence)
  2. 4–5 P-E-E-C paragraphs
  3. Conclusion
  4. spelling, punctuation and grammar proofread (2 min)

Key AOs

  • Argument + evidence
  • Language/structure/form
  • Context
  • spelling, punctuation and grammar: 4 marks (P1 + P2 Sec A)

title: Anthology Comparison — 30 marks
content_html:
30 marks

Anthology Comparison (Poetry)

Used in: Paper 2 Section B — Poetry Anthology

What the Examiner Wants

The anthology comparison question gives you one named poem from the AQA anthology and asks you to compare it with another poem of your choice from the same cluster. You must analyse how both poets present a theme (such as conflict, love, or power), using language analysis (AO2) and contextual understanding (AO3) to build a sustained comparison (AO1).

Key Fact

You choose which poem to compare it with. Spend 30 seconds deciding which poem gives you the most to say about the given theme — don’t just pick your favourite. The best comparisons show both similarity and difference.

Mark Scheme Levels (30 marks)

LevelWhat You Need
25–30MasteringPerceptive comparison of both poems. Convincing analysis of how each poet uses language/form/structure. Well-integrated contextual links. Argument is maintained throughout.
19–24SecureClear comparison with evidence from both poems. Explained analysis of language. Some contextual understanding.
13–18DevelopingPoints made about both poems but comparison may be implicit or uneven. Some language analysis.
7–12EmergingSimple points about one or both poems. Limited evidence. Mostly descriptive.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose your second poem — Pick the poem from the same cluster that gives you the richest comparison for the stated theme. Consider both similarities AND differences for a nuanced response.
  2. 2
    Plan: two columns — Draw a quick two-column plan: left column for the named poem, right for your chosen poem. Note two or three language techniques from each, plus one structural or form observation each.
  3. 3
    Write a comparative opening — Name both poems, state the theme, and give your overarching comparison argument in one or two sentences. Avoid treating the poems separately — connect them from the start.
  4. 4
    Write comparative paragraphs — Each paragraph should discuss BOTH poems together around a shared idea, not one poem then the other in separate blocks. Use connectives: “Similarly…”, “In contrast…”, “Whereas [Poem A]… [Poem B]…”, “Both poets…”
  5. 5
    Analyse language and form in both poems — Comment on specific words, imagery, and techniques in each poem. Also consider form and structure: rhyme scheme, free verse, voice, stanza length. These are often where the comparison is most interesting.
  6. 6
    Link to context for each poet — Brief contextual links (poet’s background, time of writing, social/historical circumstances) can elevate Secure to Mastering. Keep each context link brief but pointed.

Timing

Choose + plan
3 min Write
38 min Conclude & check
4 min

Allow approximately 45 minutes. Four to five paragraphs comparing both poems is the target. The most common mistake is running out of time on the named poem and barely discussing the second — weave them together from the start to prevent this.

Introducing similarity

“Both [Poem A] and [Poem B] present [theme] through [shared technique/idea]…”

“Like [Poet A], [Poet B] uses [technique] to suggest…”

Introducing contrast

“In contrast, whereas [Poem A] [approach], [Poem B] [different approach]…”

“While [Poet A] presents [theme] as [X], [Poet B] portrays it as [Y]…”

Comparing methods

“[Poet A] achieves [effect] through [technique], while [Poet B] relies instead on [technique]…”

Compare how poets present the effects of conflict. You must compare the poem printed below with one other poem from the anthology you have studied.
[Named poem: “Remains” by Simon Armitage]

Comparative opening: both poems + argument

Both “Remains” by Simon Armitage and “War Photographer” by Carol Ann Duffy explore the lasting psychological damage inflicted on those who witness conflict, suggesting that the effects of war extend far beyond the battlefield and into the domestic lives of those who return.

Comparative paragraph: weaving both poems together

Armitage uses visceral, colloquial language to convey the soldier’s inability to escape his memories: the looter’s image is described as “dug in behind enemy lines”, a military metaphor that suggests the trauma is now itself an occupying force in the speaker’s mind. Similarly, Duffy’s photographer finds that the suffering he has witnessed “half-formed ghost[s]” in his developing trays — the spectral imagery implying that the dead are never fully absent. Where Armitage emphasises the visceral, unprocessed nature of the trauma through present-tense narration, Duffy’s third-person perspective creates a sense of detachment that reflects how the photographer must emotionally distance himself to survive.

Examiner: Mastering — Integrated comparison, confident language analysis across both poems, distinct observations about form and perspective.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Writing about each poem separately — A “Poem A then Poem B” structure earns Developing at best. Examiners want to see continuous comparison. Weave both poems into every paragraph.
  • ✗
    Choosing a poem you can’t quote accurately — In the exam you must rely on memory for your chosen poem. Pick one you know well and have practised quoting from.
  • ✗
    Focusing only on content, not methods — “Both poems are about war” is not enough. You must compare HOW language, structure, and form are used to present the theme.
  • ✗
    Uneven coverage of the two poems — Both poems should receive broadly equal analytical attention. If you notice you’ve written three paragraphs on the named poem and only one on your choice, adjust mid-essay.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
45 min total

Structure

  1. Choose your poem (30 sec)
  2. Two-column plan
  3. Comparative opening
  4. 4–5 paragraphs (both poems per para)
  5. Conclusion

Connectives

  • Both poets…
  • Similarly… / Likewise…
  • In contrast… / Whereas…
  • While [A] presents… [B]…

title: Unseen Poetry Analysis — 24 marks
content_html:
24 marks

Unseen Poetry Analysis

Used in: Paper 2 Section C — Question 1 (Unseen Poetry)

What the Examiner Wants

The unseen poetry analysis question asks you to respond to a poem you have never studied before. You are given the poem in the exam paper. The examiner wants to see that you can apply your analytical skills to an unfamiliar text — identifying how language, structure, and form create meaning and effect. There is no “right answer”: your personal interpretation, backed by evidence, is exactly what is being tested.

Key Fact

You cannot revise the content of the unseen poem — but you CAN revise the skills. Practise applying language and structure analysis to poems you haven’t studied. The more you practise the process, the more confident you’ll be in the exam.

Mark Scheme Levels (24 marks)

LevelWhat You Need
21–24MasteringPerceptive, sensitive analysis of how language, structure, and form work together. Convincing personal interpretation supported by well-chosen evidence. Confident use of subject terminology.
15–20SecureClear explanation of how the poet uses language and structure. Relevant evidence and terminology. Some awareness of form.
9–14DevelopingSome analytical points with evidence. Terminology used but may not always enhance the analysis.
1–8EmergingSimple observations. Limited evidence. Mainly descriptive or focused on subject matter rather than method.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the poem twice — First read: get the overall meaning and mood. Second read: annotate for language (striking words, techniques, imagery) and structure (stanza length, rhyme, line breaks, shifts in tone or voice).
  2. 2
    Identify the tone and theme — What is the poem’s emotional register? (Melancholic? Angry? Celebratory?) What is the central idea or message? This gives your analysis a direction before you start writing.
  3. 3
    Choose three to four moments to analyse — Select specific moments where the language is particularly interesting, surprising, or purposeful. Avoid trying to comment on every single line — depth beats breadth.
  4. 4
    Analyse language and structure together — For each moment, name the technique, embed the quotation, explain the effect, and say WHY the poet might have made that choice. Also comment on at least one structural feature (e.g. enjambment, caesura, stanza breaks, the volta if it’s a sonnet).
  5. 5
    Comment on form — Is it a sonnet, ballad, free verse, dramatic monologue? Does the form reinforce or contrast the content? Even one clear observation about form can earn marks.
  6. 6
    Write a conclusion with a personal response — AQA rewards genuine personal engagement. End with a sentence stating your overall interpretation of what the poem is doing and why you find the poet’s approach effective.

Timing

Read & annotate
5 min Write
22 min Conclude & check
3 min

Allow approximately 30 minutes for 24 marks. Spend five minutes reading and annotating before you write a single word of your response. This is time well spent — students who rush to write without annotating produce thinner analysis.

When you annotate an unseen poem, look for:

  • Imagery: metaphor, simile, personification, symbolism
  • Sound devices: alliteration, sibilance, assonance, onomatopoeia
  • Tone and mood: word choices that carry emotional weight (connotations)
  • Repetition: anaphora, refrain, recurring imagery
  • Structure: enjambment, caesura, line length variations, stanza breaks
  • Form: sonnet, free verse, ballad, dramatic monologue, ode
  • Voice: first person (personal)? second person (direct address)? Third person (detached)?
  • Shifts: Does the tone, focus, or speaker change at any point? (Often at a volta or final stanza)
Language: technique + effect

The poet uses an extended metaphor of drowning throughout the poem, culminating in the image of “waves of silence pressing down”. The verb “pressing” suggests an active, suffocating force, transforming emotional isolation into something physical and inescapable — as if grief is not merely felt but endured as a bodily experience.

Structure: enjambment

The enjambment that runs across stanzas three and four reinforces this sense of relentlessness: the lines spill forward without pause, mimicking the inability of the speaker to stop the tide of emotion even when they wish to.

Personal response

I find this technique particularly effective because it allows the poem to enact, not just describe, the experience of grief — placing the reader inside the sensation rather than observing it from outside.

Examiner: Mastering — Perceptive language and structure analysis, personal response integrated, confident use of terminology.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Retelling what the poem is about — The examiner has read the poem. You must analyse HOW it achieves its effect, not WHAT it describes.
  • ✗
    Only commenting on language, not structure or form — Structure and form observations are part of AO2 and often the most insightful points you can make. Always include at least one structural comment.
  • ✗
    Panicking because you don’t know the poem — Not knowing the poem is the point. Every student is in the same position. Apply your skills systematically using the annotation checklist.
  • ✗
    Commenting on every single line — Select three to four key moments and analyse them in depth. Examiners reward analytical quality, not coverage of every technique in the poem.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
30 min total

What to Annotate

  • Striking word choices
  • Language techniques
  • Structural choices
  • Tone shifts / volta
  • Form

Key AOs

  • Personal response + evidence
  • Language & structure analysis

title: Unseen Poetry Comparison — 8 marks
content_html:
8 marks

Unseen Poetry Comparison

Used in: Paper 2 Section C — Question 2 (Unseen Poetry)

What the Examiner Wants

Question 2 of the unseen poetry section gives you a second short poem and asks you to compare it with the first poem (from Question 1) on a specific focus. You need to write a focused comparison of how both poets use language and form to present a particular idea or feeling. This tests (comparison with evidence) and (analysis of language and form).

Key Fact

This question is only 8 marks — keep it brief and focused. You do not need to analyse the second poem in as much depth as in Question 1. Aim for two or three comparison points, not a full essay.

Mark Scheme Levels

LevelWhat You Need
7–8MasteringPerceptive comparison of how both poets use language/form/structure. Convincing analysis with well-chosen evidence from both poems.
5–6SecureClear comparison. Evidence from both poems. Relevant language analysis.
3–4DevelopingSome comparison. Points made about both poems but not always clearly linked. Some evidence used.
1–2EmergingSimple comments on one or both poems. Mostly descriptive. Little comparison.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the second poem and the question focus — The question will specify a focus (e.g. “how the poets present sadness”). Note two or three moments from each poem that relate to that focus.
  2. 2
    Identify a similarity and a difference — The best 8-mark responses show both. What do the poets agree on or share? Where do they diverge in approach, tone, or method?
  3. 3
    Write two or three integrated comparison paragraphs — Each paragraph discusses BOTH poems together. Use comparative connectives: “Similarly…”, “In contrast…”, “Whereas Poem 1… Poem 2…”. Keep paragraphs tight and focused.
  4. 4
    Analyse language briefly in each poem — Embed a short quotation from each and explain the technique/effect. You don’t need the depth of Question 1 — one technique per poem per paragraph is enough.

Timing

Read & note
2 min Write
10 min Check
2 min

Allow around 10–15 minutes. Two or three focused comparison paragraphs is all you need for 8 marks. Do not write a full essay — this is a compact, focused comparison task.

Similarity

“Both poems present [theme/feeling] through [shared technique], suggesting…”

“Like the first poem, the second poet uses [technique] to convey…”

Difference

“In contrast to [Poem 1’s approach], [Poem 2] uses [different technique], creating…”

“Whereas [Poem 1] presents [feeling] as [X], [Poem 2] portrays it as [Y]…”

In this poem, how does the poet present loneliness? Compare this with how loneliness is presented in the poem from Question 1. [8 marks]

Similarity: both poems + evidence

Both poems present loneliness as a physical sensation rather than an emotional state. In Poem 1, the “weight of empty rooms” uses tactile imagery to make isolation feel bodily and oppressive. Similarly, the second poet describes “cold settling in the bones”, a metaphor that transforms emotional isolation into physical discomfort — both poets suggesting that loneliness cannot be separated from the body.

Difference: form and structure

However, the two poems differ significantly in form. Poem 1’s fragmented free verse — with frequent caesura and short, broken lines — mimics the fractured inner life of the speaker, whereas the second poem’s regular quatrains and consistent rhyme scheme create an impression of resigned acceptance, as though loneliness has become so familiar it now feels ordered and inevitable.

Examiner: 7–8 — Integrated comparison, evidence from both poems, analysis of both language and form, similarity and difference both discussed.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Writing about each poem separately — “First poem: [paragraph]. Second poem: [paragraph]” is not a comparison. Interweave them in each paragraph.
  • ✗
    Writing too much — This is 8 marks, not 24. Two or three focused paragraphs is the target. Spending 20+ minutes on this wastes time you need elsewhere in the exam.
  • ✗
    Only noting similarities — The most insightful comparisons show both similarity and difference. Even a subtle contrast in tone, form, or emotional effect is worth pointing out.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
15 min total

Structure

  1. Read both poems + note focus
  2. 1 similarity + 1 difference
  3. 2–3 integrated paragraphs

Connectives

  • Both poems… / Similarly…
  • In contrast… / Whereas…
  • Unlike [Poem 1]…

title: 4 marks — Retrieval
content_html:
4 Marks — Retrieval (Paper 1 Q1 / Paper 2 Q1)

What the Question Asks

This is the opening question on both Paper 1 and Paper 2. It tests whether you can find specific information that is directly stated in the text. You are not being asked to analyse, interpret, or infer — just locate facts. On Paper 1, you choose the correct answer from four multiple-choice questions (1 mark each). On Paper 2, you pick the four true statements from a list of eight (1 mark each).

Key Fact

This question is worth only 4 marks but it is the easiest on the paper. You should aim for full marks every time. There is no excuse for dropping marks here if you read carefully.

How Marks Are Allocated

The marking is simple and absolute — there are no levels, no partial credit, and no judgement calls from the examiner.

Paper Format Marks How It Works
Paper 1 Q1 4 multiple-choice questions (choose A, B, C, or D) 4 marks (1 each) Correct = 1 mark. Wrong = 0 marks. No half marks.
Paper 2 Q1 8 statements — shade 4 that are TRUE 4 marks (1 each) Each correct shade = 1 mark. If you shade more than 4 boxes, you score 0 for the entire question.
Key Fact

Paper 2 warning: If you shade five or more boxes instead of exactly four, the examiner will mark the whole question as zero — even if all four correct answers are among your choices. Only ever shade four.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the line references carefully. The question will tell you exactly which lines to focus on (e.g. "lines 1 to 6"). Underline these lines in the source. Do not look beyond them — the answer will not be outside the specified section.
  2. Read the specified section slowly and deliberately. Read it twice if you have time. Pay attention to specific details: names, numbers, descriptions, and facts. As you read, underline or circle key details that stand out.
  3. Go through each statement or option one at a time. For each one, ask yourself: "Can I point to the exact words in the text that prove this?" If you cannot, it is probably wrong. Do not rely on what "sounds right" — rely on what is written.
  4. Eliminate confidently wrong answers first. Cross out any option that is clearly contradicted by the text or not mentioned at all. This narrows your choices and reduces the chance of error.
  5. Double-check tricky options against the exact wording. Some wrong answers are designed to be almost right. They may change a number, swap a detail, or exaggerate what the text says. Compare the statement word-for-word against the source. If even one detail is wrong, the whole statement is wrong.
  6. Shade or circle your final answers cleanly. Make sure you have answered exactly the right number of questions. On Paper 2, count your shaded boxes — there must be exactly four.

Timing

Spend no more than 4–5 minutes on this question. Here is why:

  • Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks. That works out to roughly 1.3 minutes per mark. A 4-mark question should take around 5 minutes.
  • Paper 2 is also 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks, so the same calculation applies.
  • This is the most straightforward question on the paper. The harder questions (evaluation, comparison, writing) need more time, so getting through Q1 quickly gives you extra minutes where they matter most.
  • If you are spending more than 5 minutes, you are overthinking it. Trust the text, not your gut.
Key Fact

Think of Q1 as a warm-up. It gets you reading the source carefully, which helps you with every question that follows. But do not linger — move on quickly.

Model Answer

Question: Read again the first part of Source A, from lines 1 to 6. Choose four statements below which are TRUE. Shade the boxes of the ones you think are TRUE.

Answer: B, C, D, E

Why this scores 4/4:

  • B — "Workers were not allowed to speak during the shift" — The text states: "Silence was strictly enforced; no worker dared utter a word." This directly supports the statement.
  • C — "The foreman carried a pocket watch" — The text states: "The foreman checked his brass pocket watch." A direct match.
  • D — "Conditions were described as unbearable by a former employee" — The text includes: "One former hand called the conditions 'unbearable.'" The word is right there in the source.
  • E — "Women outnumbered men on the factory floor" — The text states: "Of the workforce, the majority were women and girls." This confirms the statement.

Every answer can be traced to a specific line in the extract. The student only shaded four boxes. This is a clean, confident, full-mark answer.

Weak Answer

Answer: A, B, F, H

Score: 1/4 (only B is correct from the actual text)

What went wrong:

  • A — "The factory employed over 200 workers" ❌ — This is not stated anywhere in lines 1–6. The student probably assumed this because they know Victorian factories were large. This is background knowledge, not retrieval. The text does not give a number.
  • B — ✅ — Correct. Directly supported by the text.
  • F — "The factory operated 24 hours a day" ❌ — Again, this sounds plausible for a Victorian factory, but the text does not say this. The student is guessing based on what they think they know, not what they can see on the page.
  • H — "The machines were steam-powered" ❌ — This is a trap. The text mentions machines but does not specify what powered them. The student has made an assumption. Close is not good enough — if the text does not say it, the statement is not true according to the source.

This student lost 3 easy marks because they trusted their own knowledge instead of the text. They also missed D and E, which were clearly stated in the extract, suggesting they did not read the lines carefully enough.

Common Mistakes

  • Using background knowledge instead of the text. This is the number one error. It does not matter what you know about the topic. The question asks what is stated in the source. If you cannot point to the exact line, do not choose it.
  • Shading more than four boxes on Paper 2. If you are unsure, some students shade a fifth box "just in case." This automatically scores you zero for the entire question. Always shade exactly four.
  • Reading beyond the specified lines. The question says "lines 1 to 6" — do not use information from line 7 onwards. A statement might be true later in the text but false within the specified section. Stick to the lines you are told.
  • Falling for "almost right" statements. Examiners deliberately include options that are close to what the text says but change one detail — a number, a name, or a degree of certainty. For example, the text might say "most workers" but the statement says "all workers." Read precisely.

Key Terminology

You do not need to use specialist terminology in your answer for this question — you are simply selecting correct options. However, understanding these terms will help you approach Q1 with the right mindset:

  • Retrieval — Finding and selecting information that is explicitly stated in the text. No interpretation needed.
  • Explicit information — Details that are directly and clearly stated in the text, not implied or suggested.
  • Inference — Reading between the lines to work out what is suggested but not directly said. This is not what Q1 asks for — save it for Q2.
  • Line reference — The specific lines of the source the question directs you to. You must stay within these lines.
  • Distractor — A wrong answer designed to look plausible. Examiners include these to test whether you are reading the text or guessing.
  • Source — The passage or extract printed in the exam booklet that you are reading and answering questions on.
Quick Reference
Marks: 4 marks (1 per correct answer)
Timing: 4–5 minutes maximum
Paper 1 Q1: 4 multiple-choice questions — pick one letter each
Paper 2 Q1: 8 statements — shade exactly 4 true ones
Golden Rule: Only choose what the text directly states — never guess from background knowledge
Warning: Shading 5+ boxes on Paper 2 = automatic zero
Stick to the lines: Only use the section specified in the question
Other Guides
8 marks — Language Analysis 8 marks — Structure Analysis 8 marks — Summary 16 marks — Comparison 20 marks — Evaluation 40 marks — Creative Writing 40 marks — Transactional Writing

title: 8 marks — Language Analysis
content_html:
What the Question Asks

This question asks you to analyse specific language choices the writer has made and explain the effect those choices have on the reader. You must focus only on the lines specified in the question. The examiner wants to see that you can identify interesting words, phrases, and techniques — then explain why the writer chose them and how they make the reader think or feel.

This appears as Question 2 on Paper 1 (fiction) and Question 3 on Paper 2 (non-fiction). Both are worth 8 marks and both require the same core skill: close analysis of language.

Key Fact

The magic formula for every point: identify the technique → quote it → explain the effect on the reader. If any of these three elements are missing, you will not reach the top levels.

How Marks Are Allocated

AQA uses four levels to mark this question. Read the descriptors carefully — the jump from Developing to Secure is where most students get stuck, and it comes down to one thing: explaining the effect in detail.

LevelWhat the Examiner Sees
MasteringPerceptive, detailed analysis. You select precise quotes. You explore nuanced effects — what the word connotes, how it makes the reader feel, and why the writer chose that word over another. Your vocabulary is sophisticated and your explanations feel insightful, not formulaic.
SecureClear, explained analysis. You name techniques, quote accurately, and give developed explanations of effect. Your points make sense and show genuine understanding of how language works. This is a solid, competent answer.
DevelopingSome understanding. You identify some language features and attempt to explain effects, but explanations are thin, vague, or generic (e.g., "this is effective because it creates imagery"). You may feature-spot without fully explaining why it matters.
EmergingSimple, general comments. You make basic observations about the text or copy out quotes without analysing them. Little or no discussion of effect. Answers may be very short or off-topic.
Key Fact

The difference between Developing and Secure is depth of explanation. Saying "the metaphor is effective" is Developing. Explaining exactly what it suggests and how it affects the reader's understanding is Secure. Going further to explore connotations and alternative readings pushes you into Mastering.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the specified lines twice. First read: understand the overall mood, tone, or impression. Second read: underline or circle 3–4 interesting language choices — words, phrases, or patterns that stand out. Don't just look for "techniques" — look for words that feel deliberate or powerful.
  2. Choose your best 3–4 quotes. Pick quotes where you can say something meaningful about the effect. A single powerful word can be better than a long phrase. If you can't explain why it's interesting, don't use it — choose a different quote.
  3. Name the technique or language feature. Be specific. Don't just say "language technique" — say metaphor, verb choice, sibilance, semantic field, etc. But remember: naming the technique alone scores nothing. The effect is what earns marks.
  4. Explain the effect in detail. Ask yourself three questions about each quote: What does this word/phrase suggest or connote? How does it make the reader feel? Why has the writer chosen this specific word? Push yourself beyond your first thought — your second or third idea is usually the more perceptive one.
  5. Use precise analytical vocabulary. Words like connotes, implies, evokes, reinforces, and suggests show the examiner you are analysing rather than describing. Avoid weak phrases like "this shows" or "this is effective."
  6. Write 3–4 developed paragraphs. Quality beats quantity. Three well-analysed points will outscore six shallow ones. Each paragraph should follow the pattern: technique → quote → effect → deeper exploration of effect.

Timing

Spend 10–12 minutes on this question.

  • Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes. Section A (reading) should take about 1 hour. Q2 is worth 8 of the 40 reading marks, so roughly 10–12 minutes is proportionate.
  • Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes. Section A (reading) should take about 1 hour. Q3 is again worth 8 marks, so the same timing applies.
  • Budget your time like this: 2–3 minutes reading and annotating the lines, then 8–9 minutes writing 3–4 paragraphs.
Key Fact

Do not spend 20 minutes on an 8-mark question. If you over-run here, you steal time from the 40-mark writing question — which is worth five times as many marks. Set a timer when you practise.

Model Answer

Question: How does the writer use language to describe the abandoned house?

The writer uses personification in 'the windows stared blankly', giving the house an unsettling, lifeless quality — as if it once watched the world but has now lost its will to see. The verb 'stared' implies a fixed, unblinking gaze, which connotes something hollow or dead, while the adverb 'blankly' reinforces the absence of life or purpose. This makes the reader feel the house is a presence, not just a building, which creates a creeping sense of unease.

The adjective 'bleached' suggests the colour has been drawn out of the house over time, like something long exposed to sun and neglect. The connotation of fading life subtly implies decay without stating it directly — 'bleached' is associated with bones, driftwood, and things left behind. This draws the reader into the atmosphere of abandonment and makes the house feel almost like a corpse.

The sibilance in 'silence settling slowly' creates a hushed, creeping effect through the repetition of soft 's' sounds. This slows the reader's pace, mimicking the oppressive stillness the writer wants us to feel. The verb 'settling' is particularly effective, as it suggests the silence is a physical substance — like dust — that gathers and thickens, reinforcing the sense that the house has been undisturbed for a long time.

Why this answer works:

  • Precise technique identification: personification, adjective choice, sibilance — all correctly named.
  • Short, embedded quotes: quotes are woven into sentences, not dumped in.
  • Layered effect analysis: each point goes beyond the first observation. The answer explores connotations ("bones, driftwood"), reader response ("creeping sense of unease"), and writer's purpose ("mimicking the oppressive stillness").
  • Analytical vocabulary: uses "connotes," "implies," "reinforces," "evokes" — not "this shows" or "this is effective."
  • Individual word analysis: zooms in on specific words within quotes ('stared', 'blankly', 'settling') rather than discussing the whole phrase vaguely.

Weak Answer

Question: How does the writer use language to describe the abandoned house?

The writer uses personification: 'the windows stared blankly'. This is effective. There is also sibilance in 'silence settling slowly'. The writer uses these techniques to describe the house. The language makes the reader feel like the house is old.

What went wrong — annotated mistakes:

  • ❌ "This is effective" — says nothing. This is the single most common mistake at GCSE. The examiner already knows you think it's effective — you need to explain how and why. What feeling does it create? What does the word suggest?
  • ❌ Feature-spotting without analysis. The student identifies sibilance correctly but then does nothing with it. Naming a technique without explaining its effect earns almost no credit.
  • ❌ Vague, generic effect: "the house is old." This is too general. How does the language make it feel old? What specific word creates that impression? The answer doesn't connect the language choice to the effect.
  • ❌ No exploration of connotations. The student never asks "what does this word suggest?" — which is the core skill being tested.
  • ❌ Too short. Four sentences for 8 marks is not enough. This answer offers only surface-level observations. At least 3 developed paragraphs are needed.
  • ❌ Quotes are not analysed at word level. The student quotes the full phrase but doesn't zoom in on individual word choices like 'stared' or 'blankly'.

Common Mistakes

  • "This is effective" / "This creates imagery." These are empty statements. The examiner wants to know what kind of effect and what kind of imagery. Replace "this is effective" with a specific explanation: "This creates a sense of decay" or "This connotes vulnerability."
  • Feature-spotting (naming techniques without explaining effects). Writing "The writer uses a simile" and moving on does not earn marks. The technique is only the starting point — the effect is where the marks are. Aim for the ratio: 20% identification, 80% explanation.
  • Writing about the wrong lines. If the question says "lines 1 to 6," everything outside those lines is irrelevant. You will get zero marks for analysing language from other parts of the text. Underline the specified section before you start.
  • Retelling the story instead of analysing language. Don't write "The writer describes an abandoned house that is old and nobody lives there anymore." That's summary, not analysis. Focus on how the writer uses specific words and devices, not what happens.

Key Terminology

You don't need to use every term below in every answer — but you should be comfortable with all of them. The best answers use terminology naturally, not as a checklist.

  • Metaphor — describing something as if it is something else (e.g., "the house was a skeleton"). Creates a direct comparison that shapes how the reader imagines the subject.
  • Simile — a comparison using "like" or "as" (e.g., "the walls sagged like tired shoulders"). Draws a parallel that gives the reader a vivid mental image.
  • Personification — giving human qualities to something non-human (e.g., "the door groaned"). Makes objects feel alive or emotionally charged.
  • Connotation — the associations or feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning. For example, "crimson" connotes danger or passion in a way "red" does not. This is arguably the most important term for this question.
  • Semantic field — a group of words related to the same topic or theme (e.g., "crumbled," "dust," "rubble" = semantic field of destruction). Shows a pattern of meaning across the text.
  • Sibilance — repetition of 's' sounds (e.g., "silence settling slowly"). Often creates a soft, sinister, or hushed effect.
  • Plosive sounds — harsh, explosive consonant sounds like 'b', 'p', 'd', 't' (e.g., "battered," "broken," "torn apart"). Often creates a violent, forceful, or aggressive tone.
  • Adjective / verb / adverb choice — you don't always need a named "device." Analysing a single powerful word choice (e.g., why the writer chose "lurched" instead of "moved") is just as valid and often more impressive.
  • Imagery — language that creates a picture in the reader's mind. Be specific about what kind of imagery (visual, auditory, tactile) and what it makes the reader picture.
  • Tone — the overall mood or attitude conveyed by the language (e.g., menacing, nostalgic, bleak). Useful for linking individual language choices to the writer's broader purpose.
  • Juxtaposition — placing two contrasting ideas or images side by side for effect (e.g., describing beauty and decay in the same sentence).
  • Pathetic fallacy — using weather or natural surroundings to reflect mood or emotion (e.g., storm clouds to suggest danger).
Key Fact

You can reach Top band (7–8 marks):without naming a single literary device — if your analysis of word choices and their connotations is detailed and perceptive. The examiner rewards quality of analysis, not a list of technique names. Analysing why

title: 8 marks — Summary
content_html:
Paper 2 Question 2: Summary (8 marks)

What the Question Asks

This question gives you two non-fiction sources and asks you to summarise the differences (or occasionally similarities) between them on a specific topic — for example, attitudes towards working conditions, experiences of travel, or views on education. You must read both sources, pull out relevant details, and compare them using inference (reading between the lines), not just copy out quotations.

Key Fact

This is a synthesis question. You must weave both sources together in your response — not write about Source A then Source B separately. Every point should connect the two sources.

How Marks Are Allocated

LevelWhat the Examiner Is Looking For
MasteringPerceptive. Detailed and nuanced synthesis of both sources. Discriminating use of evidence — short, well-chosen references woven into your own sentences. Clear inferences that go beyond the obvious.
SecureClear. Developed synthesis across both sources. Relevant inferences supported by appropriate references. Differences are explained, not just stated.
DevelopingSome understanding. Inferences attempted but may be vague or underdeveloped. Some reference to both sources, but comparison may be unbalanced or surface-level.
EmergingSimple. Identifies some relevant information from one or both sources. Little or no inference. May describe rather than compare.
Key Fact

To hit Mastering, you need inference (what is implied, not just stated), synthesis (linking both sources in the same point), and precision (short, embedded quotations — not long copied chunks).

Step-by-Step Method

  1. Read the question carefully and underline the focus. The question will tell you exactly what to compare — e.g. "differences between the attitudes of the writers towards working conditions." Circle the key words: differences, attitudes, working conditions. Everything you write must connect to these words.
  2. Annotate both sources for relevant details. Spend 3–4 minutes re-reading the relevant sections. In the margin, jot one-word summaries of the writer's attitude at each point (e.g. "sympathetic," "proud," "critical"). Underline short phrases you could quote — aim for 2–3 word quotations, not whole sentences.
  3. Plan 3–4 paired points. On your question paper, quickly pair up your annotations: Source A point → contrasting Source B point. Each pair becomes one paragraph. For example: "A = workers suffering / B = workers thriving." This takes 1–2 minutes but prevents rambling.
  4. Write using a comparative structure. For each point, follow this pattern: State what Source A suggests → embed a short quotation → infer what this implies → use a connective (In contrast / However / Whereas) → state what Source B suggests → embed a short quotation → infer what this implies. This guarantees synthesis.
  5. Infer, don't just identify. After every quotation, push yourself to write what it suggests or implies about the writer's attitude. The difference between Developing and Mastering is the quality of your inferences. Ask yourself: "What does this tell me about how the writer feels?"
  6. Check your answer. In the final minute, re-read your response and ask: Have I used both sources in every paragraph? Have I actually addressed the specific focus (e.g. attitudes, not just conditions)? Have I inferred, not just described?

Timing

Spend 12–15 minutes on this question. Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes for 80 marks. That means roughly 1 minute per mark, plus reading time. For 8 marks, 12–15 minutes is proportionate and gives you enough time to plan and write 3–4 developed comparative points.

Break it down like this:

  • 3–4 minutes: Re-read and annotate both sources for the stated focus
  • 1–2 minutes: Plan your paired points
  • 7–8 minutes: Write your response (3–4 paragraphs)
  • 1 minute: Check and proofread
Key Fact

Don't over-write this answer. 3–4 well-developed comparative paragraphs is enough for full marks. Writing more than necessary steals time from the 20-mark and 40-mark questions later on the paper.

Model Answer

Question: Write a summary of the differences between the attitudes of the writers towards working conditions.

Source A's writer views the factory conditions with sympathy for the workers, suggesting they are 'ground down' by the relentless pace. This implies the conditions are dehumanising, reducing people to little more than machinery themselves. In contrast, Source B's writer regards the same type of factory as a place of 'vigour and purpose', seeing the noise and motion as signs of productivity rather than suffering.

Source A focuses on the physical toll of the work — the aching backs, the dust — suggesting the writer sees the cost to human health as unacceptable. Source B, however, dwells on wages earned and pride taken, implying the writer believes hardship is offset by economic reward.

Both sources acknowledge the difficult environment, but Source A presents this as exploitation, whilst Source B frames it as an opportunity for the working class to better themselves — a fundamentally different ideological position about labour and human dignity.

Why this scores highly:

  • Synthesis throughout: Every paragraph connects both sources directly — the comparison is built into each point, not bolted on afterwards.
  • Short, embedded quotations: 'ground down' and 'vigour and purpose' are woven into the student's own sentences, not dropped in as standalone chunks.
  • Inference is developed: The student doesn't just say "Source A is negative" — they explain what the negativity implies (dehumanisation, exploitation). This is the difference between Developing and Mastering.
  • The final paragraph draws a wider conclusion: Identifying the "fundamentally different ideological position" shows perceptive, discriminating reading — exactly what the top band requires.
  • Clear, precise language: No waffle, no repetition, no unnecessary retelling of the sources.

Question: Write a summary of the differences between the attitudes of the writers towards working conditions.

Source A says the conditions were bad. Source B says they were okay. In Source A it says the workers were 'ground down'. In Source B it talks about wages. They have different views about working conditions. Source A is negative and Source B is positive.

What goes wrong here:

  • ❌ No inference: "The conditions were bad" and "they were okay" are surface-level observations. There is no attempt to explain why the writer thinks this or what their attitude reveals. This caps the answer at Emerging–2.
  • ❌ Sources treated separately: The student writes about Source A, then Source B, without connecting them. There is no synthesis — just two descriptions side by side.
  • ❌ Quotation is dropped in, not used: 'Ground down' is mentioned but not explained or interpreted. The student never tells us what this quotation implies about the writer's attitude.
  • ❌ Vague labels instead of analysis: "Source A is negative and Source B is positive" is the most common weak answer move. The examiner already knows this — what they want is how and why the attitudes differ.
  • ❌ Too short and undeveloped: This is essentially one point repeated in different ways. A Secure–4 answer needs 3–4 distinct developed points.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing about only one source. This is surprisingly common under pressure. If you only discuss Source A, you cannot score above Developing no matter how good your analysis is. Every paragraph must reference both sources.
  • Copying out long quotations instead of summarising. The question says "write a summary." If you're quoting full sentences, you're not summarising — you're retelling. Keep quotations to 2–4 words and embed them in your own sentences.
  • Describing what happens instead of inferring attitudes. "Source A describes a dusty factory" is description. "Source A's writer emphasises the dust to suggest the conditions are harmful and neglected" is inference. The mark scheme rewards inference at every level above Emerging.
  • Using vague comparative words without development. Saying "Source A is more negative than Source B" earns almost nothing on its own. You must explain in what way — negative about what? Negative because of what evidence? What does this negativity imply about the writer's broader attitude?

Key Terminology

  • Synthesis — combining information from both sources into a single, connected point (rather than discussing them separately).
  • Inference — reading between the lines; identifying what a writer implies or suggests, not just what they directly state.
  • Attitude — the writer's viewpoint, feeling, or position towards the subject. Questions often ask about attitudes specifically, so use this word in your answer.
  • Implies / suggests / conveys — use these verbs to signal that you are making an inference. They show the examiner you're going beyond the surface.
  • In contrast / However / Whereas / Conversely — comparative connectives that signal a difference. Use one per paragraph to keep your synthesis visible.
  • Similarly / Likewise / Both writers — use these if the question asks about similarities, or if you want to acknowledge a shared element before highlighting a difference.
  • Perspective — the writer's particular way of seeing or interpreting something, shaped by their context, values, or experience.
Quick Reference
Question: Paper 2, Q2
Marks: 8
Timing: 12–15 minutes
Skill: Synthesis & Summary
Sources: Must use BOTH
Aim for: 3–4 comparative points with inference
Top tip: Embed short quotations (2–4 words) — don't copy sentences
Formula: Source A suggests… [quote + inference]. In contrast, Source B implies… [quote + inference].

title: 1 Mark — Recall Questions
content_html:
1 mark

Recall Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

Recall questions test whether you know a specific fact, term, or piece of information. The examiner wants one precise answer — nothing more. These questions use command words like “Name,” “State,” “Give,” or “What is.”

Marking

What You Need
1A correct, specific answer that directly addresses the question
Vague, incorrect, or no response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question carefully — Identify exactly what is being asked. “Name the organ” and “Name the organelle” require very different answers.
  2. 2
    Give the specific answer — Write the term, name, or fact. Use correct scientific terminology (e.g. “mitochondria” not “the part that makes energy”).
  3. 3
    Do not explain — This is worth 1 mark. Adding unnecessary explanation wastes time and cannot earn you extra marks.

Timing

Recall — 1 min

One minute maximum. Write your answer and move on. If you cannot remember, leave a gap and return at the end.

Name the type of bond formed when metals react with non-metals. [1 mark]

Full mark

Ionic bond.

Examiner: 1/1 — Clear, correct, no unnecessary detail.

State the function of the ribosomes in a cell. [1 mark]

Full mark

Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

Examiner: 1/1 — Uses the correct term “protein synthesis.”

Give the unit used to measure electrical resistance. [1 mark]

0 marks — wrong unit

Volts.

Full mark

Ohms (Ω).

Examiner: A common confusion. Resistance is measured in ohms, not volts. Volts measure potential difference.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Confusing similar terms — “Mitosis” and “meiosis,” “evaporation” and “condensation,” “current” and “voltage” are commonly mixed up. Learn the precise definition of each.
  • ❌
    Being vague — “The thing that carries blood” will not earn the mark. The examiner wants “artery” or “vein” (and the correct one for the context).
  • ❌
    Wasting time explaining — If a question says “Name” or “State,” it wants a fact, not an explanation. Extra detail earns no additional marks.

← Back to Exam Technique

1 min total

  1. Read the question carefully
  2. Give the specific term or fact
  3. Move on — do not explain
