title: 2 Marks — Describe Questions
content_html:
2 marks

Describe Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

“Describe” questions ask you to state what happens, what you see, or what a pattern or trend shows. You do not need to explain why — just state the facts clearly. These questions often relate to processes, trends in data, or what you would observe in a practical.

Marking

What You Need
2Two clear, correct descriptive points that address the question directly
1One correct point or two vague points
No relevant description or an explanation instead of a description

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what to describe — Is it a process (e.g. “Describe how vaccination works”), a trend (e.g. “Describe the pattern in the graph”), or an observation (e.g. “Describe what you would see”)?
  2. 2
    Make two distinct points — Each point should cover a different aspect. For a graph, state the trend and use data. For a process, state the steps in order.
  3. 3
    Use scientific language but do not explain — The word “because” is a warning sign. If you catch yourself writing “because,” you are explaining, not describing.

Timing

Describe — 2 min

About two minutes. Write two clear sentences and move on.

Describing a trend

“As [variable X] increases, [variable Y] increases/decreases. For example, at [data point 1]… and at [data point 2]…”

Describing a process

“First, [step 1 happens]. Then, [step 2 happens].”

Describing an observation

“You would see [observation 1]. The [substance/object] would [observation 2].”

Describe the trend shown in the graph of enzyme activity against temperature. [2 marks]

Full marks

As temperature increases from 10°C to 37°C, the rate of enzyme activity increases. Above 37°C, the rate of activity decreases rapidly.

Examiner: 2/2 — Two clear points about the trend, with data from the graph.

Describe the test for carbon dioxide gas. [2 marks]

Full marks

Bubble the gas through limewater. If carbon dioxide is present, the limewater turns milky (cloudy).

Examiner: 2/2 — States the test and the positive result.

Describe the trend in the graph of stopping distance against speed. [2 marks]

1 mark — no data

As speed goes up, stopping distance goes up because there is more kinetic energy.

Full marks

As speed increases, stopping distance increases. The relationship is not linear — stopping distance increases more steeply at higher speeds (e.g. at 30 mph it is 23 m, but at 60 mph it is 73 m).

Examiner: The weak answer uses “because” (explaining, not describing) and lacks data. The strong answer describes the pattern with specific values.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Explaining instead of describing — If the question says “Describe,” do not write “because.” State what happens, not why it happens.
  • ❌
    Not using data from the graph — When describing a trend, quote specific values from the axes. “It goes up” is worth less than “It increases from 20 to 85 between 0 and 60 seconds.”
  • ❌
    Only making one point — Two marks means two points. Check you have stated two distinct observations or steps.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
2 min total

Formula

  1. Identify what to describe
  2. Make two distinct points
  3. Use data if a graph is given
  4. Do not explain — just state

title: 2 Marks — Calculate Questions
content_html:
2 marks

Calculate Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

Calculate questions test your ability to use scientific formulae, substitute values correctly, and arrive at a numerical answer with the right units. The examiner awards marks for your working as well as the final answer — so even if your arithmetic is wrong, a correct method can still earn marks.

Marking

What You Need
2Correct substitution into the formula AND correct final answer with appropriate units
1Correct substitution but wrong calculation, OR correct formula stated but not applied, OR correct answer with no working shown
No relevant working and incorrect answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Write the formula — Write out the equation you need. In physics, the formula sheet is provided but you still need to select the right one. In chemistry, you may need to recall the formula (e.g. relative formula mass, moles calculations).
  2. 2
    Substitute the values — Replace each symbol with the numbers from the question. Check units match — convert if needed (e.g. km to m, minutes to seconds, cm³ to dm³).
  3. 3
    Calculate and show your working — Write each step of the calculation. If you make an arithmetic error, the examiner can still award marks for your method if they can follow your working.
  4. 4
    State the answer with units — Write the final answer clearly, including the correct unit (e.g. J, N, mol, Ω). If the question asks you to give your answer to a certain number of significant figures or decimal places, do so.

Timing

Calculate — 2–3 min

About two to three minutes. Write the formula, substitute, calculate, and check your units.

A car has a mass of 1200 kg and is travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car. Use the equation: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed² [2 marks]

Full marks

KE = 0.5 × m × v²
KE = 0.5 × 1200 × 15²
KE = 0.5 × 1200 × 225
KE = 135,000 J (or 135 kJ)

Examiner: 2/2 — Formula stated, values substituted correctly, correct answer with unit.

Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate (CaCO3). Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16. [2 marks]

Full marks

Mr = 40 + 12 + (16 × 3)
Mr = 40 + 12 + 48
Mr = 100

Examiner: 2/2 — Clear working, each element accounted for, correct final answer. No unit needed for relative formula mass.

A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A flowing through it. Calculate the resistance. [2 marks]

1 mark — no formula or working

24 Ω

Full marks

R = V ÷ I
R = 12 ÷ 0.5
R = 24 Ω

Examiner: The answer alone may only score 1 mark (or 2 if an “allow” applies). Always show working to guarantee full marks.

FromToMultiply by
kmm× 1000
cmm÷ 100
gkg÷ 1000
cm³dm³÷ 1000
minutesseconds× 60
hoursseconds× 3600
kJJ× 1000
kWW× 1000

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not showing working — If you write only the final answer and it is wrong, you score zero. If you show correct substitution, you score at least 1 mark even with a calculation error.
  • ❌
    Forgetting to convert units — A common error is using grams when the formula requires kilograms, or cm when it needs metres. Always check the units before substituting.
  • ❌
    Missing units on the answer — “135,000” is incomplete. The examiner needs to see “135,000 J.” Some questions state the unit for you, but if they do not, you must provide it.
  • ❌
    Using the wrong formula — Read the question carefully. “Calculate the force” and “calculate the work done” use different equations even though both involve force.

← Back to Exam Technique

2–3 min total

Formula

  1. Write the formula
  2. Substitute the values
  3. Calculate step by step
  4. State answer with units

title: 3 Marks — Explain Questions
content_html:
3 marks

Explain Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

“Explain” questions require you to give a reason or mechanism for something happening. Unlike “Describe” questions, you must say why or how. The examiner is looking for a chain of logic: cause → effect, or statement → reasoning.

Marking

What You Need
3Three valid points, or two well-developed points with a clear chain of reasoning
2Two correct points or one point with good development
1One basic relevant point
No scientifically correct points

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the scientific concept — What topic area does this question relate to? What scientific principle explains the phenomenon?
  2. 2
    State what happens — Start with a clear factual statement about the process or observation.
  3. 3
    Explain why using scientific reasoning — Link the cause to the effect. Use “This means that…” or “This is because…” to build a chain of reasoning.
  4. 4
    Develop or add a third point — Either develop one of your points further or add a third distinct reason. Use subject-specific terminology to show depth of understanding.

Timing

Explain — 3–4 min

About three to four minutes. Write a short paragraph with a clear chain of cause and effect.

Cause → Effect chain

“[Statement of what happens]. This is because [scientific reason]. This means that [consequence/further development].”

Three-point approach

“Firstly, [point 1 with reason]. Secondly, [point 2 with reason]. Additionally, [point 3 with reason].”

Explain why the rate of photosynthesis increases as light intensity increases. [3 marks]

Full marks

As light intensity increases, more light energy is available for the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. This means that more chlorophyll molecules can absorb light energy, increasing the rate at which water is split and ATP is produced. As a result, more glucose is synthesised per unit of time, until another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes limiting.

Examiner: 3/3 — Three linked points: more light energy available, more absorption by chlorophyll, and the idea of a limiting factor.

Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points. [3 marks]

Full marks

Ionic compounds form a giant lattice structure made up of positive and negative ions. There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong electrostatic forces, so the melting point is high.

Examiner: 3/3 — Structure identified, nature of bonding explained, linked to energy required to break bonds.

Explain why a skydiver reaches terminal velocity. [3 marks]

1 mark — lacks scientific detail

The skydiver stops accelerating because the air resistance is equal to gravity.

Full marks

When the skydiver first jumps, the force of gravity (weight) is greater than the air resistance, so there is a resultant downward force causing acceleration. As speed increases, air resistance increases. Eventually, air resistance equals the weight of the skydiver, so the resultant force is zero and acceleration stops — the skydiver falls at a constant speed called terminal velocity.

Examiner: The weak answer gets the conclusion right but does not explain the process. The strong answer traces the chain: unbalanced forces → acceleration → increasing air resistance → balanced forces → constant speed.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing instead of explaining — “The rate increases” describes what happens but does not explain why. Always include the scientific reason using “because” or “this means that.”
  • ❌
    Missing the chain of reasoning — An explanation needs to link cause to effect. “Ionic compounds have strong bonds so high melting points” jumps from A to C. You must go through B: what type of bonds, and why they require a lot of energy to break.
  • ❌
    Using vague language — Avoid “the particles move around more.” Be specific: “The particles gain kinetic energy so collide more frequently and with greater energy.”
← Calculate (2 marks) Compare and Explain (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
3–4 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the scientific concept
  2. State what happens
  3. Say why (cause → effect)
  4. Develop or add a third point

title: 4 Marks — Compare and Explain Questions
content_html:
4 marks

Compare and Explain Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

These questions ask you to identify similarities or differences between two things and then explain why those differences or similarities exist. The examiner is looking for two skills: accurate comparison and scientific reasoning. You need comparative language (“whereas,” “however,” “both”) alongside clear scientific explanations.

Marking

What You Need
4Two clear comparisons, each with a developed scientific explanation
3Two comparisons with one well-explained, or one very well-developed comparison plus a second basic point
2Two basic comparisons without explanation, or one comparison with explanation
1One basic comparison or one relevant scientific point
No relevant comparison or scientific content

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what you are comparing — Read the question to establish the two things being compared (e.g. two organisms, two materials, two processes, two data sets).
  2. 2
    State the first comparison using comparative language — Use “whereas,” “however,” “in contrast” or “both” to make the comparison explicit. Do not write about each thing separately — put them together in one sentence.
  3. 3
    Explain the scientific reason for the first comparison — Link the difference or similarity to the underlying science. Use “This is because…”
  4. 4
    Repeat for a second comparison + explanation — Make a second distinct point comparing the two things, then explain it scientifically. This earns the remaining marks.

Timing

Plan
1 min Write
4 min

About five minutes total. Spend a minute identifying two comparison points before writing.

Comparison + explanation

“[Thing A] has/does [feature], whereas [Thing B] has/does [different feature]. This is because [scientific reason].”

Similarity + explanation

“Both [Thing A] and [Thing B] [shared feature]. This is because they both [scientific reason].”

Compare the structures of animal cells and plant cells. Explain the differences. [4 marks]

Full marks

Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, whereas animal cells do not have a cell wall. This is because the cell wall provides structural support and rigidity to the plant, allowing it to stand upright without a skeleton. Additionally, plant cells contain chloroplasts, whereas animal cells do not. This is because plants make their own glucose by photosynthesis, which requires chloroplasts to absorb light energy, while animals obtain glucose by eating food.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two clear comparisons (cell wall, chloroplasts), both using comparative language, each with a developed scientific explanation.

Compare the properties of metals and non-metals. Explain the differences. [4 marks]

2 marks — comparison without explanation

Metals conduct electricity but non-metals do not. Metals are shiny and non-metals are dull.

Full marks

Metals are good conductors of electricity, whereas most non-metals are insulators. This is because metals have delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry charge. In contrast, metals are malleable (can be bent into shape), whereas non-metals are brittle. This is because the layers of metal ions can slide over each other while maintaining the metallic bonding, but in non-metals the rigid covalent bonds break when force is applied.

Examiner: The weak answer states two comparisons but explains neither. The strong answer pairs each comparison with the underlying scientific reason.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing about each thing separately — “Metals conduct electricity. Non-metals do not.” This is two separate statements, not a comparison. Use “whereas” or “however” to link them.
  • ❌
    Comparing without explaining — Stating the differences earns only half the marks. You must explain why the differences exist using scientific reasoning.
  • ❌
    Making the same point twice — “Metals are good conductors” and “non-metals are bad conductors” is one comparison, not two. Find a genuinely different property for your second point.
← Explain (3 marks) Extended Response (6 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the two things to compare
  2. State comparison 1 + explain why
  3. State comparison 2 + explain why
  4. Use comparative language throughout

title: 6 Marks — Extended Response Questions
content_html:
6 marks

Extended Response Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

The 6-mark extended response is the highest-value question on each paper. It is marked using a levels of response mark scheme, which means the examiner reads your whole answer and decides which level it fits into. There is an asterisk (*) next to the question to show that quality of written communication is assessed. The examiner wants a logically structured, detailed answer that uses scientific terminology accurately and builds a clear argument or explanation.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureDetailed, coherent explanation with a logical structure; accurate and relevant scientific terminology; all key points addressed; clear line of reasoning throughout
DevelopingSome relevant scientific points with some explanation; logical sequence attempted but may lack coherence; some scientific terminology used
EmergingSimple, basic statements; limited scientific vocabulary; disorganised or list-like response
No relevant scientific content

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan before you write (2–3 minutes) — Jot down 4–5 key scientific points you need to include. Put them in a logical order. This planning stage is the difference between Developing and Secure.
  2. 2
    Write a brief opening statement — One sentence that shows you understand the question and sets the direction of your answer.
  3. 3
    Develop each point in a logical sequence — Each point should connect to the next. Use connectives: “This means that…,” “As a result…,” “Furthermore…,” “However…” to build a chain of reasoning. Use correct scientific terminology throughout.
  4. 4
    If it’s an evaluation question — Discuss advantages and disadvantages, or arguments for and against. Reach a conclusion or judgement supported by your scientific reasoning.
  5. 5
    Re-read your answer — Check that your answer flows logically, uses correct spelling of scientific terms, and addresses every part of the question.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
7 min Check
1 min

About ten minutes total. This is the biggest question on the paper — do not rush it. Planning is essential for a Secure response.

Building a chain of reasoning

“This means that… / As a result… / Therefore… / Consequently…”

Adding points

“Furthermore… / In addition… / Another factor is…”

Evaluating / contrasting

“However… / On the other hand… / A disadvantage of this is…”

Concluding

“Overall… / In conclusion… / The most significant factor is… because…”

Describe how the body responds to a bacterial infection and explain how vaccination can prevent the disease from developing. [6 marks]

Secure — 6 marks

When bacteria enter the body, white blood cells detect foreign antigens on the surface of the pathogens. Lymphocytes are activated and produce specific antibodies that are complementary in shape to the antigens on the bacteria. These antibodies bind to the antigens, causing the bacteria to clump together (agglutination) so that they can be destroyed by phagocytes, which engulf and digest the pathogens.

After the infection has been cleared, memory lymphocytes remain in the blood. If the same pathogen enters the body again, these memory cells recognise the antigen and produce the correct antibodies much more quickly and in greater quantities. This is called the secondary immune response, and it is usually fast enough to destroy the pathogen before symptoms develop.

Vaccination works by introducing a dead or weakened form of the pathogen (or just its antigens) into the body. This stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease. As a result, if the person is later exposed to the live pathogen, their immune system can mount a rapid secondary response, preventing the disease from developing.

Examiner: Secure, 6/6 — Comprehensive and logically sequenced. Covers initial immune response, memory cells, secondary response, and how vaccination exploits this. Accurate scientific terminology throughout (antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, phagocytes, memory cells, secondary immune response). Clear line of reasoning from infection to vaccination.

Describe how the body responds to a bacterial infection and explain how vaccination can prevent the disease from developing. [6 marks]

Emerging — 2 marks

White blood cells fight off the bacteria. They make antibodies. A vaccine has a dead version of the pathogen. It helps your body fight it next time.

Examiner: Emerging — basic statements with no development or chain of reasoning. No explanation of how antibodies work, no mention of memory cells, no link between vaccination and the secondary immune response. List-like rather than a coherent explanation.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    No plan = disorganised answer — Students who skip planning almost always produce Emerging–2 responses because their points are jumbled and lack a logical flow. Spend two minutes planning.
  • ❌
    Writing a list of facts — The examiner is assessing your ability to construct a coherent explanation, not list bullet points. Use full sentences and connectives to build an argument.
  • ❌
    Vague scientific language — “White blood cells fight bacteria” is Emerging. “Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies complementary to the pathogen’s antigens” is Secure. Precision matters.
  • ❌
    Not answering every part of the question — If the question says “describe AND explain,” you must do both. Ignoring half the question caps you at Developing regardless of quality.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10 min total

  1. Plan 4–5 key points
  2. Brief opening statement
  3. Develop points in logical sequence
  4. Use scientific terminology
  5. Evaluate if required (pros/cons)
  6. Re-read and check

title: 2 Marks — Describe Questions
content_html:
2 marks

Describe Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

“Describe” questions ask you to state what happens, what you see, or what a pattern or trend shows. You do not need to explain why — just state the facts clearly. These questions often relate to processes, trends in data, or what you would observe in a practical.

Marking

What You Need
2Two clear, correct descriptive points that address the question directly
1One correct point or two vague points
No relevant description or an explanation instead of a description

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what to describe — Is it a process (e.g. “Describe how vaccination works”), a trend (e.g. “Describe the pattern in the graph”), or an observation (e.g. “Describe what you would see”)?
  2. 2
    Make two distinct points — Each point should cover a different aspect. For a graph, state the trend and use data. For a process, state the steps in order.
  3. 3
    Use scientific language but do not explain — The word “because” is a warning sign. If you catch yourself writing “because,” you are explaining, not describing.

Timing

Describe — 2 min

About two minutes. Write two clear sentences and move on.

Describing a trend

“As [variable X] increases, [variable Y] increases/decreases. For example, at [data point 1]… and at [data point 2]…”

Describing a process

“First, [step 1 happens]. Then, [step 2 happens].”

Describing an observation

“You would see [observation 1]. The [substance/object] would [observation 2].”

Describe the trend shown in the graph of enzyme activity against temperature. [2 marks]

Full marks

As temperature increases from 10°C to 37°C, the rate of enzyme activity increases. Above 37°C, the rate of activity decreases rapidly.

Examiner: 2/2 — Two clear points about the trend, with data from the graph.

Describe the test for carbon dioxide gas. [2 marks]

Full marks

Bubble the gas through limewater. If carbon dioxide is present, the limewater turns milky (cloudy).

Examiner: 2/2 — States the test and the positive result.

Describe the trend in the graph of stopping distance against speed. [2 marks]

1 mark — no data

As speed goes up, stopping distance goes up because there is more kinetic energy.

Full marks

As speed increases, stopping distance increases. The relationship is not linear — stopping distance increases more steeply at higher speeds (e.g. at 30 mph it is 23 m, but at 60 mph it is 73 m).

Examiner: The weak answer uses “because” (explaining, not describing) and lacks data. The strong answer describes the pattern with specific values.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Explaining instead of describing — If the question says “Describe,” do not write “because.” State what happens, not why it happens.
  • ❌
    Not using data from the graph — When describing a trend, quote specific values from the axes. “It goes up” is worth less than “It increases from 20 to 85 between 0 and 60 seconds.”
  • ❌
    Only making one point — Two marks means two points. Check you have stated two distinct observations or steps.
← Recall (1 mark) Calculate (2 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
2 min total

Formula

  1. Identify what to describe
  2. Make two distinct points
  3. Use data if a graph is given
  4. Do not explain — just state

title: 2 Marks — Calculate Questions
content_html:
2 marks

Calculate Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

Calculate questions test your ability to use scientific formulae, substitute values correctly, and arrive at a numerical answer with the right units. The examiner awards marks for your working as well as the final answer — so even if your arithmetic is wrong, a correct method can still earn marks.

Marking

What You Need
2Correct substitution into the formula AND correct final answer with appropriate units
1Correct substitution but wrong calculation, OR correct formula stated but not applied, OR correct answer with no working shown
No relevant working and incorrect answer

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Write the formula — Write out the equation you need. In physics, the formula sheet is provided but you still need to select the right one. In chemistry, you may need to recall the formula (e.g. relative formula mass, moles calculations).
  2. 2
    Substitute the values — Replace each symbol with the numbers from the question. Check units match — convert if needed (e.g. km to m, minutes to seconds, cm³ to dm³).
  3. 3
    Calculate and show your working — Write each step of the calculation. If you make an arithmetic error, the examiner can still award marks for your method if they can follow your working.
  4. 4
    State the answer with units — Write the final answer clearly, including the correct unit (e.g. J, N, mol, Ω). If the question asks you to give your answer to a certain number of significant figures or decimal places, do so.

Timing

Calculate — 2–3 min

About two to three minutes. Write the formula, substitute, calculate, and check your units.

A car has a mass of 1200 kg and is travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car. Use the equation: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed² [2 marks]

Full marks

KE = 0.5 × m × v²
KE = 0.5 × 1200 × 15²
KE = 0.5 × 1200 × 225
KE = 135,000 J (or 135 kJ)

Examiner: 2/2 — Formula stated, values substituted correctly, correct answer with unit.

Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate (CaCO3). Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16. [2 marks]

Full marks

Mr = 40 + 12 + (16 × 3)
Mr = 40 + 12 + 48
Mr = 100

Examiner: 2/2 — Clear working, each element accounted for, correct final answer. No unit needed for relative formula mass.

A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 0.5 A flowing through it. Calculate the resistance. [2 marks]

1 mark — no formula or working

24 Ω

Full marks

R = V ÷ I
R = 12 ÷ 0.5
R = 24 Ω

Examiner: The answer alone may only score 1 mark (or 2 if an “allow” applies). Always show working to guarantee full marks.

FromToMultiply by
kmm× 1000
cmm÷ 100
gkg÷ 1000
cm³dm³÷ 1000
minutesseconds× 60
hoursseconds× 3600
kJJ× 1000
kWW× 1000

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not showing working — If you write only the final answer and it is wrong, you score zero. If you show correct substitution, you score at least 1 mark even with a calculation error.
  • ❌
    Forgetting to convert units — A common error is using grams when the formula requires kilograms, or cm when it needs metres. Always check the units before substituting.
  • ❌
    Missing units on the answer — “135,000” is incomplete. The examiner needs to see “135,000 J.” Some questions state the unit for you, but if they do not, you must provide it.
  • ❌
    Using the wrong formula — Read the question carefully. “Calculate the force” and “calculate the work done” use different equations even though both involve force.

← Back to Exam Technique

title: 3 Marks — Explain Questions
content_html:
3 marks

Explain Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

“Explain” questions require you to give a reason or mechanism for something happening. Unlike “Describe” questions, you must say why or how. The examiner is looking for a chain of logic: cause → effect, or statement → reasoning.

Marking

What You Need
3Three valid points, or two well-developed points with a clear chain of reasoning
2Two correct points or one point with good development
1One basic relevant point
No scientifically correct points

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the scientific concept — What topic area does this question relate to? What scientific principle explains the phenomenon?
  2. 2
    State what happens — Start with a clear factual statement about the process or observation.
  3. 3
    Explain why using scientific reasoning — Link the cause to the effect. Use “This means that…” or “This is because…” to build a chain of reasoning.
  4. 4
    Develop or add a third point — Either develop one of your points further or add a third distinct reason. Use subject-specific terminology to show depth of understanding.

Timing

Explain — 3–4 min

About three to four minutes. Write a short paragraph with a clear chain of cause and effect.

Cause → Effect chain

“[Statement of what happens]. This is because [scientific reason]. This means that [consequence/further development].”

Three-point approach

“Firstly, [point 1 with reason]. Secondly, [point 2 with reason]. Additionally, [point 3 with reason].”

Explain why the rate of photosynthesis increases as light intensity increases. [3 marks]

Full marks

As light intensity increases, more light energy is available for the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. This means that more chlorophyll molecules can absorb light energy, increasing the rate at which water is split and ATP is produced. As a result, more glucose is synthesised per unit of time, until another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes limiting.

Examiner: 3/3 — Three linked points: more light energy available, more absorption by chlorophyll, and the idea of a limiting factor.

Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points. [3 marks]

Full marks

Ionic compounds form a giant lattice structure made up of positive and negative ions. There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these many strong electrostatic forces, so the melting point is high.

Examiner: 3/3 — Structure identified, nature of bonding explained, linked to energy required to break bonds.

Explain why a skydiver reaches terminal velocity. [3 marks]

1 mark — lacks scientific detail

The skydiver stops accelerating because the air resistance is equal to gravity.

Full marks

When the skydiver first jumps, the force of gravity (weight) is greater than the air resistance, so there is a resultant downward force causing acceleration. As speed increases, air resistance increases. Eventually, air resistance equals the weight of the skydiver, so the resultant force is zero and acceleration stops — the skydiver falls at a constant speed called terminal velocity.

Examiner: The weak answer gets the conclusion right but does not explain the process. The strong answer traces the chain: unbalanced forces → acceleration → increasing air resistance → balanced forces → constant speed.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Describing instead of explaining — “The rate increases” describes what happens but does not explain why. Always include the scientific reason using “because” or “this means that.”
  • ❌
    Missing the chain of reasoning — An explanation needs to link cause to effect. “Ionic compounds have strong bonds so high melting points” jumps from A to C. You must go through B: what type of bonds, and why they require a lot of energy to break.
  • ❌
    Using vague language — Avoid “the particles move around more.” Be specific: “The particles gain kinetic energy so collide more frequently and with greater energy.”
← Calculate (2 marks) Compare and Explain (4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
3–4 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the scientific concept
  2. State what happens
  3. Say why (cause → effect)
  4. Develop or add a third point

title: 4 Marks — Compare and Explain Questions
content_html:
4 marks

Compare and Explain Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

These questions ask you to identify similarities or differences between two things and then explain why those differences or similarities exist. The examiner is looking for two skills: accurate comparison and scientific reasoning. You need comparative language (“whereas,” “however,” “both”) alongside clear scientific explanations.

Marking

What You Need
4Two clear comparisons, each with a developed scientific explanation
3Two comparisons with one well-explained, or one very well-developed comparison plus a second basic point
2Two basic comparisons without explanation, or one comparison with explanation
1One basic comparison or one relevant scientific point
No relevant comparison or scientific content

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify what you are comparing — Read the question to establish the two things being compared (e.g. two organisms, two materials, two processes, two data sets).
  2. 2
    State the first comparison using comparative language — Use “whereas,” “however,” “in contrast” or “both” to make the comparison explicit. Do not write about each thing separately — put them together in one sentence.
  3. 3
    Explain the scientific reason for the first comparison — Link the difference or similarity to the underlying science. Use “This is because…”
  4. 4
    Repeat for a second comparison + explanation — Make a second distinct point comparing the two things, then explain it scientifically. This earns the remaining marks.

Timing

Plan
1 min Write
4 min

About five minutes total. Spend a minute identifying two comparison points before writing.

Comparison + explanation

“[Thing A] has/does [feature], whereas [Thing B] has/does [different feature]. This is because [scientific reason].”

Similarity + explanation

“Both [Thing A] and [Thing B] [shared feature]. This is because they both [scientific reason].”

Compare the structures of animal cells and plant cells. Explain the differences. [4 marks]

Full marks

Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, whereas animal cells do not have a cell wall. This is because the cell wall provides structural support and rigidity to the plant, allowing it to stand upright without a skeleton. Additionally, plant cells contain chloroplasts, whereas animal cells do not. This is because plants make their own glucose by photosynthesis, which requires chloroplasts to absorb light energy, while animals obtain glucose by eating food.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two clear comparisons (cell wall, chloroplasts), both using comparative language, each with a developed scientific explanation.

Compare the properties of metals and non-metals. Explain the differences. [4 marks]

2 marks — comparison without explanation

Metals conduct electricity but non-metals do not. Metals are shiny and non-metals are dull.

Full marks

Metals are good conductors of electricity, whereas most non-metals are insulators. This is because metals have delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry charge. In contrast, metals are malleable (can be bent into shape), whereas non-metals are brittle. This is because the layers of metal ions can slide over each other while maintaining the metallic bonding, but in non-metals the rigid covalent bonds break when force is applied.

Examiner: The weak answer states two comparisons but explains neither. The strong answer pairs each comparison with the underlying scientific reason.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing about each thing separately — “Metals conduct electricity. Non-metals do not.” This is two separate statements, not a comparison. Use “whereas” or “however” to link them.
  • ❌
    Comparing without explaining — Stating the differences earns only half the marks. You must explain why the differences exist using scientific reasoning.
  • ❌
    Making the same point twice — “Metals are good conductors” and “non-metals are bad conductors” is one comparison, not two. Find a genuinely different property for your second point.
← Explain (3 marks) Extended Response (6 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5 min total

Formula

  1. Identify the two things to compare
  2. State comparison 1 + explain why
  3. State comparison 2 + explain why
  4. Use comparative language throughout

title: 6 Marks — Extended Response Questions
content_html:
6 marks

Extended Response Questions

Used in: All papers (Biology, Chemistry, Physics)

What the Examiner Wants

The 6-mark extended response is the highest-value question on each paper. It is marked using a levels of response mark scheme, which means the examiner reads your whole answer and decides which level it fits into. There is an asterisk (*) next to the question to show that quality of written communication is assessed. The examiner wants a logically structured, detailed answer that uses scientific terminology accurately and builds a clear argument or explanation.

Level Descriptors

LevelWhat You Need
SecureDetailed, coherent explanation with a logical structure; accurate and relevant scientific terminology; all key points addressed; clear line of reasoning throughout
DevelopingSome relevant scientific points with some explanation; logical sequence attempted but may lack coherence; some scientific terminology used
EmergingSimple, basic statements; limited scientific vocabulary; disorganised or list-like response
No relevant scientific content

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan before you write (2–3 minutes) — Jot down 4–5 key scientific points you need to include. Put them in a logical order. This planning stage is the difference between Developing and Secure.
  2. 2
    Write a brief opening statement — One sentence that shows you understand the question and sets the direction of your answer.
  3. 3
    Develop each point in a logical sequence — Each point should connect to the next. Use connectives: “This means that…,” “As a result…,” “Furthermore…,” “However…” to build a chain of reasoning. Use correct scientific terminology throughout.
  4. 4
    If it’s an evaluation question — Discuss advantages and disadvantages, or arguments for and against. Reach a conclusion or judgement supported by your scientific reasoning.
  5. 5
    Re-read your answer — Check that your answer flows logically, uses correct spelling of scientific terms, and addresses every part of the question.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
7 min Check
1 min

About ten minutes total. This is the biggest question on the paper — do not rush it. Planning is essential for a Secure response.

Building a chain of reasoning

“This means that… / As a result… / Therefore… / Consequently…”

Adding points

“Furthermore… / In addition… / Another factor is…”

Evaluating / contrasting

“However… / On the other hand… / A disadvantage of this is…”

Concluding

“Overall… / In conclusion… / The most significant factor is… because…”

Describe how the body responds to a bacterial infection and explain how vaccination can prevent the disease from developing. [6 marks]

Secure — 6 marks

When bacteria enter the body, white blood cells detect foreign antigens on the surface of the pathogens. Lymphocytes are activated and produce specific antibodies that are complementary in shape to the antigens on the bacteria. These antibodies bind to the antigens, causing the bacteria to clump together (agglutination) so that they can be destroyed by phagocytes, which engulf and digest the pathogens.

After the infection has been cleared, memory lymphocytes remain in the blood. If the same pathogen enters the body again, these memory cells recognise the antigen and produce the correct antibodies much more quickly and in greater quantities. This is called the secondary immune response, and it is usually fast enough to destroy the pathogen before symptoms develop.

Vaccination works by introducing a dead or weakened form of the pathogen (or just its antigens) into the body. This stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease. As a result, if the person is later exposed to the live pathogen, their immune system can mount a rapid secondary response, preventing the disease from developing.

Examiner: Secure, 6/6 — Comprehensive and logically sequenced. Covers initial immune response, memory cells, secondary response, and how vaccination exploits this. Accurate scientific terminology throughout (antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, phagocytes, memory cells, secondary immune response). Clear line of reasoning from infection to vaccination.

Describe how the body responds to a bacterial infection and explain how vaccination can prevent the disease from developing. [6 marks]

Emerging — 2 marks

White blood cells fight off the bacteria. They make antibodies. A vaccine has a dead version of the pathogen. It helps your body fight it next time.

Examiner: Emerging — basic statements with no development or chain of reasoning. No explanation of how antibodies work, no mention of memory cells, no link between vaccination and the secondary immune response. List-like rather than a coherent explanation.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    No plan = disorganised answer — Students who skip planning almost always produce Emerging–2 responses because their points are jumbled and lack a logical flow. Spend two minutes planning.
  • ❌
    Writing a list of facts — The examiner is assessing your ability to construct a coherent explanation, not list bullet points. Use full sentences and connectives to build an argument.
  • ❌
    Vague scientific language — “White blood cells fight bacteria” is Emerging. “Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies complementary to the pathogen’s antigens” is Secure. Precision matters.
  • ❌
    Not answering every part of the question — If the question says “describe AND explain,” you must do both. Ignoring half the question caps you at Developing regardless of quality.
← Compare and Explain (4 marks) Recall (1 mark) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10 min total

Must Cover

  1. Plan 4–5 key points
  2. Brief opening statement
  3. Develop points in logical sequence
  4. Use scientific terminology
  5. Evaluate if required (pros/cons)
  6. Re-read and check

title: Listening Comprehension Strategies (Paper 1 Section A)
content_html:
Paper 1 — Section A

Listening Comprehension Strategies

Spanish (8692) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 1 tests your ability to understand spoken Spanish across the three themes: People and Lifestyle, Popular Culture, and Communication and the World Around Us. You will hear a range of recordings — monologues, conversations, announcements, and messages — and answer questions in English or Spanish.

At Foundation tier, the language is slower and more predictable. At Higher tier, speakers talk at a more natural pace with less repetition and more complex structures. Each extract is played twice.

Question Types

TypeWhat You Do
Multiple choiceChoose the correct answer (A, B, C, or D) from options in English or Spanish
MatchingMatch speakers or descriptions to images, statements, or categories
Short answerWrite brief answers in English or Spanish based on what you hear
True/false/not mentionedDecide whether statements match the recording

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the questions before you listen — Use every second of reading time. Underline key words in each question. If the question says “Where does María go?”, you know to listen for a place. Predict the kind of vocabulary you need.
  2. 2
    First listen: get the gist — Don’t panic if you miss words. Focus on understanding the overall message. Jot down any key words you catch (times, places, opinions).
  3. 3
    Second listen: confirm and fill gaps — Now target the specific answers. Check your initial notes against what you hear. Listen for negatives (no, nunca, ni…ni) and time markers (ayer, la semana pasada, el año que viene) that can change the meaning completely.
  4. 4
    Watch for distractors — AQA often includes information designed to trick you. A speaker might mention several places but only one is the answer. The correct answer usually comes after a contrast word like pero (but) or sin embargo (however).
  5. 5
    Answer every question — Never leave a blank. For multiple choice, eliminate obviously wrong answers and make an educated guess from what remains.

Timing

Read Qs 1st Listen 2nd Listen + Write

You control nothing here — the audio is played for you. Use every pause to read ahead, check your answers, and prepare for the next question.

Opinion Markers

Positive: me gusta, me encanta, me mola, es genial, es estupendo, me parece bien

Negative: no me gusta, odio, detesto, es fatal, es horrible, me parece mal

Mixed: por un lado… por otro lado, depende, no está mal

Time Markers

Past: ayer, la semana pasada, el año pasado, cuando era joven

Present: hoy, normalmente, todos los días, cada semana

Future: mañana, la semana que viene, el año próximo, voy a, tengo la intención de

Connectives & Contrast

pero (but), sin embargo (however), aunque (although), porque (because), ya que (since), además (furthermore), también (also)

You hear: “Antes iba al cine todos los fines de semana, pero ahora prefiero quedarme en casa y ver películas en línea.”

Question: What does this person prefer to do now?
A. Go to the cinema   B. Stay at home and watch films online   C. Go out with friends

Correct: B

Key clue: “pero ahora prefiero” — the word pero (but) signals a change. Everything before it (antes iba al cine) is what they used to do. The answer is what comes after the contrast: quedarme en casa y ver películas en línea.

Trap: Students who hear “cine” and immediately choose A miss the contrast. Always listen for pero, sin embargo, and aunque — they flip the meaning.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Choosing the first thing you hear — AQA plants distractors early. The speaker might say “Fui a la playa pero al final nos quedamos en el hotel”. The answer is hotel, not beach.
  • ✗
    Ignoring negatives — “No quiero ir” is the opposite of “Quiero ir”. Listen carefully for no, nunca, ni…ni, tampoco.
  • ✗
    Confusing similar-sounding words — casa (house) vs caza (hunting), pero (but) vs perro (dog), hombre (man) vs hambre (hunger). Context is everything.
  • ✗
    Leaving answers blank — There is no penalty for guessing. Always write something — even an educated guess gives you a chance.
Dictation →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference

  2. Underline key words
  3. Predict vocabulary

During Listening

  1. 1st play: gist + key words
  2. 2nd play: confirm + fill gaps
  3. Watch for pero / sin embargo

title: Dictation Technique and Common Errors (Paper 1 Section B)
content_html:
Paper 1 — Section B

Dictation Technique & Common Errors

Spanish (8692) • Part of Paper 1 (Listening)

What the Question Asks

In the dictation section, you hear short sentences in Spanish and must write them down exactly as you hear them. Every word must be spelled correctly, including accents. The sentences test vocabulary from all three themes and include a range of tenses.

Foundation tier: simpler sentences with high-frequency vocabulary. Higher tier: longer sentences with more complex grammar and less common words.

How Marks Are Allocated

What You Need
Full marksEvery word spelled correctly, including accents. Each correct word scores individually.
PartialCorrect words earn marks even if others are wrong. You are not penalised for extra words.
0 per wordIncorrect spelling, missing accents on words where the accent changes meaning, or missing words

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    First play: listen to the whole sentence — Do not write yet. Focus on understanding the meaning and structure. How many words are there? What tense is being used?
  2. 2
    Pause: write what you can — Write down as much as you can. Leave gaps for words you are unsure about. Use dashes or blanks to hold the space.
  3. 3
    Second play: fill gaps and check — Focus on the words you missed. Check verb endings carefully: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. Check accents on key words.
  4. 4
    Apply phonics rules — Spanish spelling is highly phonetic. If you can hear the sound, you can usually spell the word. Use your knowledge of Spanish phonics to decode unfamiliar words.
  5. 5
    Final check: grammar sense — Does the sentence make grammatical sense? Check subject-verb agreement, gender agreement (el/la, -o/-a), and tense consistency.

Timing

1st Listen Write 2nd Listen + Check

The pace is controlled by the audio. Use every pause productively — write fast, check fast.

SoundSpellingExample
/k/ before e, iququiero, porque, quince
/k/ before a, o, uccasa, como, cuando
/th/ or /s/ before e, ic or zcine, hacer, zapato
/g/ before e, iguguitarra, guerra, seguir
/kh/ (throaty) before e, ig or jgente, gimnasio, joven
/ny/ñespañol, año, niño
/ly/ or /y/llllamar, calle, pollo
silent letterhhacer, hoy, hay
/rr/ (rolled)rr or initial rperro, rápido, alrededor
/b/ (same sound)b or vbien, viajar, beber, vivir

Accents that change meaning:

sí (yes) vs si (if) • él (he) vs el (the) • está (is — location/state) vs esta (this) • habló (he spoke) vs hablo (I speak)

b vs v confusion:

beber (to drink), vivir (to live), haber (to have), viajar (to travel), trabajar (to work), llover (to rain)

Double letters:

llave (key), llevar (to carry/wear), perro (dog), corre (he runs), correo (post/email)

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Missing accents — In dictation, missing accents cost marks, especially where they change meaning: habló (he spoke) vs hablo (I speak). Learn the accent rules.
  • ✗
    Confusing b and v — In Spanish, b and v sound identical. You must know the spelling: bien (b), viajar (v). There is no shortcut — learn the words.
  • ✗
    Forgetting silent h — hacer, hay, hoy, hablar all start with a silent h. If the word sounds like it starts with a vowel, consider whether it has an h.
  • ✗
    Wrong verb endings — -o (I), -a/-e (he/she), -an/-en (they). Listen carefully to the final syllable — it tells you who is doing the action.
← Listening Comprehension Reading Comprehension →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5–8 min total

Dictation Formula

  1. 1st listen: understand, don’t write
  2. Pause: write what you can
  3. 2nd listen: fill gaps
  4. Apply phonics rules
  5. Check grammar sense

Key Accent Rules

habló = he spoke (preterite)
hablo = I speak (present)
Always check: does the accent change meaning?

title: Reading Comprehension Strategies (Paper 3 Section A)
content_html:
Paper 3 — Section A

Reading Comprehension Strategies

Spanish (8692) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 3 tests your ability to understand written Spanish. Section A contains a range of texts — adverts, emails, articles, blogs, and literary extracts — with questions that test comprehension at different levels: identifying key details, understanding opinions, drawing inferences, and recognising tenses.

Foundation and Higher tiers share some questions (overlap questions), but Higher includes more complex texts and inferential questions.

Question Types

TypeWhat You Do
Multiple choiceSelect the correct answer from options (English or Spanish)
MatchingMatch people, descriptions, or opinions to correct categories
Short answer (English)Answer questions in English based on the Spanish text
Short answer (Spanish)Answer questions in Spanish (Higher tier)
True/false/not mentionedAssess whether statements match the text

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the questions first — Before reading the text, read all the questions. This tells you what to look for and saves time. Underline key words in each question.
  2. 2
    Skim the text for gist — Read the whole text quickly. What is it about? Who is speaking? What is the general opinion? Don’t get stuck on unknown words.
  3. 3
    Scan for specific answers — Go back to each question and find the relevant section of the text. Look for synonyms — the text often rephrases the question using different vocabulary.
  4. 4
    Use cognates and word families — Many Spanish words look like English: importante (important), problema (problem), información (information). Also use word roots: if you know trabajar (to work), you can guess trabajador (worker/hardworking).
  5. 5
    Watch for negatives and qualifiers — A single no, nunca, or ni…ni changes the entire meaning. Similarly, demasiado (too much) and bastante (quite) are different from muy (very).
  6. 6
    Check tenses — AQA tests whether you can distinguish past, present, and future. “Fui al cine” (I went — past) is different from “Voy al cine” (I go — present) and “Iré al cine” (I will go — future).

Timing

Read Qs Skim text Answer Check

Foundation: 45 minutes for the whole paper. Aim for roughly 1 minute per mark. Leave 5 minutes at the end to re-read your answers. Higher: 60 minutes — same strategy, more time for the complex final questions.

Dealing with Unknown Words

Strategy 1 — Cognates: responsable, técnico, economía, contaminación — these look like English and mean the same thing.

Strategy 2 — Word families: From comer (to eat), you can guess comida (food/meal), comedor (dining room). From vivir (to live), vivienda (housing).

Strategy 3 — Context: If a sentence says “Compré una [unknown word] en la panadería”, you know it must be something you buy at a bakery.

Strategy 4 — False friends warning: sensible = sensitive (NOT sensible), embarazada = pregnant (NOT embarrassed), éxito = success (NOT exit), actual = current (NOT actual).

Text: “El año pasado, mi hermana y yo fuimos de vacaciones a Barcelona. Visitamos la Sagrada Familia y comimos paella en un restaurante cerca de la playa. El único problema fue que hacía demasiado calor.”

Q: What was the only problem? [1 mark]

Full mark

It was too hot.

Key clue: “El único problema fue que hacía demasiado calor” — único problema = only problem, demasiado calor = too hot. Do not write “it was hot” — the word demasiado (too much) is essential for full marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Falling for false friends — sensible means sensitive, not sensible. Actual means current, not actual. Keep a mental list of the most common false friends.
  • ✗
    Missing tense distinctions — If the question asks what someone will do, don’t give what they did. Check the verb ending: -é, -ó (past), -o, -a (present), -á, -é (future).
  • ✗
    Writing too much in English answers — If the question is worth 1 mark, a short phrase is enough. Over-writing wastes time and can introduce errors.
  • ✗
    Ignoring qualifiers — Bastante (quite), demasiado (too), and un poco (a bit) are crucial for accurate answers. Don’t skip them.

title: Translation: Spanish to English (Paper 3 Section B)
content_html:
Paper 3 — Section B

Translation: Spanish → English

Spanish (8692) • Part of Paper 3 (Reading)

What the Question Asks

You are given a short passage in Spanish (approximately 50 words) and must translate it into English. The passage covers vocabulary and grammar from across the specification. It is the final question on Paper 3 and is worth 10 marks.

How Marks Are Allocated

Description
9–10All content translated accurately. Occasional minor errors that do not affect meaning.
7–8Most content translated accurately. A few minor errors or omissions.
5–6A reasonable attempt. Some accurate sections but gaps or errors in places.
3–4Limited accuracy. Several sections poorly translated or missing.
1–2Very limited. Only isolated words or phrases correctly translated.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the whole passage first — Get the overall meaning before you start translating. What is the topic? What tenses are used? Understanding context helps you translate tricky words.
  2. 2
    Translate sentence by sentence — Work through the passage one sentence at a time. Identify the verb, the subject, and any time markers first.
  3. 3
    Do not translate word for word — Spanish word order differs from English. “Me gusta mucho la música” is “I really like music”, not “Me pleases much the music”. Aim for natural English.
  4. 4
    Use context for unknown words — If you don’t know a word, use the rest of the sentence. “Compré un regalo para mi madre” — even if you forget regalo, you know you bought something for your mum. Write “I bought a present for my mum” or your best guess — never leave a gap.
  5. 5
    Re-read your English version — Does it read naturally? Does it make sense? Check you have not accidentally changed the tense or missed a negative.

Timing

Read Translate Re-read

Allow 10–12 minutes for this question. It is worth 10 marks — spend time on it. Leave 2–3 minutes to re-read your English and smooth out awkward phrasing.

Spanish text: “El verano pasado, fui de vacaciones a Málaga con mi familia. Nos alojamos en un hotel cerca de la playa. Hacía mucho sol y nadé en el mar todos los días. El año que viene, me gustaría visitar América del Sur.”

Full marks

“Last summer, I went on holiday to Malaga with my family. We stayed in a hotel near the beach. It was very sunny and I swam in the sea every day. Next year, I would like to visit South America.”

Examiner notes: All content accurately conveyed. Tenses correct: fui (went — preterite), nos alojamos (we stayed), hacía (it was — imperfect for weather), me gustaría (I would like — conditional). Natural English throughout.

6/10 — tense errors + unnatural English

“The past summer, I go of holidays to Malaga with my family. We stay in a hotel close of the beach. It did much sun and I swim in the sea all the days. The year that comes, I would like to visit America of the South.”

Examiner: Key meaning conveyed, but errors throughout. “I go” should be “I went” (past tense). “The past summer” is unnatural English — “Last summer” is better. “Much sun” should be “very sunny.” Word-for-word translation produces unnatural English that costs marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Translating word for word — “Tengo quince años” is “I am fifteen years old”, not “I have fifteen years.” Spanish idioms must be turned into natural English.
  • ✗
    Getting tenses wrong — “Fui” (I went) vs “voy” (I go) vs “iré” (I will go). The wrong tense changes the whole answer. Look at time markers for clues.
  • ✗
    Leaving gaps — A blank earns zero. An approximate translation or educated guess can still earn marks. Always write something.
  • ✗
    Ignoring the imperfect tense — “Hacía calor” = “It was hot” (description, not a one-off event). “Hizo calor” = “It was hot” (on a specific day). Understanding the imperfect/preterite distinction matters at Higher.

Quick Reference
10–12 min total

Translation Formula

  1. Read the whole passage
  2. Translate sentence by sentence
  3. Aim for natural English
  4. Guess unknown words from context
  5. Re-read your English version

Marks: 10

Time: 10–12 minutes

title: Translation: English to Spanish (Paper 4)
content_html:
Paper 4 — Translation

Translation: English → Spanish

Spanish (8692) • Part of Paper 4 (Writing)

What the Question Asks

You are given five English sentences and must translate each one into Spanish. The sentences test a range of tenses (present, past, future, conditional), key vocabulary from the themes, and grammatical accuracy. Worth 10 marks (Foundation) or 10 marks (Higher, with harder grammar).

How Marks Are Allocated

Each sentence is marked individually. You earn marks for conveying the meaning accurately with correct grammar and spelling. Minor errors that don’t affect communication may still earn partial credit.

Per SentenceWhat You Need
2Meaning fully conveyed with accurate grammar and spelling
1Meaning partially conveyed — some errors but the message is understandable
Meaning not conveyed, or so many errors that the sentence is incomprehensible

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the English sentence carefully — Identify the subject, verb, tense, and any tricky elements (negatives, time phrases, opinions). Know what you need before you start writing.
  2. 2
    Translate the verb first — Get the tense and person right. “I go” = voy (present), “I went” = fui (preterite), “I used to go” = iba (imperfect), “I will go” = iré (future).
  3. 3
    Build the sentence around the verb — Add the subject (if needed — Spanish often omits it), the object, and any extras (time phrases, opinions, connectives).
  4. 4
    Check gender and agreement — Adjectives must agree with their noun: el chico alto but la chica alta. Articles too: el/la, un/una.
  5. 5
    Check accents and spelling — Missing accents on key words can change meaning. Write clearly so the examiner can read your answer.

Timing

Translation — 10–12 min (2 min per sentence)

Aim for about 2 minutes per sentence. If you are stuck on one, move on and come back. A partially correct sentence scores more than a blank.

English: I do not like to listen to music.

Full marks

No me gusta escuchar música.

Key points: No before me gusta for the negative. Infinitive escuchar after gustar. No article needed before música in this context.

English: Yesterday I recycled all my rubbish.

Full marks

Ayer reciclé toda mi basura.

Key points: Ayer at the start (time phrase). Preterite reciclé (accent essential on the é). Toda agrees with feminine basura.

English (Higher): I am going to eat after going to the gym.

Full marks

Voy a comer después de ir al gimnasio.

Key points: Near future voy a + infinitive. Después de + infinitive for “after doing.” Al = a + el (contraction). This sentence tests three grammar points at once.

English (Higher): I would love to go on a long trip with you.

1/2 — meaning conveyed but grammar errors

Me encantaría ir en un viaje largo contigo. ✔

Me gustaria ir a un viaje largo con tu. — Two errors: missing accent on gustaría, and con tu should be contigo.

Key Grammar to Check

Ser vs Estar: Soy alto (permanent) vs Estoy cansado (temporary state)

Por vs Para: por (because of, through, duration) vs para (for the purpose of, in order to, deadline)

Preterite vs Imperfect: Fui (I went — one-off) vs Iba (I used to go — repeated/description)

Reflexive verbs: Me levanto (I get up), se llama (he/she is called)

Negatives: No quiero (I don’t want), Nunca voy (I never go), No tengo ni dinero ni tiempo (I have neither money nor time)

Agreements: Las casas blancas (feminine plural), un amigo simpático (masculine singular)

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Wrong tense — “I went” must be preterite (fui), not present (voy). Always check the English tense before translating.
  • ✗
    Missing accents on preterite verbs — hablé (I spoke), comió (he ate), vivió (he lived). These accents are not optional — they show the tense.
  • ✗
    Gender errors on adjectives — “Mi madre es simpático” should be simpática. Always match the adjective to the noun’s gender.
  • ✗
    Using English word order — In Spanish, adjectives usually come after the noun: “una casa grande”, not “una grande casa”.

Quick Reference
10–12 min total

Translation Formula

  1. Read the English carefully
  2. Translate the verb first (correct tense!)
  3. Build the sentence around it
  4. Check gender agreement
  5. Check accents + spelling

Marks: 10 (5 sentences × 2)

Time: 10–12 minutes

title: Writing Tasks: Photo, 50-Word, 90-Word and 150-Word (Paper 4)
content_html:
Paper 4 — Writing

Writing Tasks: Photo, 50-Word, 90-Word & 150-Word

Spanish (8692) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 4 tests your ability to write in Spanish. The tasks increase in length and complexity. Foundation and Higher tiers have different combinations:

TaskFoundationHigher
Photo description5 sentences about a photo [10 marks]—
50-word taskEmail/message with bullet points [10 marks]—
GrammarFill gaps with correct Spanish [5 marks]—
Translation (Eng → Spa)[10 marks][10 marks]
90-word taskStructured writing [15 marks][15 marks]
150-word task—Open writing [25 marks]

The 90-word and 150-word tasks are marked on communication (content + response to bullet points), range of language (variety of vocabulary and structures), and accuracy (grammar + spelling).

Step-by-Step Method

Photo Description (Foundation only) — 10 marks

  1. 1
    Write 5 clear sentences — Each sentence scores up to 2 marks. Describe what you see: people, actions, setting, weather, clothes, objects.
  2. 2
    Use a range of structures — Don’t start every sentence with “Hay”. Mix it up: “En la foto hay…”, “Puedo ver…”, “Una mujer está comiendo…”, “Hace sol”.
  3. 3
    Include opinions where possible — “Parece que la familia está contenta” shows more than just description.

50-Word Task (Foundation only) — 10 marks

  1. 1
    Address every bullet point — There are usually 5 bullet points. Miss one and you lose marks for communication.
  2. 2
    Write approximately 50 words — Going slightly over is fine, but significantly under will cost you.
  3. 3
    Keep it simple and accurate — At Foundation, accuracy matters more than complexity. A correct simple sentence beats an incorrect complex one.

90-Word Task — 15 marks

  1. 1
    Plan before writing — Read the bullet points. Note the tense each one requires (the bullet points often require past, present, and future). Plan 2–3 sentences per bullet point.
  2. 2
    Cover all bullet points equally — Don’t write half your words on the first bullet point and rush the rest. Spread your content evenly.
  3. 3
    Show off your grammar — Use connectives (porque, sin embargo, además), opinions (creo que, en mi opinión), and different tenses. This boosts your “range of language” mark.
  4. 4
    Check your work — Read through for gender agreement, verb endings, and spelling. Fix errors before moving on.

150-Word Task (Higher only) — 25 marks

  1. 1
    Plan with “fancy phrases” — Before writing, note 3–4 impressive structures you want to include: subjunctive (quiero que sea), conditional (me gustaría), si clauses (si tuviera dinero, iría).
  2. 2
    Cover both bullet points in depth — Unlike the 90-word task, you have only 2 bullet points but more space. Develop each with opinions, reasons, and examples.
  3. 3
    Use a wide range of tenses — Preterite, imperfect, present, near future, simple future, conditional, and subjunctive (Higher). Variety = higher marks.
  4. 4
    Write a short conclusion — End with a summary opinion or a look to the future. This shows structure and maturity.

Timing

Photo [8 min] 50-word [8 min] 90-word [15 min] 150-word [20 min]

Foundation (1 hour): Photo 8 min, 50-word 8 min, Grammar 5 min, Translation 10 min, 90-word 15 min, check 4 min.
Higher (1 hr 15 min): Translation 10 min, 90-word 15 min, 150-word 25 min, check 5 min.

Use these to boost your “range of language” mark:

SpanishEnglishWhen to Use
Lo mejor es que…The best thing is that…Opinions
Lo peor fue que…The worst thing was that…Past opinions
Si tuviera la oportunidad, me gustaría…If I had the opportunity, I would like to…Conditional + subjunctive
Ojalá pudiera…I wish I could…Subjunctive wishes
Aunque sea difícil, vale la pena…Although it is difficult, it is worth…Concession
Cuando sea mayor…When I am older…Future + subjunctive
Estoy convencido/a de que…I am convinced that…Strong opinions
A mi modo de ver…In my view…Introducing opinions
Por un lado… por otro lado…On one hand… on the other…Balanced argument
Debo admitir que…I must admit that…Nuanced views

Task: You are writing to your Colombian friend about your school. Write approximately 90 words in Spanish. Mention: what your school is like / what you did yesterday at school / what you will do after your exams. [15 marks]

14/15 — strong answer

Mi instituto es bastante grande y moderno. Hay muchas instalaciones, por ejemplo, un gimnasio y una biblioteca. Lo mejor es que los profesores son muy simpáticos y nos ayudan mucho.

Ayer tuve clases de matemáticas y ciencias. Hicimos un experimento en el laboratorio, que fue muy interesante. Sin embargo, lo peor fue que tuve demasiados deberes.

Después de mis exámenes, voy a celebrar con mis amigos. Además, me gustaría viajar a España porque quiero mejorar mi español.

Examiner: All three bullet points covered. Three tenses used (present, preterite, near future + conditional). “Fancy phrases” used naturally: Lo mejor es que, Sin embargo, Lo peor fue que, Me gustaría. Excellent range of vocabulary. One minor slip prevents full marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Missing a bullet point — Each bullet point carries marks. If you skip one, you cap your score. Always check you have covered every bullet.
  • ✗
    Using only one tense — Even if the bullet points don’t explicitly ask for past/future, find ways to include them. “Range of language” rewards variety.
  • ✗
    Going way under the word count — If the task says 90 words, writing 40 words will severely limit your marks. Plan to write 85–100 words.
  • ✗
    Memorising pre-learned answers — examiners can spot generic, memorised text. Adapt your “fancy phrases” to the specific question. Relevance matters.

  2. Multiple tenses used?
  3. Opinions + connectives?
  4. Gender agreement checked?
  5. Accents on verbs?

title: Role-Play and Reading Aloud (Paper 2)
content_html:
Paper 2 — Tasks 1 & 2

Role-Play & Reading Aloud

Spanish (8692) • Part of Paper 2 (Speaking, 25%)

What the Tasks Ask

Task 1: Role-Play [10 marks]

You are given a scenario (e.g. buying a ticket, booking a hotel, visiting a doctor) with instructions in English. You must play your role in Spanish, responding to the examiner’s questions and giving information as specified on the card. You have one “unpredictable” question where you must think on your feet.

Task 2: Reading Aloud [10 marks]

You are given a short passage in Spanish (around 35–50 words) and must read it aloud clearly and accurately. The examiner then asks you questions about the passage, which you answer in Spanish.

How Marks Are Allocated

CriterionRole-PlayReading Aloud
Communication5 tasks completed successfully (2 marks each)Clear, accurate reading (up to 5 marks)
Questions—Answers to follow-up questions (up to 5 marks)

Step-by-Step: Role-Play

  1. 1
    Use your preparation time wisely — You get time to study the card before the exam starts. Plan what you will say for each bullet point. Think about the tense required and any tricky vocabulary.
  2. 2
    Listen carefully to the examiner — The examiner plays the other role. Listen to their questions — they often contain clues. If they ask “¿Cuánto cuesta?”, you need to give a price.
  3. 3
    Use full sentences — Don’t just say “sí” or “no”. For 2 marks per task, you need to convey the message clearly. “Sí, me gustaría reservar una habitación doble, por favor” is much better than “Sí”.
  4. 4
    Prepare for the “!” (unpredictable) question — One task on the card has an exclamation mark — this is the unpredictable element. You won’t know the question in advance. Stay calm, listen, and give any reasonable answer in Spanish.
  5. 5
    If you make a mistake, correct yourself — Self-correction shows awareness and does not cost marks. Say it again correctly and move on.

Step-by-Step: Reading Aloud

  1. 1
    Read through the passage silently first — In your preparation time, identify any tricky words. Practise the pronunciation in your head. Note where the natural pauses fall (commas, full stops).
  2. 2
    Read at a steady pace — Do not rush. Speak clearly and at a natural speed. Pause at punctuation marks. The examiner is listening for pronunciation and fluency, not speed.
  3. 3
    Apply Spanish pronunciation rules — Every vowel is always the same sound. A = “ah”, E = “eh”, I = “ee”, O = “oh”, U = “oo”. The letter h is always silent. J sounds like the “ch” in Scottish “loch.”
  4. 4
    Answer the follow-up questions — After reading, the examiner asks questions related to the passage. Listen carefully, answer in Spanish, and try to extend your answers with opinions or reasons.

Timing

Role-Play [~3 min] Reading Aloud + Qs [~4 min]

The speaking exam is short. You have preparation time before it starts, then the actual exam is 7–9 minutes (Foundation) or 10–12 minutes (Higher) for all three tasks combined.

Letter/ComboSoundExample
j“ch” as in Scottish “loch”joven, trabajar, rojo
ll“y” soundllamar, calle, lluvia
ñ“ny” soundaño, español, niño
halways silenthacer, hoy, hora
z“th” (Castilian) or “s”zapato, plaza, diez
c before e/i“th” (Castilian) or “s”cine, hacer, ciencia
qu“k” soundque, quiero, quince
gu before e/ihard “g”guitarra, guerra
rrrolled “r”perro, correr, arroz

Tip: Both Castilian (“th” for z/c) and Latin American (“s”) pronunciation are accepted by AQA. Be consistent — don’t mix them.

Scenario: You are at a train station in Spain. The teacher plays the ticket seller.

1. Say where you want to go. 2. Ask about the price. 3. Say when you want to travel. 4. Ask about the journey time. 5. ! (Unpredictable question)

Strong response

1. “Quisiera un billete de ida y vuelta a Sevilla, por favor.” (I would like a return ticket to Seville, please.)

2. “¿Cuánto cuesta el billete?” (How much does the ticket cost?)

3. “Quiero viajar el viernes por la mañana.” (I want to travel on Friday morning.)

4. “¿Cuánto dura el viaje?” (How long does the journey take?)

5. Examiner: “¿Con quién viaja usted?” → “Viajo con mi familia. Somos cuatro personas.”

Examiner: All 5 tasks completed clearly. Polite register used (quisiera). The unpredictable question was answered confidently with an extended response.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Answering in English — Everything you say must be in Spanish. Even if you are unsure, say something in Spanish rather than switching to English.
  • ✗
    One-word answers — “Sí” alone rarely earns full marks. Extend: “Sí, me gustaría una mesa para dos personas, por favor.”
  • ✗
    Rushing the reading aloud — Slow down. Mispronouncing words because you are reading too fast loses marks. Clarity beats speed.
  • ✗
    Anglicising pronunciation — Spanish vowels are always pure. A is always “ah”, never the English “ay”. Practise reading Spanish aloud before the exam.

Role-Play Formula

  1. Use prep time to plan each task
  2. Listen to examiner’s questions
  3. Full sentences, not one-word answers
  4. Self-correct if you slip up

Reading Aloud Formula

  1. Read silently first
  2. Read at a steady pace
  3. Pause at punctuation
  4. Extend follow-up answers
