title: Photo Card Discussion (Paper 2)
content_html:
Paper 2 — Task 3

Photo Card Discussion

Spanish (8692) • Part of Paper 2 (Speaking, 25%)

What the Task Asks

You are given a photo related to one of the three themes. You must:

  1. Describe the photo in Spanish
  2. Answer two questions linked to the photo
  3. Hold a general conversation on the theme, answering further questions from the examiner

This is the longest and highest-value speaking task. At Higher tier, the conversation goes deeper and requires more complex language.

How Marks Are Allocated

CriterionWhat It Means
Communication & ContentHow much relevant information you convey; how well you respond to questionsUp to 10
Range of LanguageVariety of vocabulary, structures, and tensesUp to 10
AccuracyGrammar, gender, verb endings, pronunciationUp to 10
Pronunciation & IntonationClarity, natural Spanish sounds, correct stressUp to 10

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Preparation: describe the photo mentally — During prep time, plan 4–5 sentences about the photo. Cover: who is in it (hay una familia), what they are doing (están comiendo), where they are (en un restaurante), the weather/time if visible, and an opinion (parece divertido).
  2. 2
    Describe the photo confidently — Use a variety of structures: “En la foto puedo ver…”, “Hay…”, “Una persona está [gerund]…”, “Parece que…”. Don’t just list objects — describe actions and give opinions.
  3. 3
    Answer the two linked questions — These relate to the photo’s theme. Give developed answers (2–3 sentences each). Include an opinion + reason: “Creo que es importante porque…”
  4. 4
    General conversation: extend every answer — The examiner will ask broader questions on the theme. Never give one-sentence answers. Use the PALM technique:
    Point — state your answer
    Amplify — add detail or example
    Link — connect to another idea
    Mix tenses — add a past or future comment
  5. 5
    Show off your best Spanish — This is your chance to demonstrate range. Use subjunctive phrases (quiero que, es importante que), conditionals (me gustaría, iría), and impressive connectives (sin embargo, no obstante, a pesar de que).

Timing

Photo desc [1–2 min] 2 questions [2 min] Conversation [3–5 min]

The general conversation is the longest section. Keep talking — silence costs marks. If you don’t understand a question, ask: “¿Puede repetir, por favor?”

Opening

“En la foto puedo ver…” / “En esta foto hay…”

Actions

“Una persona está [comiendo / jugando / hablando]…”

“Parece que están [disfrutando / trabajando / descansando]…”

Setting

“Están en [un parque / un restaurante / la playa]…”

“Al fondo se puede ver…” (In the background you can see…)

Opinion

“Creo que la foto muestra…” / “Me parece que…”

“En mi opinión, parece [divertido / relajante / interesante]…”

Examiner asks: “¿Qué haces para mantenerte en forma?” (What do you do to keep fit?)

Strong answer using PALM

P (Point): “Para mantenerme en forma, juego al fútbol dos veces por semana.”

A (Amplify): “Además, intento comer de manera saludable. Por ejemplo, como mucha fruta y verdura.”

L (Link): “Sin embargo, debo admitir que a veces como demasiado chocolate.”

M (Mix tenses): “El año pasado, hice una carrera de cinco kilómetros y me gustaría hacerla otra vez.”

Examiner: Excellent response. Four tenses (present, past, conditional), connectives (además, sin embargo), an example, and a personal opinion. This is exactly what earns top marks for communication and range.

Weak answer — too short, one tense

“Juego al fútbol.”

Examiner: Message conveyed but minimal. Only one tense, no opinion, no development. This would score low for range and communication. Always extend your answers.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Short, undeveloped answers — “Sí, me gusta.” earns minimal marks. Always add why, an example, or a contrasting point. Use the PALM technique.
  • ✗
    Only using the present tense — The mark scheme rewards multiple tenses. Find ways to include the past (“el año pasado…”) and future (“en el futuro me gustaría…”) even when the question doesn’t ask for them.
  • ✗
    Staying silent when stuck — If you don’t understand, ask: “¿Puede repetir, por favor?” or “¿Qué significa…?” Silence scores nothing; asking for help is allowed.
  • ✗
    Reciting memorised answers — Examiners can tell when an answer has been memorised and doesn’t fit the question. Adapt your prepared phrases to the specific context.

title: Listening Comprehension Strategies (Paper 1 Section A)
content_html:
Paper 1 — Section A

Listening Comprehension Strategies

German (8662) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 1 tests your ability to understand spoken German across the three themes: People and Lifestyle, Popular Culture, and Communication and the World Around Us. You will hear a range of recordings — monologues, conversations, announcements, and messages — and answer questions in English or German.

At Foundation tier, the language is slower and more predictable. At Higher tier, speakers talk at a more natural pace with less repetition and more complex structures. Each extract is played twice.

Question Types

TypeWhat You Do
Multiple choiceChoose the correct answer (A, B, C, or D) from options in English or German
MatchingMatch speakers or descriptions to images, statements, or categories
Short answerWrite brief answers in English or German based on what you hear
True/false/not mentionedDecide whether statements match the recording

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the questions before you listen — Use every second of reading time. Underline key words in each question. If the question says “Where does Lukas go?”, you know to listen for a place. Predict the kind of vocabulary you need.
  2. 2
    First listen: get the gist — Don’t panic if you miss words. Focus on understanding the overall message. Jot down any key words you catch (times, places, opinions).
  3. 3
    Second listen: confirm and fill gaps — Now target the specific answers. Check your initial notes against what you hear. Listen for negatives (nicht, nie, kein) and time markers (gestern, letzte Woche, nächstes Jahr) that can change the meaning completely.
  4. 4
    Watch for distractors — AQA often includes information designed to trick you. A speaker might mention several places but only one is the answer. The correct answer usually comes after a contrast word like aber (but) or jedoch (however).
  5. 5
    Answer every question — Never leave a blank. For multiple choice, eliminate obviously wrong answers and make an educated guess from what remains.

Timing

Read Qs 1st Listen 2nd Listen + Write

You control nothing here — the audio is played for you. Use every pause to read ahead, check your answers, and prepare for the next question.

Opinion Markers

Positive: es gefällt mir, ich mag, ich liebe, es ist toll, es ist wunderbar, es macht Spaß

Negative: es gefällt mir nicht, ich hasse, es ist furchtbar, es ist schrecklich, es nervt mich

Mixed: einerseits… andererseits, es kommt darauf an, es ist nicht schlecht

Time Markers

Past: gestern, letzte Woche, letztes Jahr, als ich jünger war, früher

Present: heute, normalerweise, jeden Tag, jede Woche, meistens

Future: morgen, nächste Woche, nächstes Jahr, ich werde, ich habe vor

Connectives & Contrast

aber (but), jedoch (however), obwohl (although), weil (because), da (since), außerdem (furthermore), auch (also), trotzdem (despite that)

You hear: “Früher bin ich jedes Wochenende ins Kino gegangen, aber jetzt bleibe ich lieber zu Hause und schaue Filme online.”

Question: What does this person prefer to do now?
A. Go to the cinema   B. Stay at home and watch films online   C. Go out with friends

Correct: B

Key clue: “aber jetzt” — the word aber (but) signals a change. Everything before it (früher bin ich ins Kino gegangen) is what they used to do. The answer is what comes after the contrast: zu Hause bleiben und Filme online schauen.

Trap: Students who hear “Kino” and immediately choose A miss the contrast. Always listen for aber, jedoch, and obwohl — they flip the meaning.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Choosing the first thing you hear — AQA plants distractors early. The speaker might say “Ich wollte an den Strand fahren, aber am Ende sind wir im Hotel geblieben”. The answer is hotel, not beach.
  • ✗
    Ignoring negatives — “Ich will nicht gehen” is the opposite of “Ich will gehen”. Listen carefully for nicht, nie, kein, weder…noch.
  • ✗
    Confusing similar-sounding words — Kirche (church) vs Kirsche (cherry), Meer (sea) vs mehr (more), Rat (advice) vs Rad (wheel/bicycle). Context is everything.
  • ✗
    Leaving answers blank — There is no penalty for guessing. Always write something — even an educated guess gives you a chance.
Dictation →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
35 min total

Before Listening

  1. Read all questions first
  2. Underline key words
  3. Predict vocabulary

During Listening

  1. 1st play: gist + key words
  2. 2nd play: confirm + fill gaps
  3. Watch for aber / jedoch

title: Dictation Technique and Common Errors (Paper 1 Section B)
content_html:
Paper 1 — Section B

Dictation Technique & Common Errors

German (8662) • Part of Paper 1 (Listening)

What the Question Asks

In the dictation section, you hear short sentences in German and must write them down exactly as you hear them. Every word must be spelled correctly, including umlauts (ä, ö, ü) and the Eszett (ß). The sentences test vocabulary from all three themes and include a range of tenses.

Foundation tier: simpler sentences with high-frequency vocabulary. Higher tier: longer sentences with more complex grammar and less common words.

How Marks Are Allocated

What You Need
Full marksEvery word spelled correctly, including umlauts and capitalisation of nouns. Each correct word scores individually.
PartialCorrect words earn marks even if others are wrong. You are not penalised for extra words.
0 per wordIncorrect spelling, missing umlauts on words where they change meaning, or missing words

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    First play: listen to the whole sentence — Do not write yet. Focus on understanding the meaning and structure. How many words are there? What tense is being used? Is it a main clause or a subordinate clause?
  2. 2
    Pause: write what you can — Write down as much as you can. Leave gaps for words you are unsure about. Use dashes or blanks to hold the space.
  3. 3
    Second play: fill gaps and check — Focus on the words you missed. Check verb endings carefully: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. Check umlauts on key words.
  4. 4
    Apply German spelling rules — German spelling is largely phonetic. Long vowels often appear with -h (fahren) or doubled (Meer). Short vowels are followed by doubled consonants (Mutter). The ch sound after i/e is different from after a/o/u.
  5. 5
    Final check: capitalisation and grammar — All German nouns start with a capital letter — this is a free mark. Check the verb is in position 2 in main clauses and at the end in subordinate clauses (weil, dass, obwohl).

Timing

1st Play: Listen Only Pause: Write 2nd Play: Check

The pace is set by the recording. Use the pauses wisely — write quickly and check your spelling before the next sentence begins.

Umlauts (ä, ö, ü)

Umlauts change meaning: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful), Bruder (brother) vs Brüder (brothers), Apfel (apple) vs Äpfel (apples). Always write the dots — they count.

Eszett (ß) vs ss

After long vowels and diphthongs: Straße, Fuß, groß. After short vowels: dass, Wasser, Schloss. Getting this wrong is a common error.

Capitalisation

Every noun in German is capitalised: Schule (school), Freund (friend), Wochenende (weekend). This includes abstract nouns: Gesundheit (health), Freiheit (freedom).

ie vs ei

ie = long “ee” sound: Spiel, Lied, viel. ei = “eye” sound: Arbeit, Freizeit, mein. Mixing these up is one of the most common dictation errors.

You hear: “Am Wochenende fahre ich gern mit meiner Familie in die Stadt, um einzukaufen.”

Correct dictation

Am Wochenende fahre ich gern mit meiner Familie in die Stadt, um einzukaufen.

Key checks: Wochenende — capital W (noun). Familie — capital F. Stadt — capital S. einzukaufen — separable verb with zu in the middle. Missing any capital letter or misspelling einzukaufen as two words loses marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Forgetting to capitalise nouns — schule instead of Schule. Every noun needs a capital letter in German — no exceptions.
  • ✗
    Missing umlauts — fur instead of für, uber instead of über. If you can’t type the umlaut, write ue, ae, or oe instead.
  • ✗
    Confusing ie and ei — Speil instead of Spiel. Remember: ie sounds like “ee”, ei sounds like “eye”.
  • ✗
    Leaving blanks — Write your best guess. A phonetic attempt may still earn the mark if it’s close enough.
← Listening Comprehension Reading Comprehension →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5–8 min total

Dictation Checklist

  1. 1st play: listen only — don’t write
  2. Pause: write what you heard
  3. 2nd play: fill gaps + check
  4. Capitalise all nouns
  5. Check umlauts and ß

Key Rule

ie = “ee” sound • ei = “eye” sound

title: Reading Comprehension Strategies (Paper 3 Section A)
content_html:
Paper 3 — Section A

Reading Comprehension Strategies

German (8662) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 3 tests your ability to understand written German. Section A contains a range of texts — adverts, emails, articles, blogs, and literary extracts — with questions that test comprehension at different levels: identifying key details, understanding opinions, drawing inferences, and recognising tenses.

Foundation and Higher tiers share some questions (overlap questions), but Higher includes more complex texts and inferential questions.

Question Types

TypeWhat You Do
Multiple choiceSelect the correct answer from options (English or German)
MatchingMatch people, descriptions, or opinions to correct categories
Short answer (English)Answer questions in English based on the German text
Short answer (German)Answer questions in German (Higher tier)
True/false/not mentionedAssess whether statements match the text

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the questions first — Before reading the text, read all the questions. This tells you what to look for and saves time. Underline key words in each question.
  2. 2
    Skim the text for gist — Read the whole text quickly. What is it about? Who is speaking? What is the general opinion? Don’t get stuck on unknown words.
  3. 3
    Scan for specific answers — Go back to each question and find the relevant section of the text. Look for synonyms — the text often rephrases the question using different vocabulary.
  4. 4
    Use cognates and word families — Many German words look like English: Musik (music), Telefon (telephone), Information (information). Also use word roots: if you know arbeiten (to work), you can guess Arbeiter (worker) and Arbeitgeber (employer).
  5. 5
    Watch for negatives and tense changes — A text might describe what someone used to do (Früher hat er…) versus what they do now (Jetzt…). Negatives (nicht, kein, nie, niemand) flip the meaning. Don’t confuse past and present.
  6. 6
    Break apart compound words — German is famous for long compound nouns. Krankenhaus = krank (sick) + Haus (house) = hospital. Schreibtisch = schreiben (to write) + Tisch (table) = desk. Split them up and the meaning often becomes clear.

Timing

Skim Answer Questions Check

Foundation: 45 minutes for Section A + B. Spend roughly 30–35 minutes on comprehension, leaving 10–15 for the translation. Higher: 60 minutes total — about 40–45 on comprehension.

German builds long words by joining smaller words together. The last word in the compound is the core meaning; earlier words modify it.

CompoundPartsMeaning
HandschuhHand + Schuh (shoe)Glove
HausaufgabeHaus (house) + Aufgabe (task)Homework
GeburtstagsfeierGeburtstag (birthday) + Feier (party)Birthday party
UmweltverschmutzungUmwelt (environment) + Verschmutzung (pollution)Environmental pollution

Text: “Letztes Jahr habe ich mein Praktikum in einem Büro gemacht. Es war ziemlich langweilig. Nächstes Mal möchte ich lieber in einem Krankenhaus arbeiten.”

Question: Where would the writer like to work next time?

Correct: In a hospital

Key clue: “Nächstes Mal möchte ich lieber in einem Krankenhaus arbeiten” — nächstes Mal (next time) tells you this is about the future, not the past. Krankenhaus = hospital. The office (Büro) is what they did before — a distractor.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Panicking over long compound words — Split them into parts. Sehenswürdigkeiten looks terrifying, but it means “sights/tourist attractions” (things worth seeing).
  • ✗
    Confusing tenses — “Ich habe gespielt” (I played) vs “Ich spiele” (I play) vs “Ich werde spielen” (I will play). The question might ask about the past but the distractor is in the present.
  • ✗
    False friends — Gift means poison (not gift), bekommen means to receive (not to become), aktuell means current (not actual). Don’t assume a word means the same as its English lookalike.
  • ✗
    Answering in the wrong language — If the question says “Answer in English”, make sure you write in English. If it says “Answer in German”, write in German. Check every time.
← Dictation Translation into English →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
45–60 min total

Reading Strategy

  1. Read questions first
  2. Skim text for gist
  3. Scan for specific answers
  4. Use cognates + word families
  5. Split compound words apart

Watch Out For

  1. False friends (Gift, bekommen)
  2. Tense changes (past vs present)
  3. Negatives (nicht, kein, nie)

title: Translation: German to English (Paper 3 Section B)
content_html:
Paper 3 — Section B

Translation: German → English

German (8662) • Part of Paper 3 (Reading)

What the Question Asks

You are given a short passage in German (approximately 50 words) and must translate it into English. The passage covers vocabulary and grammar from across the specification. It is the final question on Paper 3 and is worth 10 marks.

How Marks Are Allocated

Description
9–10All content translated accurately. Occasional minor errors that do not affect meaning.
7–8Most content translated accurately. A few minor errors or omissions.
5–6A reasonable attempt. Some accurate sections but gaps or errors in places.
3–4Limited accuracy. Several sections poorly translated or missing.
1–2Very limited. Only isolated words or phrases correctly translated.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the whole passage first — Get the overall meaning before you start translating. What is the topic? What tenses are used? Understanding context helps you translate tricky words.
  2. 2
    Translate sentence by sentence — Work through the passage one sentence at a time. Identify the verb, the subject, and any time markers first.
  3. 3
    Do not translate word for word — German word order differs from English, especially in subordinate clauses. “Ich spiele gern Fußball, weil es Spaß macht” is “I like playing football because it is fun”, not “I play gladly football, because it fun makes”. Aim for natural English.
  4. 4
    Use context for unknown words — If you don’t know a word, use the rest of the sentence. “Ich habe ein Geschenk für meine Mutter gekauft” — even if you forget Geschenk, you know you bought something for your mum. Write “I bought a present for my mum” or your best guess — never leave a gap.
  5. 5
    Re-read your English version — Does it sound natural? Check for awkward phrasing caused by following German word order too closely. Tidy up articles, prepositions, and tenses.

Timing

Read Passage Translate Check English

Allow 10–12 minutes for this question. Do not rush — accuracy matters more than speed. Leave time to re-read your English version at the end.

Verb at the End

In subordinate clauses starting with weil (because), dass (that), obwohl (although), or wenn (when/if), the verb goes to the end. “Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin” = “I’m staying at home because I am ill.”

Separable Verbs

Separable verbs split in main clauses: “Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf” = “I get up at seven o’clock.” The prefix (auf-) goes to the end. In subordinate clauses, they rejoin: “weil ich früh aufstehe”.

Perfect Tense

The past participle goes to the end: “Ich habe gestern Tennis gespielt” = “I played tennis yesterday.” Don’t forget to translate both parts of the verb.

German passage: “Letzten Sommer bin ich mit meiner Familie nach Spanien gefahren. Wir haben in einem kleinen Hotel übernachtet. Das Wetter war wunderbar und ich habe jeden Tag im Meer geschwommen.”

Strong translation

“Last summer I went to Spain with my family. We stayed in a small hotel. The weather was wonderful and I swam in the sea every day.”

Key points: bin…gefahren → “went” (not “have driven”). übernachtet → “stayed (overnight)”. im Meer geschwommen → “swam in the sea”. Natural English phrasing earns full marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Translating word for word — German word order is different from English. Rearrange your translation to sound natural in English.
  • ✗
    Missing the perfect tense — “Ich habe…gespielt” has two parts. Make sure you translate it as past tense (“I played”), not present (“I have playing”).
  • ✗
    Falling for false friends — Gift = poison, bekommen = to receive, sensibel = sensitive. Always check context.
  • ✗
    Leaving gaps — An educated guess is better than a blank. Use context clues to work out unknown words.
← Reading Comprehension Translation into German →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10–12 min total

Translation Formula

  1. Read the whole passage first
  2. Translate sentence by sentence
  3. Don’t go word for word
  4. Use context for unknown words
  5. Re-read for natural English

Marks: 10 • Time: 10–12 min

title: Translation: English to German (Paper 4)
content_html:
Paper 4 — Translation

Translation: English → German

German (8662) • Part of Paper 4 (Writing)

What the Question Asks

You are given five English sentences and must translate each one into German. The sentences test a range of tenses (present, past, future, conditional), key vocabulary from the themes, and grammatical accuracy. Worth 10 marks (Foundation) or 10 marks (Higher, with harder grammar).

How Marks Are Allocated

Each sentence is marked individually. You earn marks for conveying the meaning accurately with correct grammar and spelling. Minor errors that don’t affect communication may still earn partial credit.

Per SentenceWhat You Need
2Meaning fully conveyed with accurate grammar and spelling
1Meaning partially conveyed — some errors but the message is understandable
Meaning not conveyed, or so many errors that the sentence is incomprehensible

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the English sentence carefully — Identify the subject, verb, tense, and any tricky elements (negatives, time phrases, opinions). Know what you need before you start writing.
  2. 2
    Translate the verb first — Get the tense and person right. “I go” = ich gehe (present), “I went” = ich bin gegangen (perfect), “I used to go” = ich ging (imperfect), “I will go” = ich werde gehen (future).
  3. 3
    Build the sentence around the verb — Remember: the conjugated verb is always in position 2 in a main clause. Time – Manner – Place word order applies: “Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus in die Stadt”.
  4. 4
    Check cases and gender — German has four cases (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive). The most common errors involve accusative (den, einen for masculine) and dative (dem, einem after mit, in, zu). Know the gender of common nouns.
  5. 5
    Check spelling, umlauts, and capitalisation — All nouns must be capitalised. Umlauts change meaning: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful). Write clearly so the examiner can read your answer.

Timing

Read Translate Check

Allow 10–12 minutes for this question. Spend about 2 minutes per sentence, with time left to check your grammar and spelling.

CaseWhenMasculineFeminineNeuter
NominativeSubject of sentenceder / eindie / einedas / ein
AccusativeDirect object; after für, gegen, ohne, umden / einendie / einedas / ein
DativeIndirect object; after mit, nach, aus, zu, bei, von, seitdem / einemder / einerdem / einem

Top tip: Only masculine changes in the accusative (der → den). The dative changes all three genders. Learn the dative prepositions as a group: mit, nach, aus, zu, bei, von, seit, gegenüber.

English: “Last weekend I went to the cinema with my friends.”

Strong translation

Letztes Wochenende bin ich mit meinen Freunden ins Kino gegangen.

Key points: Letztes Wochenende (time phrase first). bin…gegangen (perfect tense with sein for movement). mit meinen Freunden (dative plural after mit). ins Kino (in das contracted). Verb in position 2: bin.

Weak translation

Letzte Wochenende ich habe ins Kino mit meine Freunde gegangen.

Errors: Letzte should be Letztes (neuter agreement). ich habe — wrong auxiliary (gehen uses sein). meine Freunde — should be meinen Freunden (dative after mit). Verb not in position 2. This would likely score 0–1.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Wrong auxiliary in perfect tense — Movement verbs (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen) use sein, not haben. “I went” = ich bin gegangen, not ich habe gegangen.
  • ✗
    Wrong case after prepositions — mit always takes the dative: mit meinem Bruder, not mit mein Bruder. Learn which prepositions take which case.
  • ✗
    Verb not in position 2 — In main clauses, the conjugated verb must be the second element. “Gestern bin ich schwimmen gegangen”, not “Gestern ich bin schwimmen gegangen”.
  • ✗
    Forgetting noun capitalisation — kino instead of Kino. All German nouns must start with a capital letter.
← Translation into English Writing Tasks →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10–12 min total

Translation Formula

  1. Read the English carefully
  2. Translate the verb first (correct tense!)
  3. Build the sentence around it
  4. Check cases + gender
  5. Check umlauts + capitalisation

Marks: 10 (5 sentences × 2)

Time: 10–12 minutes

title: Writing Tasks: Photo, 50-Word, 90-Word and 150-Word (Paper 4)
content_html:
Paper 4 — Writing

Writing Tasks: Photo, 50-Word, 90-Word & 150-Word

German (8662) • 25% of GCSE

What the Paper Asks

Paper 4 tests your ability to write in German. The tasks increase in length and complexity. Foundation and Higher tiers have different combinations:

TaskFoundationHigher
Photo description5 sentences about a photo [10 marks]—
50-word taskEmail/message with bullet points [10 marks]—
GrammarFill gaps with correct German [5 marks]—
Translation (Eng → Ger)[10 marks][10 marks]
90-word taskStructured writing [15 marks][15 marks]
150-word task—Open writing [25 marks]

The 90-word and 150-word tasks are marked on communication (content + response to bullet points), range of language (variety of vocabulary and structures), and accuracy (grammar + spelling).

Step-by-Step Method

Photo Description (Foundation only) — 10 marks

  1. 1
    Write 5 clear sentences — Each sentence scores up to 2 marks. Describe what you see: people, actions, setting, weather, clothes, objects.
  2. 2
    Use a range of structures — Don’t start every sentence with “Es gibt”. Mix it up: “Auf dem Foto sehe ich…”, “Eine Frau trägt…”, “Im Hintergrund kann man…sehen”, “Das Wetter ist sonnig”.
  3. 3
    Include opinions where possible — “Es scheint, dass die Familie glücklich ist” shows more than just description and demonstrates a subordinate clause.

50-Word Task (Foundation only) — 10 marks

  1. 1
    Address every bullet point — There are usually 5 bullet points. Miss one and you lose marks for communication.
  2. 2
    Write 8–12 words per bullet — Keep it simple but accurate. One or two sentences per bullet point is enough.
  3. 3
    Show range — Use different sentence starters, connectives (und, aber, weil, obwohl), and at least two tenses.

90-Word Task — 15 marks

  1. 1
    Plan before you write — Spend 2 minutes planning. Note which bullet points need which tense. Jot down key vocabulary.
  2. 2
    Address all bullet points — There are usually 4 bullet points. Each one should get roughly equal treatment (2–3 sentences).
  3. 3
    Show range of tenses — Include at least three tenses: present (ich spiele), past (ich habe gespielt), and future (ich werde spielen) or conditional (ich würde spielen).
  4. 4
    Use complex structures — Subordinate clauses (weil, dass, obwohl, wenn), opinions with justifications (Ich finde es toll, weil…), and varied connectives impress examiners.

150-Word Task (Higher only) — 25 marks

  1. 1
    Plan carefully — This is the highest-value writing question. Spend 3–5 minutes planning. Map each bullet point to a paragraph.
  2. 2
    Aim for 150–180 words — Going slightly over is fine. Going significantly under means you probably haven’t addressed all bullet points fully.
  3. 3
    Demonstrate ambitious language — Use a mix of tenses (including conditional and pluperfect if possible), subjunctive (Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich…), and complex sentence structures. This is where you show off.
  4. 4
    Proofread — Check verb endings, cases, word order in subordinate clauses, and noun capitalisation. Two minutes of checking can save several marks.

Mark Scheme: 90-Word and 150-Word Tasks

CriterionTop BandMiddle BandLower Band
CommunicationAll bullet points addressed with relevant detail and opinionsMost bullet points addressed; some detailLimited response; bullet points missed
Range of LanguageWide variety of vocabulary and structures; multiple tenses; complex sentencesSome variety; mostly familiar vocabulary; at least 2 tensesRepetitive; basic vocabulary; limited tenses
AccuracyMostly accurate; minor errors only; verbs, cases, and word order secureSome errors but meaning generally clearFrequent errors that impede communication

Opinions

Meiner Meinung nach… (In my opinion…), Ich bin der Meinung, dass… (I believe that…), Ich finde es wichtig, dass… (I find it important that…)

Justifications

weil (because), da (since/as), denn (because — no word order change), deshalb (therefore), aus diesem Grund (for this reason)

Comparisons

besser als (better than), schlechter als (worse than), genauso…wie (just as…as), im Vergleich zu (compared to)

Conditional / Subjunctive

Wenn ich die Wahl hätte, würde ich… (If I had the choice, I would…), Es wäre besser, wenn… (It would be better if…), Ich würde gern… (I would like to…)

Write approximately 90 words in German about healthy living. You must write about: what you eat and drink, what sport you do, what you did last week to stay healthy, your plans for next year.

Strong answer

Normalerweise esse ich viel Obst und Gemüse, weil es gesund ist. Ich trinke meistens Wasser, obwohl ich manchmal Cola trinke.

Zweimal pro Woche spiele ich Fußball in einer Mannschaft und am Wochenende gehe ich oft schwimmen, da es Spaß macht.

Letzte Woche bin ich jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule gefahren und ich habe auch eine Stunde Yoga gemacht.

Nächstes Jahr werde ich einen Marathon laufen, weil ich fitter werden möchte. Außerdem habe ich vor, weniger Zucker zu essen.

Why this works: All 4 bullet points addressed. Four tenses used (present, present with manchmal, perfect, future). Complex structures: weil, obwohl, da. Opinions + justifications. Varied vocabulary. Would score in the top band for all three criteria.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Missing a bullet point — Every bullet point is worth marks. Even a single sentence addressing it is better than nothing.
  • ✗
    Sticking to one tense — Writing only in the present tense limits your range marks. Force in at least one past and one future tense, even if the question doesn’t explicitly ask for it.
  • ✗
    Wrong word order in subordinate clauses — After weil, dass, obwohl, wenn, the verb goes to the end: “weil ich Fußball spiele”, not “weil ich spiele Fußball”.
  • ✗
    Repetitive vocabulary — Using gut and schlecht for every opinion. Try: toll, wunderbar, fantastisch, furchtbar, schrecklich, langweilig.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference

Writing Checklist

  1. Address every bullet point
  2. Use 3+ tenses (present, past, future)
  3. Include opinions + reasons
  4. Use subordinate clauses (weil, dass)
  5. Check verb position + cases
  6. Capitalise all nouns

title: Role-Play and Reading Aloud (Paper 2)
content_html:
Paper 2 — Tasks 1 & 2

Role-Play & Reading Aloud

German (8662) • Part of Paper 2 (Speaking, 25%)

What the Tasks Ask

Task 1: Role-Play [10 marks]

You are given a scenario (e.g. buying a ticket, booking a hotel, visiting a doctor) with instructions in English. You must play your role in German, responding to the examiner’s questions and giving information as specified on the card. You have one “unpredictable” question where you must think on your feet.

Task 2: Reading Aloud [10 marks]

You are given a short passage in German (around 35–50 words) and must read it aloud clearly and accurately. The examiner then asks you questions about the passage, which you answer in German.

How Marks Are Allocated

CriterionRole-PlayReading Aloud
Communication5 tasks completed successfully (2 marks each)Clear, accurate reading (up to 5 marks)
Questions—Answers to follow-up questions (up to 5 marks)

Step-by-Step: Role-Play

  1. 1
    Use your preparation time wisely — You get time to study the card before the exam starts. Plan what you will say for each bullet point. Think about the tense required and any tricky vocabulary.
  2. 2
    Listen carefully to the examiner — The examiner plays the other role. Listen to their questions — they often contain clues. If they ask “Was kostet das?”, you need to give a price.
  3. 3
    Use full sentences — Don’t just say “ja” or “nein”. For 2 marks per task, you need to convey the message clearly. “Ja, ich möchte ein Einzelzimmer mit Dusche buchen, bitte” is much better than “Ja”.
  4. 4
    Prepare for the “!” (unpredictable) question — One task on the card has an exclamation mark — this is the unpredictable element. You won’t know the question in advance. Stay calm, listen, and give any reasonable answer in German.
  5. 5
    If you get stuck, paraphrase — Can’t remember Fahrkarte (ticket)? Say “Ich brauche etwas für den Zug” (I need something for the train). Communication is what matters.

Step-by-Step: Reading Aloud

  1. 1
    Use prep time to read silently — During your preparation, read the passage in your head. Identify any tricky words and practise their pronunciation mentally.
  2. 2
    Read slowly and clearly — Rushing leads to errors. Pause naturally at commas and full stops. The examiner needs to understand every word.
  3. 3
    German pronunciation rules — ch after i/e is soft (like “sh” in some accents): ich, nicht. After a/o/u it’s harder (throat sound): Buch, noch. w = “v” sound: Wasser. v = “f” sound: Vater. z = “ts”: Zeit. sp/st at the start = “shp/sht”: Spaß, Straße.
  4. 4
    Answer the follow-up questions — The examiner asks questions about the passage. Use the text to help you — the answers are often contained within it. Give full-sentence answers where possible.

Timing

Role-Play (~3 min) Read Aloud (~2 min) Follow-Up Qs (~2 min)

The examiner controls the timing. Focus on clear communication rather than speed. If you need a moment to think, say “Also…” (well…) or “Moment mal…” (just a moment).

Letter/ComboSoundExample
ch (after i/e)Soft, breathy “h”ich, nicht, Milch
ch (after a/o/u)Throaty, like clearing throatBuch, noch, Kuchen
w“v” soundWasser, Woche, Wohnung
v“f” soundVater, viel, Verkehr
z“ts” soundZeit, Zimmer, Zug
sp- / st-“shp” / “sht” at word startSpaß, Sport, Straße, Stadt
äLike “e” in “bed”Mädchen, später
öRound lips, say “e”schön, möchte
üRound lips, say “ee”für, über, Glück

Scenario: You are at a train station in Germany. The teacher plays the ticket seller.

1. Say where you want to go • 2. Say when you want to travel • 3. Ask how much the ticket costs • 4. Ask what platform the train leaves from • 5. ! (unpredictable)

Strong answers

1. “Ich möchte nach München fahren, bitte.”
2. “Ich möchte morgen um zehn Uhr reisen.”
3. “Was kostet eine Hin- und Rückfahrkarte?”
4. “Von welchem Gleis fährt der Zug ab?”
5. Examiner: “Warum fahren Sie nach München?” → “Ich besuche meine Großeltern dort.”

Key points: Full sentences, correct verb forms, polite register (bitte), specific vocabulary (Hin- und Rückfahrkarte, Gleis). The unpredictable question gets a reasonable response.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    One-word answers — “Ja” on its own scores 0. Always give a full sentence: “Ja, ich möchte…”
  • ✗
    Anglicised pronunciation — Saying w as English “w” instead of German “v”. Saying z as English “z” instead of “ts”. These errors are very noticeable.
  • ✗
    Panicking on the unpredictable question — It’s always related to the scenario. Listen carefully, think for a second, and give any reasonable answer. “Ich weiß nicht” (I don’t know) is better than silence, but a real answer scores more.
  • ✗
    Reading too fast — Speed does not earn marks. Clear, accurate pronunciation does. Slow down at tricky words.

  2. Use full sentences
  3. Listen to the examiner’s clues
  4. Stay calm on the “!” question
  5. Paraphrase if stuck

Reading Aloud

  1. Read slowly and clearly
  2. w = “v”, z = “ts”
  3. sp/st = “shp/sht”

title: Photo Card Discussion (Paper 2)
content_html:
Paper 2 — Task 3

Photo Card Discussion

German (8662) • Part of Paper 2 (Speaking, 25%)

What the Task Asks

You are given a photo related to one of the three themes. You must:

  1. Describe the photo in German
  2. Answer two questions linked to the photo
  3. Hold a general conversation on the theme, answering further questions from the examiner

This is the longest and highest-value speaking task. At Higher tier, the conversation goes deeper and requires more complex language.

How Marks Are Allocated

CriterionWhat It Means
Communication & ContentHow much relevant information you convey; how well you respond to questionsUp to 10
Range of LanguageVariety of vocabulary, structures, and tensesUp to 10
AccuracyGrammar, gender, verb endings, pronunciationUp to 10
Pronunciation & IntonationClarity, natural German sounds, correct stressUp to 10

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Preparation: describe the photo mentally — During prep time, plan 4–5 sentences about the photo. Cover: who is in it (es gibt eine Familie), what they are doing (sie essen zusammen), where they are (in einem Restaurant), the weather/time if visible, and an opinion (es sieht gemütlich aus).
  2. 2
    Describe the photo confidently — Use a variety of structures: “Auf dem Foto kann ich…sehen”, “Es gibt…”, “Eine Person macht gerade…”, “Es scheint, dass…”, “Im Hintergrund sehe ich…”. Don’t just list objects — describe actions and give opinions.
  3. 3
    Answer the two linked questions — These relate to the photo’s theme. Give developed answers (2–3 sentences each). Include an opinion + reason: “Ich glaube, dass es wichtig ist, weil…”
  4. 4
    General conversation: extend every answer — The examiner will ask broader questions on the theme. Never give a one-sentence answer. Use the PALM technique: Point (state your answer), Amplify (add detail), Link (connect to another idea), Mix tenses (add a past or future reference).
  5. 5
    Show off your German — This is your chance to demonstrate everything you know. Use subordinate clauses (weil, obwohl, dass, wenn), varied tenses, conditional (Ich würde gern…), comparatives (besser als, mehr als), and idiomatic phrases (meiner Meinung nach).

Timing

Photo (~1 min) Linked Qs (~2 min) Conversation (~4–6 min)

The conversation section is where most marks are available. Don’t rush the photo — but save your energy for the extended discussion.

Use PALM to structure every answer in the conversation section:

StepWhat It MeansExample
PointState your answer clearly“Ich treibe gern Sport.”
AmplifyAdd detail or explanation“Am liebsten spiele ich Fußball in einer Mannschaft.”
LinkConnect to another idea“Außerdem gehe ich oft schwimmen, weil es entspannend ist.”
Mix tensesAdd a past or future reference“Letztes Jahr habe ich einen Halbmarathon gelaufen und nächstes Jahr werde ich an einem Triathlon teilnehmen.”

This technique transforms a one-sentence answer into a developed response worth top-band marks.

Photo: A family eating a meal together in a garden on a sunny day.

Strong description

“Auf dem Foto kann ich eine Familie sehen, die zusammen im Garten isst. Es gibt vier Personen — zwei Erwachsene und zwei Kinder. Das Wetter ist sonnig und warm. Auf dem Tisch gibt es viel Essen — Salat, Brot und Obst. Die Familie sieht glücklich aus und ich denke, dass sie ein Sommerfest feiern.”

Why this works: Describes who, what, where. Gives specific detail (food items, weather). Includes an opinion with a dass-clause. Uses varied structures: kann ich…sehen, es gibt, sieht…aus, ich denke, dass…

Starting Phrases

Auf dem Foto kann ich…sehen (In the photo I can see…) • Es gibt… (There is/are…) • Im Vordergrund/Hintergrund… (In the foreground/background…) • Man kann…erkennen (You can make out…)

Describing People

Eine Frau/Ein Mann trägt… (A woman/man is wearing…) • Die Leute lachen/reden/essen (The people are laughing/talking/eating) • Ein Kind spielt mit… (A child is playing with…)

Opinions

Es sieht gemütlich/lustig/interessant aus (It looks cosy/fun/interesting) • Ich glaube, dass… (I believe that…) • Es scheint, dass… (It seems that…) • Meiner Meinung nach… (In my opinion…)

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Listing objects instead of describing — “Es gibt einen Tisch. Es gibt Stühle. Es gibt Essen.” is repetitive. Vary your structures and describe actions, not just objects.
  • ✗
    One-sentence answers in the conversation — “Ja, ich mag Sport” is too short. Use PALM to develop every answer into 3–4 sentences with opinions, reasons, and different tenses.
  • ✗
    Sticking to present tense only — The examiner will ask about past experiences and future plans. If they don’t, volunteer them: “Letztes Jahr habe ich…”, “In Zukunft werde ich…”
  • ✗
    Long pauses without filler — If you need to think, use German fillers: “Also…” (well), “Ich würde sagen, dass…” (I would say that), “Das ist eine gute Frage…” (that’s a good question). Silence costs marks.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10–12 min total

PALM Technique

  1. Point — state your answer
  2. Amplify — add detail
  3. Link — connect ideas
  4. Mix tenses — past/future

Photo Description Checklist

  1. Who is in the photo?
  2. What are they doing?
  3. Where are they?
  4. Your opinion

title: Listening Comprehension
content_html:
40–50 marks

Listening Comprehension

Paper 1: Listening — AQA/L — 25% of GCSE

What the Examiner Wants

The listening paper tests your ability to understand spoken French across a range of contexts — from short announcements and conversations to longer monologues and interviews. You hear each recording twice. The examiner wants you to pick out key details, understand opinions, and recognise tenses — not translate every single word.

Question Types

Type What You Do Tip
Multiple choice Select A, B, C, or D Eliminate wrong answers — distractors are deliberate
True / False / Not mentioned Tick the correct box If the recording doesn't say it, it's "Not mentioned"
Matching Match statements to speakers or categories Read ALL options before listening
Short answer Answer in English or French Check how many details are needed (1 mark = 1 detail)

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the questions BEFORE listening — Use the 5-minute reading time. Underline key words in each question. Predict what vocabulary you might hear.
  2. 2
    First listen: get the gist — Don't panic if you miss words. Focus on the overall meaning and jot down any key details you catch. Note the tense (past, present, future).
  3. 3
    Second listen: confirm and fill gaps — Now target the specific answers you're unsure about. Listen for the exact phrase that answers each question.
  4. 4
    Watch for distractors — AQA deliberately includes words that sound like the right answer but aren't. If someone says "Je voulais aller à la plage mais j'ai décidé d'aller au cinéma", the answer is cinema, not beach.
  5. 5
    Check your answers make sense — Re-read your answer in context. If the question asks "What did Marie do at the weekend?" and you've written "she will go shopping," the tense is wrong.

Timing

Read
5 min Listen 1
~13 min Listen 2
~13 min Check
4 min

You cannot control the pace — the audio plays automatically. Use every second of reading time before each section. Write answers during the pauses between recordings.

Negatives that change everything

ne...plus (no longer) — "Je ne joue plus au tennis" = I no longer play tennis

ne...jamais (never) — "Il n'a jamais visité Paris" = He has never visited Paris

ne...que (only) — "Elle n'aime que le chocolat" = She only likes chocolate

Opinion words (positive vs negative)

génial / formidable / chouette = great — vs — affreux / nul / ennuyeux = awful / rubbish / boring

J'adore vs Je déteste — listen for the verb, not just the topic

Time markers (tense clues)

hier / la semaine dernière / l'année dernière = past

demain / le week-end prochain / l'année prochaine = future

d'habitude / normalement / tous les jours = present habit

You hear: "Le week-end dernier, je suis allée au centre commercial avec mes amies. Je voulais acheter une nouvelle robe mais c'était trop cher, alors j'ai acheté un jean et un tee-shirt. Après, on a mangé dans un restaurant italien — c'était délicieux!"

Q: What did the speaker buy? (2 marks)

Distractor identified

Trap: "une nouvelle robe" sounds like the answer — but she says "mais c'était trop cher" (but it was too expensive), so she did NOT buy a dress.

Correct answer

Answer: A pair of jeans and a t-shirt (2 marks — one detail per mark).

Examiner note: Students who write "a dress" would get 0 for that detail. Always listen for qualifiers like mais, cependant, pourtant (but/however).

You hear: "D'habitude, je vais au collège à pied, mais aujourd'hui il pleut alors ma mère m'a emmené en voiture."

Q: How does the speaker usually get to school?

Weak Answer

Picks up wrong detail

By car.

This student heard "en voiture" and wrote it down without noticing the time marker "aujourd'hui" (today) — the question asks about the USUAL routine.

Strong Answer

Correct — identifies "d'habitude"

On foot / walking.

"D'habitude" (usually) + "à pied" (on foot) = the habitual method. "Aujourd'hui" signals today is different.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing the distractor — AQA includes tempting wrong answers deliberately. If someone mentions two activities but only did ONE, make sure you identify which one actually happened.
  • ❌
    Ignoring tenses — "J'irai" (I will go) is future, "je suis allé" (I went) is past. If the question asks what someone DID, a future-tense answer is wrong.
  • ❌
    Not reading the question carefully — If it says "Give TWO details," one detail = one mark. Don't leave marks on the table by writing only one thing.
  • ❌
    Leaving blanks — Never leave an answer blank. For multiple choice, you have a 25% chance of guessing correctly. For short answers, write your best guess.

← Back to Exam Technique

35 min (F) / 45 min (H)

Strategy

  1. Read questions first
  2. First listen: get the gist
  3. Second listen: confirm details
  4. Watch for distractors
  5. Check tenses match

title: Dictation
content_html:
8 marks

Dictation

Paper 4: Writing — AQA/W — Question 1

What the Examiner Wants

Dictation is new to the AQA French GCSE from 2026. You hear short French sentences and must write them down exactly as spoken. The examiner is testing your ability to recognise spoken French and convert it accurately into written form — including correct spelling, accents, and grammar.

Marking Criteria

Aspect What Earns Marks What Loses Marks
Spelling Correct French spelling throughout Phonetic English spelling, e.g. "je mapel" instead of je m'appelle
Accents All accents present and correct Missing accents: eleve instead of élève
Grammar Correct agreements and verb forms Wrong endings: les maison instead of les maisons
Word boundaries Words correctly separated Running words together: ilyavait instead of il y avait

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    First hearing: listen to the whole sentence — Do NOT write yet. Get the overall meaning. How many words? What tense? What's the subject?
  2. 2
    Second hearing: write it down — Now write, leaving small gaps for any words you're unsure about. Focus on getting the structure right.
  3. 3
    Third hearing: check and correct — Fill in gaps, check accents, verify agreements (plural nouns, adjective endings, verb conjugations).
  4. 4
    Apply grammar logic — Even if you're unsure what you heard, apply rules: les + noun = plural (add -s), elle est + adjective = feminine (add -e), past participle with être = agreement.
  5. 5
    Final scan for accents — Check every e: does it need é, è, or ê? Check ç before a/o/u. Check à (preposition) vs a (verb).

Timing

Hear 1
Listen Hear 2
Write Hear 3
Check

You hear each sentence three times with pauses. The whole dictation section takes about 8 minutes. Use every second of the pauses to review your spelling and accents.

Accent aigu (é) — "ay" sound

élève, école, café, répéter, téléphone

Only appears on the letter e. Most common accent in French.

Accent grave (è, à, ù)

mère, père, frère, très, après

à (to/at) vs a (has) — this distinction matters!

où (where) vs ou (or)

Accent circonflexe (ê, î, ô, û, â)

être, fête, hôpital, île, goût

Often replaces an old 's' — compare hôpital with English "hospital."

Cédille (ç)

français, garçon, leçon, reçu, commençons

Only before a, o, u — makes 'c' sound like 's' instead of 'k.'

You hear: "Ma sœur est allée au marché et elle a acheté des légumes frais."

Common student attempt

Ma soeur est alle au marche et elle a achete des legumes frais.

Errors: Missing œ ligature in sœur, missing ée agreement on allée (feminine subject with être), missing accents on marché, acheté, and légumes.

Correct version

Ma sœur est allée au marché et elle a acheté des légumes frais.

Key checks: allée has an extra -e because ma sœur is feminine and the verb uses être. Every accent is essential for full marks.

You hear: "Il y avait beaucoup de monde à la fête."

Weak Attempt

Multiple errors

Il ya avait boucoup de monde a la fete.

Errors: ya should be y avait (word boundary), boucoup should be beaucoup, a needs accent (à), fete needs circumflex (fête).

Strong Attempt

All details correct

Il y avait beaucoup de monde à la fête.

Word boundaries clear, spelling accurate, accents present. Full marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Forgetting past-participle agreements — With être verbs, the past participle agrees with the subject: elle est allée, ils sont arrivés.
  • ❌
    Confusing homophones — a / à, et / est, ou / où, on / ont, son / sont. Use grammar context to decide: "il a mangé" (has eaten) vs "il va à Paris" (to Paris).
  • ❌
    Rushing to write on the first hearing — Listen to the whole sentence first. If you start writing immediately, you may mishear word boundaries and lose the overall meaning.
  • ❌
    Anglicising spellings — French words that look like English are often spelled differently: différent (not "different"), intéressant (one 'r', not two), développer (one 'l', two 'p').

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
~8 min total

Checklist

  1. Listen first, write second
  2. Check accents (é è ê ç à)
  3. Past participle agreements
  4. Homophones (a/à, et/est)
  5. Word boundaries

title: Reading Comprehension
content_html:
40–50 marks

Reading Comprehension

Paper 3: Reading — AQA/R — 25% of GCSE

What the Examiner Wants

The reading paper tests your ability to understand written French across a range of text types — adverts, emails, articles, blog posts, and literary extracts. Questions progress from simple retrieval to inference and analysis. The examiner wants you to extract specific details, understand opinions and attitudes, identify tenses, and — at Higher — draw conclusions from unfamiliar language.

Question Types

Type What You Do Tip
Multiple choice Select A, B, C, or D Read ALL options — the most obvious choice is sometimes the trap
Matching Match people to statements or headings to paragraphs Cross off options as you use them
True / False / Not mentioned Decide based on the text only "Not mentioned" means the text simply doesn't say it
Short answer (English) Answer in English Don't copy French — the examiner needs to see you've understood it
Short answer (French) Answer in French — often just a word or phrase from the text You can lift words directly from the text

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Skim the text first — Read the title, any headings, and the first sentence of each paragraph. Get the gist: Who? What? Where? When?
  2. 2
    Read the questions — Underline key words. Note what each question is actually asking: a fact, an opinion, a reason, or a time?
  3. 3
    Scan for answers — Questions usually follow the order of the text. Find the relevant section and read it carefully. Look for synonyms — the question might say "happy" while the text says content or ravi.
  4. 4
    Use context clues for unknown words — If you don't know a word, look at the words around it. "Le chat a grimpé dans l'arbre" — even if you don't know grimpé, you can guess "climbed" from cat + tree.
  5. 5
    Check your answers against the text — Re-read the relevant sentence. Does your answer actually match what the French says? Watch for negatives (ne...pas) and qualifiers (seulement, parfois, rarement).

Timing

Skim
5 min Section A
15 min Section B
17 min Section C
8 min Check
5 min

Foundation: 45 minutes total. Higher: 60 minutes total. Section A is easiest — don't spend too long on it. Save time for the harder questions in Section B and the translation in Section C.

Cognates (words that look like English)

chocolat, téléphone, important, délicieux, aventure, réserver

About 30% of French words resemble English — use them as anchors.

Near-cognates (need a small adjustment)

école = school, étrange = strange, bibliothèque = library, magasin = shop (not magazine!)

False friends (look similar but mean something different)

actuellement = currently (NOT actually), blessé = injured (NOT blessed)

regarder = to watch (NOT to regard), assister à = to attend (NOT to assist)

journée = day (NOT journey), librairie = bookshop (NOT library)

Word families (spot the root)

travail (work) → travailler (to work) → travailleur (worker)

nager (to swim) → nageur (swimmer) → natation (swimming)

Read this extract from an email:

"Salut! Le week-end dernier, je suis allée à un concert avec ma meilleure amie. Le groupe était français et j'ai adoré la musique, mais malheureusement il y avait trop de monde et on ne pouvait pas bien voir la scène. La prochaine fois, je vais acheter des billets VIP!"

Q1: What was the problem at the concert? (1 mark)

Q2: What will the speaker do differently next time? (1 mark)

Q1: Finding the negative

The key phrase is "malheureusement il y avait trop de monde et on ne pouvait pas bien voir la scène".

Answer: There were too many people / she couldn't see the stage properly.

Q2: Identifying the future

"La prochaine fois" signals the future. "Je vais acheter des billets VIP" = near future tense.

Answer: She will buy VIP tickets.

Text: "Mon père travaille dans un hôpital. Avant, il était professeur mais il a décidé de changer de carrière parce qu'il voulait aider les malades."

Q: Why did the speaker's father change career?

Weak Answer

Incomplete understanding

Because he was a teacher and worked in a hospital.

This describes WHAT he did, not WHY he changed. The student didn't understand "parce qu'il voulait aider les malades."

Strong Answer

Identifies the reason

Because he wanted to help sick people.

The key is "parce que" (because) — everything after it is the reason.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Falling for false friends — actuellement means "currently," NOT "actually." Blessé means "injured," not "blessed." Always think: does this meaning make sense in context?
  • ❌
    Missing negatives — ne...pas, ne...plus, ne...jamais, ne...rien completely change the meaning. "Il ne mange plus de viande" means he NO LONGER eats meat — the opposite of what you'd get if you missed the negative.
  • ❌
    Confusing tenses — "Elle jouait au tennis" (she used to play) vs "Elle a joué au tennis" (she played) vs "Elle jouera au tennis" (she will play). Tenses matter.
  • ❌
    Not answering the question asked — If the question asks "Why?" give a reason. If it asks "When?" give a time. If it asks "How many?" give a number. Read the question word carefully.

  3. Scan for answers in order

title: Translation into English
content_html:
10 marks

Translation into English

Paper 3: Reading — AQA/R — Section C

What the Examiner Wants

You must translate a short French passage (approximately 50 words at Foundation, 50 words at Higher) into English. The examiner wants an accurate and natural-sounding translation — not a word-for-word literal version. You need to show you understand the French AND can express it properly in English.

Marking Criteria

Band What You Need
Band 3 The translation is accurate with only occasional minor errors. The English reads naturally.
Band 2 Generally accurate with some errors. The meaning is mostly clear but some phrases are awkward or inaccurate.
Band 1 Limited accuracy. Some meaning comes through but there are significant errors or omissions.
— No relevant content.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the whole passage first — Understand the overall topic and context before translating anything. Is it about school? Holidays? Family? This helps you make sensible guesses for tricky words.
  2. 2
    Translate sentence by sentence — Work through systematically. Don't skip ahead. Underline any words you're unsure about and come back to them.
  3. 3
    Don't translate word-for-word — French word order and idioms differ from English. "Il me manque" literally means "he me misses" but should be translated as "I miss him." "J'ai douze ans" literally means "I have twelve years" but should be "I am twelve years old."
  4. 4
    Identify tenses and translate them correctly — "je jouais" = I used to play / I was playing (imperfect). "j'ai joué" = I played (perfect). "je jouerai" = I will play (future). Get the tense right.
  5. 5
    Read your translation back as English — Does it sound natural? Would an English speaker say this? If it reads awkwardly, rephrase. "I have hunger" should be "I'm hungry." "It makes beautiful" should be "The weather is nice."

Timing

Read
1 min Translate
5 min Check
2 min

The translation is part of the Reading paper and is worth 10 marks. Spend around 8 minutes on it. Don't rush — accuracy matters more than speed.

Expressions with avoir (to have)

J'ai faim → I'm hungry (NOT "I have hunger")

J'ai soif → I'm thirsty

J'ai chaud / froid → I'm hot / cold

J'ai peur → I'm scared

J'ai raison / tort → I'm right / wrong

J'ai besoin de → I need

Impersonal expressions

Il fait beau / mauvais → The weather is nice / bad

Il y a → There is / there are

Il faut → You must / it is necessary to

Il s'agit de → It's about

Reflexive verbs

Je me lève → I get up (NOT "I myself lift")

Il s'appelle → His name is / He is called

Je m'intéresse à → I'm interested in

On s'amuse bien → We have a good time

Translate into English:

"L'année dernière, je suis allé en France avec ma famille. Nous avons loué une maison près de la plage. Chaque matin, je me levais tôt pour nager dans la mer. C'était génial parce qu'il faisait très chaud. L'année prochaine, nous irons en Espagne."

Literal (weak) attempt

"The year last, I am gone in France with my family. We have rented a house near of the beach. Each morning, I myself lifted early for to swim in the sea. It was great because it made very hot. The year next, we will go in Spain."

Natural (strong) translation

"Last year, I went to France with my family. We rented a house near the beach. Every morning, I got up early to swim in the sea. It was great because the weather was very hot. Next year, we will go to Spain."

Key differences: Natural English word order, correct tense translation (je suis allé = I went, not "I am gone"), idioms correctly rendered (il faisait chaud = the weather was hot, not "it made hot"), prepositions adjusted (en France = to France, not "in France").

Translate: "Quand j'étais petit, j'avais peur des araignées mais maintenant ça ne me dérange plus."

Weak Translation

Tense errors + literal phrasing

"When I was small, I have fear of the spiders but now that not me disturbs more."

Strong Translation

Natural English with correct tenses

"When I was little, I was scared of spiders but now it doesn't bother me any more."

Why it's better: "petit" = little (not "small" for a person), "j'avais peur" = I was scared (imperfect, ongoing state), "ne...plus" = no longer / any more, "déranger" = to bother (not "disturb").

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Translating word-for-word — French sentence structure is different. "Je ne sais pas" is "I don't know," not "I not know not." Rearrange to make natural English.
  • ❌
    Wrong tense — "J'ai mangé" = I ate (past), NOT "I have eaten" (present perfect). "Je mangeais" = I used to eat / I was eating (imperfect). Context tells you which English tense is best.
  • ❌
    Skipping words you don't know — Never leave a gap. Make your best guess using context. If you don't know "mairie" but the sentence is about going somewhere in a town, guess "town hall" or "council building."
  • ❌
    Not reading your English back — Your translation should read like normal English. If it sounds weird when you read it aloud in your head, rephrase it.

← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
~8 min total

Checklist

  1. Read the whole passage first
  2. Translate sentence by sentence
  3. Don't go word-for-word
  4. Check tenses are correct
  5. Read back as natural English

title: Translation into French
content_html:
20 marks

Translation into French

Used in: Paper 4 — Writing (Higher only)

What the Examiner Wants

You translate a short English passage (approximately 50 words) into French. The examiner marks each phrase individually — you get full marks for accurate, natural-sounding French. Minor errors (small accent slips) are tolerated if meaning is clear, but grammatical mistakes that change the message cost marks.

Mark Scheme Breakdown

Descriptor What It Means
Full communication 4 per phrase Message fully conveyed — accurate grammar, vocabulary, and spelling
Good communication 3 per phrase Message mostly conveyed — minor errors that don’t affect meaning
Partial communication 2 per phrase Part of the message conveyed — some errors affect clarity
Limited communication 1 per phrase Very little of the message is conveyed
No communication Nothing relevant or comprehensible

The passage is divided into roughly 5 phrases, each worth up to 4 marks = 20 marks total.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the whole passage first — Don’t translate word-by-word immediately. Read the full English text to understand the topic and tense. Is it past, present, or future? Are there opinion phrases?
  2. 2
    Identify the tense for each sentence — Underline time markers: “last weekend” = passé composé, “every day” = present, “next year” = future. Misidentifying tenses is the number-one cause of lost marks.
  3. 3
    Translate phrase by phrase — Think about how French expresses each idea. E.g. “I am 15 years old” = J’ai quinze ans (not *Je suis quinze ans). “I am cold” = J’ai froid.
  4. 4
    Check agreements — Do adjectives agree with their nouns in gender and number? Do past participles agree with être verbs? E.g. Elle est allée (not *Elle est allé).
  5. 5
    Check accents and spelling — Missing accents change meaning: a (has) vs à (to/at), ou (or) vs où (where). Add all accents carefully.

Timing

Read
2 min Tenses
2 min Translate
6 min Check
3 min

Allow roughly 13 minutes for this question. Spending 3 minutes checking agreements and accents at the end is the single most effective way to gain extra marks.

Negatives

“I don’t like” = Je n’aime pas — remember BOTH parts: ne...pas, ne...jamais, ne...plus.

Reflexive verbs

“I get up” = Je me lève. In the past: Je me suis levé(e) — don’t forget the reflexive pronoun AND the être auxiliary.

Depuis + present tense

“I have lived here for 5 years” = J’habite ici depuis cinq ans. English uses perfect tense, but French uses present with depuis.

Il faut / On doit

“You must” / “You have to” = Il faut + infinitive OR On doit + infinitive. Don’t translate “you” literally with tu when the English is impersonal.

Partitive articles

“I eat some cheese” = Je mange du fromage. English often drops “some” but French requires du / de la / des.

Translate the following passage into French:

Last weekend, I went to the cinema with my friends. We watched an interesting film. I usually prefer comedies because they make me laugh. Next summer, I am going to visit my grandmother in Paris. I think it will be fantastic.

Phrase 1 — Passé composé (aller takes être)

Le week-end dernier, je suis allé(e) au cinéma avec mes ami(e)s.

Phrase 2 — Passé composé + adjective agreement

Nous avons regardé un film intéressant.

Phrase 3 — Present + opinion + faire construction

D’habitude, je préfère les comédies parce qu’elles me font rire.

“Make me laugh” = me font rire (faire + infinitive).

Phrase 4 — Near future (aller + infinitive)

L’été prochain, je vais rendre visite à ma grand-mère à Paris.

“Visit a person” = rendre visite à (not visiter, which is for places).

Phrase 5 — Future tense + opinion

Je pense que ce sera fantastique.

Examiner: 20/20 — all messages fully conveyed with accurate grammar, spelling, and accents.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Translating word-for-word — English and French structure sentences differently. “I am cold” = J’ai froid (not *Je suis froid). Always think about French idiom.
  • ❌
    Wrong tense — If the English says “last year,” you need passé composé or imparfait. If it says “every day,” you need the present. Misidentifying the tense is the top cause of lost marks.
  • ❌
    Forgetting agreements — Adjectives must agree in gender and number: une grande maison, des grandes maisons. Past participles with être must also agree.
  • ❌
    Missing accents — é, è, ê, ç, ù all matter. Marche (walk) vs marché (market / past participle) — one missing accent changes the meaning.
  • ❌
    Leaving blanks — Never leave a phrase untranslated. Even a partially correct attempt scores 1–2 marks. Write something for every phrase.

Quick Reference
~13 min total

Structure

  1. Read full passage
  2. Identify tenses
  3. Translate phrase by phrase
  4. Check agreements
  5. Check accents & spelling

title: Writing Tasks
content_html:
32 / 40 marks

Writing Tasks

Used in: Paper 4 — Writing (Foundation Q2–Q4 / Higher Q2–Q3)

What the Examiner Wants

The writing questions test your ability to produce French text at different lengths. Foundation builds from a short message (Q2) to a longer response (Q4, ~90 words). Higher builds to an extended piece (Q3, 130–150 words). At every level, the examiner rewards range of language, accuracy, and communication of ideas.

Content & Communication (half the marks)

Level What You Need
Tier 5 (H): All bullet points fully addressed with relevant detail and opinions throughout
Mastering Good coverage of bullet points with relevant detail; mostly clear communication
Secure Reasonable coverage, but some content is thin or unclear
Developing Some bullet points addressed, limited detail, unclear communication
Emerging Very basic responses, mostly incomprehensible

Range & Accuracy of Language (other half)

Level What You Need
Tier 5 (H): Wide range of vocabulary and structures; high accuracy; complex sentences used fluently
Mastering Good range; uses different tenses with mostly accurate grammar
Secure Reasonable range; attempts different tenses, some errors
Developing Limited range; mainly present tense; frequent errors
Emerging Very limited vocabulary; major errors throughout

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the bullet points carefully — Each question gives you 4 bullet points. You MUST address all of them. Missing a bullet point caps your content mark at Developing, regardless of quality elsewhere.
  2. 2
    Plan your tenses — The bullet points are designed to draw out at least 2–3 tenses. Typically: one about the past, one about the present, one about the future, one asking for an opinion. Map each bullet to its tense before writing.
  3. 3
    Write one paragraph per bullet point — Each paragraph should have 3–4 sentences minimum for the extended task. Start with your main point, add detail, then give a reason or opinion.
  4. 4
    Showcase your range — Use connectives (cependant, néanmoins, par conséquent, bien que), opinion phrases (à mon avis, je crois que, il me semble que), and varied vocabulary. Avoid repeating the same words.
  5. 5
    Proofread for AGOS — Agreements, Gender, Order (adjective position), Spelling. Check every adjective agrees, every verb is conjugated, and accents are in place.

Timing

Higher Tier (recommended split)

Dictation
8 min Q2
10 min Q3
27 min Translation
13 min Check
10 min

Give the most time to the longest task (Q3 on Higher, worth 32 marks). Save 10 minutes at the end to proofread everything.

Opinions

À mon avis... — In my opinion...

Je suis convaincu(e) que... — I am convinced that...

Il me semble que... — It seems to me that...

Ce qui me plaît, c’est... — What I like is...

Connectives

Cependant / Néanmoins — However / Nevertheless

Par conséquent — As a result

Bien que (+ subjunctive) — Although

Non seulement... mais aussi... — Not only... but also...

D’un côté... de l’autre côté... — On one hand... on the other hand...

Complex structures (Higher)

Si j’avais le choix, je... — If I had the choice, I would...

Après avoir fait... — After having done...

Ce dont j’ai besoin, c’est... — What I need is...

Il est essentiel que... (+ subjunctive) — It is essential that...

You are writing about your school for a French magazine. Write approximately 130–150 words in French. You must write something about each bullet point.

  • A description of your school
  • What you did at school last week
  • What you like and dislike about school
  • Your plans for after school
Bullet 1 — Present tense + description

Mon collège se trouve dans le nord de l’Angleterre et il est assez grand. Il y a environ mille élèves et les bâtiments sont modernes. Nous avons un grand terrain de sport et une bibliothèque bien équipée.

Uses location, size, numbers — specific detail scores well.

Bullet 2 — Passé composé + imparfait

La semaine dernière, j’ai passé un examen de maths qui était vraiment difficile. Pendant que je révisais, mes amis jouaient au football dehors. Néanmoins, j’ai réussi à bien me concentrer et je pense que j’ai bien répondu.

Mixes passé composé and imparfait — shows tense control.

Bullet 3 — Present + opinions

Ce qui me plaît au collège, c’est la variété des matières. J’adore les sciences parce que les expériences sont fascinantes. Cependant, je n’aime pas les cours de musique car je ne suis pas du tout musicien. À mon avis, on devrait avoir plus de choix.

Opinions with reasons + connective cependant + conditional devrait.

Bullet 4 — Future + conditional

Après avoir passé mes examens, je voudrais aller au lycée pour étudier les sciences. Si j’avais de bonnes notes, j’aimerais devenir médecin à l’avenir. Je suis convaincu que travailler dur maintenant m’aidera plus tard.

Uses après avoir + past participle, conditional, and si + imperfect — high-level structures.

Examiner: Content 15/16, Language 14/16 = 29/32 (Level 5) — excellent range, accurate tenses, all bullet points addressed with detail.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Ignoring a bullet point — If you skip one, your content mark is capped at Developing no matter how good the rest is. Even 2–3 sentences on each bullet point is enough.
  • ❌
    Only using the present tense — This caps your language mark at Developing. You MUST show past, present, and future. The bullet points are designed to push you into different tenses — take the hint.
  • ❌
    Listing without detail — “I like maths. I like English. I like science.” scores minimal marks. Develop each point with a reason or example.
  • ❌
    Repetitive vocabulary — Using bien and bon for everything shows limited range. Vary it: formidable, passionnant, génial, agréable, amusant.
  • ❌
    Writing too much or too little — The word count is a guide. Going significantly over risks more errors. Going under means you haven’t developed your ideas enough.
← Translation into French (20 marks) Role Play & Reading Aloud (15 + 15 marks) →
Quick Reference
~68 min (full writing paper)

Structure

  1. Read bullet points
  2. Plan tenses per bullet
  3. One paragraph per bullet
  4. Showcase range & connectives
  5. Proofread AGOS

title: Role Play & Reading Aloud
content_html:
15 + 15 marks

Role Play & Reading Aloud

Used in: Paper 2 — Speaking (Foundation & Higher)

What the Examiner Wants

The speaking exam begins with two structured tasks: Role Play (15 marks) and Reading Aloud (15 marks). Both are short and predictable — if you prepare the patterns, they are among the easiest marks on the whole paper.

Role Play — Mark Scheme (15 marks)

Criterion What It Means
Communication 10 2 marks per task (5 tasks). Full message = 2, partial = 1, nothing = 0
Quality of Language 5 Accuracy of grammar and pronunciation across all five tasks

Reading Aloud — Mark Scheme (15 marks)

Criterion What It Means
Pronunciation 5 Accurate pronunciation of individual words and sounds
Fluency & intonation 5 Smooth delivery with natural rhythm and appropriate intonation
Comprehension questions 5 Answering questions on the passage you’ve just read aloud

Role Play — Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Read the scenario in English — You get a card describing a situation (e.g. “You are at a restaurant in France”). Read it carefully during your preparation time.
  2. 2
    Prepare all 5 tasks — Each bullet tells you what to say or ask. If it says “Ask about…” you need a question. If it says “Say…” you need a statement. One task has a ! meaning you must respond to something unpredictable.
  3. 3
    Use proper question forms — For questions: Est-ce que..., Qu’est-ce que..., À quelle heure..., Où est.... Use a proper structure for full marks rather than relying on intonation alone.
  4. 4
    Handle the unpredictable task (!) — Listen carefully, pause briefly, then respond. Keep it simple: a short sentence is fine. If you don’t understand, ask Pouvez-vous répéter, s’il vous plaît?
  5. 5
    Speak clearly — Don’t rush. Even if your grammar isn’t perfect, clear pronunciation earns quality-of-language marks.

Reading Aloud — Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Use preparation time wisely — Read the text silently, identify tricky words, and practise them in your head. Pay attention to liaisons (e.g. les enfants = “lay-zonfon”).
  2. 2
    Read at a steady pace — Read in meaningful chunks (phrase by phrase), not word by word. Pause naturally at commas and full stops.
  3. 3
    Watch for silent letters — Final consonants are usually silent: petit (“puh-tee”), les amis (“lay-zah-mee”). Exceptions: C, R, F, L (the “CaReFuL” rule).
  4. 4
    Use French intonation — Questions rise at the end. Statements stay level or fall slightly. Try to sound natural.
  5. 5
    Answer follow-up questions — After reading, the examiner asks questions about the text. Listen carefully, refer back to the passage, and answer in French. Full sentences are not required but help.

Timing

Role Play
5 min Reading Aloud
5 min

You get 12 minutes preparation time before the exam to study your role play card and reading-aloud passage. Use every second. The actual tasks take around 5 minutes each.

Nasal vowels

an / en — as in France, enfant (nasalised “on”)

on — as in maison, bon (nasalised “o”)

in / ain / ein — as in vin, pain, plein (nasalised “a”)

Tricky sounds

r — produced at the back of the throat (not the English “r”)

u — round your lips tightly, say “ee” (tu, une)

ou — like English “oo” (nous, vous)

eu — round lips, say “uh” (deux, bleu)

Liaisons

les amis = “lay-zah-mee” — the silent s links to the next vowel

un enfant = “uh-nonfon” — the n links to the next vowel

c’est important = “say-teh-por-ton” — the t links to the vowel

Scenario: You are at a tourist information office in France. The teacher will play the role of the assistant.

  • Say where you are staying and for how long
  • Ask about things to do in the town
  • Say what you did yesterday
  • ! (Unpredictable question)
  • Ask about opening times of the museum
Task 1 — Statement (present + future)

Je reste dans un hôtel au centre-ville et je vais rester pendant une semaine.

Task 2 — Question

Qu’est-ce qu’il y a à faire dans la ville?

Task 3 — Past tense

Hier, j’ai visité le château et j’ai mangé dans un bon restaurant.

Task 4 — ! Unpredictable (e.g. “What would you like to do tomorrow?”)

Demain, je voudrais aller à la plage s’il fait beau.

Task 5 — Question

À quelle heure est-ce que le musée ouvre et ferme?

Examiner: Communication 10/10, Quality of Language 5/5 = 15/15

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not forming proper questions — If the task says “ask about...” you need a question. Using Est-ce que... or inversion is safest. Just using a questioning voice may not earn full marks.
  • ❌
    Panicking on the unpredictable task — It’s always related to the scenario. Take a breath, listen carefully, and give a simple response. Even Oui, j’aime ça or Non, je préfère... scores marks.
  • ❌
    Reading word-by-word — In the reading-aloud task, reading one word at a time sounds robotic and loses fluency marks. Practise reading in phrase chunks.
  • ❌
    Anglicising pronunciation — Don’t say French words with English sounds. The biggest giveaways: pronouncing final consonants that should be silent, and using an English “r” instead of the French guttural “r”.
  • ❌
    Not using preparation time — You have 12 minutes to prepare. Write notes on your card, practise tricky words silently, and plan your responses. Students who “wing it” consistently score lower.

Quick Reference
~10 min (+ 12 min prep)

Structure

  1. Read scenario / passage
  2. Prepare all 5 tasks
  3. Form proper questions
  4. Handle unpredictable (!)
  5. Speak clearly & naturally
