title: Photo Card & Discussion
content_html:
32 marks

Photo Card & Discussion

Used in: Paper 2 — Speaking (Foundation & Higher)

What the Examiner Wants

This is the biggest part of the speaking exam. You describe a photo, answer questions about it, then have a wider conversation on the same theme plus one additional theme. The examiner rewards opinions, multiple tenses, and developed answers beyond simple one-line responses.

Mark Scheme Breakdown

Criterion What It Means
Communication & Content 12 How well you convey ideas, respond to questions, and develop your answers
Interaction & Spontaneity 4 How naturally you respond, ask questions back, and keep conversation flowing
Range of Language 8 Variety of vocabulary, structures, and tenses
Accuracy 4 Correct grammar, verb forms, and agreements
Pronunciation & Intonation 4 Clear, natural French pronunciation

Photo Card — Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Describe what you see — Use Sur la photo, je vois... or Dans l’image, il y a.... Describe the people, place, and activity using the present tense: Un garçon joue au football dans un parc.
  2. 2
    Give your opinion about the photo — À mon avis, cette photo montre que le sport est important pour les jeunes. Always link back to the theme with a reason.
  3. 3
    Answer 3 follow-up questions — These are printed on your card (Foundation) or asked by the teacher (Higher). One will be about the past, one about the present, one about the future. Prepare a 2–3 sentence answer for each.

General Conversation — Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Know your themes — The conversation covers the same theme as your photo card, plus one additional theme. The three AQA themes are: (1) People & lifestyle, (2) Popular culture, (3) Communication & the world around us.
  2. 2
    Develop every answer with PEE — Point (J’aime le sport), Example (par exemple, je joue au rugby le samedi), Extend (parce que c’est bon pour la santé et c’est amusant).
  3. 3
    Show off your tenses — Weave in past, present, future, and conditional naturally. L’année dernière, j’ai joué au tennis. Maintenant, je préfère le rugby. L’année prochaine, je vais essayer le cricket. Si j’avais plus de temps, je ferais de la natation.
  4. 4
    Be spontaneous — If you can, ask the examiner a question back: Et vous, qu’est-ce que vous en pensez? This scores interaction marks and shows confidence.
  5. 5
    Use fillers naturally — If you need thinking time: Alors..., Eh bien..., C’est une bonne question..., En fait.... These sound natural and buy time without awkward silence.

Timing

Photo
2 min Questions
3 min Conversation
7 min

The whole task lasts around 12 minutes. The general conversation is the longest section and carries the most marks — practise speaking on each theme for at least 5 minutes without stopping.

Describing the photo

Sur la photo, je vois... — In the photo, I can see...

Il y a une personne qui... — There is a person who...

Au premier plan, on peut voir... — In the foreground, you can see...

À l’arrière-plan, il y a... — In the background, there is...

La photo a été prise... — The photo was taken...

Giving opinions

Cette photo me fait penser à... — This photo makes me think of...

Je pense que cette image montre... — I think this image shows...

Ce qui est intéressant, c’est... — What’s interesting is...

Developing answers (PEE)

Par exemple... — For example...

...parce que / car / puisque... — ...because / since...

De plus... — Furthermore...

En revanche... — On the other hand...

Photo: A family eating together at a dinner table

Theme: People & Lifestyle

Description

Sur la photo, je vois une famille qui mange ensemble autour d’une grande table. Il y a quatre personnes — les parents et deux enfants. Ils ont l’air contents et détendus. À mon avis, cette photo montre que les repas en famille sont importants pour rester proches.

Follow-up Q1 — Present tense

D’habitude, je mange des plats assez sains à la maison. Ma mère prépare souvent du poulet avec des légumes. Cependant, le week-end, on commande parfois une pizza parce que c’est plus facile et tout le monde adore ça.

Follow-up Q2 — Past tense

Le week-end dernier, nous avons mangé un rôti traditionnel le dimanche. Mon père a cuisiné et c’était délicieux. Après le repas, nous avons mangé une tarte aux pommes que ma grand-mère avait préparée.

Follow-up Q3 — Future + conditional

L’année prochaine, je voudrais apprendre à cuisiner moi-même. Si j’avais plus de temps, j’aimerais essayer la cuisine française — surtout les crêpes et les croissants. Je pense que savoir cuisiner est une compétence très utile pour l’avenir.

Examiner: Communication 11/12, Interaction 4/4, Range 7/8, Accuracy 3/4, Pronunciation 4/4 = 29/32

Question: What do you like to do in your free time?

Weak Answer

One tense, no development, repetitive

J’aime le football. Je joue le samedi. C’est bien. J’aime aussi les jeux vidéo.

Strong Answer

Multiple tenses, opinions, development

Pendant mon temps libre, j’adore jouer au football avec mes amis. On s’entraîne deux fois par semaine et le samedi, on joue des matchs contre d’autres équipes. Le week-end dernier, on a gagné trois à zéro — c’était génial! Si j’avais plus de temps libre, j’aimerais aussi apprendre à jouer de la guitare parce que j’écoute beaucoup de musique.

The strong answer uses present, past, and conditional tenses, gives specific examples, and develops each point with reasons.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    One-word or one-sentence answers — Oui, j’aime le sport. This scores minimal marks. Always develop: say what, why, when, and how you feel about it.
  • ❌
    Only using the present tense — The examiner asks questions specifically to draw out different tenses. If you only use the present, your range mark is capped. Prepare past/future/conditional answers for every topic.
  • ❌
    Long pauses and silence — Silence scores nothing. Use fillers (Alors..., Eh bien...) or rephrase. Even saying something simple is better than saying nothing.
  • ❌
    Reciting memorised answers that don’t fit — Examiners spot recited speeches immediately. Listen to the actual question and adapt. Use prepared material flexibly, not word-for-word.
  • ❌
    Forgetting to describe the photo — Some students jump straight to opinions. Spend 30–60 seconds on pure description first — it’s easy marks.

title: Short Answer Questions (1–2 marks)
content_html:
1–2 marks

Short Answer Questions

Used in: All Topic Areas • R093 Exam

What the Examiner Wants

Short answer questions test your ability to recall specific facts quickly. The command words are identify, state, or name. You do NOT need to explain or justify your answer — the examiner simply wants to see that you know the correct term, feature, or example.

These questions appear throughout the R093 paper and are your easiest marks. Get them right and move on quickly.

Mark Allocation

What You Need
2 Two correct, distinct points (1 mark each)
1 One correct point or a partially correct answer
Incorrect or no relevant response

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the command word — “Identify”, “State”, or “Name” all mean the same thing: give a short, factual answer. No explanation needed.
  2. 2
    Check how many points are needed — If the question says “identify two”, you must give two separate answers. Each one earns 1 mark.
  3. 3
    Write a concise answer — A single word, short phrase, or brief sentence is enough. Do not waste time writing paragraphs for 1-mark questions.

Timing

Read
15 sec Identify
15 sec Write
15 sec

Short answer questions should take under a minute each. The R093 paper is 1 hour 30 minutes for 70 marks, so you have roughly 1 minute 17 seconds per mark. A 1-mark question should be answered in well under a minute to bank time for the longer questions.

Identify two sectors of the media industry. [2 marks]

Full marks answer

1. Film / moving image
2. Audio / radio

Examiner: 2/2 — Two distinct, correct sectors identified.

State one purpose of a mood board. [1 mark]

Full marks answer

To visually communicate the style, colour scheme, and feel of a media product to a client.

Examiner: 1/1 — Clear purpose identified.

Name the file format commonly used for web images that supports transparency. [1 mark]

Full marks answer

PNG

Examiner: 1/1 — Correct format named.

Identify two job roles in a media production team. [2 marks]

Weak Answer (0–1 marks)

Too vague

1. Someone who makes the video
2. The person in charge

Strong Answer (2 marks)

Specific job roles

1. Camera operator
2. Director

The weak answer uses vague descriptions instead of actual job role titles. The examiner needs specific, recognised terms.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Writing too much — If the question says “identify” or “name”, a single word or short phrase is all you need. Long sentences waste time and don’t earn extra marks.
  • ✗
    Being vague — “A type of image file” won’t earn a mark. You need the specific term: “JPEG”, “PNG”, etc.
  • ✗
    Repeating the same point twice — If asked for two answers, make sure they are clearly different. “Film” and “movies” would only count as one point.
  • ✗
    Not reading the question carefully — If the question asks for a job role, don’t give a department. If it asks for a file format, don’t give a software name.
Describe & Explain (2–4 marks) →
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
~45 seconds per question

Structure

  1. Read carefully
  2. Identify key term
  3. Write precise answer

title: Describe & Explain Questions (2–4 marks)
content_html:
2–4 marks

Describe & Explain Questions

Used in: All Topic Areas • R093 Exam

What the Examiner Wants

These questions go beyond simple recall. The command words describe and explain require you to develop your points with detail. “Describe” means give features or characteristics with some detail. “Explain” means say why or how something works, linking cause to effect.

The examiner is looking for developed points — not just a list. Each point needs a follow-up sentence that adds detail, gives a reason, or provides a specific example from Creative iMedia.

Mark Allocation

What You Need
3–4 Two or more developed points with clear detail, examples, or reasoning. Subject-specific terminology used accurately.
1–2 Basic points identified but not developed, or only one point explained well. Limited use of terminology.
Nothing relevant or no creditworthy material.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the command word — Is it “describe” (give features/characteristics) or “explain” (give reasons why)? This determines how you structure your answer.
  2. 2
    Plan two developed points — For a 4-mark question, aim for two well-developed points. Each point follows the pattern: Point → Develop → Example.
  3. 3
    Write Point 1 — State your first point clearly, then expand it. For “describe”, add detail about features. For “explain”, give the reason why using connectives like “because”, “this means that”, or “as a result”.
  4. 4
    Write Point 2 — Make sure your second point is distinct from your first. Use a specific Creative iMedia example where possible (e.g. a file format, a planning document, a distribution platform).

Timing

Read
30 sec Plan
30 sec Point 1
1.5 min Point 2
1.5 min

A 4-mark question should take around 4 minutes. Don’t spend longer than 5 minutes — you need to save time for the 6–8 mark questions later in the paper.

Describe template

“One feature of [X] is… This includes… For example…”

Explain template

“One reason why [X] is important is because… This means that… For example, in a media product such as…”

Second point opener

“Another [feature/reason] is… This is significant because…”

Explain two reasons why a client brief is important in pre-production planning. [4 marks]

Point 1 — developed with reason

A client brief is important because it outlines the client’s requirements and expectations for the media product, such as the target audience, purpose, and style. This means the production team has a clear set of guidelines to follow, reducing the risk of producing something that doesn’t meet the client’s needs.

Point 2 — distinct point with example

Another reason is that it provides a reference point for reviewing the final product. If the client and production team disagree about the outcome, they can refer back to the original brief to check whether the agreed requirements were met. For example, if the brief specified a target audience of 16–25 year olds, the team can evaluate whether the visual style and language are appropriate for that age group.

Examiner: 4/4 — Two distinct, well-developed reasons with clear explanation and a relevant example.

Describe two features of a storyboard. [4 marks]

Weak Answer (1 mark)

Lists without developing

A storyboard has pictures and writing on it. It shows what the video will look like.

Strong Answer (4 marks)

Developed with specific detail

One feature of a storyboard is that it contains a sequence of frames showing the key shots in order. Each frame includes details such as camera angles (e.g. close-up, wide shot), helping the director plan how each scene will be filmed.

Another feature is that it includes annotations alongside the visuals, such as dialogue, sound effects, and transition types (e.g. cut, fade). This helps the entire production team understand what is needed for each shot before filming begins.

The weak answer is vague and undeveloped. The strong answer uses specific terminology (camera angles, transitions) and explains the purpose of each feature.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Listing without developing — Writing “it has pictures, text, and sounds” without explaining what each feature involves or why it matters only earns basic marks.
  • ✗
    Confusing “describe” with “explain” — If asked to explain, you must give a reason (“because…”). If asked to describe, you need detail and characteristics, not just reasons.
  • ✗
    No subject terminology — Generic language like “the thing that shows the pictures” loses marks. Use proper terms: “storyboard”, “visualisation diagram”, “mood board”, “script”.
  • ✗
    Only making one point for a 4-mark question — Even if your single point is excellent, you’ll cap yourself at 2 marks. Always check how many points the question requires.

← Back to Exam Technique

~4 minutes per question

Structure

  1. Read & identify command word
  2. Plan 2 developed points
  3. Point + expansion for each
  4. Use subject terminology

title: Discuss & Evaluate Questions (6–8 marks)
content_html:
6–8 marks

Discuss & Evaluate Questions

Used in: All Topic Areas • R093 Exam

What the Examiner Wants

These are the highest-value questions on the R093 paper. The command words discuss and evaluate require you to consider multiple sides of an issue and reach a reasoned conclusion. You need to show that you can weigh up advantages and disadvantages, or consider the suitability of a choice, using your knowledge of Creative iMedia concepts.

The examiner rewards answers that demonstrate depth (detailed points with evidence), breadth (multiple relevant points), and a balanced judgement in the conclusion.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Secure Detailed discussion with multiple developed points. Clear evidence and examples. Balanced evaluation with a reasoned conclusion.
Developing Some relevant points made with limited development. May lack balance or a clear conclusion. Some use of terminology.
Emerging Basic, generic statements with little or no development. No clear structure or conclusion.
— Nothing relevant.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read and plan — Underline the key focus of the question. Jot down 3 points: at least one advantage/positive and one disadvantage/negative (or “for” and “against”). A third point adds the breadth needed for Secure.
  2. 2
    Write Point 1 — State your first argument clearly. Develop it with a specific Creative iMedia example and explain its impact. Use the structure: Point → Evidence → Explain.
  3. 3
    Write Point 2 — Present the other side. If Point 1 was a positive, Point 2 should be a limitation or drawback. This shows the examiner you can see both sides.
  4. 4
    Write Point 3 (optional but recommended) — Add a further argument or address a specific context (“However, this depends on…”). This moves you into Secure territory.
  5. 5
    Write a conclusion — Make a clear judgement. “Overall, I believe… because…” The conclusion must be justified, not just a restatement of your points.

Timing

Read
1 min Plan
1 min Point 1
2.5 min Point 2
2.5 min Pt 3 + Conclusion
3 min

An 8-mark question should take around 10 minutes. This is where your careful time management on earlier questions pays off. Don’t rush the conclusion — it’s the difference between Developing and Secure.

Point 1 (advantage / positive)

“One advantage of [X] is that… For example… This is beneficial because…”

Point 2 (disadvantage / limitation)

“However, a disadvantage of [X] is… This could cause problems because… For instance…”

Point 3 (context / depends on)

“Furthermore, the suitability of [X] depends on… In some cases… but in others…”

Conclusion

“Overall, I believe [X] is [suitable/effective/the best choice] because… Although there are drawbacks, the benefits outweigh them because…”

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using social media to distribute a short promotional video for a new music festival aimed at 16–25 year olds. [8 marks]

Point 1 — Advantage with evidence

One significant advantage of using social media to distribute the video is that platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube have a very large user base within the 16–25 age group. This means the video is likely to reach the target audience directly, as these platforms are where young people spend most of their time online. The video could also be shared by users, creating organic reach without additional advertising costs.

Point 2 — Disadvantage with reasoning

However, a disadvantage is that social media platforms are saturated with content, making it difficult for the video to stand out. The average user scrolls past content within seconds, so unless the video has a strong hook in the first few seconds, it may not gain traction. The festival organisers may need to invest in paid promotion to ensure the video reaches enough people, which adds to costs.

Point 3 — Further consideration

Furthermore, the suitability of social media depends on the specific platform chosen. TikTok is ideal for short, attention-grabbing clips (under 60 seconds), whereas YouTube would be better for a longer, more cinematic promotional video. The production team would need to consider the file format and aspect ratio requirements of each platform — for example, vertical 9:16 for TikTok versus widescreen 16:9 for YouTube — which may require multiple versions of the same video.

Conclusion — Reasoned judgement

Overall, social media is an effective distribution method for this video because the target audience of 16–25 year olds are highly active on these platforms. Although there are challenges around content saturation and platform-specific requirements, the low cost and potential for viral sharing make it the most suitable primary distribution channel for a music festival targeting young people.

Examiner: 8/8 (Secure) — Three developed points with specific examples, clear balance between advantages and disadvantages, and a justified conclusion.

Evaluate the use of a visualisation diagram in the pre-production of a website for a local bakery. [6 marks]

Emerging Answer (1–2 marks)

Generic, no development

A visualisation diagram is good because it shows what the website will look like. It helps the designer plan the website. It is useful to have one.

Secure Answer (6 marks)

Developed with balance and judgement

A visualisation diagram is a useful pre-production document because it provides a visual mock-up of the website’s layout, showing the placement of elements such as the navigation bar, hero image, product gallery, and contact information. For a local bakery, this helps the client see how their branding and product photos will appear before any coding begins, reducing the risk of costly revisions later.

However, a limitation of a visualisation diagram is that it is static and does not show interactive features such as dropdown menus, hover effects, or responsive behaviour on mobile devices. The client may approve a design that looks good on paper but functions poorly in practice, meaning additional wireframes or interactive prototypes may also be needed.

Overall, a visualisation diagram is a valuable starting point for this project because it establishes the visual direction quickly and cheaply, but it should be used alongside other planning documents such as a site map and wireframes to give a complete picture of the final product.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Only arguing one side — “Discuss” and “evaluate” both require balance. If you only give positives (or only negatives), you cannot reach Secure regardless of how detailed your points are.
  • ✗
    No conclusion — The examiner specifically looks for a judgement at the end. Even a brief “Overall, I think… because…” sentence can push you up a level.
  • ✗
    Generic answers with no context — Saying “social media is good for advertising” without relating it to the specific scenario in the question (the audience, the product, the purpose) stays at Emerging.
  • ✗
    Spending too long on this question — An 8-mark question should take 10 minutes maximum. Over-writing doesn’t earn extra marks and steals time from other questions.

← Back to Exam Technique

~10 minutes per question

Structure

  1. Read & plan 3 points
  2. Point 1 with evidence
  3. Point 2 with evidence
  4. Point 3 or counter-argument
  5. Conclusion / judgement

title: Applied Scenario Questions (4–8 marks)
content_html:
4–8 marks

Applied Scenario Questions

Used in: All Topic Areas • R093 Exam

What the Examiner Wants

Applied scenario questions are a distinctive feature of R093. You are given a real-world brief or context — for example, a company launching a website, a charity creating a promotional video, or a band releasing an album cover — and asked to apply your Creative iMedia knowledge to that specific situation.

The examiner is testing whether you can use what you know in context, not just repeat textbook definitions. Every point you make must link back to the scenario. Generic answers that could apply to any situation will score poorly.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

Level What You Need
Secure Detailed, context-specific application. Multiple developed points that directly address the scenario. Clear reasoning linked to the brief’s audience, purpose, and constraints.
Developing Some application to the scenario but points are partially developed or occasionally generic. Some relevant terminology.
Emerging Basic, generic statements that show knowledge but do not apply it to the specific scenario.
— Nothing relevant.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the scenario carefully — Underline or highlight key details: Who is the client? What is the product? Who is the target audience? What is the purpose? Are there any constraints (budget, deadline, platform)?
  2. 2
    Identify what the question is really asking — Is it asking you to recommend, justify, explain suitability, or suggest improvements? The command word tells you whether you need to give options, weigh up choices, or defend a decision.
  3. 3
    Plan your points — For each point, think: What do I know? → How does this apply to THIS scenario? Write brief notes before starting your answer.
  4. 4
    Write with constant reference to the brief — Every paragraph should mention something specific from the scenario. Use phrases like “Because the target audience is [X]…”, “Since the client needs [Y]…”, or “Given the budget constraint of [Z]…”.
  5. 5
    Use subject terminology throughout — Don’t just say “a picture file” — say “a PNG file with transparency”. Don’t say “put it online” — say “distribute via the client’s social media channels”.

Timing

Read
1.5 min Plan
1 min Point 1
2 min Point 2
2 min Pt 3 + Link
1.5 min

Spend extra time reading the scenario — this is not wasted time. The more detail you extract from the brief, the more context-specific your answer will be, which is what separates Developing from Secure.

The biggest difference between a Emerging and a Secure answer is application. Compare these two approaches:

Generic (Emerging)

“JPEG is a lossy file format that compresses images. It is commonly used on the internet. It does not support transparency.”

Applied (Secure)

“JPEG would be a suitable format for the bakery’s product photos on their website because lossy compression would reduce the file size, improving page load times for customers browsing on mobile devices. However, JPEG would not be suitable for the bakery’s logo, which requires a transparent background to sit over the coloured header — PNG would be more appropriate for this element.”

Both answers demonstrate the same knowledge, but only the second one applies it to the scenario and earns full marks.

Scenario: A local animal rescue charity wants to create a 30-second promotional video to raise awareness and encourage donations. The video will be shared on social media (Instagram and Facebook). The charity has a small budget and no professional filming equipment.

Explain why a storyboard would be a useful pre-production document for this project. [4 marks]

Point 1 — Applied to charity’s constraints

A storyboard would be particularly useful for this project because the charity has a small budget and no professional equipment. By planning each shot in advance — including camera angles, shot types, and the order of scenes — the team can make the most of their limited filming time and avoid wasting resources on unnecessary retakes. For a 30-second video, every second counts, so the storyboard ensures each frame serves a clear purpose.

Point 2 — Applied to social media context

Additionally, because the video will be shared on Instagram and Facebook, the storyboard can be used to plan for the specific requirements of these platforms. For example, the team could plan a vertical (9:16) version for Instagram Stories and a square (1:1) version for Facebook posts, ensuring the key visual elements — such as the charity’s logo and donation link — remain visible in both formats. This planning at the storyboard stage prevents problems during editing.

Examiner: 4/4 — Both points are fully developed and directly linked to the scenario (budget, equipment, social media platforms). Strong use of subject terminology.

Scenario: A school wants a new website to display information about clubs, events, and term dates. The target audience is parents aged 30–50.

Recommend a suitable colour scheme for the website and explain your choice. [4 marks]

Weak Answer (1 mark)

Generic — ignores the scenario

I would use blue because blue is a nice colour and lots of websites use blue. Blue is calming and looks professional.

Strong Answer (4 marks)

Context-specific with reasoning

I would recommend a colour scheme based on the school’s existing branding colours to maintain consistency with their uniform, letterheads, and other communications. This helps parents immediately recognise the website as an official school resource, which builds trust.

As the target audience is parents aged 30–50, the colour scheme should use muted, professional tones rather than bright, playful colours that might suit a younger audience. A dark navy blue for headers with a white background and grey accents would ensure high readability and a professional appearance. Good colour contrast also improves accessibility for users with visual impairments, which is important for a school that serves a diverse community.

The weak answer names a colour but doesn’t link the choice to the school context, target audience, or purpose. The strong answer references the audience, brand consistency, and accessibility — all specific to this scenario.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Ignoring the scenario — The single biggest mistake. If the question gives you a bakery, a charity, or a band, your answer must reference that specific context. Generic textbook answers stay at Emerging.
  • ✗
    Not reading the full brief — Scenario questions contain crucial details (target audience, budget, platform). Students who skim the brief miss constraints that should shape their answer.
  • ✗
    Describing instead of applying — Defining what a mood board is doesn’t answer why a mood board would be useful for this particular project. Always ask yourself: “So what? Why does this matter here?”
  • ✗
    Forgetting the target audience — Almost every scenario question involves a target audience. Your recommendations should explicitly address their needs, preferences, and habits. A website for elderly users needs different design choices to one for teenagers.

~8 minutes per question

Structure

  1. Read the scenario carefully
  2. Highlight key details
  3. Apply knowledge to context
  4. Link every point back to the brief
  5. Use subject terminology

title: Short Answer Questions
content_html:
1–4 marks

Short Answer Questions

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

Short answer questions use command words like define, state, identify, describe, and give an example. The number of marks tells you exactly how many distinct points to make. One clear, technically accurate point per mark.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
4Four distinct, relevant points using correct technical terminology.
3Three relevant points with accurate terminology.
2Two relevant points with some technical language.
1One relevant point, even if loosely expressed.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Check the mark allocation — A 2-mark question needs exactly 2 points. Writing 5 points wastes time and earns no extra credit.
  2. 2
    Identify the command word — “Define” means give the meaning. “Describe” means say what it is and how it works. “Explain” means say why.
  3. 3
    Use technical terminology — Say “RAM is volatile” not “RAM loses its data when you turn it off”. The examiner rewards precise vocabulary.
  4. 4
    One point per line — Write each point on a new line or use bullet points. This makes it easy for the examiner to award marks.

Timing

Read
10s Write
1–3 min Check
15s

Allow roughly 1 minute per mark. A 3-mark question should take about 3 minutes. Do not over-write.

Define (1 mark)

“[Term] is [precise definition using technical vocabulary].”

Describe (2 marks)

“[Feature] works by [how it operates].”

“This means that [consequence or purpose].”

Explain (3 marks)

“[Concept] is [definition].”

“It works by [mechanism].”

“This is important because [reason/consequence].”

Common Mistakes

  • Repeating the question as the answer — “The clock speed is the speed of the clock” earns zero marks. Define it properly.
  • Writing too much for low-mark questions — A paragraph for a 1-mark question wastes time you need for 8-mark answers.
  • Vague language instead of technical terms — “It makes it faster” is too vague. Say what makes it faster and why.
  • Forgetting units in data representation — Binary values need the correct number of bits. File sizes need bytes/KB/MB.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
~1 min per mark

Steps

  1. Check mark allocation
  2. Identify command word
  3. Use technical terminology
  4. One point per line

title: Algorithm Tracing & Trace Tables
content_html:
3–6 marks

Algorithm Tracing & Trace Tables

Used in: Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

Trace table questions give you a piece of pseudocode or Python and ask you to track the values of variables as the program runs. Every row in the trace table represents one step. You must show every change, including loop iterations.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
Full marksEvery variable value recorded correctly at each step. Final output matches.
PartialMost values correct but one or two errors in loop iterations or conditional branches.
1–2Initial values correct but errors accumulate through the trace.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Draw the trace table — Create a column for each variable mentioned in the code, plus an “Output” column if the code prints anything.
  2. 2
    Set initial values — Write the starting values of all variables in the first row. If a variable has not been assigned yet, leave it blank.
  3. 3
    Execute line by line — Follow the code exactly as a computer would. When a variable changes, start a new row and write the new value.
  4. 4
    Track loops carefully — For each iteration, write a new row. Count iterations on your fingers if needed. Off-by-one errors are the most common mistake.
  5. 5
    Double-check the output — After completing the trace, verify that any print/output statements match the values in your table at that point.

Timing

Setup
1 min Trace
4 min Verify
1 min

Allow 5–6 minutes for a trace table question. Take your time — one wrong value early on cascades through the entire table.

Common Mistakes

  • Off-by-one errors in loops — Check whether the loop starts at 0 or 1, and whether the condition is < or <=. This changes the number of iterations.
  • Forgetting to update the loop counter — In a while loop, the counter must be incremented inside the loop body.
  • Confusing = and == — A single = assigns a value; == compares. In a trace, only = changes the variable.
  • Not showing every step — Even if a variable does not change, show it was checked. The examiner awards marks for each correct row.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
5–6 min total

Steps

  1. Draw trace table with columns
  2. Set initial values
  3. Execute line by line
  4. Track each loop iteration
  5. Verify output

title: Binary & Hex Calculations
content_html:
2–4 marks

Binary & Hex Calculations

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

These questions test your ability to convert between binary, hexadecimal, and denary, perform binary addition and shifts, and calculate file sizes. You must show your working — even if your final answer is wrong, method marks are available for correct steps.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
Full marksCorrect answer with clear working shown. Correct units (bits, bytes, KB, MB).
PartialCorrect method but arithmetic error, or correct conversion but wrong/missing units.
1Some correct working even if the final answer is wrong.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the conversion type — Binary to denary? Denary to hex? Binary addition? Know which method to use before you start writing.
  2. 2
    Write out place values — For binary: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. For hex: split binary into nibbles (groups of 4 bits). This prevents silly errors.
  3. 3
    Show every step — Write the place values above your binary number. Show carries in addition. The examiner awards method marks for correct working.
  4. 4
    Check for overflow — If a binary addition result needs more than 8 bits, note that overflow has occurred. This is often worth a mark.
  5. 5
    Include units — Always state whether your answer is in bits, bytes, KB, or MB. Missing units can lose you marks on file size calculations.

Timing

Read
15s Calculate
2 min Check
1 min

Allow 3–4 minutes. Write place values out every time — it takes 10 seconds and prevents most errors.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting place values — Students who try to convert in their head make arithmetic errors. Always write 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above the binary digits.
  • Mixing up nibble order for hex — Split from the right: 10110011 becomes 1011 | 0011 (B3), not 1 | 0110 | 011.
  • Not noting overflow — If 11010110 + 01101010 exceeds 8 bits, state that overflow has occurred. This is a separate mark.
  • Missing units in file size calculations — Image size = resolution x colour depth. Sound size = sample rate x bit depth x duration. Always convert to the unit asked for.
  • Binary shift direction — A left shift multiplies by 2; a right shift divides by 2 (integer division). Bits shifted off the end are lost.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
3–4 min total

Steps

  1. Identify conversion type
  2. Write out place values
  3. Show every step
  4. Check for overflow
  5. Include units

title: Multiple Choice Questions
content_html:
1 mark each

Multiple Choice Questions

Used in: Paper 1 & Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

Multiple choice questions test your recall of key definitions, components, and concepts. Each question has four options (A–D) and only one correct answer. These questions appear at the start of both papers and are designed to be answered quickly.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
1Select the correct answer from four options. No working required.
0Incorrect answer or no answer given.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question carefully — Look for keywords like “not”, “most likely”, or “best describes”. These change the meaning completely.
  2. 2
    Try to answer before looking at options — If you know the answer already, find it in the list. This prevents you being misled by distractors.
  3. 3
    Eliminate wrong answers — Cross out options you know are wrong. Even removing one or two increases your chances if you need to guess.
  4. 4
    Never leave a blank — There is no negative marking. A guess gives you a 25% chance; a blank gives you 0%.

Timing

Read
10s Decide
15s Check
5s

Spend no more than 30 seconds per MCQ. If you are stuck, mark it and move on — come back at the end.

Common Mistakes

  • Misreading “not” in the question — Questions like “Which is NOT an example of…” catch students who skim too quickly.
  • Changing a correct answer — Your first instinct is usually right. Only change if you spot a clear error in your reasoning.
  • Spending too long on one question — Each MCQ is worth 1 mark. Do not sacrifice time for higher-mark questions later.
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
30 seconds per question

Steps

  1. Read question carefully
  2. Answer before looking at options
  3. Eliminate wrong answers
  4. Never leave a blank

title: Extended Response Questions
content_html:
6–8 marks

Extended Response Questions

Used in: Paper 1 (typically the final question)

What the Examiner Wants

Extended response questions ask you to discuss, explain, or evaluate a computing topic in depth. These are marked using a levels-based mark scheme, meaning the examiner reads your whole answer and places it in a band. Quality of reasoning matters more than number of points.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
7–8Comprehensive discussion with multiple well-developed points. Clear, logical structure. Accurate technical terminology throughout. Balanced evaluation with a justified conclusion.
5–6Good discussion with several relevant points. Mostly accurate terminology. Some structure and reasoning.
3–4Basic discussion with some relevant points. Limited use of technical terms. May lack structure.
1–2Limited response with one or two simple points. Inaccurate or missing terminology.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan for 2 minutes — Jot down 3–4 points you want to make. If the question asks you to “discuss”, plan both sides (advantages and disadvantages).
  2. 2
    Write in paragraphs — Each paragraph covers one main point. Start with a topic sentence, then develop with explanation and an example.
  3. 3
    Use the PEE structure — Point (make a claim), Explanation (say why), Example (give a concrete computing example).
  4. 4
    Write a conclusion — Summarise your argument and state your overall judgement. This pushes you into the top band.
  5. 5
    Proofread — Check spelling of technical terms (e.g. “algorithm” not “algorythm”) and ensure your logic flows.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
8 min Check
2 min

Allow 10–12 minutes for an 8-mark extended response. This is the most valuable question on the paper — do not rush it.

Point 1 (Advantage)

“One advantage of [topic] is that [point].”

“This is because [explanation]. For example, [specific computing example].”

Point 2 (Disadvantage)

“However, a disadvantage is that [counter-point].”

“This means that [consequence]. For instance, [example].”

Conclusion

“Overall, [topic] is [judgement] because [strongest reason].”

Common Mistakes

  • Writing a list instead of paragraphs — Bullet points will not reach the top band. The examiner wants connected reasoning.
  • One-sided answers to “discuss” questions — If the question says “discuss”, you must cover both sides to reach Secure.
  • No conclusion — A conclusion shows you can weigh up arguments. Without one, you cap at Developing.
  • Vague examples — “Like in a computer” is not an example. Be specific: “A solid-state drive has no moving parts, so it accesses data faster than an HDD.”
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
10–12 min total

Steps

  1. Plan 3–4 points (2 min)
  2. Write in paragraphs (PEE)
  3. Cover both sides if “discuss”
  4. Write a conclusion
  5. Proofread technical terms

title: Writing Pseudocode & Programs
content_html:
4–8 marks

Writing Pseudocode & Programs

Used in: Paper 2

What the Examiner Wants

These questions ask you to write an algorithm in OCR pseudocode or a high-level programming language (usually Python). The examiner checks that your logic is correct, your syntax is consistent, and your solution handles the requirements stated in the question.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
Full marksCorrect, complete solution with consistent syntax. Handles edge cases. Clear variable names and indentation.
Most marksMostly correct logic with minor syntax errors. The algorithm would work for normal inputs.
Some marksCorrect structure (loops, selection) but logical errors or missing steps.
1–2Some relevant code elements but the algorithm would not run correctly.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Read the question twice — Underline what the program must do: inputs, processing, outputs, and any validation requirements.
  2. 2
    Plan the structure — Decide which constructs you need: sequence, selection (if/elif/else), iteration (for/while), and any functions or procedures.
  3. 3
    Declare variables clearly — Use meaningful names. If using OCR pseudocode, follow their conventions: variable = value, array[index].
  4. 4
    Indent consistently — Every line inside a loop or if-statement must be indented. The examiner uses indentation to understand your logic.
  5. 5
    Dry-run your code — Mentally trace through with a sample input. Does it produce the expected output? Fix any bugs before moving on.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
5 min Test
2 min

Allow 8–10 minutes for a coding question. Spending 2 minutes planning saves you from rewriting the whole answer.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing Python and pseudocode syntax — Pick one and be consistent. Do not write print() in pseudocode or OUTPUT in Python.
  • Forgetting to initialise variables — A counter or total must be set to 0 before a loop. Missing this causes incorrect results.
  • Infinite loops — Every while loop needs a condition that will eventually become false. Check that you update the loop variable.
  • Not reading input correctly — If the question says “the user enters a number”, you need an input statement and possibly a type conversion (int()).
← Back to Exam Technique
Quick Reference
8–10 min total

Steps

  1. Read question twice
  2. Plan constructs needed
  3. Use meaningful variable names
  4. Indent consistently
  5. Dry-run with sample input

title: Section B - Specialist Technical Principles
content_html:
30 marks

Section B — Specialist Technical Principles

Short answer & extended response questions

What the Examiner Wants

Section B tests in-depth knowledge of specialist technical principles: selection of materials, forces and stresses, ecological and social footprint, sources and origins, stock forms, scales of production, and surface treatments. You will answer several short questions (2–5 marks) and one extended response. The examiner wants detailed, technical answers that show depth of understanding.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
2 marksA correct point with brief explanation
3–5 marksTwo or more points, each with explanation and/or examples
6+ marksExtended response with clear structure, multiple points, and technical detail

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Identify the command word — “Explain” means give a reason WITH a because; “Describe” means say what happens; “Evaluate” means weigh up pros and cons.
  2. 2
    Link to the context — If the question names a product or material, make sure your answer refers to that specific context.
  3. 3
    Use the PEE structure — Point, Evidence, Explain. State your point, give a specific example or technical detail, then explain why it matters.
  4. 4
    Match points to marks — For a 4-mark question, aim for 2 developed points. For a 2-mark question, one clear point with explanation is enough.

Timing

Read
6 min Answer
20 min Check
4 min

Aim for about 30 minutes on Section B. Spend slightly longer on the extended response question.

Short Answer (2–5 marks)

“One reason [X] is used is because [property/advantage]…”

“This is important because [consequence/benefit for the product or user].”

Extended Response

“[Material/process] is suitable because [property]. For example, [specific detail].”

“However, a disadvantage is [limitation], which means [consequence].”

“Overall, [material/process] is the best choice because [concluding judgement].”

Explain two reasons why a manufacturer might choose injection moulding for a plastic phone case. [4 marks]

Point 1 + Evidence + Explain

Injection moulding is ideal for mass production because once the mould is made, thousands of identical cases can be produced quickly and cheaply. This keeps the unit cost low, which is essential for a consumer product sold in large quantities.

Point 2 + Evidence + Explain

The process also produces a high-quality surface finish straight from the mould, meaning no additional finishing is needed. This reduces production time and labour costs while ensuring a consistent appearance for every case.

Common Mistakes

  • Generic answers — Writing “it is strong” without naming the specific property (tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, etc.).
  • Ignoring the context — If the question says “for a children’s toy”, your answer must relate to that product, not products in general.
  • Only listing, not explaining — For “Explain” questions, every point needs a “because” or “this means that”.
  • Confusing ferrous and non-ferrous metals — Ferrous = contains iron (steel). Non-ferrous = no iron (aluminium, copper).
Quick Reference
30 minutes total

Steps

  1. Identify command word
  2. Link to context
  3. PEE structure
  4. Match points to marks

title: Extended Response Questions
content_html:
6–12 marks

Extended Response Questions

Used in: Sections B and C

What the Examiner Wants

Extended response questions require you to write several paragraphs. They test your ability to construct a coherent argument, use technical vocabulary, and apply knowledge to a specific context. The quality of your written communication is assessed alongside your technical knowledge.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
10–12Comprehensive answer. Multiple well-developed points with specific examples, precise technical vocabulary, clear structure, and a justified conclusion.
7–9Good answer. Several relevant points with explanation and some examples. Generally clear structure but may lack depth in places.
4–6Basic answer. Some relevant points but limited explanation. May rely on generic statements without specific detail.
1–3Limited answer. Few relevant points, vague language, no structure.

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Underline key words — Circle the command word (Discuss, Evaluate, Explain) and the topic. This prevents you going off track.
  2. 2
    Plan 3–4 key points — Jot them in the margin. For “Discuss” questions, plan arguments for AND against.
  3. 3
    Write one paragraph per point — Each paragraph: Point → Evidence/Example → Explain why it matters.
  4. 4
    Use connectives — “However”, “Furthermore”, “On the other hand” show you are building an argument, not just listing.
  5. 5
    End with a conclusion — Summarise your argument and make a clear judgement. “Overall, I believe… because…”

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
9 min Check
1 min

Allow roughly 1 minute per mark. A 12-mark question deserves about 12–15 minutes including planning time.

Opening Paragraph

“[Topic] is important in design and technology because [overview reason]…”

Supporting Paragraph

“One key advantage/factor is [point]. For example, [specific detail]. This means that [consequence/impact].”

Counter-argument

“However, [opposing point]. This is because [evidence]. As a result, [impact].”

Conclusion

“Overall, [judgement] because [strongest reason]. While [counter-point] is valid, [final justification].”

Evaluate the use of CAD/CAM in modern manufacturing. [6 marks]

Point 1 — Advantage

CAD (Computer Aided Design) allows designers to create precise 2D and 3D models that can be easily modified and shared. This speeds up the design process and reduces errors, as measurements are exact and the design can be tested virtually before production.

Point 2 — Advantage with link to CAM

CAM (Computer Aided Manufacture) works alongside CAD to produce identical components with high accuracy. CNC machines such as laser cutters and 3D printers can produce complex shapes that would be difficult to achieve by hand, ensuring consistency across batch and mass production.

Counter-argument + Conclusion

However, CAD/CAM requires significant initial investment in software and machinery, and workers need training to use the systems. Despite this, CAD/CAM has become essential in modern manufacturing because the long-term benefits of speed, accuracy, and reduced waste far outweigh the setup costs.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing a list instead of paragraphs — Bullet points without explanation will not access the higher mark bands.
  • No conclusion — Leaving out a conclusion means you cannot access the top marks for “Evaluate” or “Discuss” questions.
  • Repeating the same point — Saying the same thing in different words does not earn extra marks. Make each paragraph a new point.
  • Ignoring spelling, punctuation, and grammar — Written communication quality is assessed, so proofread your answer.
Quick Reference
~1 min per mark

Steps

  1. Underline key words
  2. Plan 3–4 points
  3. One paragraph per point
  4. Use connectives
  5. Write a conclusion

What the Examiner Wants

  2. 2

“[Technical term] is/means [definition]…”

Give one advantage of using CAD (Computer Aided Design) when designing a product. [2 marks]

Technical term + explanation

CAD allows designers to make quick modifications to a design without starting again from scratch. This saves time and reduces material waste during the development stage, as changes can be tested on screen before making a physical prototype.

title: Section C - Designing & Making Principles
content_html:
50 marks

Section C — Designing & Making Principles

Extended responses & design application

What the Examiner Wants

Section C is the biggest section and includes a mix of short answer questions and extended responses. It covers investigation and research, the work of others, design strategies, prototype development, and specialist tools and processes. The final question is usually a design-based task worth up to 12 marks where you must apply your knowledge to a real-world scenario. The examiner wants to see that you can think like a designer — not just recall facts.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

What You Need
9–12Detailed, well-structured answer with multiple points, specific examples, technical vocabulary, and a clear conclusion or judgement
5–8Several relevant points with some explanation and examples, but may lack depth or a clear conclusion
1–4Basic points with limited explanation, generic language, or missing key elements

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Plan before you write — For 6+ mark questions, spend 1–2 minutes jotting down 3–4 key points in the margin before writing your answer.
  2. 2
    Use paragraphs — Each point should be a separate paragraph. This makes your answer easier to mark and shows clear structure.
  3. 3
    Reference specific designers, materials, or processes — Naming Dyson, Starck, or a specific manufacturing process shows depth and scores highly.
  4. 4
    Include a conclusion — For evaluate/discuss questions, finish with a clear judgement that weighs up the arguments.
  5. 5
    Annotate design sketches — For design-based questions, label materials, dimensions, key features, and manufacturing methods.

Timing

Plan
8 min Write
38 min Check
8 min

Section C is worth half the paper. Allocate about 54 minutes here. The design question alone deserves 12–15 minutes.

Design Question (12 marks)

“The product should be made from [material] because [property relevant to the brief]…”

“I would manufacture this using [process] because [advantage for this product]…”

“To make this product sustainable, I would [specific action] because [environmental benefit].”

Discuss the environmental impact of using polymers in product design. You should consider both advantages and disadvantages. [9 marks]

Point 1 — Disadvantage

Most polymers are derived from crude oil, a non-renewable fossil fuel. The extraction and refining process produces significant CO2 emissions, contributing to climate change. When disposed of in landfill, polymers can take hundreds of years to decompose.

Point 2 — Advantage

However, polymers are lightweight compared to metals and timber, which reduces transportation costs and fuel consumption during distribution. For example, replacing a steel car panel with a polymer composite can reduce the vehicle’s weight and improve fuel efficiency over its lifetime.

Point 3 — Mitigation + Conclusion

Designers can mitigate the environmental impact by using bioplastics (such as PLA derived from cornstarch), designing for disassembly so parts can be recycled, and using the six Rs. Overall, polymers have significant environmental drawbacks, but careful design choices can reduce their impact considerably.

Common Mistakes

  • Not planning extended answers — Jumping straight into writing often leads to repetition and missed points.
  • Unannotated sketches — A drawing without labels and notes scores very few marks.
  • One-sided arguments — “Discuss” and “Evaluate” questions require both advantages AND disadvantages.
  • Forgetting sustainability — Many design questions expect you to consider environmental and social impact.
Quick Reference
54 minutes total

Steps

  1. Plan before writing
  2. Use paragraphs
  3. Reference specifics
  4. Include a conclusion
  5. Annotate sketches

title: Time Management Strategy
content_html:
2 hours

Time Management Strategy

AQA/W — 120 minutes, 100 marks

What the Examiner Wants

Poor time management is the number one reason students lose marks in D&T. The exam is 2 hours for 100 marks, which means roughly 1.2 minutes per mark. Many students spend too long on Section A (low marks) and run out of time on Section C (high marks). Plan your time before you start writing.

Level Descriptors (Simplified)

SectionTime
Section A — Core Technical (20 marks)20 minutes
Section B — Specialist Technical (30 marks)36 minutes
Section C — Designing & Making (50 marks)54 minutes
Final check10 minutes

Step-by-Step Formula

  1. 1
    Note your section deadlines — Write the clock times on the front of your paper: e.g. if starting at 9:00, Section A done by 9:20, Section B by 9:56, Section C by 10:50, check by 11:00.
  2. 2
    Do not over-write low-mark questions — A 2-mark question needs 2–3 sentences maximum. Save your energy for the 6–12 mark questions.
  3. 3
    Skip and return — If a question stumps you, put a small mark next to it and move on. Come back in the final 10 minutes.
  4. 4
    Use the final 10 minutes wisely — Re-read extended answers, check spelling of technical terms, and attempt any questions you skipped.

Timing

A
20 min B
36 min C
54 min Check
10 min

The golden rule: never spend more than 1.2 minutes per mark. Leave every question with an answer — even a quick bullet point scores more than a blank space.

Common Mistakes

  • Spending 40+ minutes on Section A — Section A is only 20% of the marks. Do not labour over multiple choice.
  • Leaving Section C half-finished — This is where the most marks are. If you are running short on time, write quick bullet points rather than leaving questions blank.
  • Not reading the whole paper first — Skim through all questions before starting so you know what is coming and can plan your time.
  • Perfectionism on drawings — Your design sketches need to communicate ideas clearly, not be works of art. Clear labels matter more than shading.
